title: Detect Outage - Remediation Plan Review
summary: Megan, Raj, and Brian convened on day three of an ongoing outage affecting the Detect product's event processing pipeline. Raj explained that a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer caused a cascading failure, leaving customers with zero threat monitoring visibility for approximately six hours. The remediation plan includes deploying redundant active-active processing nodes (live by end of day) and implementing a circuit breaker pattern (by Wednesday evening), with full tenant visibility restored in a phased rollout by tomorrow morning. The team aligned on communication protocols, retroactive security analysis, and a postmortem timeline.
transcript_text: Megan Lawson: Alright, I think we're all on - Raj, Brian, can you both hear me okay? Raj Kapoor: Yeah, I'm here. Audio's good. Brian Cho: Yep, I'm on. Give me one sec, I'm just pulling up the incident doc. Megan Lawson: Sure, take your time. So, uh, the reason I wanted to get us together today - obviously we're still in the middle of this, day three of the outage window - I want to make sure we have a clear remediation plan and that we're all aligned before we send anything else externally. Raj Kapoor: Yeah, agreed. I've been heads-down with the engineering team since Saturday and I think we have a pretty solid picture of the root cause at this point. Do you want me to just walk through it? Megan Lawson: Please, yeah. Go ahead. Raj Kapoor: Okay so - and Brian, let me know if the technical depth here is useful for you or if you want me to translate as I go - basically what we're looking at is a cascading failure in the event processing pipeline. The short version is we had a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer, and when that node went down, there was no fallback. So events just started backing up and then the whole downstream monitoring stack lost visibility. Brian Cho: Yeah no that's - that's helpful context actually. My team has been getting hammered with tickets since Saturday morning and I want to make sure I understand what I'm telling customers, so. Megan Lawson: How many tickets are we at now, roughly? Brian Cho: As of this morning we're at a hundred and twelve open cases specifically tied to the Detect outage. About thirty of those are priority one or two accounts. We've got a handful of customers that are, uh, pretty vocal about it. Megan Lawson: Okay. That's - yeah, that tracks with what I've been seeing from the account side. Raj, continuing on the root cause - what's the fix look like? Raj Kapoor: So the fix is two-pronged. The immediate thing we're doing - and this is already in progress, the team started on it yesterday - is deploying redundant processing nodes. So instead of relying on a single ingestion point, we're moving to an active-active configuration. That should eliminate the single point of failure entirely. Megan Lawson: And the second piece? Raj Kapoor: The second piece is implementing a circuit breaker pattern on the pipeline. So essentially, if one component starts degrading, the circuit breaker trips before it can take down the whole chain. It's a more resilient architecture overall. We should have had this from the start, honestly, but - yeah. Megan Lawson: I appreciate you saying that. I think - and I want to be candid here - I think there's going to be a postmortem conversation about how this got built the way it did, but I want to table that for now and focus on the remediation. What's the timeline looking like for full restoration? Raj Kapoor: Current estimate is we'll have the redundant nodes live by end of day today. The circuit breaker implementation is a little more involved - that's probably forty-eight hours from now, so, Wednesday evening at the earliest. But the monitoring visibility issue, the core thing customers are experiencing, that should be resolved today. Brian Cho: Okay so when you say resolved today - are we talking full visibility restored across all tenants, or is it phased? Raj Kapoor: It'll be phased. We're going to roll it out starting with, uh, our larger enterprise tenants first and then work down. Realistically all tenants should have visibility restored by tomorrow morning. Brian Cho: Okay. That's a little frustrating because I've been telling customers we're targeting end of today. Can we - is there any way to compress that timeline or is tomorrow morning pretty firm? Raj Kapoor: Brian, I get it, but I'd rather give customers a conservative timeline and hit it than promise end of day and miss. We've already got a credibility issue here. Brian Cho: Yeah, no, that's fair. That's fair. I just - I need to go back and update a lot of those tickets and some of these customers are going to push back. Megan Lawson: I can help draft the updated customer communication if that's useful, Brian. I think we should have something that acknowledges the delay, explains the phased rollout without getting too deep in the weeds technically, and gives them the concrete timeline. Brian Cho: Yeah, that would actually be really helpful. My team is stretched pretty thin right now. Megan Lawson: Raj, on the six hours of no visibility - I want to make sure I understand this correctly. During that window, customers had zero threat monitoring data? Like nothing was coming through? Raj Kapoor: Correct. Events were being ingested at the edge but they were just... queuing up and not processing. So from a customer-facing dashboard perspective, it looked like nothing was happening. No alerts, no detections, nothing. Which is - yeah, that's bad. Megan Lawson: And we're confident that there were no actual threats during that window that went undetected? Or is that - can we even say that? Raj Kapoor: That's a really important question and the honest answer is we've been doing retroactive processing of the queued events and so far we haven't identified any threats that were active during that window, but I want to be careful about saying definitively that nothing happened. We're still working through the backlog. Megan Lawson: Okay so we cannot make any affirmative statements to customers about security posture during that window. Got it. Brian, make sure your team is not - if anyone's asking that question, the answer is we're doing a full retroactive analysis and we'll communicate findings. Brian Cho: Understood. Yeah, I'll make sure that's clear in the team briefing. We've had a few customers ask exactly that and I've been kind of hedging, so it's good to have a cleaner answer. Megan Lawson: Raj, what's the ETA on completing that retroactive processing? I want to know when we can close the loop on that. Raj Kapoor: We're probably looking at another twenty-four hours to fully process and review the backlog. I'll have a summary report by Wednesday that we can share internally, and then we can figure out what we communicate to customers from there. Megan Lawson: Alright. Let's talk about the postmortem briefly - not to get into the full discussion, but I want to align on the process. Are we thinking internal postmortem first and then a customer-facing summary, or are we doing those in parallel? Raj Kapoor: I'd want to do the internal one first. We need to have our story straight before we put anything external out. I'm thinking we do a full engineering postmortem by end of this week, and then next week we can work on a customer-facing incident report. Megan Lawson: That timeline works for me. Brian, from a support perspective, is there anything you need for the postmortem process? Like data from the ticket queue or customer impact analysis? Brian Cho: Yeah, I can pull together a breakdown of affected accounts, priority tiers, how long each was impacted - that kind of thing. That should be useful for the postmortem. I'll have that ready by Thursday. Megan Lawson: Perfect. Okay, so just to summarize where we are - redundant nodes going live today, circuit breaker implementation by Wednesday, full tenant visibility restored by tomorrow morning, retroactive event analysis complete by Wednesday, internal postmortem end of this week, customer-facing incident report next week. Does that capture it? Raj Kapoor: That's accurate from my end. Brian Cho: Yeah, that matches what I've got. I'll start updating tickets this afternoon once Megan sends over draft language. Megan Lawson: Great. I'll get that to you within the hour, Brian. Raj - anything else you need from me or from the product side to unblock the engineering work? Raj Kapoor: Not right now. The team knows what they're doing. I'll send you both a status update this evening once the first phase of the rollout is done. Megan Lawson: Sounds good. Thanks both. Let's talk again Wednesday to review where we are on the circuit breaker and the retroactive analysis. I'll send a hold. Raj Kapoor: Works for me. Brian Cho: Yeah, talk Wednesday. Thanks everyone.
topics: outage remediation, incident response, customer communication, security monitoring, postmortem planning, infrastructure reliability
action_items: Megan Lawson: Draft updated customer communication explaining the phased rollout and revised timeline within the hour | Raj Kapoor: Send evening status update to Megan and Brian once the first phase of the redundant node rollout is complete | Raj Kapoor: Deliver internal retroactive event analysis summary report by Wednesday | Brian Cho: Prepare affected account breakdown with priority tiers and impact durations for the postmortem by Thursday

title: Support Case #9279 - Summit Trust Billing Inquiry
summary: Gregory Fisk, IT Director at Summit Trust, called regarding a billing discrepancy on his January invoice showing 1,400 seats for Aegis Identity when their contract specifies 1,200 seats. Sarah Chen investigated and traced the overage to approximately 200 test accounts created during a December migration that were never deprovisioned. Sarah agreed to submit a billing adjustment request to the finance team, which will take 5-7 business days to review. Gregory also received guidance on bulk deprovisioning test accounts and setting up usage threshold alerts to prevent recurrence.
transcript_text: Sarah Chen: Thank you for calling Aegis Cloud Security support, this is Sarah Chen, how can I help you today? Gregory Fisk: Hi Sarah, yeah this is Gregory Fisk, I'm the IT Director over at Summit Trust, I have a support case open - case number 9279 - regarding a billing question. Sarah Chen: Great, let me pull that up right now, Gregory - and thanks for the case number, that helps a lot. Gregory Fisk: Sure, no problem. Sarah Chen: Okay, I'm seeing case 9279 here, Summit Trust, billing inquiry submitted... looks like February 4th. So can you walk me through what you're seeing on your end? Gregory Fisk: Yeah so, uh, we received our January invoice last week and there's a line item on there that doesn't quite match what we expected based on our contract. It's showing a charge for - let me pull this up - okay, it's showing a charge for 1,400 seats under Aegis Identity, but we only have 1,200 licensed users. Sarah Chen: Okay, so a discrepancy of 200 seats on the Aegis Identity module. Got it. And just to confirm - was this your January invoice, so the billing period would have been January 1st through January 31st? Gregory Fisk: That's correct, yeah, January billing period. Sarah Chen: Alright. And do you have the invoice number handy, or should I just work from the account? Gregory Fisk: Um, give me just a second... yeah, it's INV-2026-00847. Sarah Chen: Perfect, INV-2026-00847, let me bring that up... okay, I can see the invoice. And yeah, I can see the Identity module line item - 1,400 seats at the per-seat rate. Let me cross-reference this against your contract terms and your provisioned seat count. Gregory Fisk: Right, and I mean, our contract was renewed in October, I believe, and at that time we explicitly set the seat count at 1,200. So I'm not sure where the 1,400 is coming from. Sarah Chen: Yeah, that's a fair question. Let me look at the contract record... okay so I'm seeing the renewal executed October 14th, 2025, and the contracted seat count for Aegis Identity is listed as 1,200 seats. So you're correct there. Gregory Fisk: Right, so where's the 1,400 coming from? Is there some kind of overage charge? Because we weren't notified of any overage. Sarah Chen: That's actually a good point and let me dig into the usage data for January. Our billing system will sometimes pick up peak concurrent provisioned users during the billing cycle, and if that number exceeded your contracted seat count at any point, it can trigger overage billing depending on how your contract is structured. Gregory Fisk: Hmm. I wasn't aware that was how it worked. We haven't had 1,400 active users - I mean our headcount isn't even close to that. Sarah Chen: Understood, and that's worth looking at more closely. So I'm pulling up the provisioning logs for your account for January... okay so what I'm seeing here is interesting - there were 1,400 user accounts in a provisioned state within the Aegis Identity system during January, but let me look at whether those were all active or if some were in, like, a pending or deprovisioned queue. Gregory Fisk: Yeah, we did do a migration in December where we were onboarding users from a legacy system, and I know there were some test accounts created during that process. Could those still be showing as provisioned? Sarah Chen: That could very well explain it. If test accounts or staging accounts were created and not explicitly deprovisioned, the system would count those against your seat total. Do you know approximately how many test accounts were created during that migration? Gregory Fisk: I'd have to check with my team but, uh, off the top of my head I'm thinking maybe 150 to 200 accounts, something in that range. We were testing SSO integrations with a few internal apps. Sarah Chen: Okay, so that does line up with the discrepancy - 1,200 contracted plus roughly 200 test accounts would get you to the 1,400 that was billed. The system doesn't differentiate between test and production users unless they're tagged and excluded explicitly, which is something we'd typically walk customers through during a migration engagement. Gregory Fisk: Right, well, that's - I mean, that's a process thing we probably should have caught on our end too, so I'm not going to sit here and say it's entirely on Aegis. But the question now is what do we do about the invoice. Sarah Chen: Absolutely, and that's a reasonable question. So what I can do from a support side is document the root cause here - essentially the overage was driven by non-production test accounts that weren't deprovisioned post-migration - and submit a billing adjustment request to our finance team. That goes to them with my notes and they review it. Gregory Fisk: Okay. And what's the typical turnaround on something like that? Sarah Chen: Usually 5 to 7 business days for the review, and then if a credit or adjustment is approved it would appear on your next billing cycle. I can't guarantee the outcome of the review, but given that the overage appears to be tied to test accounts from a migration, it's a scenario our billing team has handled before. Gregory Fisk: That's fine. I'd appreciate you submitting that. And - sorry, one more thing - those test accounts, I need to get those cleaned up regardless. Is there a way to bulk deprovision them, or does someone have to go in and do it one by one? Sarah Chen: Yeah, there's a bulk deprovision option in the Aegis Identity admin console - if you go to User Management and then Provisioning, you can filter by account status, creation date, and there's also a tag-based filter if any of those test accounts were tagged during setup. You can select multiple accounts and deprovision them in one action. Gregory Fisk: Okay good, that's helpful. I'll have my team take care of that this week. We definitely don't want to have the same issue on the February invoice. Sarah Chen: That makes sense, and I'd actually recommend doing it sooner rather than later so that the February billing period doesn't pick up the elevated seat count again. If you want, I can send you a quick knowledge base article that walks through the bulk deprovision steps - sometimes it's easier to have that written out. Gregory Fisk: Yeah, that would be useful, if you could send that to the email on the case that'd be great. Sarah Chen: Will do. I'll send that along with a summary of what we discussed today and the billing adjustment request reference number once I've submitted it. Should all come through within the next hour or so. Gregory Fisk: Perfect. And just - out of curiosity - going forward, is there a way to get some kind of alert or notification if our seat count gets close to the contracted limit? Because I'd rather know proactively than find out on an invoice. Sarah Chen: That's actually a really good question. There are usage threshold alerts you can configure in the admin console - under Account Settings, Billing and Usage, you can set a threshold, say 90% of your contracted seat count, and you'll get an email notification when you hit it. That's probably worth setting up. Gregory Fisk: Yeah, I'll definitely look into that. I don't think we have that configured right now. Sarah Chen: I'll include a note about that in the follow-up email as well, just so you have the steps. Is there anything else I can help you with on this call today? Gregory Fisk: No, I think that covers it. I appreciate you walking through all of this - it's helpful to understand what actually happened rather than just having a number on a bill that doesn't make sense. Sarah Chen: Of course, that's what we're here for. I'll get everything documented and submitted, and you should hear back from the billing team within that 5 to 7 business day window. If you have any other questions in the meantime, feel free to reply to the case email and it'll come back to me. Gregory Fisk: Sounds good. Thanks Sarah. Sarah Chen: Thank you Gregory, have a good rest of your day.
topics: billing dispute, seat overage, migration cleanup, identity management, billing adjustment, provisioning
action_items: Sarah Chen: Submit billing adjustment request to finance team for the 200-seat overage on invoice INV-2026-00847 and send reference number to Gregory | Sarah Chen: Email Gregory the knowledge base article on bulk deprovisioning and include steps for configuring usage threshold alerts | Gregory Fisk: Have IT team bulk deprovision the ~200 test accounts created during the December migration before the February billing period closes | Gregory Fisk: Configure usage threshold alerts in the admin console under Account Settings > Billing and Usage

title: Weekly Engineering Standup

Mike Romano reported being 60% through the event ingestion refactor, with the end-of-March deadline assessed at roughly 60-40 odds due to uncertainty around Kafka configuration and redundant node setup. Tyler Washington completed alert deduplication work and will assist by spiking on the Kafka investigation to help reduce risk. Tom Bradley will communicate to product that the March target stands but carries acknowledged technical uncertainty, while Chris Lee continues weekly syncs with Priya's team on the Comply v2 April launch.

Okay, so usual format - let's do a quick status round, then I want to spend some time on the Detect pipeline work and the Comply v2 timeline. Mike, you want to kick us off? Mike Romano: Sure. So on my end, I've been heads down on the event ingestion refactor. We're about sixty percent through the work - the new queue partitioning is done, and I've got a draft PR up for the retry logic. Still need to wire up the dead letter queue handling and then we can start integration testing. Chris Lee: And that's all under the Detect reliability track, right? Mike Romano: Yeah, exactly. Chris Lee: Yeah those have been in the backlog forever, good to finally get to them. Any blockers? Tyler Washington: Not right now. I might need some time with Mike later this week to ask a few questions about how the ingestion layer works because some of the dashboard stuff pulls from there, but nothing blocking me today. Mike Romano: Yeah that's fine, just ping me, we can do a quick thirty minutes. Tyler Washington: Cool, thanks. Chris Lee: Okay, Tom, anything from your side before we get into the weeds on the pipeline stuff? Tom Bradley: Yeah, a couple things. One - I had a conversation with product Friday and they're asking again about the timeline for the Detect reliability work. They want to know if we're still comfortable with end of March. And two - the Comply v2 launch is tracking for early April, so I want to make sure we haven't over-allocated anyone against Detect to where we can't support any last-minute Comply stuff. Chris Lee: Right, yeah - on the end of March question, I think we're okay but it's tight. Mike, do you want to give your honest read on that? Mike Romano: Honestly? End of March for the core pipeline changes is doable, but that's assuming we don't hit anything weird in integration testing. If the testing surfaces issues - which it might - we're looking at a week or two of buffer that we don't really have. So I'd call it like... sixty-forty we hit the date. Tom Bradley: Okay so not super confident. That's useful to know now rather than in three weeks. Mike Romano: Yeah, I'd rather flag it now. I don't want to sandbag the estimate but I also don't want to commit to something and then miss it. Tom Bradley: I get it. What would it take to move the odds more in our favor? Like is this a resourcing thing or just inherent uncertainty in the work? Mike Romano: Bit of both, honestly. The dead letter queue piece and the circuit breaker pattern - those are well-understood, I'm not worried about them. The part I'm less sure about is how the redundant node setup interacts with our current Kafka config. We haven't fully mapped that out yet. Chris Lee: Could Tyler help spike on the Kafka piece? Is that something he could pick up, or is it too deep in your area? Tyler Washington: I mean, I could take a look at it. I'm not as familiar with our Kafka setup as Mike is, but I've worked with Kafka before. It might take me a bit to get context but I'm not opposed to it. Mike Romano: The risk there is the ramp-up time kind of eats into whatever time savings you'd get. But - if Tyler can do some of the investigation work and document what he finds, that could at least give me clearer inputs so I'm not going in blind. That might actually help. Chris Lee: Okay let's do that. Tyler, can you carve out time this week to start pulling on that thread? Just document what you find, even if it's rough notes - Mike, you can work off that. Tyler Washington: Yeah, works for me. Chris Lee: Good. Tom, does that give you enough to go back to product with, or do they need a harder commitment? Tom Bradley: I'll tell them end of March is still the target but flag that there's some technical uncertainty we're actively working down. I'd rather do that than give them a false sense of confidence. They won't love it but they'll deal with it. Chris Lee: Yeah, that's the right call. Okay - on the Comply v2 resource question, I don't think we have a huge exposure there. The team that's been carrying that work is mostly on the platform side. The main thing I'd watch is if QA needs help in late March, early April - that's where it could bleed over. Tom Bradley: Who's the primary contact on that side, is it still Priya's team? Chris Lee: Yeah, Priya owns it. I've been syncing with her weekly. She hasn't raised any red flags yet - the on-demand reporting piece is apparently in pretty good shape, and the multi-framework stuff for SOC 2, PCI, HIPAA is mostly done. The ISO 27001 mapping was the last thing to come in. Tom Bradley: Okay good. Keep that sync going, and just make sure she knows to flag us early if she needs anything from this team. Chris Lee: Will do. Alright, anything else on Comply before we move on?... No? Okay. Let me just do a quick check on the sprint board - we've got eight tickets in progress, two in review. I'll plan to take a look Thursday then. Alright, I think that covers everything - Tom, anything before we close out? Tom Bradley: No, I'm good. Good check-in, appreciate the transparency on the timeline stuff. Keep me posted if anything changes. Chris Lee: Will do. Alright everyone, have a good week. Mike Romano: Thanks, you too. Tyler Washington: Yeah, take it easy.

title: Aegis / Redwood Clinical - ISO 27001 Preparation
summary: Daniel Okafor and solutions architect Kevin O'Brien met with Thomas Hargrove of Redwood to introduce Comply v2 and discuss support for their ISO 27001 certification journey. Thomas shared that Redwood is in early stages of ISO prep, with a formal audit targeted for Q1 2027, and highlighted pain points around evidence collection and continuous monitoring. Kevin walked through Comply v2's on-demand reporting engine, which maps live environment data to Annex A controls and supports multi-framework coverage including HIPAA and SOC 2. The team agreed on a clear set of next steps: activating Comply v2 on Redwood's tenant, running a baseline report, and scheduling a technical working session with Thomas and his security analyst Priya.
transcript_text: Daniel Okafor: Hey Thomas, can you hear us okay? Thomas Hargrove: Yeah, loud and clear - good to hear from you guys, it's been a couple weeks. Daniel Okafor: Good, good - yeah sorry it took us a bit to get this on the calendar, things have been moving fast on our end with the Comply v2 launch and everything. Daniel Okafor: Actually that's kind of why we're here today, right, so - Thomas, I also want to introduce Kevin, he's our solutions architect and he's going to be the technical lead on your ISO 27001 prep work. Kevin O'Brien: Hey Thomas, great to meet you - I've been looking forward to this one, Daniel's told me a lot about what Redwood is trying to accomplish this year. Thomas Hargrove: Likewise, yeah, and honestly the timing could not be better because our CISO has been breathing down my neck about ISO 27001 since like January, so - any help getting a clearer picture of where we stand is going to be huge. Daniel Okafor: Yeah, absolutely, and I think that's exactly where Comply v2 is going to change the game for you - um, before we dive in though, Thomas, can you just give Kevin a quick sense of where you are in the ISO journey? Like, have you done a formal gap assessment yet or are you still kind of in the early stages? Thomas Hargrove: Yeah so we're - we're pretty early if I'm being honest. We had an external consultant come in back in February, they did a high-level gap assessment, and the short version is we have a lot of work to do on the information security management side, particularly around evidence collection and demonstrating continuous monitoring, which as a healthcare organization is like, that's a big deal for us. Kevin O'Brien: Right, and that's such a common pain point, especially in healthcare - the auditors want to see a continuous thread of evidence, not just a snapshot, and that's historically been really painful to pull together manually. Thomas Hargrove: Oh god, yeah, the last time we went through a HIPAA audit my team spent like three weeks just pulling logs and documentation together - it was a nightmare. Kevin O'Brien: Three weeks, yeah - that's - I mean that's not unusual but it's also exactly the kind of thing we built Comply v2 to eliminate, so let's talk about what that actually looks like in practice. Thomas Hargrove: Please, yeah, walk me through it. Kevin O'Brien: So - okay so the big thing with v2, and this just went GA on April 7th so it's very fresh, is the on-demand reporting engine. You can now generate a full ISO 27001 readiness report at any point, and it maps your current control posture directly to the Annex A controls - so you're not having to manually cross-reference anything, the platform does that work for you. Thomas Hargrove: Wait, so it's actually mapping to the specific Annex A controls? Like, is that - is it just a template thing or is it actually pulling live data from our environment? Kevin O'Brien: Live data - so it's pulling from your Detect telemetry, your Identity configurations, your Protect backup logs, and then surfacing all of that against the control framework. So when an auditor asks you to demonstrate, say, A.12.4 on event logging and monitoring, you can literally generate that section of the report on the spot. Thomas Hargrove: Okay that is - yeah that is genuinely impressive, I wasn't expecting that level of granularity. Kevin O'Brien: And it's not just ISO either - you mentioned HIPAA a second ago - the same report engine covers HIPAA, SOC 2, and PCI DSS as well, so if you ever need to spin up a HIPAA evidence package, it's the same workflow, same interface. Thomas Hargrove: Yeah that multi-framework piece is something we specifically asked for in our renewal discussions, so it's great to see that actually shipped - Daniel you might remember that conversation. Daniel Okafor: I do, yeah, I have the notes from that call - it was definitely on the roadmap and I'm glad we could deliver on it before your audit cycle. Kevin O'Brien: So Thomas, one thing I want to make sure we cover - in terms of your timeline, do you have a target date for the ISO 27001 certification audit? Because that's going to shape how we structure the onboarding to Comply v2. Thomas Hargrove: Our CISO is targeting Q1 2027 for the formal audit, so we have - you know, roughly eight or nine months, which sounds like a lot but when you factor in the remediation work it's going to go fast. Kevin O'Brien: Eight months is actually a really solid runway for this - um, what I'd typically recommend for organizations at your stage is we start with a baseline report run in the first two weeks, just to get a concrete picture of where you are against the framework, and then we build a remediation roadmap from those gaps. Thomas Hargrove: Yeah and that baseline report - is that something Kevin can help us interpret, or is it pretty self-explanatory on the platform? Daniel Okafor: Both, honestly - the report is designed to be readable by a non-specialist, we have like a traffic light system for control status, but Kevin and I will absolutely walk through it with you line by line on a follow-up call. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah I was going to say - I'd actually love to do a working session with you and maybe whoever on your team is going to be the compliance lead, we can go through the report together and I can explain what each gap actually means in practical terms, not just the framework language. Thomas Hargrove: That would be - yeah that would be incredibly helpful, I have a security analyst, her name is Priya, she's been leading the internal ISO prep work and she would get a lot out of that kind of session. Kevin O'Brien: Perfect, let's make sure Priya is on the next call - I'll send a calendar invite for a technical working session, maybe two weeks out, that gives you time to get Comply v2 activated and run that first report. Thomas Hargrove: That works - and just so I understand the activation piece, is that something I need to loop in my IT team for, or is it more of a - like a configuration thing on the Aegis side? Kevin O'Brien: It's pretty lightweight on your end - since you're already running Detect and Identity, the data connectors are mostly already in place, we just need to enable the Comply v2 module on your tenant and do a quick configuration review to make sure all your data sources are mapped correctly, should take maybe an hour of your team's time. Thomas Hargrove: Oh wow, okay, yeah that's much less overhead than I was anticipating - I was kind of bracing myself for like a big implementation project. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah that's the benefit of being on the full platform - you're not starting from scratch, we're just unlocking capabilities that the underlying data already supports. Thomas Hargrove: You know, I'll be honest - when we were evaluating platforms last year, one of the things that tipped us toward Aegis was exactly that, the idea that everything would be integrated rather than bolted together, and it's good to see that actually playing out in practice. Daniel Okafor: That means a lot to hear, Thomas - and we want to make sure it keeps playing out that way through the audit, so Kevin's going to be your dedicated point of contact for all things Comply through this ISO process. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, consider me on speed dial - seriously, if you or Priya hit questions on the platform or you're not sure how to interpret something in the report, just reach out, that's what I'm here for. title: Aegis / Cobalt Software - Q2 Planning

title: SOC 2 Audit Preparation - Internal
summary: Raj Kapoor convened a meeting with Tyler, Ravi, Brian, and Mike to prepare for an upcoming SOC 2 Type II audit with a 90-day observation period starting March 1st. The team reviewed key control areas including access control, change management, incident tracking, monitoring, vendor management, and employee security training. Several gaps were identified, including a broken Zendesk-PagerDuty integration, inconsistent hotfix documentation, alert fatigue in the monitoring system, and incomplete security training completions. Action items were assigned to each team member with tight deadlines before the observation window opens.
transcript_text: Raj Kapoor: Alright, I think we've got everyone on. Let me just do a quick roll call - Tyler, Raj, Ravi, Brian, Mike - okay yeah looks like we're all here. Tyler Washington: Yep, I'm here. Ravi Gupta: Here. Brian Cho: Yeah, good to go. Mike Romano: Here, sorry I'm like thirty seconds late, had a thing. Raj Kapoor: No worries. Okay so, the reason I pulled everyone together today - as you all know we've got our SOC 2 Type II audit window coming up, and I want to make sure we're not scrambling at the last minute. The auditors are going to want evidence going back several months so we need to be organized now. Tyler Washington: Do we have the audit window confirmed? Last I heard it was still tentative. Raj Kapoor: Yeah, it got confirmed last week. We're looking at a roughly ninety-day observation period, starting March first and running through end of May. Auditors will do their fieldwork in June. Mike Romano: Okay, so we've got like three days before the observation period actually kicks off. That's not a ton of runway. Raj Kapoor: Right, which is why we're doing this now. I want to go through the key control areas and figure out who owns what. Tyler, I was going to start with you on the access control and change management side. Tyler Washington: Sure. So for access control, I think we're in pretty decent shape. We've got access reviews running quarterly, last one was - uh, I want to say January fifteenth? I'd have to double-check the exact date. And we're logging provisioning and deprovisioning events through Aegis Identity. Mike Romano: Are those logs being retained for the right duration? SOC 2 auditors are going to want to see at minimum a year of retention depending on the trust service criteria. Tyler Washington: That's actually a good question. Ravi, you're closer to the logging infrastructure - what are we configured to right now? Ravi Gupta: So right now I believe we're at thirteen months retention for the identity and access logs specifically. I set that up back in Q3. For the broader system logs it's a bit more varied - some are at ninety days, some at a year. I can pull together a full inventory this week if that's helpful. Raj Kapoor: Yeah, please do that. And flag anything that's under a year, we should probably normalize that before March first if we can. Ravi Gupta: I can have something by Wednesday. Raj Kapoor: Perfect. Okay, change management - Tyler, where are we on that? Tyler Washington: So we've got the change advisory board process documented, and most production deploys are going through the proper approval workflow in Jira. The one gap I'm a little worried about is the hotfix process - we've had a few cases where engineers pushed directly to prod without a formal ticket and then backdated the documentation. Mike Romano: Yeah, that's going to be a problem. Auditors will look at commit history and deployment logs and they'll see the timing doesn't line up. Tyler Washington: It happened, I think, twice in the past quarter. Both times it was legitimate emergencies but still - the process wasn't followed. Raj Kapoor: We need to tighten that up going forward during the observation period. Can we add a gate in the CI/CD pipeline so that anything touching production requires a ticket reference? Like, a hard gate, not just a reminder. Ravi Gupta: Yeah that's doable. I can build that out. It'll probably take me a day or two, I'd want to test it in staging first so we don't break the deployment pipeline. Raj Kapoor: Good. Let's get that in before March first. Brian, I want to pull you in here - from a support perspective, do you have visibility into how incidents are being tracked and escalated? That's going to come up under the availability trust service criteria. Brian Cho: Yeah so we use PagerDuty for alerting and Zendesk for the customer-facing ticket side. I'd say the process is reasonably well documented. The thing I want to flag is that we don't always have great linkage between a customer ticket and the underlying incident record. Like, if a customer reports something and we tie it to a system incident, that connection isn't always formally captured. Mike Romano: Is that a manual process right now or is there supposed to be an integration? Brian Cho: It's supposed to be integrated but honestly it's kind of broken. The Zendesk to PagerDuty link works maybe sixty percent of the time. My team has been working around it manually. Raj Kapoor: Okay, that's a gap we need to address. Even if the auditors don't specifically flag the integration, if they pull a sample of incidents and can't trace them end to end, that's going to be a finding. Brian Cho: I agree. I've been meaning to get someone to look at that integration for like two months, it just keeps getting deprioritized. Raj Kapoor: Mike, can you take a look at the Zendesk PagerDuty integration and see what's going on? I don't want to put more on Ravi's plate. Mike Romano: Yeah, I can take that. I'll coordinate with Brian to understand what's actually failing. My guess is it's probably an API auth token that expired or something like that, but I won't know until I look. Brian Cho: That would actually make sense, we rotated some credentials in December. Mike Romano: Yeah, I'll take a look. Should be fixable pretty quickly if that's the case. Raj Kapoor: Okay good. Let me pivot to monitoring and threat detection. We use Aegis Detect for that internally - Ravi, what's the state of our alerting coverage? Are we logging the right events? Ravi Gupta: So coverage is pretty good overall. We're monitoring login anomalies, privilege escalations, API rate limit breaches, network egress outliers - basically the standard playbook. One thing I've been meaning to raise is that we have some alert fatigue going on. The tuning hasn't been updated in a while and we're getting a lot of low-signal alerts that people are starting to ignore. Tyler Washington: That's actually a risk from an audit perspective too. If auditors see a bunch of unacknowledged alerts in the system that's going to raise questions about whether we're actually reviewing them. Ravi Gupta: Exactly. I'd like to do a tuning pass before the observation period starts. Maybe a half-day exercise where we go through the alert configs and suppress or recategorize the noisy ones. Raj Kapoor: Let's schedule that. Who needs to be in that session? Ravi Gupta: Me, Tyler probably, and it might be worth having Brian there since some of the alerts feed into the support escalation queue. Brian Cho: Works for me. Let's try to do that Tuesday or Wednesday this week. Raj Kapoor: Okay I'll send a calendar invite. Now - vendor management and third-party risk. This is one that I feel like we always underinvest in until an auditor asks about it. Do we have current SOC 2 reports for our critical vendors? Tyler Washington: Uh, I know we have CloudPrime's compliance reports and we have something for Zendesk but it might be out of date. I'd have to check. Mike Romano: Yeah that's something we should inventory. I can take a first pass at it - I'll pull together a list of our critical third-party vendors and check what compliance documentation we have on file versus what's missing. Raj Kapoor: That would be great. We also need to make sure we have BAAs in place for anything that touches customer data. I know that's more of a legal thing but someone needs to chase it down. Tyler Washington: I can loop in legal and make sure those are accounted for. That's probably a quick check. Raj Kapoor: Good. Okay, let me just summarize what we've got so far in terms of action items. Ravi, you're doing the log retention inventory by Wednesday and the CI/CD gate for production deployments before March first. Mike, you're looking at the Zendesk PagerDuty integration and taking a pass at the vendor compliance documentation. Tyler, you're following up with legal on BAAs and keeping the access review records organized. Brian, you're participating in the alert tuning session. Does that all sound right? Ravi Gupta: That tracks for me. Mike Romano: Yep. Tyler Washington: Good with me. Brian Cho: Same. Raj Kapoor: One more thing I want to raise before we wrap up - employee security training. Auditors consistently ask about this. Do we have completion records for security awareness training for all staff? Tyler Washington: We ran a training in November and I believe we got pretty close to a hundred percent completion but there were a handful of people who didn't finish it. I'm not sure if we ever followed up. Mike Romano: That handful is going to matter to an auditor. If there are any outstanding completions we need to chase those down and document that we followed up, even if we can't get everyone to retroactively complete it. Raj Kapoor: Agreed. Tyler, can you pull the completion report from our LMS and send it around? We can figure out who still needs to complete it and decide if we want to issue a new training cycle or just document the exceptions. Tyler Washington: Yeah, I'll get that today. Raj Kapoor: Alright. I think we're in reasonable shape but there's clearly work to do before March first. Let's plan to do a quick check-in next Friday to see where things stand. I'll set up a shared tracker so everyone can update their items. Brian Cho: That works. I'll keep an eye on the tracker. Raj Kapoor: Okay, I think that's everything for today. Thanks everyone, let's get this stuff done.
topics: soc 2 audit, access control, change management, incident tracking, vendor management, security training
action_items: Ravi Gupta: Complete log retention inventory by Wednesday and build a CI/CD hard gate requiring ticket references for all production deployments before March 1st | Mike Romano: Investigate and fix the broken Zendesk-PagerDuty integration and compile a vendor compliance documentation inventory | Tyler Washington: Pull LMS security training completion report today, follow up with legal on BAAs for vendors touching customer data, and organize access review records | Raj Kapoor: Send calendar invite for alert tuning session (Tuesday or Wednesday) and set up a shared tracker for all action items with a check-in planned for next Friday

title: Support Case #6977 - Brightpath Commerce Slow Backup Performance
summary: Kendra Wallace from a retail company contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding severely degraded backup performance, with nightly jobs taking 4-6 hours instead of the usual 90 minutes over the past three weeks. David Kim identified a likely root cause: Kendra's environment is running backup agent version 3.4.1, which has a known change block tracking issue that causes over-scanning, while a fix was released in version 3.6.0 in late January. David acknowledged a process gap in that Kendra was not notified about the update. The resolution plan includes upgrading to 3.6.0 and a follow-up call on Monday, with escalation to senior engineering promised if the issue persists.
transcript_text: David Kim: Hi, is this Kendra? This is David Kim calling from Aegis Cloud Security support, I have case number 6977 pulled up here. Kendra Wallace: Yes, hi David, thanks for calling back. I've been waiting on this - we submitted that ticket two days ago. David Kim: I completely understand, and I apologize for the delay getting back to you. I want to make sure we get this sorted out today. So you're seeing slow backup performance with Aegis Protect - can you walk me through what you're experiencing? Kendra Wallace: Yeah, so - I mean, it's been terrible honestly. Our nightly backup jobs are taking, uh, somewhere between four and six hours to complete. They used to finish in under ninety minutes. This started maybe three weeks ago, and it's just... it's not getting better. David Kim: Four to six hours, okay, that's a significant regression. And this is consistent every night, or are there certain nights where it's worse than others? Kendra Wallace: It's pretty much every night. I mean, maybe slightly worse on weekends but honestly it's bad across the board. And look, we're a retail company - we have a lot of transaction data, inventory records, customer data - we can't have backup windows bleeding into our morning operations. David Kim: Right, yeah, that makes total sense and that's a real operational concern. Um, let me ask - what's the approximate data volume you're backing up each night? Do you have a rough figure? Kendra Wallace: It's around, uh, two to two and a half terabytes per night. That hasn't changed dramatically. I mean, we've grown a little but nothing that should cause this kind of slowdown. David Kim: Got it. And have you made any changes on your end around that time - network configuration, storage infrastructure, anything like that? Or was this kind of just one day it started being slow? Kendra Wallace: Not that I'm aware of. I mean, I had my team look into it and we didn't push any major infrastructure changes around that time. So we're kind of pointing the finger at your platform, honestly. David Kim: I hear you, and I'm not here to deflect blame - I want to find the root cause wherever it is. Let me pull up your account and look at the job logs from the last couple weeks here. Kendra Wallace: Please do. And while you're at it, I want to flag - we're running incremental backups, not full backups, so the fact that it's taking this long is extra concerning to me. David Kim: Yeah, that's a really good point, incremental jobs should absolutely not be taking that long. Okay, I'm in your account now... I can see the job history here. Hmm. Okay so I'm seeing some things. Kendra Wallace: What are you seeing? Because my team has been asking me for answers and I don't have any. David Kim: So I can see that your backup jobs are completing, but the throughput rate has dropped significantly. You're running at roughly 120 to 140 megabytes per second, whereas historically your jobs were running closer to 400 or 500. That's the bottleneck. Kendra Wallace: Okay so something changed on your end then. Because we didn't touch anything. David Kim: It could be a few things - I want to dig into this more before I point fingers anywhere. One thing I'm noticing is that your backup agent version - you're running 3.4.1, and we released 3.6.0 back in late January. There were some performance optimizations in that release, specifically around incremental change detection. Kendra Wallace: Wait - so you're saying there might be a performance issue in the version we're running and there's already a fix out? David Kim: I don't want to say definitively that's the cause yet, but it is worth flagging. There was a known issue in 3.4.x where under certain conditions the change block tracking mechanism could - um - essentially over-scan, meaning it's processing more data than it needs to. Kendra Wallace: David, that sounds like exactly what's happening. Why weren't we notified about this? This feels like something we should have gotten an email about or... I don't know, something. David Kim: That's fair feedback and I'm going to note that in the case. Customers on affected versions should have been flagged for that update and I'll look into why that didn't happen for your account. That's a process gap we need to close. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, I mean - look, I like Aegis, we've been customers for over a year and overall we've been happy. But this kind of thing is frustrating. We're a retail business, our data pipeline is critical, and three weeks of bad backups is not something I can just shrug off. David Kim: Absolutely, and I'm not asking you to shrug it off. Let's focus on getting you fixed first and then I'll make sure the right people on our side hear this feedback. So - upgrading to 3.6.0, that's the immediate step I'd recommend. Can your team do that tonight? Kendra Wallace: We can probably do it tonight or tomorrow night. What's involved in the upgrade? Is there any downtime, any risk? David Kim: It's a rolling upgrade, so there's minimal impact. The agent restarts but the restart window is typically under two minutes. You'd want to do it outside your backup window obviously, but it shouldn't cause any data issues or anything like that. Kendra Wallace: Okay. And what if we do the upgrade and it's still slow? Then what? David Kim: If you're still seeing the issue after the upgrade, the next thing I'd want to look at is your network egress path - specifically whether there's any throttling or rate limiting happening between your environment and our ingestion endpoints. I can also set you up with enhanced logging on the next backup run so we get more granular telemetry. Kendra Wallace: Okay, that's fine. I mean I'm hopeful the upgrade fixes it but I've been hopeful before with this and it hasn't gotten better on its own. David Kim: I get it. I don't want to just give you hope and disappear - here's what I'll do. I'm going to send you the upgrade instructions in writing right after this call, and I'll personally follow up with you on Monday morning to check on how the backup ran. I'll keep this case open until we confirm the performance is back to where it should be. Kendra Wallace: Monday morning works. But David, if we're still seeing the same numbers Monday, I need escalation. I can't keep going back to my team with 'we're looking into it.' David Kim: Completely fair. If the upgrade doesn't resolve it and we don't have a clear answer by Monday, I'll escalate this to our senior engineering team and loop in your account manager. You have my word on that. Kendra Wallace: Alright. I'll hold you to that. Go ahead and send me those upgrade instructions and I'll get my team moving on it tonight. David Kim: Will do. I'll have that in your inbox within the next thirty minutes. And Kendra - again, I'm sorry this dragged on as long as it did. We'll get it resolved. Kendra Wallace: Appreciate it. Talk Monday. David Kim: Talk Monday. Thanks Kendra, take care.
topics: backup performance, agent version update, technical issue, customer retention, notification gap, escalation
action_items: David Kim: Send upgrade instructions to Kendra's inbox within 30 minutes of the call | Kendra Wallace: Schedule agent upgrade to version 3.6.0 tonight or tomorrow night outside the backup window | David Kim: Follow up Monday morning to confirm backup performance improvement and keep the case open | David Kim: Investigate why Kendra's account was not notified about the known issue in version 3.4.x and escalate to senior engineering and account manager if unresolved

title: Aegis / Quantum Edge - Renewal Concerns
summary: Maria Santos met with Brianna Foster and Leo Marquez to address a serious six-hour outage on March 10-11 that caused a loss of visibility in Aegis Detect, breaching their 99.5% uptime SLA. The customer expressed eroded confidence in platform reliability and revealed they are actively evaluating a competitor, SentinelShield, which is offering aggressive pricing and a 99.9% SLA. Additional concerns included platform stagnation, upcoming compliance needs (SOC 2, HIPAA), and budget constraints going into renewal. Maria outlined next steps including a renewal proposal with an SLA credit, pricing adjustments, access to the upcoming Comply v2 product, and an engineering call to address Leo's infrastructure concerns.
transcript_text: Maria Santos: Hi Brianna, thanks for making time today - I know you're probably slammed this week. Brianna Foster: Yeah, honestly it's been a rough couple of weeks, but, um, we needed to have this conversation so here we are. Maria Santos: I totally understand, and I appreciate you being direct about that - I'd rather we just get into it than dance around things. Brianna Foster: I also pulled in Leo from our security engineering team because honestly he's the one who's been living in your platform day to day and he has, uh, a lot of thoughts. Maria Santos: Hey Leo, good to have you on - I've seen your support tickets come through and I definitely want to make sure we address what you've been seeing. Leo Marquez: Yeah, hi Maria. I'll be honest, I've been pretty frustrated. Like, the past week especially has been... not great. March tenth through the eleventh. We had a six-hour window where Aegis Detect just... went dark. No alerts, no visibility, nothing. And we're a tech company, we have compliance obligations, we have customers who depend on us being secure - that's not a minor inconvenience. Leo Marquez: And what made it worse honestly was that we didn't even find out from Aegis. We noticed it ourselves because our dashboards just stopped updating. Like, how does that happen? Maria Santos: You're right, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it - that was a significant failure on our part, both the outage itself and the communication lag. We should have been proactively reaching out to you within the first hour. Leo Marquez: I mean, we got the postmortem email a few days later, which was fine, but like... six hours is a really long time to be flying blind from a threat monitoring standpoint. Anything could have happened in that window. Brianna Foster: And look, I don't want to be overdramatic about it, but it does make us question the reliability of the platform as a whole. If this happened once, what's to say it doesn't happen again? Maria Santos: That's a completely fair question and I want to give you a real answer on that, not just reassurances. The root cause was a single point of failure in the event ingestion pipeline - essentially one component failed and it cascaded. The engineering team has since implemented redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern, so that specific failure mode is addressed. Leo Marquez: Okay but how do we know that? Like, I appreciate the explanation but we're being asked to renew a contract and our confidence in the infrastructure is shaken. Do you have documentation on the remediation? Something we can actually review? Maria Santos: Yes, absolutely - I can get you the full technical remediation report, and I can also set up a call with our engineering team if that would be helpful so you can ask questions directly. I think that would be more valuable than just a document. Brianna Foster: That could be useful, yeah. Leo, would you want to do that? Leo Marquez: I mean, yeah, I'd want to dig into the architecture changes. But I still think the broader question is around SLAs. Like, what is our actual SLA for Detect uptime and were we compensated for that breach? Maria Santos: So your current contract has a 99.5% uptime SLA for Detect, and the six-hour outage did breach that. I'm going to be honest with you - I've been working with our team on a service credit for the affected period, and I have something concrete to bring to you today. Brianna Foster: Okay, I mean, that's something at least. What are we talking? Maria Santos: I want to frame it in the context of the overall renewal conversation rather than just throwing a number out, because I think there's a broader package we should discuss. But yes, there's a meaningful credit on the table. Brianna Foster: Okay, fair enough. Let's talk about the renewal then, because there's more to it than just the outage. We've also been, um, we've been doing some evaluations of other options in the market. Maria Santos: I'd expect nothing less, honestly. Can you tell me more about what you've been looking at? Brianna Foster: We've been talking to SentinelShield. They reached out to us actually, right around the time the outage happened - which, great timing on their part. And we took the meeting because, you know, we felt like we should at least understand our options. Maria Santos: That makes sense. What's been their pitch to you? Leo Marquez: They're aggressive on pricing, I'll say that. And they're making a lot of claims about uptime guarantees - 99.9% SLA on their detection product. Which, after what we just went through, that's an appealing number. Yeah, and they have a... I don't want to overstate it, but they have a slick demo. We've only done one call so we're early in that conversation. But Brianna, you want to tell her the other stuff? Brianna Foster: Right, so, the other thing is we've been feeling like the platform as a whole isn't growing fast enough for where we're headed. We're scaling up, we're going to have some significant compliance requirements in the next twelve months - SOC 2, we're looking at HIPAA as we move into a new vertical - and we need a platform that can grow with us. Maria Santos: Okay, so that's actually a really important thing for me to flag here, because this is directly relevant. Aegis Comply v2 just launched - well, it's going live next month, April seventh - and it has on-demand reporting for SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001 all in one place. That's new functionality that directly addresses what you're describing. Leo Marquez: Wait, when does that launch? Because we've been on Comply and honestly it's felt a little stagnant. Like the reporting has been clunky. Maria Santos: April seventh is the GA date. I can get you access to the release notes and if you want, we can get you into an early preview or at least a demo of v2 before renewal conversations close. The on-demand piece is a big deal - you're not waiting for scheduled reports, you can pull a SOC 2 report whenever an auditor asks. Leo Marquez: That would actually be helpful to see. Bri, that's kind of the thing we were complaining about last month, right? Having to wait for the reporting cycle. Brianna Foster: Yeah, it is. I mean, I don't want to get too excited about something that's not live yet - we've been burned before with roadmap promises. But okay, I'd like to see a demo. Maria Santos: Totally fair, and I hear you on the roadmap skepticism - I'll make sure what I show you is real and shipping, not vaporware. So let me make sure I understand everything on the table: the outage and infrastructure trust, the SLA credit, the competitive evaluation with SentinelShield, and the compliance roadmap for the next year. Did I miss anything? Brianna Foster: Pricing. Our budget for next year is tighter than it was when we signed. We need the renewal to reflect that reality. Maria Santos: Okay. And where does the renewal land relative to your budget right now - like, are we talking ten percent, twenty percent, is there a number you're working against? Brianna Foster: We need to come down meaningfully on the total. I don't want to throw out a number yet because I want to see what you put together first. But SentinelShield is significantly cheaper for what looks like comparable coverage. Maria Santos: I want to make sure we're comparing apples to apples there, because sometimes what looks comparable in a demo is missing pieces - especially around the identity and backup modules which I know you rely on. But I'll build something out. Can I ask what your renewal deadline is internally? Brianna Foster: Our contract is up end of April. So we're not in a panic, but we're not that far out either. And we'd want whatever's next decided by, I don't know, first week of April so legal has time. Maria Santos: Okay, that gives us a couple weeks which is tight but workable. Here's what I'm going to do - I'll put together a renewal proposal that includes the SLA credit, a pricing option that reflects your budget situation, and I'll bundle in access to Comply v2. And I'll also coordinate the engineering call for Leo. Does that feel like a reasonable next step? Brianna Foster: Yeah, that's reasonable. I'd want to see that by end of this week if possible so we have time to react. Maria Santos: I can commit to Thursday. Leo, any final things from your end that you want to make sure are in scope? Leo Marquez: Just the engineering call on the remediation. That's the thing that'll determine for me whether I recommend staying or not. The business case is Brianna's call but technically, I need to feel confident in the infrastructure before I can sign off on anything. Maria Santos: Understood. I'll set that up for early next week. Thank you both - I know this wasn't an easy conversation but I'd rather have it openly and I'm committed to getting you to a place where you feel good about where things are going. Brianna Foster: Okay. We'll see what you come back with. Thanks Maria.

title: Comply v2 - Launch Readiness Review
summary: Megan and Chris conducted a launch readiness review for Comply v2, targeting an April 7th release. A recent Detect outage pulled two engineers off the project for four days, causing a 5-6 day slip on the HIPAA and ISO 27001 reporting engine, which has formatting issues in staging. The API is in good shape with beta customers, but customer-facing documentation for HIPAA and ISO 27001 is still in first draft and poses the biggest launch risk. They aligned on key deadlines, escalation paths, and a follow-up check-in for the following Tuesday.
transcript_text: Megan Lawson: Hey Chris, you on? Chris Lee: Yeah, yeah I'm here. Sorry, just closing out a Slack thread real quick. Megan Lawson: No worries. So, okay, let's just dive in. We've got about - I have a hard stop at two so maybe forty minutes or so. Chris Lee: Yeah same, that works for me. Megan Lawson: Okay. So the main thing I wanted to go through today is just the launch readiness checklist for Comply v2. April 7th is, you know, it's coming up fast and I want to make sure we're actually aligned on where things stand. Chris Lee: Yeah, agreed. I think overall we're in decent shape but there are a few things I want to flag, um, before we get too deep into the checklist stuff. Megan Lawson: Sure, go ahead. Chris Lee: So the Detect outage last week - and I know that's kind of a separate workstream - but it pulled two of my engineers off Comply work for almost four days. Priya and Damon were both on the incident response rotation. Megan Lawson: Right, I was aware of that. How much did that actually set you back? Like in real terms. Chris Lee: It's, uh, it's probably a five to six day slip on the on-demand reporting engine specifically. The SOC 2 and PCI DSS templates are done, those were finished before the outage. But the HIPAA and ISO 27001 report generation - those are still being validated in staging and we've got some edge cases we're still working through. Megan Lawson: Okay so the four frameworks are going to be ready, it's just - what exactly is the validation issue with HIPAA and ISO? Chris Lee: It's less a code issue and more a data mapping issue. The way we're pulling control evidence from the customer's environment, for HIPAA specifically, there are like three or four controls where the evidence mapping isn't lining up correctly with the report template. So the output looks weird. It's not wrong necessarily but it's not clean. Megan Lawson: When you say not clean, are we talking cosmetic or are we talking inaccurate? Chris Lee: Cosmetic, mostly. The data is correct, the control mapping is correct, it just, um, the way it renders in the PDF export has some formatting gaps and one section where the evidence summary is truncated. Megan Lawson: Okay, that's - that's manageable. Can we get that resolved by say March 31st? Chris Lee: That's actually what I wanted to talk through because Priya thinks she can get it done by the 30th, but that's also assuming she doesn't get pulled back into the Detect remediation work. And honestly I don't know what the situation is going to look like next week. Megan Lawson: I talked to the Detect team lead on Friday and my understanding is the redundant node work and the circuit breaker implementation should be wrapped up by end of this week. So I don't anticipate any more pulls from your team after that. Chris Lee: Okay, good. That's, uh, that's helpful to know. I'll confirm that with Priya and make sure she's fully back on Comply starting Monday. Megan Lawson: Yeah do that. And loop me in if anything changes because I need to know by the 1st at the latest whether we have a go or a no-go situation with any of the four frameworks. Chris Lee: Understood. Okay, what else is on the checklist? Megan Lawson: So the other big one is the customer-facing documentation. I checked in with the content team yesterday and the HIPAA and ISO 27001 user guides are still in first draft. SOC 2 and PCI DSS are done and reviewed. So there's a dependency there too. Chris Lee: That's not on my team but yeah, that tracks with what I've been hearing. Is that a blocker for the launch? Megan Lawson: It depends. I mean technically we could launch with SOC 2 and PCI DSS fully documented and say HIPAA and ISO 27001 docs are coming within two weeks of GA. But I don't love that from a product narrative standpoint because we've been marketing all four frameworks as day-one capabilities. Chris Lee: Right, and if a customer goes to generate a HIPAA report on day one and then there's no documentation to help them interpret it, that's a support headache. Megan Lawson: Exactly. So I'm going to push the content team hard this week. I think the ISO guide is actually closer than they're letting on, that one might just need a round of SME review. The HIPAA one is more complicated because compliance and legal both have to sign off on the language. Chris Lee: Do you want me to have anyone on my team do a technical review pass on the HIPAA doc? Just to make sure the control descriptions are accurate? Megan Lawson: Actually yeah, that would be helpful. Can you give me a name? I'll connect them directly with Aisha on the content team. Chris Lee: Damon would be the right person for that. He did a lot of the control mapping work on the HIPAA side so he'd be best positioned to review it. Megan Lawson: Perfect. I'll send an intro today. Okay, um, what about the API? Where does the on-demand report generation API stand? Because we've got a couple of enterprise customers who want to integrate directly. Chris Lee: The API is actually in pretty good shape. We finished the endpoint work two weeks ago, it's been in internal testing and we're doing beta access with two customers right now - NorthBridge Financial is one of them. Feedback has been fine, no major issues. There's a rate limiting question we're still finalizing but that's a configuration decision, not an engineering one. Megan Lawson: Okay good. What's the rate limiting question specifically? Chris Lee: It's basically how many on-demand report generations we allow per customer per day. Right now the default is set at ten but some customers during beta have been asking about higher limits. NorthBridge specifically asked about a hundred per day. Megan Lawson: A hundred per day? That's... I mean, what's the infrastructure cost implication on that? Chris Lee: It's manageable at current scale but if we have, you know, twenty enterprise customers all hitting a hundred per day simultaneously that could be a compute cost issue. I'd want to think about it as a tiered limit - so like standard tier gets ten, enterprise gets fifty, and then anything above that is a custom contract discussion. Megan Lawson: That actually makes sense. I'll take that to the pricing conversation - we have a sync with the revenue team on Thursday so I'll raise it then. But yeah, don't change the default before I talk to them. Chris Lee: Yep, no changes on that until you say so. Megan Lawson: Okay. What else - oh, the SSO integration for Comply. Is that still in scope for v2 or did we descope that? Chris Lee: That got descoped in the February planning cycle. It's on the v2.1 roadmap. Comply v2 will use the standard Aegis Identity authentication, same as the other modules. So it's not SSO-native within Comply specifically but customers who have Identity set up get SSO passthrough through that. Megan Lawson: Right, okay, I remember now. I just wanted to make sure we hadn't quietly put it back in scope somewhere. Alright, so let me just summarize where I think we are. Engineering is tracking, HIPAA and ISO 27001 reporting has a formatting issue that Priya's resolving by the 30th, API is solid, documentation is the bigger risk. Does that sound right to you? Chris Lee: Yeah that's accurate. I'd also add that we still need to do the final performance test on the report generation under load. We have that scheduled for March 28th. Megan Lawson: Good, make sure I get the results of that as soon as they're available. And if anything fails on that load test I want to know same day, don't wait for a report. Chris Lee: Will do. I'll make sure you're on the distribution for the test results. Megan Lawson: Okay, I think we're good. Let's plan to do a quick check-in again next Tuesday, maybe thirty minutes, and by then we should know the state of the Priya work and I should have an update from the content team. Chris Lee: Works for me. I'll send a hold. Megan Lawson: Great. Thanks Chris. Chris Lee: Yeah, talk soon.
