title: Aegis / Meridian Capital - Service Reliability Discussion
summary: Suki Nakamura from a financial services firm expressed serious concern over a six-hour threat monitoring outage on Monday that left her security team blind during ongoing regulatory audit conversations. Ravi Gupta acknowledged a known architectural single point of failure in Aegis Detect's event processing pipeline and outlined remediation steps including redundant nodes and a circuit breaker pattern targeted for end-of-month deployment. Suki disclosed that her CISO has initiated a formal vendor review and that the company is actively evaluating competitor SentinelShield. The call concluded with concrete commitments: Ravi will send an infrastructure audit summary by Monday, the technical fix will ship by end of March, and a follow-up check-in call is scheduled for two weeks out.
transcript_text: Rachel Torres: Hi Suki, thanks so much for making time for us today, I know your schedule has been pretty packed this week. Suki Nakamura: Yeah, it has been, honestly. Hi Rachel, hi everyone. Lisa Park: Hi Suki, I'm Lisa Park, I work alongside Rachel on your account - I don't think we've actually spoken before, so just wanted to introduce myself quickly. Suki Nakamura: Oh right, yes, Rachel mentioned you'd be joining. Nice to meet you Lisa. Rachel Torres: And I've also got Ravi Gupta on the line, he's one of our DevOps engineers and he can speak a lot more technically to some of the stuff we're going to cover today. Ravi Gupta: Hey Suki, good to be here. Suki Nakamura: Good, okay. So look, I'll be honest with you Rachel, I agreed to this call but I'm - I'm not in a great headspace about things right now, and I think you probably know why. Rachel Torres: We do, and that's exactly why we wanted to get on the phone rather than just send another email. I want to give you the space to tell us everything that's on your mind. Suki Nakamura: Okay. So, you know, Monday was - it was a really bad day for us. We had no visibility into threat monitoring for, what, like six hours? Six hours, Rachel. In financial services, that's not a minor inconvenience, that's a serious risk event. Rachel Torres: Completely understood, and I'm not going to minimize that at all. Suki Nakamura: Our security team was essentially flying blind. We had regulators - we have ongoing audit conversations happening, and I had to get on a call with our CISO on Monday afternoon and explain why our threat monitoring platform was just... not working. That's not a conversation I ever want to have. Ravi Gupta: Yeah, and Suki, I want to jump in here because I think it's important that you hear directly from me on the technical side of what happened. Can I - is it okay if I walk through it? Suki Nakamura: Please. Yes. I want to understand what actually happened because the status page updates were... they were not sufficient. Ravi Gupta: Yeah, and I hear you on that, the communications piece is something we're addressing separately. But on the technical side - what happened was we had a cascading failure in our event processing pipeline. There was essentially a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer, and when that component went down, it took the whole pipeline with it rather than failing gracefully. Suki Nakamura: Right. So there was no redundancy built in. Ravi Gupta: That's - yeah, that's the honest answer. There wasn't sufficient redundancy at that layer, and that's a design gap that we've already started addressing. We're implementing redundant processing nodes and we're adding a circuit breaker pattern so that if one node degrades, traffic gets redistributed rather than causing a full outage. Suki Nakamura: Okay, and when does that actually get shipped? Because I've been in software long enough to know that 'we're implementing' can mean a lot of different things. Rachel Torres: That's a completely fair push. Ravi, do you want to give Suki the timeline? Ravi Gupta: Yeah, so the redundant nodes are already being staged in our dev environment, and we're targeting end of this month for the circuit breaker rollout to production. We're not waiting on this one. Suki Nakamura: End of March. Okay. And what happens between now and end of March if something goes wrong again? Ravi Gupta: So in the interim we've actually increased monitoring frequency on that specific pipeline component and we have an on-call rotation specifically watching it. It's not the permanent fix but it's not nothing either. Suki Nakamura: I appreciate you explaining it, Ravi, I do. But I have to be candid with you all - this isn't just about the technical fix for me. The bigger issue is that this shook my confidence, and frankly my leadership's confidence, in Aegis Detect as a platform we can rely on. Lisa Park: Can you tell us a bit more about what that looks like internally? Like, is this something your leadership is actively asking questions about? Suki Nakamura: Yes. My CISO has asked me to do a formal review of our threat monitoring vendor options. And I don't love that I'm in that position, because we've been with Aegis for, what, almost two years now, and up until Monday I would have said we were pretty happy. But this... this was bad timing on a lot of levels. Rachel Torres: I really appreciate you being so direct with us Suki, that kind of honesty helps us actually address what matters. Can I ask - is the review something that's already in motion, or is it more of a... a contingency your CISO is preparing for? Suki Nakamura: It's in motion. We've - look, I'll be transparent. We've been talking to SentinelShield. They actually reached out to us a few weeks ago, coincidentally, and we had a demo scheduled that we were going to deprioritize, and now... we're not deprioritizing it. Rachel Torres: Okay. Thank you for telling us that. Suki Nakamura: I'm not saying it to be threatening, I'm saying it because I think you deserve to know where we're at. We haven't made any decisions. But I'd be lying if I said we weren't looking. Rachel Torres: No, and I - I genuinely appreciate that, Suki. Look, we're not going to sit here and tell you not to do your due diligence, that would be unreasonable. What I do want to make sure is that you're evaluating us based on a full picture, not just this week. Suki Nakamura: And that's fair, but the full picture does include this week. That's part of the picture. Rachel Torres: Absolutely. No question. And we own that. Suki Nakamura: I guess what I want to understand from you all is - is this a one-off? Or is this symptomatic of something deeper in how Detect is architected? Because those are two very different stories. Ravi Gupta: That's exactly the right question and I want to give you a real answer, not a canned one. The honest truth is - the single point of failure that caused this outage was a known architectural limitation that we hadn't yet prioritized fixing. We knew it existed. We underestimated the blast radius. That's on us. Suki Nakamura: I... okay. I actually appreciate that you said that, Ravi. That's more honest than I expected. Ravi Gupta: We've done a full audit of similar single points of failure across the Detect infrastructure this week, and the circuit breaker implementation addresses the highest risk ones. I can share that audit summary with you if that would be helpful - obviously redacted where appropriate, but I think seeing the scope of what we've reviewed might give you some confidence. Suki Nakamura: Yes. Yes I'd want to see that. That's the kind of thing I can actually bring to my CISO - something substantive. Rachel Torres: We'll get that to you by end of day Monday, Ravi can you confirm that works on your end? Ravi Gupta: Yeah, Monday works, I'll have it ready. Suki Nakamura: Okay. And look, I do want to say - the other piece of this that's been frustrating, and this is maybe more on the compliance side, is that I need to be able to demonstrate to our regulators that we have continuous monitoring in place. When Detect goes down, that argument falls apart. And in our industry, that's not academic. Lisa Park: That's such an important point, and actually - I don't want to pivot too hard here because I know we're focused on Detect today - but we do have some things coming in Comply that might actually help you build a stronger narrative around that for regulators, around your overall monitoring posture. Suki Nakamura: Maybe, but right now I need Detect to work before I worry about how we report on it. Lisa Park: That's completely fair. You're right, one thing at a time. Suki Nakamura: So where do we land today? I want to make sure I leave this call with a clear picture of what you're committing to and by when. Rachel Torres: Okay, let me summarize and you can tell me if I'm missing anything. Ravi's going to send over the infrastructure audit summary by Monday. We're committing to end-of-month production deployment of the circuit breaker fix and redundant nodes. And I'd like to schedule a follow-up call in two weeks - not to sell you anything, just to check in and make sure the interim monitoring is holding and answer any questions that come up from your internal review. Suki Nakamura: Two weeks. Okay. Yeah, I can do that. And Rachel - I do want to be clear, I'm not trying to be difficult here. I'm trying to do right by my organization. Rachel Torres: I know that. And honestly, the fact that you're still talking to us and being this candid tells me that you haven't given up on us yet, and we're not going to give up on you either. Suki Nakamura: We'll see. Send me that audit doc and let's talk in two weeks. Rachel Torres: Absolutely. Thanks Suki, we'll be in touch Monday.

title: Detect Outage - Customer Impact Assessment
summary: The team convened an urgent internal call to address a significant outage of their Detect product that left customers without security monitoring for approximately six hours overnight. A single point of failure in the event ingestion pipeline caused a cascading failure, and critically, the company's own internal alerting also failed because the health checks were tied to the same broken pipeline - meaning a customer, not the team, flagged the outage. title: Support Case #1514 - Meridian Capital Granular Restore Request
summary: Jason Hoffman from Meridian contacted Aegis support (Sarah Chen) regarding the lack of granular file-level restore capabilities in Aegis Protect. An analyst had accidentally overwritten config files on an EBS-backed EC2 trading platform, requiring a two-hour manual workaround involving spinning up a temporary instance to retrieve the files. Sarah confirmed that file-level restore is not currently supported and documented a formal feature request covering granular file-level restore from EBS snapshots, restore-to-alternate-path functionality, and a file metadata preview capability. The case will be logged, Jason's colleague Marcus Webb will be added, and the CSM will be looped in for follow-up.
transcript_text: Sarah Chen: Hi Jason, thanks for joining - this is Sarah Chen from Aegis support, I'll be handling case number 1514 for you today. Jason Hoffman: Hey Sarah, yeah thanks for getting on a call, I appreciate it - email threads on this kind of thing just go in circles. Sarah Chen: Totally understand, it's a lot easier to just talk through it directly. So I pulled up the case before hopping on - looks like you're looking at granular restore capabilities within Aegis Protect, is that the right starting point? Jason Hoffman: Yeah, exactly. So the short version is - we had an incident internally, nothing catastrophic, but one of our analysts accidentally overwrote a set of config files in our trading platform environment, and we needed to restore just those specific files, not the whole VM or the whole volume. Sarah Chen: Okay, got it. And when you went into Protect to try and do that, what did you run into? Jason Hoffman: So, the restore options we're seeing are basically - restore the full snapshot, or restore at the volume level. There's no way that I can find to, uh, drill down and say I want this specific directory, or these three files from this snapshot point. Sarah Chen: Right, yeah, so that's - that's actually an accurate read of where the product is today. Granular file-level restore, like truly arbitrary path-based restore from within a snapshot, that's not currently a supported workflow in Protect. Jason Hoffman: Okay. I mean, I kind of suspected that was going to be the answer but I wanted to confirm it rather than assume. Sarah Chen: No, absolutely right to ask. So let me just - can I ask a few more questions about the specific scenario so I can make sure I capture this accurately for the feature request ticket? Jason Hoffman: Sure, go ahead. Sarah Chen: So the workload in question - is this an EC2 instance, a VM in a private cloud environment, or something else? Jason Hoffman: It's EC2, yeah. We're running on CloudPrime, the trading platform environment specifically is in us-east-1. The config files in question are on an EBS volume attached to the instance. Sarah Chen: Okay, EBS-backed EC2, us-east-1. And the snapshots are being managed through Protect - so you've got a backup policy applied to that instance? Jason Hoffman: Correct, we've got an hourly snapshot policy on that environment. So the snapshots exist, they're there, it's just - we can't get to individual files without restoring the whole volume, which is kind of a nuclear option for what we actually need. Sarah Chen: Yeah, that makes complete sense. Restoring a full volume just for a handful of config files is a lot of overhead, especially if the instance needs to stay up or there are dependency concerns. In this case, how did you ultimately resolve it - were you able to get the files back another way? Jason Hoffman: Yeah, we ended up spinning up a temporary EC2 instance, restoring the volume to that, mounting it, pulling the files manually, and then copying them back. It worked but it was, uh, it was probably a two-hour process for something that should have taken ten minutes. Sarah Chen: Yeah, that's a pretty painful workaround. I want to be transparent with you - that manual approach is essentially what the product forces today if you need file-level granularity, and I completely acknowledge that's not a great experience. Jason Hoffman: Right. And look, for a financial services environment, uh, we have pretty strict RTO requirements on certain systems. A two-hour workaround process isn't something I can count on operationally. It kind of worked this time but it's not a repeatable procedure I'd want to rely on. Sarah Chen: Understood. And that's exactly the kind of context that's valuable to document. Can I ask - what kind of RTO are you targeting for this class of restore, roughly? Jason Hoffman: For the trading platform environment specifically, we're targeting fifteen minutes or under for file-level restores. Obviously full system recovery has a different SLA, but for - you know, config corruption or an accidental overwrite scenario - fifteen minutes is kind of our threshold. Sarah Chen: Fifteen minutes, got that. And are we talking about, like, structured file types - configs, CSVs, that kind of thing - or do you also need to think about database-level granularity, like individual records or tables? Jason Hoffman: For now, the ask is really around file-level. Flat files, config files, maybe log archives in some cases. Database granularity is a whole other conversation, we manage that separately through our DBA team with native tooling. Sarah Chen: Perfect, that actually simplifies things from a scoping standpoint. So I'm going to log this as a formal feature request - granular file-level restore for EBS-backed workloads, with the ability to browse the snapshot contents and select specific paths or directories for restore. Does that capture what you're looking for? Jason Hoffman: Yeah, that's the core of it. I'd also add - the ability to restore to an alternate location would be useful. So not necessarily back to the original path, but maybe restore to a staging directory so we can validate before we overwrite anything in production. Sarah Chen: Oh, that's a good addition - restore to alternate path, so you can do a staged recovery rather than directly overwriting in place. I'll include that. Anything else that comes to mind? Jason Hoffman: Um - I mean, the ability to preview the file before restoring it would be nice. Like, just a basic metadata view, see the file size, timestamp, confirm it's the right version before you commit. But I'd call that a nice-to-have, not a blocker. Sarah Chen: Got it, I'll flag that as a secondary ask - snapshot file browser with metadata preview. That's actually come up on a couple other accounts so it's good to have it documented with your name attached to it. Jason Hoffman: Sure. And just so I understand the process - what happens with a feature request like this? Does it just go into a backlog somewhere, or is there some kind of review cycle? Sarah Chen: So, the way it works is - I submit this into our product feedback system, it gets triaged by the Protect product team, and they assess it based on request volume, impact, and technical feasibility. High-priority items from enterprise accounts like yours do tend to get escalated for roadmap consideration, but I can't give you a commitment on timeline. Jason Hoffman: That's fair. I'm not expecting a date, I just want to know it's not going into a black hole. Sarah Chen: It won't - you'll have a case number attached to this, and I'll make sure your CSM gets looped in so there's a human who can give you updates on it. Speaking of which, do you want me to copy anyone specific at Meridian on the case documentation? Jason Hoffman: Yeah, if you could copy Marcus Webb on my team - he's the one who actually went through the whole workaround process, so he'll want visibility into any updates. Sarah Chen: Marcus Webb, got it, I'll add him to the case. And just to close the loop - is there anything else on the immediate side that's blocking you, or is this more of a forward-looking ask at this point? Jason Hoffman: It's forward-looking. The immediate incident is resolved, we're not down or anything. It's more - I don't want to be in that situation again and have the same painful workaround be my only option. Sarah Chen: Completely reasonable. Alright, so to summarize - I've got the feature request documented: granular file-level restore from EBS snapshots, restore to alternate path support, and file metadata preview as a secondary ask. Case 1514, I'll get Marcus added, and I'll loop in your CSM for follow-up. Does that cover everything? Jason Hoffman: Yeah, that covers it. Thanks for being straightforward about where the product is today - I'd rather have an honest answer than get told it's coming soon and then wait a year. Sarah Chen: Yeah, I think that's the only way to have a useful conversation. Alright, Jason - I'll get the case updated today and you should see the documentation in your portal within the hour. Thanks for your time. Jason Hoffman: Sounds good, thanks Sarah.
topics: feature request, granular restore, backup and recovery, rto compliance, aws ebs, workaround
action_items: Sarah Chen: Submit formal feature request (Case 1514) for granular file-level restore from EBS snapshots, alternate path restore, and file metadata preview into the Protect product feedback system | Sarah Chen: Add Marcus Webb to Case 1514 documentation and loop in Meridian's CSM for ongoing updates | Jason Hoffman: Monitor portal for case documentation update expected within the hour | Sarah Chen: Ensure CSM provides Jason with roadmap updates on the feature request to avoid it going untracked

title: Competitive Threat Assessment - Post Outage
summary: The team convened to address fallout from a six-hour platform outage that caused a complete loss of threat monitoring visibility. Competitors SentinelShield and CyberNova are actively targeting at-risk accounts, including Hartfield Financial and prospect Clearvale Systems. The group aligned on a two-part response strategy: leading with a transparent post-mortem and remediation narrative now, followed by a Comply v2 launch touchpoint in early April to show forward momentum. Key concerns include a potential liability issue involving a customer who claims an actual security incident occurred during the outage window.
transcript_text: Megan Lawson: Okay, I think we've got everyone now - can you all hear me okay? Tom Bradley: Yeah, loud and clear. James Mitchell: Good here. Brian Cho: Yep, I'm on. Megan Lawson: Alright, so - I want to just dive right in because honestly we don't have a lot of time and there's a lot to cover. The outage last week was bad. I don't think any of us are going to sugarcoat that. Six hours of zero threat monitoring visibility is not something our customers are just going to brush off, and our competitors are absolutely going to use this against us. James Mitchell: Yeah, I've already seen it happening. I had two accounts reach out to me directly asking if we had a formal post-mortem they could share internally, and one of them - Hartfield Financial - mentioned that SentinelShield had already been in contact with their procurement team. Megan Lawson: Of course they have. That's - I mean, that's exactly what I'd do too if I were them, but still. It's frustrating. Daniel Okafor: Same thing on my end. I've got a prospect, Clearvale Systems, mid-market, they were this close to signing - and now their CTO is asking pointed questions about our reliability track record. And I didn't have great answers for him, which is not a position I want to be in. Tom Bradley: And what are the competitors actually saying? Like are they sending specific messaging or is it more just, hey, we heard you had some trouble? James Mitchell: From what I can gather, SentinelShield is going in with a pretty polished pitch around their multi-region redundancy story. They're positioning it as, um, you know, 'we were built for this, our architecture doesn't have single points of failure' - which, I mean, honestly Tom, that's landing because it's hitting on exactly what went wrong with us. Tom Bradley: Look, I'm not going to sit here and pretend the architecture wasn't a problem. It was. The event ingestion pipeline had a clear single point of failure and it cascaded. We know what happened. We've already deployed the redundant processing nodes and the circuit breaker pattern is in place. But yeah - the damage from a perception standpoint, that's real and it's going to take time. Megan Lawson: How long do you think before we can point to, like, meaningful uptime numbers post-fix? Because that's what customers are going to want. Tom Bradley: I mean, realistically - we need at least 30, 60 days of clean data before we can say anything with confidence. And even then, some customers are going to want third-party validation, not just us saying we're fine. Daniel Okafor: That's a long time in a competitive sales cycle. Megan Lawson: It is. And Brian, what's the support side looking like right now? How many tickets are still open related to the outage? Brian Cho: So we had - ugh - we had a spike of about 340 tickets come in during and immediately after the outage. We've closed most of them, but there are still about 40 open, mostly from customers who want detailed impact reports, like specifically which alerts they missed during the window, what events weren't processed. And a handful of those customers are, uh, pretty heated. I had one escalation yesterday where the customer's security team is claiming they had an actual incident during the outage window and they're saying our lack of visibility may have delayed their response. Megan Lawson: Oh, that's - okay, that's a liability issue. Is legal aware of that one? Brian Cho: Yes, I looped them in this morning. We're handling it carefully. Megan Lawson: Good. Okay. So, let's talk competitive positioning because that's really why we're on this call. James, Daniel - what are you hearing beyond SentinelShield? Are VaultEdge or CyberNova showing up in these conversations? James Mitchell: VaultEdge has come up a couple of times but honestly more in the backup and recovery conversation than detect, which makes sense - that's their strength. The Hartfield situation is really squarely about Detect, so it's SentinelShield that's the immediate threat there. Daniel Okafor: Yeah, and for Clearvale, the CTO actually mentioned CyberNova as well - which surprised me a little. They don't usually show up in the mid-market space at that price point. But apparently CyberNova reached out proactively with some kind of competitive displacement offer. I don't know the specifics but - the timing is not a coincidence. Megan Lawson: Of course it's not. They've been watching the news feeds. All of them have. And we would do the same thing - I'm just annoyed we're on the receiving end of it right now. Daniel Okafor: Can we talk about what our counter-narrative actually is? Because right now I feel like we're reactive and I don't have a clean story to bring back to Clearvale. Megan Lawson: That's fair. Tom, can you give me something concrete that James and Daniel can take into customer conversations? Like what's actually different now? Tom Bradley: Yeah, so - here's what I can say with confidence. The root cause was identified within a couple of hours of the incident starting. We had the fix scoped within 24 hours. Redundant processing nodes are live, the circuit breaker pattern is deployed, and we've now got automated failover testing on a weekly cadence that we didn't have before. That's real. That's not just spin. Brian Cho: Okay, that's good. That's something. But I think we also need to be honest with customers that this was a significant failure and we're taking it seriously, rather than just trying to gloss over it with technical jargon. Customers can smell a cover-up story from a mile away. Megan Lawson: Completely agree with Brian on that. The transparency piece is actually a differentiator if we do it right. Most vendors try to minimize, and if we lead with a really candid post-mortem - like genuinely owning what went wrong - that can actually build trust. It doesn't feel that way right now but it can. Daniel Okafor: I hope you're right about that, Megan, but I've got to be honest - when I'm sitting across from a CTO who's already been called by two competitors, a transparency narrative is a tough sell in that moment. They want to know it won't happen again, and I can't guarantee that. James Mitchell: Nobody can guarantee that. SentinelShield can't guarantee it either, they've had outages too - it was, what, eighteen months ago they had that authentication service issue? I think it was over four hours. Megan Lawson: Yeah, use that. That's a legitimate point - every platform has incidents, the question is how you respond and what you've built to prevent recurrence. I'll work with marketing to get some battlecard updates out this week. The current ones are obviously not reflecting any of this. Daniel Okafor: The battlecards honestly haven't been updated in like, four months anyway. That's been a frustration for a while. No offense, Megan. Megan Lawson: No, you're - you're right, and I own that. That's on us. It's something we've deprioritized and this situation is kind of exposing why that was a mistake. James Mitchell: For what it's worth, one thing that might actually help us in the near term - and this is sort of looking ahead - is the Comply v2 launch coming up. Brian Cho: That's actually a smart angle, James. When does Comply v2 go GA, is it still early April? Megan Lawson: April 7th is the date, assuming nothing slips. Tom? Tom Bradley: We're on track. I don't anticipate any delays on that one. The on-demand SOC 2 and HIPAA reporting features are basically done, we're in final QA. Megan Lawson: Okay, good. So let's make sure we're sequencing this right for the accounts that are at risk. We want to get in front of them with the post-mortem and remediation story now, and then have a follow-up touch in early April when Comply v2 drops. That gives us two meaningful reasons to engage rather than just one awkward apology call. James Mitchell: That makes sense. I'll reach out to Hartfield early next week and see if I can get a call with their CISO. I think going above the procurement level is the right move there. Megan Lawson: Yeah, do that. And Daniel, for Clearvale - do you think the deal is still salvageable or are we in real trouble there? Daniel Okafor: Honestly? I think it's 50-50 at this point. The CTO is open to hearing us out but he's clearly been spooked. If we come in with a really strong story and maybe some kind of SLA commitment that's better than what we've offered previously, I think we have a shot. But if we fumble the next conversation, I think we lose it. Megan Lawson: Alright. Let's not fumble it. Brian, can you make sure that anyone from sales who needs a detailed technical summary of the incident and the remediation has it by end of day Monday? Something they can actually share with customers, not just internal-facing. Brian Cho: Yeah, I'll coordinate with Tom's team and have something ready. I'd say Monday EOD is doable. Megan Lawson: Good. Alright, I think we have a plan - it's not a great situation but we know what we're dealing with. Let's just make sure we're communicating internally as things develop. If anyone hears of more competitive activity from SentinelShield or CyberNova specifically, flag it in Slack immediately, don't wait for the next sync. Tom Bradley: Agreed. Thanks everyone. James Mitchell: Thanks, talk soon. Daniel Okafor: Yep, thanks. Brian Cho: Thanks all.

title: Aegis / Stratos Cloud - Audit Preparation

title: URGENT: Blackridge Investments - Complete Loss of Threat Visibility
summary: Julia Tran from Blackridge Investments called Aegis Cloud Security support in a critical situation where her firm has had zero threat visibility for over three hours due to a known event processing pipeline failure. Marcus Williams confirmed the outage is a cascading failure affecting multiple customers on the same processing cluster, with engineering estimating restoration within two more hours. Julia expressed serious frustration over the lack of proactive communication, a single point of failure in the architecture, and the operational impact of having analysts manually reviewing logs. She disclosed they have been evaluating a competitor (SentinelShield) and has a board meeting next week where she must explain the security blind spot. Marcus committed to a formal incident report, SLA review, AE loop-in, and a direct phone call upon service restoration.
transcript_text: Marcus Williams: Thank you for calling Aegis Cloud Security support, this is Marcus Williams, how can I help you today? Julia Tran: Marcus, hi, this is Julia Tran from Blackridge Investments and I need you to understand right now that this is a critical, critical situation - we have zero threat visibility, zero, and it has been that way for over three hours. Marcus Williams: Okay, Julia, I hear you, I'm pulling up your account right now - can you give me your account ID or the email on file so I can get in faster? Julia Tran: It's Blackridge Investments, B-L-A-C-K-R-I-D-G-E, account number BRI-04471, and I also already submitted a ticket, ticket number... uh, I have it here somewhere - it's AGS-229183. Marcus Williams: Got it, pulling up AGS-229183 right now, okay I see the ticket came in about... forty minutes ago, and I can see you've flagged it P1 which is absolutely appropriate, let me just get into your Detect dashboard here. Julia Tran: Forty minutes ago - Marcus, I have been trying to get someone on the phone for forty minutes, do you understand what it means for a financial services firm to have no threat monitoring? We are a target, we are constantly a target, and right now we are essentially flying blind. Marcus Williams: You're absolutely right and I sincerely apologize for the wait time, that is not acceptable and I'm going to flag that separately, but right now my full focus is on getting your visibility restored - can you describe exactly what you're seeing on your end? Like, are you getting any events at all or is it completely flat? Julia Tran: Completely flat. The event feed in Aegis Detect, it just... stopped. No alerts, no events, nothing. The last event we see in the dashboard is timestamped at 7:14 AM this morning and it is now almost 10:30 and I have a team of analysts sitting here staring at a dead screen. Marcus Williams: Okay, 7:14 AM, so that's roughly three hours and fifteen minutes of no event ingestion, and this is across all your event sources or is it specific to certain integrations? Julia Tran: Everything. CloudPrime CloudTrail, our on-prem SIEM feed, our endpoint agents - all of it. It's not an integration issue, everything on our side is green, logs are generating, I can confirm that, it's something on your end. Marcus Williams: Understood, and uh - I want to be transparent with you, Julia. I'm looking at our internal monitoring right now and I am seeing... okay, yeah, there is a known issue with the Detect event processing pipeline that our engineering team is actively working on. Julia Tran: A known issue? A KNOWN issue? Why was I not notified? Why did I have to call in and wait forty minutes to find out there is a known issue? This is - I'm sorry, I'm trying to stay calm here but this is completely unacceptable. Marcus Williams: That is a completely fair and valid point and I - I don't have a good answer for why proactive communication didn't go out sooner and I own that on behalf of Aegis, that should have happened. Julia Tran: So what is the issue exactly? What is wrong with the pipeline? And more importantly when is it going to be fixed because I need a number, I need an ETA right now. Marcus Williams: So what I can see from our internal status is that there was a cascading failure in the event ingestion layer - it looks like a single component went down and it took the rest of the processing queue with it, engineering is working on isolating and restarting the affected nodes. Julia Tran: A single component took down the whole thing? There's no redundancy? I mean - are you serious? We are paying for an enterprise security platform and there is a single point of failure in the core monitoring pipeline? Marcus Williams: I - yeah, I understand why that is alarming and frankly it is a legitimate architectural concern that I know our engineering leadership is going to have to answer for, I'm not going to try to spin that. Julia Tran: How long has this been affecting customers? Is it just us or is this broader? Marcus Williams: It appears to be affecting multiple customers on the same processing cluster, so no, it's not just Blackridge, but I want to be clear that doesn't make it better - it actually makes it worse from an impact standpoint. Julia Tran: Multiple customers. Multiple customers with no threat visibility. In financial services. Marcus, I need you to get me an ETA and I need you to escalate this to your highest level right now, like I want to talk to a manager, I want to talk to whoever owns this incident. Marcus Williams: Yes, absolutely, I am escalating this to our P1 incident team right now as we speak and I will get you a direct line to our senior incident manager - I'm also going to stay on this call with you so you're not bounced around. Julia Tran: Okay, and while we're waiting - I have to be honest with you, Marcus, and I want you to pass this up the chain - we have been evaluating SentinelShield for the past couple months as a potential alternative and right now, today, this is making that decision very easy. Marcus Williams: I hear you, and I'm not going to try to do a sales pitch right now because that would be tone deaf - what I will say is that I want us to earn your trust back and that starts with fixing this, right now, today. Julia Tran: We have a board meeting next week where I have to present on our security posture and I was planning to highlight our Aegis deployment as a strength - now I'm going to have to explain why we had a multi-hour blind spot in our threat monitoring and that is not a conversation I want to have. Marcus Williams: And that is - look, I'm really sorry you're in that position, and something I can help with is making sure you have a full incident report with timeline, root cause, and remediation steps that you can bring to that board meeting, that's something we can absolutely provide. Julia Tran: That would be helpful, yes, I'll need that in writing, and I want our account executive looped in too because there are going to be SLA conversations that need to happen. Marcus Williams: Completely understood, I'm noting all of that - formal incident report, AE looped in, SLA review - all of that is going on the ticket right now. Julia Tran: And Marcus, in the meantime, what are we supposed to do? Like, what is your recommendation for us right now? Do we have any interim visibility at all? Marcus Williams: So in terms of interim steps - your raw logs are still being generated on your sources, which you mentioned, so your team can monitor those directly as a stopgap, I know that's painful and manual but it's something, and I'd also recommend pulling your last 24-hour threat summary from before the outage to have a baseline. Julia Tran: Yeah, we're already doing that, we've had two analysts manually reviewing CloudTrail for the last two hours - that's two people pulled off other work to compensate for your platform being down. Marcus Williams: And that operational impact is going to be part of the SLA conversation, I'm documenting it. Julia Tran: Okay - do you have any update from engineering yet? Any ETA at all? Marcus Williams: I'm checking the internal incident channel right now and... okay, engineering is saying they've isolated the failed node and are in the process of restarting the processing queue, they're estimating restoration within the next two hours, but I want to be careful about that number because they're still in active remediation. Julia Tran: Two more hours. So potentially five-plus hours total of no threat monitoring. I just - I want to make sure that is in writing somewhere because that is five hours of SLA breach and I will be referencing that. Marcus Williams: It is documented, I'm timestamping everything in the ticket and I'll make sure the incident report captures the full outage window from 7:14 AM through restoration. Julia Tran: And what happens to events that were supposed to be ingested during the outage window - are those just lost? Or will they be backfilled? Marcus Williams: That is a really important question and I want to get you a definitive answer from engineering rather than guess - my understanding is that events queued during the outage should be recoverable and backfilled once the pipeline is restored, but I will confirm that explicitly and follow up in writing. Julia Tran: Okay. Please do that. And Marcus, I need you to call me the moment visibility is restored, not an email, a phone call. Marcus Williams: You have my word, I will call you directly the moment we confirm restoration on your account, and I'm going to be monitoring your account specifically - I'll have your number pulled up and I will call you. Julia Tran: Alright. I'm going to hold you to that. And Marcus - just so you know, I genuinely hope Aegis can turn this around because switching vendors is a nightmare and I don't want to do it, but right now I need to see accountability and I need to see real action. Marcus Williams: I hear you, Julia, and I promise you that accountability starts right now with this call - I've got everything documented, escalation is in progress, and you will hear from me the moment there is any update. Thank you for your patience even though I know you're in an incredibly difficult position.

title: Identity Team - Q2 Roadmap
summary: The team held a Q2 roadmap planning session for the Identity product, covering three major themes: JIT provisioning and SCIM improvements, adaptive MFA policies, and an Identity audit trail integrated with the Comply module. Technical leads discussed specific failure modes in SCIM sync, a redesigned attribute mapping UI with inline validation, and a phased approach to adaptive MFA starting with location and device posture signals. The session also touched on competitive pressure from SentinelShield, lingering customer trust concerns following a March Detect outage, and cross-team alignment with the Comply team around SOC 2 reporting gaps.
transcript_text: Alex Reyes: Alright, I think we've got everyone - Sofia, you just joined right? Sofia Petrov: Yeah, sorry, I was just finishing up a Slack thread with the Detect team about the post-mortem follow-ups. Jordan Whitfield: Oh no worries at all, we were just doing the usual five minutes of 'can everyone hear me' so you didn't miss anything. Mike Romano: Ha, classic. Okay so, yeah, are we recording this? I want to make sure the folks who couldn't make it can catch up. Alex Reyes: Yep, recording is on. Okay so - Q2 roadmap planning for Identity. I'm really excited about this one honestly, I think we have a genuinely strong quarter ahead of us. Ananya Sharma: Same, and I feel like Q1 kind of lit the fire a little bit? Like, the Comply v2 launch last week showed what we can do when we're really coordinated, and I want that energy for Identity. Alex Reyes: Totally agree with that. Comply v2 was a good moment for the org. And honestly, Identity has been in a bit of a holding pattern, so I think customers are ready to see some movement from us. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, I've been looking at the support ticket volume and there's a pretty clear cluster around SSO configuration - specifically around just-in-time provisioning. Like, that's coming up again and again. Alex Reyes: Right, and that's actually on my list as a Q2 priority. So let me just share my screen and walk through the draft roadmap so we're all looking at the same thing. Mike Romano: Perfect. Alex Reyes: Okay so - three big themes for Q2. First is JIT provisioning and SCIM improvements, second is adaptive MFA policies, and third is what I'm calling the Identity audit trail, which ties into the Comply integration story. Jordan Whitfield: Oh, I love that the audit trail piece connects to Comply. That feels like a really natural cross-module story and honestly something we should be talking about in sales materials too. Alex Reyes: A hundred percent, and that was actually a direct ask from - I think it was the Fortiguard Pro competitive deal we almost lost last quarter? The customer specifically said they wanted IAM events surfaced in their compliance reports. Ananya Sharma: Yeah I remember that one. That was painful. But it's good that it's shaping actual roadmap items rather than just becoming a post-deal retrospective that nobody reads. Alex Reyes: Exactly. Okay so let's go a level deeper on each one. Mike, you've been thinking about the SCIM work - do you want to take JIT provisioning? Mike Romano: Sure, yeah. So the current state is that JIT provisioning exists but it's kind of half-baked - you can provision users on first login but there's no good story around attribute mapping or role assignment from the IdP side. So what I'm proposing is we build out a proper attribute mapping UI, add support for group-based role assignment, and fix the SCIM endpoint inconsistencies that have been causing sync failures. Sofia Petrov: The sync failures specifically - do we have a sense of scope there? Because I know Ananya you've been in the weeds on that. Ananya Sharma: Yeah so there are basically three distinct failure modes. One is race conditions when you have concurrent provisioning requests, two is the SCIM patch operation not handling partial updates correctly, and three is just some gnarly edge cases around deprovisioning when a user is in multiple groups. None of them are insurmountable but they're all kind of annoying in their own way. Alex Reyes: How long are we thinking for that piece - like, just a rough estimate at this point. Ananya Sharma: If Mike and I take it together I'd say four to five weeks? We'd want to do it properly with good test coverage because the last thing we need is a reliability issue on top of everything the Detect outage already stirred up in terms of customer trust. Mike Romano: Yeah that's a fair point. The March outage definitely put everyone a bit more on edge about stability. I think that's actually - it's a good forcing function for us to be really disciplined about testing this quarter. Sofia Petrov: Agreed. And I think the customers who were affected by Detect are going to be watching us closely, so any Identity work we ship needs to feel rock solid. Alex Reyes: Okay so let's pencil in JIT and SCIM as weeks one through five roughly. Jordan, for the attribute mapping UI - have you had a chance to look at any of the existing flows? Because I know there's some legacy stuff in there. Jordan Whitfield: I have, yeah, and honestly it's - it's not terrible but it's also not great. The configuration screens feel like they were designed for an engineer rather than an IT admin, which is probably accurate. I've started sketching out a redesigned attribute mapping flow that uses a more visual drag-and-drop approach and gives you inline validation so you can see if your mappings are going to work before you save. Ananya Sharma: Oh that inline validation piece is really smart, because right now you basically have to save, trigger a test login, see that it broke, go back and try to figure out what happened. It's a terrible loop. Jordan Whitfield: Right, exactly! And it generates a disproportionate number of support tickets because people just - they don't know what they did wrong. So if we can surface that feedback in the moment it should meaningfully reduce support load too. Alex Reyes: Love it. Okay, adaptive MFA policies - Sofia, this is yours I think. Sofia Petrov: Yeah so the vision here is moving away from static MFA rules - like, everyone in this role gets MFA - toward something that's context-aware. So you'd factor in things like login location, device posture, time of day, whether it's an unusual access pattern. And based on that you can either prompt for MFA, step up authentication, or in low-risk scenarios maybe let it through without friction. Mike Romano: That's a big feature though, right? Like, are we scoping the full adaptive engine or is this a first iteration? Sofia Petrov: Definitely first iteration. I'm thinking we start with location and device posture as the two signal inputs, build the policy engine to be extensible so we can add more signals later, and ship that as a beta in Q2. Full GA with more signals would be Q3. Jordan Whitfield: That's a really sensible scope. And I think shipping it as beta is smart - we can get real customer feedback on the policy configuration experience before we commit to the full design. Alex Reyes: Yeah and honestly from a competitive standpoint this is overdue. SentinelShield has had something like this for a while and we keep getting asked about it in enterprise deals. Ananya Sharma: Ugh, yeah. Every time SentinelShield comes up in a deal it's like - okay, what's their talking point this time. But I do think our implementation can be more tightly integrated with the rest of the platform, which is a real differentiator. Alex Reyes: That's exactly the angle. Like, the fact that adaptive MFA signals can feed into the Identity audit trail and then surface in Comply reports - that's something SentinelShield can't do because they don't have the compliance layer. Mike Romano: Okay so then the audit trail - this is the one I'm most excited about personally. Can we talk through what the data model looks like? Because I want to make sure we're designing this in a way that Comply can actually consume it cleanly. Ananya Sharma: Yeah absolutely. So the idea is that every significant Identity event - login, logout, MFA challenge, provisioning change, role assignment, policy update - gets written to a structured event log with a consistent schema. And then we expose that via an internal API that Comply can query when it's generating reports. Sofia Petrov: And the Comply team is on board with this? Like, have you guys talked to them? Alex Reyes: I had a quick chat with Priya on the Comply team last week, yeah. She was really enthusiastic about it. Apparently identity access events are one of the biggest gaps in what they can currently include in SOC 2 reports, so this would actually unlock a lot for their customers too. Jordan Whitfield: That's great to hear. I think cross-team stuff like this is where the platform story really shines and it's something we should be doing more of in general. Alex Reyes: Agreed. Okay so - I think we have a pretty solid shape for Q2. JIT and SCIM improvements, adaptive MFA beta, Identity audit trail. Mike, do you want to take a first pass at breaking these down into epics in Jira before our next planning session? Mike Romano: Yeah I can do that by end of week. I'll also flag any dependencies I see on shared infrastructure so we can get those on the radar early. Alex Reyes: Perfect. And Jordan - are you good to share the attribute mapping designs in Figma this week so the team can give feedback async? Jordan Whitfield: Absolutely, I'll post the link in the Identity channel tomorrow morning. I'm really happy with where it's heading and I want everyone's eyes on it before I get too attached to any particular direction. Alex Reyes: Ha, the designer's curse. Okay, I think that covers everything - honestly this was one of the more energizing planning sessions we've had in a while. I feel good about where we're headed. Ananya Sharma: Yeah, same. Q2 is going to be a good one. Sofia Petrov: Alright, thanks everyone. Talk soon.
topics: roadmap planning, identity & access management, scim / provisioning, adaptive mfa, compliance integration, competitive landscape
action_items: Mike Romano: Break Q2 roadmap themes (JIT/SCIM, adaptive MFA, audit trail) into epics in Jira and flag shared infrastructure dependencies by end of week | Jordan Whitfield: Share redesigned attribute mapping designs in Figma in the Identity channel by tomorrow morning for async team feedback | Ananya Sharma: Collaborate with Mike Romano on JIT provisioning and SCIM improvements, targeting a four-to-five week timeline with strong test coverage | Alex Reyes: Follow up with Priya on the Comply team to formalize cross-team alignment on the Identity audit trail API integration

title: Support Case #5889 - Ridgeline Logistics Detect Latency Issues
summary: Priya Patel from Aegis support contacted Paula Schneider of Ridgeline (a manufacturing/logistics company) regarding a multi-day alert latency issue with the Aegis Detect product. Priya confirmed the problem was caused by a cascading failure in Aegis's event processing pipeline, not anything on the customer's side, and apologized for the lack of proactive communication. Paula expressed concern about the security gap created by hour-long alert delays across their OT and manufacturing environments, and noted potential SLA violations and cyber insurance reporting requirements. Priya committed to a two-hour written update with fix timeline and backfill status, and offered to involve the account manager for remediation and service credit discussions.
transcript_text: Priya Patel: Hi Paula, thanks for jumping on the call, this is Priya Patel from Aegis support - I'm the team lead on your case, case number 5889. Paula Schneider: Yeah, hi Priya. Thanks for getting back to me. I've been waiting on this for - honestly it's been a couple of days now and we're not in a great spot. Priya Patel: I completely understand, and I apologize for the delay on our end. I've been reviewing the case notes and I want to make sure I fully understand what you're seeing. Can you walk me through the issue from your perspective? Paula Schneider: Sure. So, we're in manufacturing, right, we've got a lot of OT systems, warehouse management, fleet tracking - a pretty broad attack surface. And we rely heavily on Aegis Detect to give us real-time visibility into what's happening across those environments. Priya Patel: Right, right. Paula Schneider: And starting - I want to say Monday, maybe Sunday night - we started noticing that alerts are coming in with a significant lag. Priya Patel: Yeah, I hear you, an hour of latency on threat alerts is - that's a serious problem. I'm not going to sugarcoat that. Paula Schneider: And what's frustrating is we didn't get any notification from Aegis about a known issue or anything. I had my team spending two days thinking it was something on our side, misconfiguration, network issue - we went through all of it. Priya Patel: That is - yeah, I'm really sorry about that. And that's actually directly relevant to what I want to talk to you about today. So, I do need to be transparent with you about something. Paula Schneider: Okay... Priya Patel: We have been dealing with an incident on our end - specifically in the Detect event processing pipeline. There was a cascading failure that started affecting event ingestion, and it resulted in significant delays across, um, a subset of our customer environments. Ridgeline is one of them. Paula Schneider: So this is - this is an Aegis-side issue. It's not us. Priya Patel: Correct. This is on our side. And I want to be clear - you should have received proactive communication about this and you didn't, and that's a failure on our part. I'm genuinely sorry for that. Paula Schneider: I mean, Priya, I - okay. I appreciate you being straight with me but this is pretty bad. We're a logistics and manufacturing company, we've got operational technology on the floor, we've got systems that if something gets through undetected because our monitoring is delayed by an hour- Priya Patel: Absolutely, I understand the stakes. Can I ask - during this window, do you have any secondary monitoring in place, like a SIEM or anything that's been catching events that Detect was missing? Paula Schneider: We have a LogVault instance but it doesn't have the same coverage, especially not on the endpoint side. So no, we don't have full coverage. That's why we pay for Detect. Priya Patel: Understood. Okay. So let me tell you where we are from a resolution standpoint. The root cause has been identified - it was essentially a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer. Our engineering team is actively deploying a fix, which includes redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern to prevent this kind of cascading failure from happening again. Paula Schneider: Okay. And when is that fix going out? Priya Patel: The fix is being rolled out now. I don't have a precise ETA to give you right this minute but we're talking hours, not days. I can commit to getting you a status update within the next two hours with a hard timeline. Paula Schneider: Hours. Okay. I mean - and what about the events that were delayed? Are we going to get backfill on those or are those just gone? Priya Patel: That's a really important question and I want to give you an accurate answer rather than guess. The events are queued - they're not lost - but some of the time-sensitive context on those alerts may be degraded. I need to confirm with our engineering team exactly what the backfill situation looks like for your tenant specifically. Can I get back to you on that in the same two-hour update? Paula Schneider: Yeah, I need that answer. Because if we've had a gap in coverage for four days and we don't know what was missed - that's something I'm going to have to report internally and potentially to our cyber insurance carrier. Priya Patel: Completely valid. And I'll make sure we give you the full picture so you have what you need for any internal reporting. On that note, would it be helpful if I also looped in your account manager to discuss - you know, once this is resolved - what remediation looks like from a business standpoint? Service credits, that kind of conversation. Paula Schneider: Yes. I mean, yes, that conversation needs to happen. We're - look, I'm not trying to be difficult, I actually like the Detect product when it works. But this is a significant breach of the SLA as far as I'm concerned. Priya Patel: I think that's a fair characterization and I'm not going to push back on that. We'll get your account manager involved and make sure that conversation happens. In the meantime, is there anything else I can do right now - additional logging access, a direct line to our on-call engineer - anything that would help you feel more in control of the situation while we're in this window? Paula Schneider: Actually yeah - can you set me up with a direct escalation path? Like if something happens in the next few hours and I need to reach someone, I don't want to go through the general support queue. Priya Patel: Absolutely. I'm going to give you my direct line right now, and I'll also send you the on-call bridge number for our Detect engineering team. You call either of those and you'll get a response in under ten minutes. Paula Schneider: Okay. That's - that's helpful, thank you. Priya Patel: And Paula, I want to reiterate - this situation is not okay, and I'm not treating it as business as usual. You'll have a written update from me in two hours with the fix timeline, the backfill status, and a summary of the incident for your records. Does that work? Paula Schneider: Yeah, that works. I'll be watching for it. And Priya - I do appreciate you being upfront about it being on your end. I've dealt with vendors who will dance around that for a week, so. Priya Patel: Of course. title: INCIDENT: Detect Pipeline Failure - War Room
summary: A critical outage call was convened to address a complete failure of the Detect event processing pipeline that began around 9:14 AM Pacific. The ingestion pipeline's single primary node hit a memory ceiling and crashed due to lack of redundancy, a known tech debt issue that had been flagged but not prioritized. The outage went unannounced on the status page for approximately 90 minutes, causing enterprise customers including Harmon Financial and TerraLogix to escalate, with some customers mistakenly fearing a security breach. The team aligned on immediate actions: a stopgap fix involving a secondary node and temporary load balancer, a public customer statement clarifying there was no breach, and a post-mortem timeline, while acknowledging that 30-40% of event data during the outage window may be unrecoverable.
transcript_text: Brian Cho: Okay, I think we've got everyone. Tom, you there? Brian's on, Ananya's on - Sofia, can you confirm? Sofia Petrov: Yeah I'm here, sorry, I was just pulling up the dashboards. Brian Cho: Good. Okay, let's not waste time. Tom, do you want to kick us off or should I? Tom Bradley: I'll start. So, uh, at approximately 9:14 AM Pacific we started seeing alerts - or rather, the absence of alerts - from the Detect event processing pipeline. The ingestion layer just... stopped. No events coming through, no throughput, and the monitoring didn't catch it immediately which is its own problem we're going to talk about. Brian Cho: When you say the monitoring didn't catch it - are we talking about our internal alerting or the customer-facing status stuff? Tom Bradley: Both, honestly. Internal alerting had a lag, and the status page wasn't updated until... Ananya, when did we actually post to the status page? Ananya Sharma: It was around 10:40, so that's - yeah, that's about an hour and a half after the initial failure. Tom Bradley: Ananya, I appreciate you saying that but that's a process failure, not a you failure. We shouldn't have a single person making the call on when to post. That's a systemic issue. Brian Cho: I mean - I agree with that, but we can talk process later. Right now I've got customers blowing up my team's queue and I need to understand what actually happened technically so I can give my support engineers something to say. Tom Bradley: Right, yeah. Sofia, you want to walk through the technical failure? You were in the weeds on this from the start. Sofia Petrov: Sure. So the event ingestion pipeline - basically it's a single primary node that handles all incoming threat event data before it fans out to the processing workers. That node hit a memory ceiling, started throwing OOM errors, and because we don't have a circuit breaker or any redundancy on that node, it just cascaded. Everything downstream starved out. Brian Cho: Wait, so there's literally one node doing all of the ingestion? That's... okay I'm not an engineer but that sounds like a really bad design. Tom Bradley: It's not ideal, no. It's - look, it's a legacy architecture decision and it's been on the roadmap to address. We just hadn't prioritized it. Ananya Sharma: It was flagged in the Q4 tech debt review, Tom. I flagged it. Tom Bradley: I know you did. And I'm not - look, this is not the time for that conversation. Yes, it was flagged, yes, it should have been prioritized, and now we're dealing with the consequences. Brian Cho: How long until that stopgap is live? Sofia Petrov: Best case? Another hour, maybe ninety minutes. But I don't want to commit to that publicly yet. Tom Bradley: Brian, what are you hearing from customers? Like, who's screaming the loudest right now? Brian Cho: I mean, everyone in the enterprise tier is screaming. We've got - let me just look at my notes here - Harmon Financial has escalated twice, they're threatening to call their account manager directly. TerraLogix is asking whether this is a breach, which is a great question to get at 10 in the morning. And we've got at least a dozen mid-market customers who are just, you know, sitting there with a broken security product and no visibility into their threat environment. Tom Bradley: TerraLogix thinks it's a breach? We need to get ahead of that immediately. Brian Cho: I know, I've got one of my senior support reps on the phone with them right now. But Tom, I need an actual statement I can give customers about what happened. Something honest that doesn't make us look like we don't know what we're doing. Tom Bradley: The problem is we're still root-causing. I don't want to put out a statement that's wrong. Brian Cho: Tom, we know enough. It's a pipeline failure. It's not a breach. Sofia, while I'm doing that - can you document what you know so far about the failure sequence? We're going to need a timeline for the post-mortem. Sofia Petrov: Already started. Brian Cho: Oh, that's - yeah, that's going to be a very bad conversation to have with customers in regulated industries. Are we sure about that? Is there any way to replay the events? Ananya Sharma: We have some buffering at the source layer but it's limited. I'd say we can recover maybe sixty to seventy percent of what was lost. The rest is... gone. Brian Cho: Okay.
