title: Support Case #2638 - Pineridge Systems CloudPrime S3 Backup Connector
summary: Priya from Aegis Cloud Security support and senior engineer Sarah Chen joined a call with Yuki Tanaka, Security Lead at Pineridge, to troubleshoot a failing CloudPrime S3 backup connector issue (Case 2638). Yuki reported that backup jobs were failing with a 403 error since the previous Thursday, despite no known IAM permission changes. Sarah identified two likely causes: a misconfigured connector endpoint (using the generic s3.amazonaws.com instead of the region-specific us-west-2 endpoint) and potentially restrictive CloudPrime Service Control Policies updated during a routine policy review around the same time. Yuki updated the endpoint setting live on the call and agreed to test the backup job, check SCP policies with their CloudPrime admin, and share CloudTrail logs with the Aegis team.
transcript_text: Priya Patel: Hi, this is Priya from Aegis Cloud Security support, I have Sarah on the line with me as well - she's one of our senior engineers on the Protect side. Am I speaking with Yuki? Yuki Tanaka: Yeah, hi, Yuki Tanaka here, Security Lead at Pineridge. Thanks for getting back to me, I know I submitted the case like yesterday afternoon so I appreciate the quick turnaround. Priya Patel: Of course, yeah. So we've pulled up Case 2638 - the CloudPrime S3 backup connector issue. Before Sarah digs in, do you want to just give us a quick rundown of what you're seeing on your end? Yuki Tanaka: Sure, yeah. So basically, we set up the S3 connector in Aegis Protect about three weeks ago, it was working fine initially. But starting around, I want to say, last Thursday or Friday, we started seeing backup jobs failing partway through. They initiate, they run for a bit, and then just... stop. No completion, no error that makes a ton of sense. Sarah Chen: Okay, and when you say no error that makes sense - what is the error message actually showing? Like is it a timeout, a permissions thing, or something else? Yuki Tanaka: It says - let me actually pull it up - it says, uh, 'connector write operation terminated, upstream response code 403.' But here's the thing, the IAM permissions haven't changed. Like, nothing on our CloudPrime side changed that week. Priya Patel: Got it, a 403. Yeah that's a good starting point. Sarah, do you want to walk through what that typically maps to in the connector? Sarah Chen: Yeah, so a 403 from the S3 connector can actually come from a few different places, it's not always what it looks like on the surface. The first thing I'd want to rule out is whether the IAM role that Aegis Protect is assuming has the right combination of permissions - specifically s3:PutObject, s3:GetBucketLocation, and then also the bucket policy itself. Sometimes people set up the IAM role correctly but the bucket policy has a deny statement that overrides it. Yuki Tanaka: Okay, so the bucket policy can override the IAM role permissions - yeah, that's a good call, I can check that. We were pretty careful when we set this up but it's possible something got changed on the bucket side. Sarah Chen: Exactly, yeah. And the other thing - do you happen to know if the S3 bucket has any VPC endpoint policies or SCPs at the organization level? Like CloudPrime Service Control Policies? Those can also silently block writes even when IAM looks clean. Yuki Tanaka: Hmm. SCPs... we do have some org-level policies but I'd have to check with our CloudPrime admin to see if anything changed there. We had a routine policy review around that time actually, now that I think about it. Priya Patel: That's actually really useful context, yeah. That timing aligns with when you started seeing the failures, so it's worth checking whether any of those policy changes could have inadvertently restricted the role Aegis is using. Yuki Tanaka: Yeah, I can loop in our CloudPrime admin after this call. Is there a specific role name or ARN I should reference? I want to make sure they're looking at the right thing. Sarah Chen: Yes, so in your Aegis Protect console, if you go to Integrations and then Connector Settings for the S3 connector, you'll see the IAM role ARN that Aegis is using listed under Authentication Details. That's the one your admin should be checking. Yuki Tanaka: Okay, let me - hold on, I actually have the console open. Integrations... Connector Settings... yeah, okay I see it. The ARN is there, I can copy that out. Sarah Chen: Perfect. And while you're in there, can you also check what region the connector is configured to target? The reason I ask is - we've seen a specific edge case where if the bucket is in one region but the connector config still has the default us-east-1 endpoint, it can cause issues that surface as 403s rather than the more obvious region mismatch error. Yuki Tanaka: Oh interesting. Uh, the bucket is in us-west-2. And the connector says... endpoint is set to s3.amazonaws.com, no region specified explicitly. Sarah Chen: Yeah, so that could actually be a contributing factor. The generic s3.amazonaws.com endpoint will route to us-east-1 by default, and depending on your bucket's config - especially if you have bucket policies that restrict access to specific regions or VPCs - that cross-region request can get blocked. Yuki Tanaka: So I should change that endpoint to the region-specific one? Like s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com? Sarah Chen: Exactly, yeah, that would be the recommended change. You'd want to update that in the connector settings and then re-test a backup job. It's a pretty quick change to make. Yuki Tanaka: Okay, that makes sense. And should I do that before or after I check the SCP stuff with the CloudPrime admin? Like what order would you tackle these? Priya Patel: I'd actually do the endpoint fix first since you can do that right now without needing anyone else, and then run a test job. If it still fails, then you have a cleaner picture to bring to your CloudPrime admin - you can rule out the endpoint issue and focus the conversation on the policy side. Yuki Tanaka: That's a good approach, yeah. Okay, I'm going to make that endpoint change now actually, while we're on the call. Bear with me a second. Sarah Chen: Take your time. Yuki Tanaka: Alright, updated. Saved. So I'll kick off a test backup - it's going to take a few minutes to run. I might not know the result before we hang up but at least I know what to look for. Priya Patel: That's totally fine. We'll keep the case open and you can reply directly to the case email with the results. If it still 403s after the endpoint fix, Sarah can pull the connector logs from our side and do a deeper trace. Sarah Chen: Yeah, and if you want to share the CloudTrail logs from your CloudPrime account for that time window, that would help a lot too - it'll show exactly what API call was being made and why it was denied. Yuki Tanaka: Yep, I can pull CloudTrail logs. We have a 30-day retention window so that's no problem. I'll grab the logs from last Thursday through today and attach them to the case. Priya Patel: Perfect, that would be really helpful. Okay, so to summarize where we are - you're testing the endpoint fix first, and then pending that result, you'll check with your CloudPrime admin about the SCP policy review and share CloudTrail logs with us. Does that all sound right? Yuki Tanaka: Yeah, that's the plan. One other thing - is there any way to configure Aegis Protect to retry backup jobs automatically if they fail? Right now it seems like it just stops and I have to manually re-trigger it. Sarah Chen: Yes, there is actually. In the connector settings, under Advanced Options, there's a Retry Policy section - you can configure the number of retry attempts and the backoff interval. It's not enabled by default so it might just be turned off in your config. Yuki Tanaka: Oh, I didn't even know that was there. I'll look for that when I'm in the settings. That'll help in the meantime even if the root cause isn't fully resolved yet. Priya Patel: Yeah, definitely. It won't fix the underlying issue but it should reduce the manual overhead while we sort this out. Yuki Tanaka: Alright, I think I have enough to work with. I appreciate you both jumping on this - Sarah, the region endpoint thing especially, I wouldn't have caught that on my own. Sarah Chen: Happy to help. It's one of those things that trips people up because the error message doesn't point directly at it. Hopefully that's the main culprit. Priya Patel: We'll keep an eye on the case and respond as soon as you send over the test results and the CloudTrail logs. Shouldn't be more than a business day turnaround from us. Yuki Tanaka: Works for me. Thanks again, talk soon. Priya Patel: Thanks Yuki, take care.
topics: aws s3 connector, backup failure, 403 error, iam permissions, service control policies, connector configuration
action_items: Yuki Tanaka: Run a test backup job after updating the S3 connector endpoint to s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com and report results back via the case email | Yuki Tanaka: Loop in CloudPrime admin to review SCPs and bucket policies referencing the IAM role ARN found in Aegis Protect Connector Settings | Yuki Tanaka: Pull CloudTrail logs from last Thursday through today and attach them to Case 2638 | Yuki Tanaka: Enable the Retry Policy in the S3 connector Advanced Options to reduce manual re-triggering of failed jobs

title: Detect Outage - Post-Incident Review
summary: Tom Bradley led a post-incident review of the Detect outage from March 10th, which caused approximately six hours of no threat monitoring for customers due to a cascading failure in the event ingestion pipeline caused by a single point of failure. Tom explained the deployed fixes including redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern, while Megan noted upcoming product improvements including a status indicator and a potential heartbeat alert feature. Diana highlighted customer concerns about lack of visibility, particularly among enterprise and mid-renewal accounts, and the team aligned on next steps for customer communications. Key action items include Tom delivering a formal post-incident report, Megan evaluating roadmap prioritization, and Diana coordinating customer calls.
transcript_text: Tom Bradley: Alright, I think we're all here - let me just pull up my notes real quick. Diana Reeves: Yeah I'm here, go ahead. Megan Lawson: Same, I've got about twenty minutes before my next thing so let's try to be efficient. Tom Bradley: Okay so - this is the post-incident review for the Detect outage, March 10th through the 18th, well, the outage itself was March 10th, we're just closing it out today. Diana Reeves: Right, and just to frame this - I had a lot of customer conversations this week, so I want to make sure we're aligned on what we're telling them going forward. Tom Bradley: Totally fair, we'll get there. So let me just walk through the timeline and root cause first, and then we can talk about the fix and the comms piece. Megan Lawson: Sounds good. Tom Bradley: So the incident started around 2:14 AM Pacific on March 10th. The event ingestion pipeline - this is the core processing layer that pulls in telemetry from customer environments - it had a cascading failure. Basically one node went down, and because we had a single point of failure in that ingestion layer, the whole pipeline backed up and eventually stopped processing. Megan Lawson: And that's what caused the six-hour window with no visibility? Tom Bradley: Correct. For approximately six hours, customers were not getting threat monitoring alerts. Events were being generated on their end, but we weren't processing them, so nothing was surfacing in the Detect dashboard. Diana Reeves: Six hours is - I mean, that's a long time for a security product. Some of my customers were pretty upset, understandably. Tom Bradley: I know, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it - this was a significant failure. The good news is we've done a full root cause analysis and the fix is already deployed. Diana Reeves: Can you explain the fix at a level I can actually relay to customers? Like, not super deep in the weeds but enough that it's credible. Tom Bradley: Yeah, so there are two main things. First, we've added redundant processing nodes to the event ingestion layer. So if one node fails, traffic automatically routes to backup nodes - no more single point of failure. Second, we've implemented what's called a circuit breaker pattern, which basically means if one part of the pipeline starts to degrade, it isolates that failure instead of letting it cascade through the whole system. Diana Reeves: Okay, that's actually pretty explainable. Redundancy and failure isolation - I can work with that. Megan Lawson: And just to add to that - from a product standpoint, we're also looking at adding a visible status indicator in the Detect UI so customers can see in real-time whether the pipeline is healthy. That's not shipped yet but it's on the near-term roadmap. Diana Reeves: When's that realistically landing? Megan Lawson: Uh, we're targeting end of April, but I don't want to over-promise. It depends on a few other things in the queue. Diana Reeves: Can we at least tell customers it's in progress? Because right now they're asking 'how do I even know if Detect is working' and I don't have a great answer. Megan Lawson: Yeah, absolutely tell them it's in progress. That's a real commitment, end of April is the target. Tom Bradley: I do want to flag one thing - and this is a bit of a sore spot for me - our alerting on the pipeline health itself was inadequate. We didn't catch this until customers started reaching out. That's not acceptable. Megan Lawson: Yeah, how did we find out? Was it a customer ticket? Tom Bradley: It was - one of Diana's team's accounts, actually. Flagged that they hadn't seen any alerts in a few hours and opened a support ticket. Diana Reeves: Yeah, that was Thornfield Financial. They've got a pretty attentive security team, fortunately. Tom Bradley: So we are adding internal monitoring on the ingestion pipeline itself - not just the output but the pipeline health metrics. That's already in place as of this week. Diana Reeves: Good. I think one of the things I keep hearing from customers is - they feel like they're flying blind sometimes with Detect. And this incident kind of reinforced that. I don't say that to be harsh, I just think it's worth naming. Tom Bradley: No, I - yeah. I hear that. And honestly some of it is a product maturity issue, some of it is infrastructure. Megan, is there anything we can prioritize in the short term to help with that visibility gap beyond the status indicator? Megan Lawson: We've been talking about a heartbeat alert feature - basically Detect would proactively notify customers if it stops receiving telemetry from their environment for more than, say, fifteen minutes. That would at least give them a signal on their end. Diana Reeves: Oh, that would be huge actually. Can we pull that forward? Megan Lawson: Let me take a look at the roadmap this week. I think there's room to move it up, but I need to see what it bumps. I'll come back to both of you by end of week. Tom Bradley: Okay. And on the customer communication side - Diana, what's the current state? Did we send a post-incident report to affected accounts? Diana Reeves: We sent an initial communication on March 10th when the incident was resolved, but we have not sent a formal PIR document yet. I've been waiting on the root cause writeup from engineering. Tom Bradley: Yeah that's on me, I'll have that to you by tomorrow morning. Full technical summary, the fix, and what we're doing to prevent recurrence. Diana Reeves: Okay, and then I'll adapt it into customer-facing language and get it out by end of week. Some of our enterprise accounts are going to want a call, not just an email - particularly the ones who are mid-renewal. Megan Lawson: Do you want me or Tom on any of those calls, or are you handling them with your CSMs? Diana Reeves: Probably Tom for anyone who wants a technical deep-dive. I'll flag the specific accounts and we can coordinate. I don't think it'll be more than three or four. Tom Bradley: Yeah, I'm available for that. Just loop me in with at least a day's notice if you can. Diana Reeves: Will do. Alright, I think I have what I need. Tom - PIR doc tomorrow, and Megan - roadmap check by end of week on the heartbeat feature? Tom Bradley: Correct. Megan Lawson: Yep, I've got it. Diana Reeves: Okay, good. Thanks both - let's close this one out.
topics: outage post-mortem, infrastructure reliability, customer communication, product visibility, roadmap prioritization, renewal risk
action_items: Tom Bradley: Deliver the full technical PIR document (root cause, fix, and prevention measures) to Diana by tomorrow morning | Diana Reeves: Adapt PIR into customer-facing language and send to affected accounts by end of week, coordinating calls with enterprise and mid-renewal accounts | Megan Lawson: Review roadmap by end of week to assess feasibility of pulling forward the heartbeat alert feature | Tom Bradley: Make himself available for technical deep-dive calls with up to three or four enterprise customers flagged by Diana

title: Identity Team - Sprint Retro
summary: The team held a sprint 22 retrospective covering the period of March 14-27 for the Identity team. The Detect outage on the 10th impacted sprint capacity, causing two tickets (MFA enforcement policy UI and SSO session timeout configuration) to slip into sprint 23. Completed work included SCIM provisioning bug fixes, SSO metadata refresh refactor, and partial IAM role hierarchy implementation. The team identified estimation issues with the SSO refactor, a test environment credential delay, and an upcoming Comply v2 integration as key concerns heading into sprint 23.
transcript_text: Nina Kowalski: Alright, I think we're all here - let me just pull up the retro board real quick. Tyler Washington: Yeah I'm here, just give me one second, my Slack is going crazy right now. Sofia Petrov: Same, the Detect outage stuff is still causing a lot of noise even two weeks later. Mike Romano: Yeah, let's try to stay focused on Identity sprint stuff today though - we can't let the Detect fallout bleed into every single retro. Nina Kowalski: Agreed, okay so - I have the board up. We finished sprint twenty-two, March fourteenth through the twenty-seventh. Let me walk through what we had in scope. Sofia Petrov: Before you do that, can we just acknowledge that the Detect outage on the tenth actually did affect our sprint? Like two of our tickets got deprioritized because engineers were pulled for the all-hands incident response. Mike Romano: That's fair, yeah. I was pulled in for almost a full day on the fourteenth doing coordination. Nina Kowalski: Okay, let's capture that as a blocker then. I'll add it to the retro notes - external incident impacted sprint capacity. That's a legit call-out. Tyler Washington: Yeah and for the record, the two tickets that slipped were the MFA enforcement policy UI work and the SSO session timeout configuration. Both moved to sprint twenty-three. Nina Kowalski: Right, okay. So let me just go through what we did complete - the SCIM provisioning bug fixes, that was four story points. The SSO metadata refresh refactor, that was eight points. And the initial IAM role hierarchy work, that was three points, partially done. Sofia Petrov: The IAM role hierarchy work is like, technically it's partially done but it's more like sixty percent done. The remaining forty percent is the gnarly part. Mike Romano: Can you say more about that? What's the gnarly part specifically? Sofia Petrov: So the inheritance logic for nested role groups - when you have, like, a role that inherits from two parents that have conflicting permission sets, we don't have a good resolution strategy defined yet. I started prototyping something but it needs design review. Mike Romano: Okay, that's actually a bigger conversation. Can we schedule a separate design session for that? I don't want to try to hash it out in retro. Sofia Petrov: Yeah definitely. I can put something on the calendar for early next week, maybe Tuesday? Tyler Washington: Tuesday works for me. Nina Kowalski: Okay I'll grab time. Back to retro - what went well this sprint? Anyone want to start? Sofia Petrov: Um, I thought the SCIM work went really smoothly. Tyler, you basically owned that end to end and it was clean. Tyler Washington: Thanks, yeah I mean the bugs were pretty well-documented so it was mostly just methodical work. Nothing too heroic. Nina Kowalski: Still, it shipped on time, no regressions in QA, which - honestly that's not always the case with provisioning stuff. I want to call that out as a win. Mike Romano: Agreed. What else went well... I think our standup cadence was better this sprint. People were actually updating tickets before standup instead of during. Nina Kowalski: Yeah that was a thing we flagged last retro so good to see it actually stick. Tyler Washington: Okay what didn't go well, or what do we want to improve. I'll just go first - I think our story point estimates for the SSO refactor were off. We said eight points, it ended up being closer to twelve or thirteen hours of actual work. Sofia Petrov: Yeah the metadata refresh logic had a bunch of edge cases around certificate rotation that we didn't scope properly. Mike Romano: That's an estimation problem or a requirements problem? Like, were the edge cases knowable upfront or did they surface during implementation? Sofia Petrov: Honestly, a little of both. Some of them we probably should have caught in grooming, but a couple were genuinely discovered mid-implementation. Mike Romano: I'd say we should add a checklist item in grooming for cert rotation scenarios specifically. We've been bitten by that in Identity more than once. Tyler Washington: That's a good action item. Nina, can you add that to the grooming template? Nina Kowalski: On it. Anything else for the what-didn't-go-well section? I also want to flag - QA had some delays because I didn't get the test environment credentials refreshed before the sprint started. That's on me, I'll make sure to do that as part of sprint kickoff going forward. Tyler Washington: Appreciate you flagging that. It did cause like a day of delay on my end when I was trying to validate the SCIM fixes. Nina Kowalski: Yeah, sorry about that. Okay - let's talk about sprint twenty-three planning. title: Aegis / Axiom Labs - Multi-Year Renewal
summary: Aisha Johnson (CSM) held a renewal planning call with Ryan Caldwell and Mina Joshi ahead of their end-of-May contract anniversary. The customer expressed strong overall satisfaction with the platform, particularly with the Identity and Comply v2 modules, while acknowledging the March Detect outage was serious but handled well. Aisha presented a three-year renewal proposal featuring an elastic seat model and enterprise API tier, and the conversation surfaced a previously unknown streaming endpoint that could solve a latency issue in the customer's internal alerting pipeline. The call concluded positively with clear next steps including a formal proposal, a technical deep dive, and looping in finance and legal for final approval.
transcript_text: Aisha Johnson: Alright, I think we're all here - Ryan, Mina, good to see you both, well, hear you both I guess. Ryan Caldwell: Ha, yeah, good to hear you too Aisha, thanks for setting this up. Aisha Johnson: Of course, of course. Mina, how are you doing? I feel like the last time we actually talked was, what, the Comply v2 early access sessions back in February? Mina Joshi: Yeah, exactly, that was a fun one. I'm good though, we've been heads down on a pretty big infrastructure push but things are starting to settle a little bit. Aisha Johnson: Good to hear. Okay so, the reason we're all here - obviously the renewal is coming up, I think you're looking at end of May for the contract anniversary, so I wanted to make sure we had plenty of runway to actually have a real conversation about it rather than just firing off a DocuSign at the last minute. Ryan Caldwell: Yeah, no, we appreciate that, and honestly our intention is very much to continue - I don't think there's any ambiguity there. We've been really happy with the platform overall. Aisha Johnson: That's great to hear, and I don't want to just take that for granted either, like I genuinely want to understand what's been working and where there are gaps, because a multi-year commitment is significant and we want to earn it. Ryan Caldwell: I appreciate that framing actually. Um, I think the honest answer is - the platform has matured a lot since we first came on board, and Detect and Identity especially have become kind of foundational for us at this point. Mina Joshi: Yeah I'd second that on the Identity side, the SSO rollout we did in Q4 went really smoothly and the MFA enforcement policies have been... I mean, they've saved us a couple of headaches for sure. Aisha Johnson: That's great to hear on Identity, we've put a lot of engineering investment there in the past two quarters so that's really validating. And Detect - I do want to address the elephant in the room, which is the March outage. Ryan Caldwell: Yeah, I was going to bring that up at some point so I'm glad you're leading with it. Look, I'm not going to sugarcoat it - six hours of no threat monitoring visibility is not okay. And I think we said that very clearly at the time. But I do want to give credit where it's due, the communication from your team during that incident was actually really good. Like the status page was updating every 20-30 minutes, we got a direct call from support, that mattered. Mina Joshi: Yeah, the comms were solid. And the post-incident report that came out like five days later - super detailed, it walked through the root cause, the single point of failure in the ingestion pipeline, and then what you were doing to fix it. That's the kind of transparency that actually builds trust, you know? Aisha Johnson: I'm really glad that landed well, and I can tell you - I've seen the engineering changes firsthand, the redundant processing nodes are live, the circuit breaker pattern is in production, I was actually on a call with our infrastructure team last week and they walked me through the current architecture and it is meaningfully more resilient than it was before. Ryan Caldwell: Yeah, we've been watching the uptime since then and it's been clean, so... we're not holding a grudge. These things happen, it's how you respond that matters. Aisha Johnson: Totally agree. Okay so let me shift gears a little - I want to talk about Comply v2 because we just launched GA on April 7th and I know Mina you were in some of the early access stuff. What's your take now that it's fully out? Mina Joshi: Honestly? It's kind of a game changer for us. The on-demand SOC 2 reporting alone - like, do you know how many hours we used to spend just pulling evidence together for audits? It was painful. Aisha Johnson: I can imagine, yeah. Mina Joshi: And now it's just... you click a button essentially. The multi-framework support is really what sold us because we're dealing with SOC 2 obviously but also we have some customers that require HIPAA alignment and having that in one place rather than three different tools is huge. Aisha Johnson: Are you also using the ISO 27001 reporting or is that one you haven't gotten to yet? Ryan Caldwell: We're looking at it, we haven't started an ISO certification process yet but it's on our roadmap for 2027 and honestly knowing that it's already built into the platform means we don't have to scramble later. That's, um, that's actually a bigger deal than it might sound. Aisha Johnson: Yeah that's a really good point, and I'd love to set up a dedicated session with our compliance team to kind of do a readiness walkthrough for ISO when you're getting closer to that timeline - just so there are no surprises. Ryan Caldwell: That would be fantastic, yeah let's put that on the list. Aisha Johnson: Okay, perfect. So let's talk about the actual renewal structure. Right now you're on Protect, Detect, Comply, and Identity - all four modules. We're looking at a three-year proposal, and the numbers I'm going to share reflect a significant improvement over your current per-seat rates. Ryan Caldwell: Yeah, I saw the preview you sent over before this call and the pricing looks competitive. I did want to ask - we're expecting to grow our headcount by probably 40% over the next 18 months, is that factored in or are we going to be renegotiating seat counts constantly? Aisha Johnson: Great question, and that's actually something I wanted to address directly. We can structure this as an elastic seat model where you have a committed baseline but you can flex up without triggering a full contract renegotiation, and we true-up annually. So you're not paying for seats you don't have yet, but you also have the headroom to grow without friction. Mina Joshi: Okay that's much better than what we had before, because I think last year we had to do like two mid-year amendments and that was annoying for everybody. Aisha Johnson: Yeah, I heard about that from the account team and that's exactly the kind of thing we want to fix. Operational friction in the contract itself is a problem we can solve. Ryan Caldwell: Appreciate that. The other thing I wanted to raise - and this is more Mina's territory but I'll let her speak to it - is around API access and integrations. We've been doing a lot more custom tooling. Mina Joshi: Yeah so we've built some internal dashboards that pull from the Detect API and it's been working well but we hit some rate limits last quarter that were kind of annoying. Is there a tier or an add-on that gives us higher throughput there? Aisha Johnson: Yes, absolutely. The enterprise API tier - which honestly I should have already flagged for you, that's on me - gives you significantly higher rate limits and also access to the real-time event streaming endpoint which I think would actually be more elegant for what you're building than polling the REST API. Mina Joshi: Oh, the streaming endpoint - I didn't know that existed. That would actually solve a completely different problem we've been having with latency in our internal alerting pipeline. Aisha Johnson: Okay yeah, let's definitely get you set up with a technical deep dive on that after this call. I'll loop in one of our solutions engineers. Mina Joshi: Yes please. Ryan, we should definitely pursue that. Ryan Caldwell: Agreed. Aisha, one thing I do want to put on the table - and I want to be clear this isn't a threat, it's just due diligence - we did get outreach from SentinelShield and VaultEdge this quarter. We're not actively shopping but I want to be transparent. Aisha Johnson: I respect that, and I'd rather know than not know. Can I ask what they led with? Like what was the pitch? Ryan Caldwell: SentinelShield was mostly on price, and VaultEdge was making some noise about their compliance module. But honestly neither of them has the breadth of what Aegis is doing - the fact that Identity, Detect, Comply, and Protect are all in one platform with a single pane of glass is something we've come to really value. Fragmented tools are a nightmare. Mina Joshi: Yeah, and integration overhead is real - like we had a point solution for compliance before and the engineering time just to keep connectors working was not trivial. Aisha Johnson: That's exactly right, and I think the platform consolidation story is only going to get stronger - we have some announcements coming in Q3 that I can't get into detail on yet but I think they're going to further differentiate us, especially in the detection space. Ryan Caldwell: Okay, color me intrigued. I'll hold you to that. Aisha Johnson: Please do! Alright, so to kind of land the plane here - I'll send over the formal three-year proposal by end of next week, it'll have the elastic seat model baked in, the enterprise API tier included, and the pricing we discussed. I'll also include a proposed roadmap check-in cadence because for a three-year commitment I want us to be doing formal QBRs at minimum. Mina Joshi: That works for us. And the technical session on the streaming API, can we try to get that on the calendar for early next week? Aisha Johnson: Absolutely, I'll send a scheduling link today. And Ryan, is there anyone else on your side who should be looped into the renewal review? Legal, procurement? Ryan Caldwell: Yeah, I'll need to loop in our VP of Finance for the final sign-off on a multi-year, and our legal team will want a pass at the contract language, but that's pretty routine. I don't anticipate any major issues. Aisha Johnson: Perfect, that's totally expected. Just let me know who to include on the proposal email and I'll make sure everyone's got what they need. This has been a really good conversation, I feel like we're in a great place. Ryan Caldwell: Same. Appreciate you always being straight with us Aisha, it makes this whole process a lot easier. Aisha Johnson: That means a lot, genuinely. Okay, I'll get those next steps moving today. Talk soon, everyone!
topics: renewal, contract negotiation, api rate limits, compliance reporting, platform outage, competitive displacement
action_items: Aisha Johnson: Send formal three-year proposal with elastic seat model, enterprise API tier, and QBR cadence by end of next week | Aisha Johnson: Send scheduling link today for technical deep dive on streaming API endpoint with a solutions engineer for early next week | Aisha Johnson: Set up a dedicated ISO 27001 readiness walkthrough session with the compliance team closer to the customer's 2027 certification timeline | Ryan Caldwell: Loop in VP of Finance and legal team on the renewal proposal for final sign-off and contract language review

title: Aegis / Harborview Banking - Threat Detection Tuning
summary: Lisa Park and Kevin O'Brien from Aegis held a threat detection tuning session with Patricia Dunn (VP of Security) and Michael Russo (Compliance Officer) from Harborview Banking, who went live on Aegis Detect seven weeks ago. The primary concerns discussed were alert fatigue from false positives driven by geo-anomaly detection for multi-timezone staff, compliance coverage gaps for FFIEC/SOX/GLBA requirements, and inefficient alert routing to a single shared SOC inbox. Kevin enabled alert mode on the privileged access monitoring ruleset during the call and identified that the data retention setting needs to be updated from 90 days to at least 12 months. A follow-up working session was planned for the week of March 16th to configure trusted location profiles and work schedule profiles for the Manila team.
transcript_text: Lisa Park: Alright, I think we've got everyone on now - Patricia, Michael, can you both hear us okay? Patricia Dunn: Yep, coming through fine on my end. Michael Russo: Good here as well. Lisa Park: Perfect, great. So, um, welcome everyone - this is our threat detection tuning session for Harborview Banking. I'm Lisa Park, account manager on the Aegis side, and I've got Kevin O'Brien with me today, he's our solutions architect who's going to be doing most of the heavy lifting on the technical side of things. Kevin O'Brien: Hey everyone, Kevin here. Looking forward to getting into the weeds on the Detect configuration with you all today. Patricia Dunn: Thanks for having us. I'm Patricia Dunn, VP of Security here at Harborview. And I've got Michael Russo on with me, he's our compliance officer - we brought him in because a lot of what we're trying to tune around has some compliance implications that we want to make sure we're capturing. Kevin O'Brien: That makes a lot of sense, actually. Good thinking bringing Michael in. We find that the compliance angle and the detection angle overlap more than people expect, especially in financial services. Michael Russo: Yeah, exactly. That's kind of been our experience too over the years. You get siloed and then you're doing double the work. Lisa Park: Totally. So, um, before we jump in - Kevin, do you want to just set the agenda for today real quick so Patricia and Michael know what to expect? Kevin O'Brien: Sure, yeah. So the plan for today is - we want to walk through your current Aegis Detect configuration, understand what alert thresholds you have set, talk about any false positive pain points you're running into, and then start mapping out what a tuned detection profile looks like for a financial services environment like yours. We'll also touch on your event source integrations, because that's usually where a lot of the noise comes from in the early onboarding phase. Patricia Dunn: That sounds right to us. The false positive issue is honestly top of mind right now. Our SOC team is getting fatigued - they're seeing a ton of alerts that aren't actionable and it's starting to affect response times on the stuff that actually matters. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, that's a really common pattern we see, especially in the first sixty to ninety days of a Detect deployment. The out-of-the-box sensitivity settings are intentionally broad - we'd rather you see too much than miss something - but you're right that it creates alert fatigue if we don't tune it down based on your specific environment. Lisa Park: How long have you been live on Detect at this point, Patricia? I want to make sure I'm thinking about the right baseline. Patricia Dunn: We went live, uh, about seven weeks ago. So mid-January, roughly. Lisa Park: Okay, seven weeks, got it. So you're past the initial noise spike but still well within the range where tuning is going to make a big difference. Kevin, does that track with what you're seeing in the tenant config? Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, let me - I'm pulling up the Harborview tenant right now. Give me one second. Okay, so I can see your event sources - looks like you've got your CloudPrime CloudTrail integrated, Azure AD sign-in logs, and your on-prem SIEM feed coming in. Is that the full picture or are there other sources we haven't connected yet? Patricia Dunn: That's the primary set, yes. We do have a Irongate firewall log feed that we were hoping to get in there as well, but we haven't prioritized it yet. It's been on the list. Kevin O'Brien: Okay, noted. The firewall logs will actually help a lot with context enrichment, so that's worth getting on the roadmap sooner rather than later. But let's not get sidetracked - we can come back to that. Agreed. So on the false positives - can you give me some examples of the alert types that are generating the most noise? Like, is it lateral movement rules, authentication anomalies, data exfil detections - what's hitting your team hardest? Patricia Dunn: It's predominantly the authentication anomaly rules. We have a large number of staff who work across multiple time zones - we've got teams in New York, Chicago, and then we have some offshore ops in Manila - and Detect keeps flagging logins from different geographic locations as suspicious. Which, you know, it's technically doing its job, but it's not... it's not calibrated to our reality. Michael Russo: Right, and from a compliance standpoint, every one of those false positive alerts has to be reviewed and documented. So it's not just a SOC fatigue issue, it's actually creating a paper trail of noise that we have to manage through as well. Lisa Park: Yeah, that's a really good point, Michael. We don't always hear that framing but it makes total sense in a regulated environment. Okay, so on the geo-anomaly detection - Kevin, walk them through how we'd handle that. Kevin O'Brien: Sure. So within Detect, there are a couple of levers here. The first is what we call trusted location profiles - you can define named network zones or geographic regions that are considered baseline for your organization. So if you tag New York, Chicago, and Manila as your standard operating locations, any authentication from those areas will be weighted differently in the risk scoring engine. It won't suppress the alert entirely, but it drops the severity from high to low or informational depending on the context. Patricia Dunn: And how granular can you get with that? Like, is it country-level, city-level, IP range? Kevin O'Brien: You can do all three, actually. Country and region is the coarser option, but you can also define IP ranges or CIDR blocks if you want to be more precise. For something like your Manila ops center where you probably have a known IP range, that's usually the cleanest approach. Patricia Dunn: That's good to know. We do have static IPs for that office so we can definitely provide those. Kevin O'Brien: Perfect. I'll note that down - we'll want to get those into the configuration as part of the tuning work. Now, the second lever is user behavior baselines. Detect builds a behavioral model for each user over time, and the longer you're on the platform, the smarter those baselines get. At seven weeks you're starting to accumulate meaningful data, but some of your frequent travelers or remote workers might need manual anchoring to suppress the noise while the model matures. Patricia Dunn: Manual anchoring - what does that look like operationally? Is that something my team does in the UI or does it require a support ticket? Kevin O'Brien: It's self-service in the UI, which is nice. There's a user profile section in the Detect console where you can flag a user as, essentially, a high-mobility user, and you can also manually mark specific past events as expected behavior. That feeds back into the model and accelerates the learning for that individual. Patricia Dunn: Okay, that's manageable. We probably have, I don't know, twenty-five to thirty users that would fit that profile across the organization. Kevin O'Brien: That's a very doable number. We can actually help you with a bulk update approach if you want - rather than going one by one. I can put together a template after this call. Patricia Dunn: That would be helpful, yeah. Lisa Park: Kevin, while we're on this topic - can we also talk a little bit about the detection rules themselves? Michael, I know you had some specific rule categories you wanted to make sure we had coverage on. Michael Russo: Right, yeah. So from a compliance perspective - we're subject to FFIEC guidelines, we have SOX obligations, and we're working toward a GLBA compliance review later this year. There are specific threat patterns that our auditors want to see monitoring controls for - things like privileged account misuse, unauthorized data access, and after-hours activity on sensitive systems. I want to make sure those aren't getting buried in the noise. Lisa Park: All of those are covered in the Detect rule library, and actually a few of them have pre-built financial services rule packs that are designed specifically for FFIEC and similar frameworks. Kevin, are those enabled in the Harborview tenant? Kevin O'Brien: Let me check. So I'm looking at the active rule sets... it looks like the standard financial services pack is enabled, but the privileged access monitoring rules are set to monitor-only mode, not alert mode. That might be why your SOC hasn't been seeing them as prominently - they're collecting data but not generating actionable alerts. Michael Russo: That should probably be flipped, right? For our auditors, we need to demonstrate that there's an active alerting control, not just passive monitoring. Kevin O'Brien: Agreed. Yeah, we can flip that to alert mode today if you want - I can walk you through it or just do it on my end with your sign-off. Michael Russo: Let's do it on your end during this call, that's fine with me. Patricia, any objection? Patricia Dunn: No, go ahead. Just make sure we document what changed and when for the audit trail. Kevin O'Brien: Already noted. I'll include that in the session summary I send over. So I'm enabling alert mode on the privileged access monitoring ruleset now. You'll start seeing those come through in your alert queue - I'd expect an initial burst over the next twenty-four hours as it catches up, and then it should normalize. Patricia Dunn: Okay, good to know. I'll give our SOC team a heads up so they're not blindsided. Kevin O'Brien: Smart. And on the after-hours activity monitoring - do you have a defined business hours window in the system? Because that's what the rule uses to determine what counts as after-hours. Patricia Dunn: I actually don't know if we configured that. Is that something that would have been set during the initial onboarding? Kevin O'Brien: It should have been, but it's one of those things that sometimes gets skipped. Let me check. Yeah, I'm seeing the business hours window is currently set to default, which is nine to five Eastern. Is that accurate for you or do you need a wider window? Patricia Dunn: It's more complicated than that because of the Manila team. Their working hours are, um, essentially our overnight hours. So if we use a static nine to five window we're going to be generating alerts on all of their normal activity. Kevin O'Brien: Right, okay. So the way to handle that is with what we call work schedule profiles - you can create multiple profiles tied to user groups, so the Manila users have a different expected hours window than your New York and Chicago staff. The rule engine applies the right profile per user when evaluating after-hours activity. Patricia Dunn: Oh, that's - yeah, that's actually exactly what we'd need. I assumed it was going to be more of a global setting. Kevin O'Brien: It's a common assumption. The flexibility is there, it's just not always surfaced well during onboarding. That's something we're working on improving. Michael Russo: From a compliance standpoint, will those profiles be documented in the configuration export? I need to be able to show auditors what the policy is and how it's applied. Kevin O'Brien: Yes, the configuration export includes work schedule profiles with user group mappings and all effective dates. It's exportable as a PDF or CSV. And that actually ties into Aegis Comply as well, when you get to that module - those configurations feed directly into the compliance reporting layer. Michael Russo: We're not on Comply yet - that's something we're evaluating for later in the year. But it's good to know those things are connected. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, Lisa can speak to that more when the time comes, but the integration is pretty seamless. It's one of the reasons the modules are designed to work together. Lisa Park: We'll definitely circle back on Comply when the time is right. Okay, let's keep moving - Kevin, do you want to touch on the alert routing and escalation configuration? Patricia, I know that was another area you flagged in your pre-call notes. Patricia Dunn: Yeah, that's on our list. Right now everything is routing to a single shared SOC inbox and it's becoming unmanageable. We need to be able to tier the alerts - critical things need to go directly to specific individuals, not just the shared queue. Kevin O'Brien: Okay, so alert routing in Detect is handled through notification policies. You can create severity-based routing rules - so critical alerts go to a specific email or PagerDuty integration, high alerts go somewhere else, and medium and low stay in the shared queue. You can also route by alert category - so data exfil alerts might go to one person, authentication alerts to another. Patricia Dunn: We do have PagerDuty. Is that integration straightforward to set up? Kevin O'Brien: Very straightforward. It's a native integration - you just drop in your PagerDuty API key and map your Detect severity levels to your PagerDuty service and escalation policy. Takes about fifteen minutes if you have the API key handy. Patricia Dunn: I can get that from our team. That would make a big difference - right now our on-call engineer doesn't find out about critical events until someone spots it in the shared inbox, which is... not ideal. Lisa Park: Yeah, that's definitely a gap we want to close quickly. Kevin, can you add that to the action items for this session? Kevin O'Brien: Already on it. So to summarize the action items so far - we're setting up trusted location profiles with the Manila IP range and the US office locations, enabling alert mode on privileged access monitoring which I've already done, setting up work schedule profiles for the Manila team, and getting the PagerDuty integration configured. Is there anything else on your list, Patricia? Patricia Dunn: I think there was one more thing - the data retention settings. Our auditors require that we retain security event logs for at least twelve months. I want to make sure Detect is configured for that. Lisa Park: Good catch. What's your current retention setting, Kevin? Kevin O'Brien: Let me look. Current setting is ninety days. So yeah, that needs to be updated. For financial services accounts we typically recommend at least twelve months, and some organizations go to twenty-four. There may be a storage implication depending on your event volume - I can run a quick estimate after the call. Patricia Dunn: Twelve months is our minimum requirement. If there's a cost implication I'd want to understand that before we change it, so yes please run that estimate. Kevin O'Brien: Will do. I'll include it in the follow-up email. It might be straightforward depending on your tier - you may already have it covered. Michael Russo: Okay. And from a compliance standpoint - same question as before - is that retention setting visible in the configuration export? Kevin O'Brien: Yes, it is. It's in the data management policy section of the export. And there's also an effective date stamp so auditors can see when the policy was set. Michael Russo: Good. That's important for us. title: Weekly Engineering Standup
summary: Raj facilitated a team standup with Ravi and Sofia covering post-mortem follow-ups from the Detect outage and the Comply v2 rollout status. Sofia identified a critical bug in Comply v2 causing SOC 2 report generation timeouts for enterprise customers with large tenant datasets, with a fix targeting early next week. The team reviewed outstanding Detect post-mortem action items, including a circuit breaker PR that needs a health check added before merging and a load testing suite formally scheduled to begin April 28th. The runbook update was also flagged as incomplete and assigned to Sofia to finish this week.
transcript_text: Raj Kapoor: Alright, I think we've got everyone now - Ravi, Sofia, good morning. Ravi Gupta: Morning, Raj. Sofia Petrov: Hey, good morning. Sorry, I was just finishing up a Slack thread - I'm here. Raj Kapoor: No worries. Okay so, usual format - let's do quick status updates, then I want to spend the bulk of the time on the post-mortem follow-ups from the Detect outage and also figure out where we are with the Comply v2 rollout now that we're ten days post-launch. Ravi Gupta: Works for me. You want me to go first? Raj Kapoor: Yeah, go ahead Ravi. Ravi Gupta: Okay, so on my end this week - I finished deploying the second set of redundant processing nodes for Detect. That's been merged and it's running in production as of, uh, Tuesday morning. The circuit breaker pattern implementation is still in review, Sofia has eyes on it. Sofia Petrov: Yeah I was going through that PR yesterday. I have a couple of comments, nothing blocking, but I do want to talk through one part of the failover logic before we merge it. I'll get to that. Ravi Gupta: Sure, yeah, let's do that. Raj Kapoor: Good. And the nodes themselves, Ravi - any issues in production so far? Any anomalies in the monitoring? Ravi Gupta: Nothing significant. There was a brief latency spike Wednesday evening, like a 200ms uptick on the ingestion side, but it self-resolved within about four minutes. I don't think it's related to the new nodes, looked more like a downstream dependency thing. I've got it in the log if you want to review it. Raj Kapoor: Okay, let's keep an eye on it but yeah doesn't sound alarming. Sofia, your update? Sofia Petrov: Sure. So I've been split this week between the circuit breaker review and the Comply v2 stuff. On Comply - we had three customers hit errors with the on-demand SOC 2 report generation, specifically around large tenant datasets. Like, if you've got a tenant with over, um, I think it was around 50,000 audit log entries in the window, the report generation was timing out. Raj Kapoor: How many customers is that affecting? Like, is this widespread? Sofia Petrov: So far it's three confirmed, but honestly I'd expect more to surface as more customers actually try to generate reports. It's not a niche edge case - any mid-to-large enterprise customer is going to be in that range. Raj Kapoor: Yeah that's... that's not great. Do we have a fix in progress? Sofia Petrov: I have a fix drafted. Basically we need to paginate the audit log query and process it in chunks rather than pulling the full dataset at once. It's not a complicated change but I want to make sure we test it properly across all four frameworks - SOC 2, PCI, HIPAA, ISO - before we push it. Raj Kapoor: How long are we talking to get that out? Sofia Petrov: Realistically? If I get uninterrupted time today and tomorrow, I can have a PR up by end of day tomorrow, and then assuming review and QA goes smoothly we're looking at early next week for production. Raj Kapoor: Okay. Can Ravi help with QA on that? Ravi Gupta: Uh, yeah, I can do that. I'd just need - Sofia, can you set up a test tenant with a large dataset so I'm not generating fake data manually? Sofia Petrov: Yeah I already have one in staging, I'll share the credentials with you. Ravi Gupta: Perfect. Raj Kapoor: Alright, good. I want that prioritized. Now, let's go back to the Detect post-mortem follow-ups because I know we've been chipping away at those for a month now and I want to make sure we're not letting things slip. Ravi, where are we on the full list? Ravi Gupta: So from the original post-mortem action items - the redundant nodes are done, as I mentioned. The alerting threshold adjustments are done, we pushed those in week one. The runbook update is... mostly done, I think there are two sections Sofia was supposed to fill in on the detection pipeline side. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, that's on me. I haven't gotten to it. I'll do it this week. Raj Kapoor: Okay, that's the runbook. What else is outstanding? Ravi Gupta: The load testing suite. We said we were going to build out a proper synthetic load test to simulate cascading failure scenarios so we can catch this kind of thing before it hits production. That one hasn't been started. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, that's a bigger lift. I mean, it's important but it's not a one-day thing. Raj Kapoor: I know it's not, but we committed to it in the post-mortem document and I don't want it to become one of those things that just... never happens. Can we put a realistic timeline on it? Sofia Petrov: I mean, if we're being honest, with the Comply bug work and the circuit breaker PR, I don't think either of us has bandwidth to start that before, um, end of April at the earliest. Raj Kapoor: End of April to start, or end of April to finish? Sofia Petrov: To start. A full load testing suite for the event ingestion pipeline - even a basic one - I'd estimate two weeks of actual work once we get into it. Raj Kapoor: Okay. Let's say we target starting that the week of April 28th, and we plan for a two-week sprint on it. That puts us at mid-May, which I think is acceptable given the other priorities. But I want it on the roadmap formally, not just as a verbal commitment. Ravi Gupta: I'll add it to Jira today. Raj Kapoor: Good. Now - Sofia, you mentioned wanting to talk through something about the circuit breaker PR. Let's do that before we run out of time. Sofia Petrov: Right, yeah. So the way Ravi has the failover logic set up, when the circuit breaker opens it routes traffic to the secondary node immediately. My concern is there's no health check before the reroute - so if the secondary node happens to also be degraded, we're just... blindly routing to a bad node. Ravi Gupta: I mean, the assumption was the secondary is always healthy because it's not under load, but yeah, I can see the issue. You're saying we should run a quick health probe before committing the reroute? Sofia Petrov: Exactly. Even just a lightweight ping with a 500ms timeout - if it fails, we surface the alert and don't silently fail over to a bad node. Raj Kapoor: That's a reasonable concern. Ravi, how much work is that to add? Ravi Gupta: Honestly not a lot. Maybe a few hours. I don't want to hold up the whole PR for it, could I add it as a follow-up ticket? Sofia Petrov: I'd rather have it in the same PR, to be honest. It's a safety thing and it's directly part of the circuit breaker behavior. I don't love shipping the pattern without it. Raj Kapoor: I agree with Sofia on this one. It's a few hours of work, let's just do it right. Update the PR and ping Sofia when it's ready. Ravi Gupta: Yeah, fair enough. I'll have it updated by end of day. Raj Kapoor: Perfect. Okay, I think we're at about time. Any other blockers before we wrap? Sofia Petrov: Nothing from me. Ravi Gupta: Same. I'm good. Raj Kapoor: Alright. To summarize - Comply timeout fix is Sofia's priority, Ravi assists with QA. Circuit breaker PR gets the health check added today, then Sofia reviews and we merge. Runbook gets finished this week. And load testing goes on the roadmap for April 28th start. I'll send a recap in Slack. Good work, everyone - talk next week.
topics: post-mortem follow-up, compliance bug, circuit breaker, load testing, incident response, runbook
action_items: Sofia Petrov: Develop and submit PR for Comply v2 audit log pagination fix by end of day tomorrow, targeting production deployment early next week | Ravi Gupta: Add health check probe to circuit breaker PR and ping Sofia for review by end of day | Sofia Petrov: Complete the two outstanding detection pipeline sections of the post-mortem runbook this week | Ravi Gupta: Add load testing suite to Jira roadmap with April 28th start date and two-week sprint plan

title: Win/Loss Analysis - Q1
summary: The team held a Q1 win-loss review revealing 34 closed-lost opportunities totaling $2.1M ACV, with SentinelShield (9 losses), VaultEdge (6), and CyberNova (4) as the primary competitors. A significant concern is the March Detect outage continuing to haunt late-stage deals, with at least five deals attributed to reliability concerns stemming from the incident. Additional issues include a lack of competitive collateral against VaultEdge on RTO claims, inconsistent loss note quality limiting pattern recognition, and execution gaps on the Customer Success and Support sides during evaluations. The team agreed on several action items and proposed monthly win-loss reviews going forward.
transcript_text: Maria Santos: Alright, I think everyone's on now - Raj, you're good? I can see you joined but your video's off. Raj Kapoor: Yeah sorry, I'm on a laptop today, camera's being weird. Audio's fine though, let's just go. Maria Santos: Okay cool. So, um, I wanted to get us all together before the end of April because we need to actually talk about Q1 win-loss - not just look at the numbers in Salesforce and call it a day. There's some stuff here that's honestly pretty troubling. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah I've been wanting to have this conversation for a few weeks. I pulled the closed-lost records going back to January and the pattern is not great. Brian Cho: Before we get into the data, I just want to say - some of what I'm hearing from the support side is also feeding into this. Like we're not just losing deals, we're losing deals to specific competitors for specific reasons and I think those reasons are avoidable. Raj Kapoor: Okay so let's just get into it. Kevin, you want to walk through what you pulled together? Kevin O'Brien: Sure. So in Q1 we had - I'm looking at my sheet here - 34 closed-lost opportunities with a total combined ACV of around 2.1 million. Of those, 22 had a named competitor as the reason or it was noted in the loss notes. SentinelShield shows up the most, 9 times. VaultEdge was 6. CyberNova was 4. The rest were kind of scattered. Maria Santos: SentinelShield nine times. That's - that's a lot. Do we know what specifically they were winning on? Kevin O'Brien: That's the frustrating part. The loss notes are inconsistent. Some AEs write paragraphs, some write 'went with competitor' and that's it. But from the ones that had detail, the recurring themes were pricing, and - this is the one that stings - reliability concerns post the March outage. Brian Cho: Yeah, I was afraid that was going to come up. The March outage is still haunting us. I've had multiple customers ask me directly about it during QBRs in the last few weeks. Raj Kapoor: How many of the Q1 losses do we think are directly attributable to the outage versus just timing? Like Q1 was already in progress when the outage happened on March 10th. Kevin O'Brien: It's hard to isolate cleanly, but deals that were in late-stage negotiation in mid-March - I counted at least five that slipped or went cold right around that window. And two of them explicitly cited it in the loss notes. One prospect said, and I'm quoting from the notes here, 'we can't afford six hours of no threat visibility in our environment.' Raj Kapoor: That's fair feedback though, right? Like I'm not going to sit here and say that's unfair. Six hours was bad. The cascading failure in the event ingestion pipeline - that should never have gotten to that point. Kevin O'Brien: And to be clear, the fix is in place. The redundant processing nodes are live, we've got the circuit breaker pattern deployed. But the optics problem is that prospects don't know that unless we tell them and apparently we're not always telling them effectively. Maria Santos: That's actually something I want to flag - do we have a leave-behind or a one-pager that specifically addresses the March incident and what we did to fix it? Because I don't have one and I've been kind of winging it in conversations. Brian Cho: We don't. And that's a gap. Like we put out a postmortem internally and we sent customer comms but there's nothing packaged for sales conversations. Raj Kapoor: Okay, that's an action item, let's flag that. Someone needs to own a one-pager on the Detect outage resolution. Kevin, can you work with product on that? Kevin O'Brien: Yeah I can do that. I'll pull in the postmortem details and frame it as a 'here's what happened, here's what we did, here's why it won't happen again' kind of thing. Should be pretty straightforward. Raj Kapoor: Good. Okay what about the VaultEdge losses - what's the pattern there? Kevin O'Brien: VaultEdge is mostly showing up in deals where Protect is the primary use case. They're undercutting us on backup pricing pretty aggressively and a couple of the notes mention their recovery time benchmarks. Apparently they're claiming sub-15-minute RTO in their pitch and we're not matching that claim in conversations. Brian Cho: Are their RTO numbers even real? Like has anyone done a head-to-head on that? Kevin O'Brien: That's exactly what I want to know. And I don't have a good answer. We need competitive testing data or at least a way to challenge those claims in the room. Right now when a prospect brings up VaultEdge's RTO numbers we're kind of just... nodding. Raj Kapoor: That's a problem. We should not be nodding. We need either our own benchmarks or a way to reframe the conversation around total recovery workflow, not just raw RTO. Because point-in-time recovery, data integrity validation - those are things we do well and VaultEdge's pitch glosses over. Maria Santos: Agreed, but it's hard to reframe in the moment when the prospect already has a datasheet in front of them. We need that collateral to exist before the call happens. Brian Cho: Yeah, I hear that. Okay let's talk about Comply for a second because that's actually - I think that's a potential bright spot even if Q1 was rough. Comply v2 just launched on April 7th and I'm curious if anyone's already seeing it move the needle in conversations. Maria Santos: It's too early to show up in win data obviously, but I've had three demos in the last two weeks where on-demand SOC 2 and HIPAA reporting was like, the thing that got the prospect excited. One of them literally said 'okay this is the first time I've actually wanted to stay on a compliance demo.' Raj Kapoor: Okay that's good to hear. But let's not let that distract from the Q1 problems. The concern I have is that we go into Q2 still carrying this reliability baggage from March and we don't have good answers for it. Maria Santos: There's also something I want to bring up that's a little uncomfortable - I think some of the Q1 losses are partially on us, meaning Customer Success. There are a couple accounts where I think we didn't stay close enough during the evaluation and competitors got more face time. That's on me to fix but I wanted to name it. Brian Cho: I appreciate you saying that. Honestly the same is true on the support side - we had a couple of escalations during March that probably scared off prospects who were watching how we handled things. Like our response time during the outage was not what it should have been. Raj Kapoor: Okay so we have a few themes here. Reliability perception from the March Detect outage, lack of competitive collateral especially against VaultEdge on Protect, and some execution gaps on our side. Does that feel like a fair summary? Kevin O'Brien: I'd add one more - loss note quality. If we can't consistently capture why we're losing, we can't fix it. The data I pulled was useful but it's incomplete and that means we're probably missing patterns. Maria Santos: Yeah that's been a chronic problem. I've brought it up in sales meetings before and it just doesn't stick. Maybe it needs to come from leadership more forcefully. Raj Kapoor: I'll take that one. I'll talk to the VP of Sales about making loss notes a required field with a minimum character count or something. It's not a technical problem, it's a process problem. Maria Santos: Good. Okay so action items - Kevin owns the Detect outage one-pager, we need someone to own a competitive brief on VaultEdge and Protect specifically, Raj you're talking to VP Sales about loss note quality, and I guess I need to tighten up the engagement model for late-stage evaluations. Brian Cho: I can take the VaultEdge competitive brief. I've been doing some informal research anyway and I'd rather have something formal to point to. Raj Kapoor: Perfect. Can we aim to have drafts of both the one-pager and the competitive brief by end of next week? That gives us something to work with before we're too deep into Q2. Kevin O'Brien: End of next week is tight but yeah, I think doable. I'll block time for it. Maria Santos: Same. Okay I think that's probably a good place to wrap. I'll send out a summary with the action items after this. Thanks everyone - this was a hard conversation but it needed to happen. Raj Kapoor: Agreed. Let's not wait until Q2 close to do this again. Monthly would be better. Brian Cho: Seconded. Alright, talk soon.
topics: win-loss analysis, competitive intelligence, reliability / outage impact, sales process, collateral gaps, q1 review
action_items: Kevin O'Brien: Create a one-pager on the March Detect outage resolution covering what happened, what was fixed, and why it won't recur | Brian Cho: Develop a formal competitive brief on VaultEdge focused on Protect and RTO benchmarking | Raj Kapoor: Speak with VP of Sales about enforcing loss note quality with required fields and minimum character counts | Maria Santos: Tighten the engagement model for late-stage evaluations to ensure Customer Success stays closer during competitive deals

title: Aegis / Silverline Brands - Comply v2 Early Access Demo
summary: Kevin O'Brien demoed Aegis Comply v2 to Dominic Flores of Silverline, with the call timed well ahead of Silverline's PCI DSS renewal audit in six weeks. The key highlights included on-demand compliance reporting (down to ~8 seconds), native support for PCI DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 in one platform, and detailed gap analysis with remediation guidance. Dominic was highly enthusiastic, noting that this addresses real pain points including slow report generation, fragmented tooling, and difficulty communicating gaps to leadership. Next steps include scheduling a hands-on walkthrough with Silverline's compliance lead after the GA release on April 7th.

Dominic Flores: That would be perfect, she'll appreciate having something to read through beforehand - okay I think we're good, this was really helpful Kevin, thanks for making time. title: Aegis / Steelpoint Manufacturing - Contract Review

That was - that was not a good situation and I know it caused real disruption for your team. Harold Jensen: Six hours, Daniel. Six hours where we had basically zero visibility into threat monitoring. In a manufacturing environment that's... I mean, our OT systems, our floor networks - we can't just go dark on threat detection for six hours. Sofia Petrov: Completely understood, and I don't want to minimize that at all. Harold, do you want me to walk through what we identified and what's been done since? I can get into the technical specifics. Harold Jensen: Yeah, go ahead. I've seen the incident report but I want to hear it from someone who actually knows what they're talking about. Sofia Petrov: Sure. So the root cause was a single point of failure in our event ingestion pipeline - basically the primary processing node went down and there was no automatic failover in place at that layer. The cascading effect hit the whole detection feed. Since then we've deployed redundant processing nodes and implemented a circuit breaker pattern so that if one component fails, it isolates rather than cascades. We've been running that in production for about a week now and it's been stable. Harold Jensen: Okay. And what's the - I guess, what's your confidence level that this doesn't happen again? Because that's really what I need to be able to tell my leadership. Sofia Petrov: I'd say we're significantly more resilient now than we were before. That specific failure mode is addressed. I won't tell you it'll never have any downtime ever, but a repeat of that exact scenario - the cascading failure - that's been architecturally corrected. Daniel Okafor: We're also - and this is something I can put in writing as part of the renewal package - we're offering an enhanced SLA on Detect uptime going forward. I want to make sure that's formalized, not just a verbal commitment. Harold Jensen: That's good. I mean, that's the kind of thing I need to see on paper. What does that SLA look like, specifically? Daniel Okafor: We're proposing 99.9% uptime on Detect, which is up from the 99.5% that was in your current contract. And there are remediation credits tied to that if we fall below. I can send you the exact language after this call. Harold Jensen: Alright. I'll have our legal team look at that language. Okay - so what else is on the table for renewal? What's the commercial side looking like? Daniel Okafor: So you're currently on a three-module package - Protect, Detect, and Comply. The base renewal would be a like-for-like at a roughly four percent uplift given, uh, standard CPI adjustments. We also have the option to add Identity if that's something you want to explore, but I don't want to push that today - I think the priority is getting the core renewal settled. Harold Jensen: Yeah, Identity is not on the table right now. We're handling IAM internally and it's not a priority to change that in the near term. The four percent - look, I expected some kind of increase, but I'm going to need to justify that internally given what happened with the outage. Daniel Okafor: That's a fair point, and I'm not going to pretend the timing isn't awkward. What I'd like to do is see if there's a middle ground - maybe we can look at the structure of the deal, whether a two-year term instead of one year gives us room to soften that increase on year one. Harold Jensen: I'd be open to hearing the numbers on that. I'll be honest with you though - and this is not meant as a threat, it's just where we are - we have been in some conversations with CyberNova over the last few weeks. Nothing formal, just exploratory. But my leadership is asking questions and I need to be able to make a strong case for staying. Daniel Okafor: I appreciate you being straight with us on that. Can I ask - is that conversation driven mainly by the outage, or is there something about the product itself that's prompting it? Harold Jensen: Honestly, it's a mix. The outage was kind of a catalyst for the conversation internally - like, if we're questioning reliability, then we should be doing due diligence. But there are also some gaps I want to talk about with Comply. We're doing a CMMC audit later this year and I wasn't sure Comply was going to cover us on that. Daniel Okafor: Yeah, that's a good segue actually. So - Sofia, you want to touch on where Comply is heading? Because there's some relevant context there. Sofia Petrov: Sure. So we have Comply v2 coming out very shortly - the GA launch is April 7th. That release includes on-demand reporting for SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001. The CMMC framework is not in that initial v2 launch, I want to be upfront about that. But it's on the roadmap and we're actively scoping it out. I don't want to give you a date I'm not confident in. Harold Jensen: Okay, I appreciate the honesty. When you say it's on the roadmap - are we talking six months, twelve months? Because my audit is Q4. Sofia Petrov: My understanding is that CMMC is targeted for H2 this year but I would not want to commit you to a timeline without getting confirmation from our product team. What I'd suggest is that we get you a written roadmap commitment as part of the renewal discussion - and if the CMMC support doesn't land in time for your audit, we should talk about what that means for how we support you through that process manually or otherwise. Harold Jensen: That's a reasonable position. I guess I'd want to see that in writing too. I've been burned before by roadmap promises that just... didn't land. Daniel Okafor: Understood. And that's - that's exactly the kind of thing I want to document. So let me just summarize what I'm hearing: enhanced SLA on Detect in writing, pricing structure that accounts for the outage context, and a written roadmap commitment on CMMC support tied to the renewal. Does that capture it? Harold Jensen: Yeah, that's the bulk of it. And I guess just... look, the relationship matters. We've been on the platform for two and a half years. I'm not trying to blow that up over one bad month. But I do need the business case to be solid. Daniel Okafor: I hear you and I think that's completely reasonable. What I'll do is put together a revised proposal document by end of this week - so Thursday or Friday - that has the updated SLA language, the two-year pricing scenario, and whatever I can lock down in writing on the product roadmap side. You can share that with your leadership and your legal team. Harold Jensen: That works. And if your product team can get on a call to walk through the CMMC roadmap directly, that might also be useful - either before or after I see the document. Sofia Petrov: I can set that up. I'll loop in our product manager on Comply and we can find a time in the next week or two. Harold Jensen: Alright. That sounds like a plan. Let's get the document first and then we can figure out next steps from there. I don't want to drag this out - our current term ends April 30th so there's not a ton of runway. Daniel Okafor: Noted, and April 30th is very much on my radar. We'll get you something this week so you have time to review before it gets tight. Harold, is there anything else you want to flag before we let you go? Harold Jensen: No, I think that covers the main stuff. Sofia, good to finally properly meet you. And Daniel - yeah, let's see what the proposal looks like. Sofia Petrov: Thanks Harold, same here. We'll be in touch. Daniel Okafor: Talk soon. Thanks for the time.
