title: Aegis / Brightpath Commerce - Competitive Evaluation
summary: Aisha Johnson (Aegis) spoke with Kendra Wallace (Brightpath) about the state of their security vendor relationship, which has been under strain following a six-hour Aegis Detect outage in March. Kendra disclosed that Brightpath has been actively evaluating SentinelShield as an alternative, driven by the outage and pre-existing alert fatigue concerns with Aegis Detect. Despite concerns about Detect, Kendra expressed satisfaction with Aegis Protect and the newly launched Comply v2 module. The call concluded with an agreement to hold a technical session in early May, bringing in Aegis engineers to address Detect reliability and alert tuning before a mid-May decision deadline ahead of the July contract renewal.
transcript_text: Aisha Johnson: Hi Kendra, thanks for making time today - I know your calendar's been pretty packed lately. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, it has been, honestly. We're in the middle of a platform migration on top of everything else so, um, timing is a little chaotic but - yeah, let's do this. Aisha Johnson: I appreciate it, really. So I wanted to carve out some time because I know we've had a few back-and-forth emails but I'd rather just talk through where things stand between Brightpath and Aegis directly. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, that's - that's probably a good idea. Because honestly Aisha, I'll just be upfront with you, we've been doing a broader security vendor evaluation over the last six weeks or so and it's been... eye-opening. Aisha Johnson: I appreciate you saying that directly, that's exactly the kind of conversation I want to have. Can you tell me more about what that evaluation has looked like? Kendra Wallace: Sure. So we've been talking to SentinelShield, we've had a couple of pretty deep demo sessions with them, and their threat monitoring story is - I mean, it's compelling. Especially after, you know, what happened in March. Aisha Johnson: Right. And I - I want to address that directly because I know the March incident is something we need to own. That was not acceptable and I understand why it's still top of mind for you. Kendra Wallace: I mean, six hours, Aisha. Six hours where we had zero threat monitoring visibility. We're a retail company, we process transactions around the clock, and we had no idea what was happening on our infrastructure for six hours. That's - that's really hard to just move past. Aisha Johnson: And it should be hard to move past, I'm not going to sit here and tell you to forget about it. What I can tell you is what we did about it - the root cause was a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer, and the engineering team has since implemented redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern so that kind of cascading failure literally cannot happen the same way again. Kendra Wallace: I saw the post-mortem doc your team sent over. And look, the transparency was appreciated, I'll give you that. But a post-mortem doesn't help me if my board is asking why we're still with a vendor that had a six-hour outage two months ago. Aisha Johnson: That's a completely fair point. Has that - has the March outage been part of what's driving the SentinelShield conversations, or was that evaluation already in flight before that happened? Kendra Wallace: Honestly? It accelerated it. We had some low-level grumblings about Aegis Detect before March - the alert fatigue issue I mentioned back in, I think it was January - but the outage kind of pushed us to actually go out and look at alternatives. So yeah, SentinelShield is now a serious contender where a few months ago they wouldn't have been. Aisha Johnson: Okay, and I - I want to come back to the alert fatigue piece because that's something I want to make sure we've addressed properly. But on SentinelShield specifically, what's resonating with you? Like what are they showing you that's landing well? Kendra Wallace: Their detection accuracy demos have been solid. They're showing us this, uh, behavioral baselining thing where it learns what normal looks like for your specific environment over time and reduces false positives significantly. And for us that's huge because our team is small, we can't have people chasing ghost alerts all day. Aisha Johnson: Yeah, and that behavioral baselining is - I mean, Aegis Detect does have adaptive thresholding that works similarly, but I hear you that we haven't done a great job of demonstrating that or helping you configure it for your environment. That's on us. Kendra Wallace: I guess what I'd say is - it's not just about features at this point, Aisha. It's about confidence. And right now my confidence in Aegis Detect specifically is pretty low. The other modules, honestly, less so. Aisha Johnson: That's a really important distinction. Can you say more about that? Because I want to understand which pieces of the platform still feel solid to you. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, so Aegis Protect has been fine - backup and recovery has done what it's supposed to do. And actually, your Comply v2 launch, the one that just happened a couple weeks ago - we actually pulled our first on-demand SOC 2 report through it last week and that was... genuinely impressive. Saved my compliance team probably two days of work. Aisha Johnson: Oh, that's great to hear - I'm really glad that landed well. The Comply v2 team worked really hard on that launch. Were you able to use any of the other frameworks, or was it primarily SOC 2 for now? Kendra Wallace: Just SOC 2 for now but we'll definitely be looking at PCI DSS next because obviously as a retailer that's a big one for us. So that part I'm not worried about. It's really Detect that's the problem. Aisha Johnson: Okay. So help me understand - if we could demonstrate, concretely, that the reliability issues with Detect are resolved and we could do a proper optimization session to address the alert tuning, is that enough to keep you from switching, or is there something more fundamental going on here? Kendra Wallace: That's a hard question to answer right now. I think - look, we're not trying to blow up our entire security stack. Switching vendors is painful and expensive and my team doesn't have bandwidth for a big rip-and-replace. So if Aegis can get its act together on Detect, yeah, there's a path. But I need to see it, not just hear about it. Aisha Johnson: That's fair. And I think show-don't-tell is the right framing here. What if we set up a dedicated technical session - I'm thinking bring in our Detect product team directly, not just a CS overlay - and we go through your specific environment, your alert configuration, and do a live walkthrough of what the redundancy architecture looks like now post-March? Kendra Wallace: Yeah, I'd be open to that. I just - I don't want it to be a sales demo. My team has sat through enough of those. I want it to be a real technical conversation where my engineers can ask hard questions. Aisha Johnson: Completely understood. I'll make sure it's the right people in the room - we'll bring the engineering lead who actually implemented the circuit breaker changes. No slides, just architecture diagrams and your real config. Kendra Wallace: Okay. That would help. And Aisha, I do want to be honest - SentinelShield is probably going to come back to us with a pricing proposal in the next week or two. So we're not in a wait-forever situation here. Aisha Johnson: I appreciate you telling me that. Genuinely. How much runway are we talking - like what's the realistic decision timeline from your side? Kendra Wallace: I'd say we need to have a clearer picture by mid-May. Our current Aegis contract comes up for renewal in July and I don't want to be scrambling at the last minute either way. Aisha Johnson: Okay, that's helpful. Mid-May gives us enough time to do this right if we move quickly. Can we target the technical session for sometime in the next two weeks? I'm thinking early May at the latest. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, early May works. Let me check with my lead engineer - her name's Priya - and I'll have her connect with you directly to get something on the calendar. She'll know better than me what questions she wants to dig into. Aisha Johnson: Perfect. And honestly, Kendra, I just want to say - I understand the frustration. What happened in March was serious and you're right to hold us accountable. I'm glad you're still willing to have this conversation rather than just, you know, walking away. Kendra Wallace: I mean, we've had a decent working relationship for two years and I'm not trying to blow that up for no reason. But I have to make the right call for Brightpath. So - yeah. Let's see what the technical session looks like. Aisha Johnson: Absolutely. I'll send you a follow-up email today summarizing what we talked about - the technical session plan, who we'll bring from our side, and the timeline. And I'll loop in Priya's contact info too. Kendra Wallace: Sounds good. And, um, one more thing - if you can also send over whatever documentation exists on the redundancy changes post-March, the actual technical docs not the marketing version, I'd like to have Priya review it before the session. Aisha Johnson: Absolutely, I'll get the engineering post-mortem and the architecture change doc - the real ones - and include those in the follow-up. No marketing fluff. Kendra Wallace: Great. Okay, I've got a hard stop in about two minutes so I'll let you go but - yeah, appreciate you reaching out for this call. It was a good conversation. Aisha Johnson: Really appreciate it, Kendra. Talk soon.
topics: churn risk, outage post-mortem, competitor evaluation, alert fatigue, contract renewal, compliance
action_items: Aisha Johnson: Send follow-up email today summarizing the technical session plan, timeline, and Priya's contact information | Aisha Johnson: Share the real engineering post-mortem and architecture change documentation (non-marketing version) with Kendra for Priya to review before the session | Aisha Johnson: Organize a technical session in early May with the Detect engineering lead (no sales slides, live architecture and config walkthrough) | Kendra Wallace: Connect Priya (lead engineer) with Aisha to schedule the technical session and prepare questions

title: Detect Outage - Escalation Bridge
summary: A critical outage call was held between Tyler (engineering), Diana (customer success/sales), and Marcus (support) regarding a complete failure of the Detect threat monitoring pipeline that began at 2:47 AM. The ingestion layer experienced a cascading failure from a single point of failure, leaving all Detect customers with zero alert visibility. The estimated restoration window is four to eight hours, potentially resulting in up to twelve total hours of downtime. The team aligned on a remediation and communication plan, including thirty-minute customer status updates, direct outreach to at-risk enterprise accounts, and a post-incident architecture review.
transcript_text: Tyler Washington: Okay, I think everyone's on - Diana, Marcus, you both there? Diana Reeves: Yeah I'm here, I've been here for like five minutes actually, I was waiting on the bridge code to work. Tyler Washington: Sorry, yeah the - the conferencing system was being weird, I don't know. Marcus? Marcus Williams: Present. I've got the incident channel pulled up and I'm looking at the logs right now. Tyler Washington: Okay good. So - Diana, before you say anything, I want to give you a status update first so we're all working from the same picture, okay? Diana Reeves: Tyler I have eight customers blowing up my phone right now, so please, go ahead, talk fast. Tyler Washington: Right. So - so the event processing pipeline went down at approximately 2:47 AM this morning. We're seeing a cascading failure that started in the ingestion layer and basically knocked out the entire threat monitoring feed for Detect. Nobody is getting alerts right now. Diana Reeves: Nobody is - okay so you're telling me that every single Detect customer is flying blind right now? Like zero visibility? Tyler Washington: That is correct, yes. Zero event processing, zero alerts going out. Diana Reeves: Tyler, this is - this is really bad. Do you understand how bad this is? We have enterprise customers who have contractual SLA commitments around monitoring uptime. Tyler Washington: I know, Diana, I know. We're - we are working it. Marcus Williams: Can I jump in here? So from a support standpoint, I've already had, uh, eleven tickets come in since about 6 AM when people started getting to work and noticed their dashboards were blank. Hartwell Financial, Crestwood Health, um, Meridian Logistics - all of them are asking for ETAs and I have nothing to give them. Diana Reeves: Okay so Marcus what are you telling them right now? What's the messaging? Marcus Williams: I'm telling them we're aware of a service disruption affecting Detect and that our engineering team is actively investigating. That's... that's basically all I have. Diana Reeves: That is not good enough, that is not - Tyler, can you give me something more concrete? What is the root cause, do we actually know? Tyler Washington: We think - and I want to be careful here because we're still digging - but we think it's a single point of failure in the ingestion layer. Basically one node failed and instead of the load distributing properly it just, uh, it cascaded. Took everything downstream with it. Diana Reeves: A single point of failure? We have a single point of failure in production in a threat monitoring pipeline? How is that even - how did that get through architecture review? Tyler Washington: Diana, I - look, I hear you and honestly I'm asking myself the same question right now but that is a conversation for after we fix it, okay? Can we focus? Diana Reeves: No, I'm sorry, I'm not letting that go because I need to understand this for when I talk to customers. Hartwell's CISO is going to ask me that exact question. Tyler Washington: Then tell him we identified an architectural gap in our event ingestion redundancy and we are remediating it. That's the honest answer and it's all we have right now. Diana Reeves: I need an ETA Tyler. What is your best estimate for restoration? Tyler Washington: Uh - okay so honestly, we're looking at somewhere between four and eight hours to get the pipeline stable again. We need to stand up redundant nodes and we don't want to rush it because if we botch the recovery we could lose event data on top of everything else. Diana Reeves: Four to eight hours. Tyler, it's already been - what, almost four hours since 2:47? So we could be looking at twelve hours total of zero threat monitoring visibility. Tyler Washington: In a worst case scenario, yes. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Marcus Williams: I've got - okay, I just got another ticket while we've been talking. Crestwood Health is saying they're, quote, evaluating alternative vendors. They're asking about SentinelShield. Diana Reeves: Of course they are. Of course. Marcus, flag that one to me directly, I'm going to call Crestwood's account lead personally. Marcus Williams: Yeah, flagging it now. Tyler Washington: Diana I want to - I want to propose something. Can we do thirty-minute status update emails going out to all affected customers? Marcus coordinates, engineering feeds me the latest, and we keep a consistent message. No more vacuum. Diana Reeves: Yes. Yes, that is the bare minimum we should be doing, why is that not already happening? Tyler Washington: Because we've been triaging the actual technical failure, Diana, we don't have unlimited people here. Diana Reeves: Marcus, can you own the customer comms cadence? I'll draft the first email template right now and get it to you in the next fifteen minutes. Marcus Williams: Yeah, I can do that. Should I loop in the CSMs for their specific accounts or keep it centralized? Diana Reeves: Loop them in but all comms go through you so we don't have five different people saying five different things. One voice. Marcus Williams: Got it. Diana Reeves: Tyler - and I'm asking this seriously, not to be combative - do we need to escalate this to the executive team? Like does Raj need to know about this right now? Tyler Washington: I already pinged Raj at 4 AM. He's aware. He's not on this bridge because we told him we'd update him at noon with status. Diana Reeves: Okay. Okay good. Alright - so Tyler, your team is on remediation, you will feed Marcus updates every thirty minutes, Marcus coordinates customer comms, I'm going to personally call Crestwood and Hartwell in the next hour. Does that - does that cover the immediate next steps? Tyler Washington: That covers it. And Diana - for what it's worth, I'm sorry. This should not have happened and I know that doesn't fix anything but... we are going to get it fixed. Diana Reeves: I know you are. I know. But Tyler, when this is over we are having a very long conversation about redundancy architecture because I cannot - I cannot go back to customers with something like this again. I just can't. Tyler Washington: Agreed. That conversation is going to happen, I promise. Okay - I need to get back to the incident. Marcus, I'll send you the first update by 10:30. Marcus Williams: I'll be watching for it. Alright, let's go.
topics: service outage, incident response, customer communication, architecture gap, churn risk, sla compliance
action_items: Diana Reeves: Personally call Crestwood Health and Hartwell Financial account leads within the next hour | Diana Reeves: Draft first customer communication email template and send to Marcus within fifteen minutes | Marcus Williams: Own customer comms cadence, coordinate with CSMs, and ensure one centralized voice for all outreach | Tyler Washington: Feed engineering status updates to Marcus every thirty minutes, starting by 10:30

title: Aegis / Clearwater Medical - Comply v2 Deployment Kickoff
summary: This was a kickoff call for Clearwater's onboarding onto Comply v2, which had just gone GA on the day of the call (April 7th). Aisha led the session alongside solutions architect Kevin O'Brien and staff engineer Mike Romano, walking Natalie and Ajay through the platform's key features including on-demand reporting, multi-framework support (HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI DSS, ISO 27001), and continuous monitoring. Ajay expressed strong enthusiasm for the on-demand reporting and continuous monitoring capabilities given painful past audit experiences. The team aligned on a fast deployment timeline targeting connector setup within the week, a baseline HIPAA report by Wednesday or Thursday, and a review call on Thursday.
transcript_text: Aisha Johnson: Alright, I think we've got everyone on now - Natalie, Ajay, good to see you both, welcome to the Comply v2 kickoff! Natalie Simmons: Thanks Aisha, really excited to finally be here, it feels like we've been building up to this for a while. Natalie Simmons: Yeah, same here, we've been looking forward to getting started - Ajay especially, he's been, uh, chomping at the bit on the compliance side. Ajay Mehta: Ha, guilty as charged - our last audit cycle was, let's just say, not fun, so anything that makes that smoother is a win in my book. Aisha Johnson: We totally hear you on that, and honestly that's exactly what Comply v2 was built for, so I think you're going to be really happy - let me also just quickly introduce Kevin and Mike who are joining me today. Kevin O'Brien: Hey everyone, Kevin O'Brien here, Solutions Architect - I'll be the one getting into the weeds with you on the technical deployment side, really glad to be on this call. Mike Romano: And I'm Mike Romano, Staff Engineer, so I'm sort of Kevin's partner in crime on the implementation - if anything breaks I'm the one you can blame. Ajay Mehta: Ha, we'll hold you to that Mike. Aisha Johnson: So before we dive in, I just want to set the agenda real quick - we're going to walk through the Comply v2 feature set, talk about your specific compliance framework needs, get into the deployment plan, and then leave time at the end for questions and next steps, does that work for you both? Natalie Simmons: That sounds perfect, yeah. Aisha Johnson: Great - so, big news, and I mean this is actually really good timing for you guys, Comply v2 went GA literally today, April 7th, so you are among the very first customers to be onboarding onto the new version. Natalie Simmons: Oh wow, we didn't realize we were that early in the queue - that's kind of exciting actually. Aisha Johnson: Yeah it's genuinely exciting, and the headline feature that I know is going to matter a lot for Clearwater specifically is the on-demand reporting - so rather than waiting for scheduled report runs, your compliance team can pull a SOC 2 or HIPAA report literally whenever they need it. Ajay Mehta: Okay that - that right there is huge, because our last HIPAA audit we were scrambling to pull together evidence at like eleven at night, so on-demand is just... yeah, that's the thing. Aisha Johnson: Yeah and the other thing I want to highlight is the multi-framework support, so Comply v2 covers SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 all in one place - Kevin, do you want to speak a bit to how that's structured under the hood? Kevin O'Brien: Sure, yeah - so the way it works is that the platform uses a unified control mapping layer, which means a single data point or evidence artifact can satisfy requirements across multiple frameworks simultaneously, so if you're doing HIPAA and SOC 2, you're not duplicating work, the system handles the cross-mapping automatically. Ajay Mehta: That is - okay that is actually really smart because that was one of my biggest pain points, I was maintaining like three separate spreadsheets for three different frameworks and it was just, ugh, it was a mess. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah the spreadsheet era is officially over for you, which is, I think, cause for celebration. Aisha Johnson: So Natalie, I know from our earlier conversations that HIPAA is obviously the primary framework given that you're in healthcare, but can you give us a sense of what else is on your radar - I believe PCI came up at some point? Natalie Simmons: Yeah, so HIPAA is definitely the big one, that's non-negotiable for us - but we also process some payment data through our patient portal so PCI DSS is relevant, and then our board has been nudging us toward ISO 27001 as more of a longer-term goal, maybe end of year. Kevin O'Brien: That's actually a really common progression we see in healthcare organizations, and the good news is you can start with HIPAA and PCI in Comply v2 and then ISO 27001 just kind of layers on without a big lift - Mike, can you talk a little bit about the deployment sequence we'd recommend here? Mike Romano: Yeah absolutely - so for Clearwater, what I'd suggest is we start with the data connector setup first, getting your cloud environment piped into the platform, and then we layer in the HIPAA framework configuration, run a baseline report, and that gives you an immediate lay of the land before we touch anything else. Natalie Simmons: How long does that initial connector setup typically take, like are we talking hours or days? Mike Romano: For a cloud environment your size, honestly, the connector piece is usually a few hours if everything goes smoothly - I'd say plan for a full day just to give yourself buffer, and then the HIPAA baseline report can actually run that same day once data is flowing. Natalie Simmons: Oh that's faster than I expected, honestly I was bracing for like a week of setup. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah v2 specifically made a big push to reduce that time to first value - the old version had a lot more manual configuration steps and we heard that feedback pretty loudly from customers, so that was a big focus area. Aisha Johnson: Ajay, while we're on the topic, what does your typical audit cycle look like - like how far in advance do auditors usually come knocking? Ajay Mehta: So for HIPAA we get maybe, um, thirty days notice if we're lucky, sometimes it's less, and then SOC 2 we're actually pursuing type two for the first time this year so that's more of an ongoing thing over like a six month observation period. Kevin O'Brien: Okay so the SOC 2 type two use case is actually perfect for Comply v2 because the continuous monitoring integration means evidence is being collected automatically throughout that observation window, so you're not trying to reconstruct what happened six months ago. Ajay Mehta: That alone might have saved me from that eleven PM scramble situation - like if I'd had this six months ago... Aisha Johnson: Ha, well you have it now - and honestly given your SOC 2 timeline, the sooner we get you live the better, because that observation period clock is sort of always ticking. Ajay Mehta: Yeah that's a really good point, I want to make sure we're not losing any time - Natalie, should we try to target getting the connectors up this week? Natalie Simmons: I think so, yeah - Mike, what do you need from us to get that started, like what does the prep checklist look like on our end? Mike Romano: So the main things are going to be CloudPrime or Azure - which cloud provider are you on? Natalie Simmons: We're primarily CloudPrime, we have a small Azure footprint but like eighty percent is CloudPrime. Mike Romano: Perfect, CloudPrime is very well-trodden ground for us - so you'll need to create an IAM role with read permissions that we can assume, I'll send you a CloudFormation template that does that in about five minutes, and then just make sure your CloudTrail logging is enabled across all regions. Natalie Simmons: CloudTrail should already be on, we turned that on a while back - I'll double check the multi-region piece but I'm pretty confident we're good there. Mike Romano: Great, that's going to make things really smooth - and once I send that template over, you or your team can run it in maybe ten minutes and then just send me the role ARN and we're off to the races. title: Product Sync - Identity Roadmap
summary: Ananya Sharma, Hannah Liu, and Nina Kowalski held a planning sync focused on the Aegis Identity Q2 roadmap. The team aligned on two primary workstreams: an MFA policy rules engine and an expanded SSO connector library, with the risk-signal/adaptive MFA layer pushed to Q3 due to scope and technical dependencies. They established a rough timeline targeting a May GA for the MFA rules engine and prioritized Okta, Azure AD, and Google Workspace as the first SSO connectors. Key process improvements were agreed upon, including locking specs two weeks before QA hand-off and including acceptance criteria upfront to enable parallel test case development.
transcript_text: Ananya Sharma: Alright, I think everyone's on - Hannah, Nina, can you both hear me okay? Hannah Liu: Yep, loud and clear. Nina Kowalski: Same here, I'm good. Ananya Sharma: Okay great. So, um, I think the main thing we wanted to get through today is the Identity roadmap for Q2, specifically around the MFA expansion and then the SSO connector work. Hannah, do you want to kind of set the stage? Hannah Liu: Yeah, for sure. So, at a high level, the ask from leadership is that we have a clearer story around Aegis Identity by end of Q2. Right now the feedback we're getting from sales is that the IAM side feels a little thin compared to what SentinelShield is putting out there. So the focus areas are - one, the MFA policy engine, and two, the SSO connector library, we want to expand that significantly. Ananya Sharma: Right, and I think the SSO connector piece is actually the more tractable one in the near term. We already have the SAML 2.0 foundation in place, so adding connectors for, say, Okta, Azure AD, that's - it's work but it's not like, greenfield work. Nina Kowalski: How many connectors are we talking about? Because from a QA standpoint, each one is basically its own test surface. Hannah Liu: Yeah, that's a fair point. I think we were penciling in something like six to eight new connectors by end of Q2. But I want to hear what's realistic from Ananya's side before we commit to that number publicly. Ananya Sharma: Six to eight is... doable, but it depends a lot on how we scope the testing cycles. Like if Nina's team needs, what, two weeks per connector for full regression? Nina Kowalski: It's not quite that bad. For a connector where the underlying SAML flow is already validated, we can probably get that down to, I'd say, a week of focused testing if we have good test environments set up. The problem is historically we've had to wait on engineering to provision those environments and that's where time gets lost. Ananya Sharma: Okay yeah, that's a real bottleneck. I actually put a ticket in - I want to say like two sprints ago - to get a dedicated staging tenant for Identity testing and it's still sitting in the infrastructure queue. Hannah Liu: I didn't know that was still open. Do you know who's blocking it? Ananya Sharma: It's not really blocked, it just hasn't been prioritized. I think the infra team has been heads down on the Detect pipeline work so everything else kind of got deprioritized. Hannah Liu: Okay, I can follow up with the infra lead on that. That actually needs to happen regardless of what we decide today, so let me just take that as an action item. Nina Kowalski: That would be great, yeah. Hannah Liu: So, going back to MFA - Ananya, what's the current state of the policy engine? I know we had some design discussions back in December but I feel like things shifted after the holidays. Ananya Sharma: Yeah, so the design did shift a bit. The original plan was to build a rules-based engine where admins could define MFA requirements per user group and per application. That's still the core of it. What changed is we're now also looking at adding a risk-signal layer, so the system can factor in things like login location, device fingerprint, time of day - and then either require step-up auth or flag it for review. Hannah Liu: Okay, that's - I mean, that's a bigger scope than what I had in my head. Is that all in scope for Q2 or is the risk-signal piece more of a later phase? Ananya Sharma: Honestly I think we should phase it. The core rules engine, that's Q2. The risk-signal layer I'd push to Q3 at the earliest. It requires integrating with some telemetry pipelines that aren't fully built out yet. Nina Kowalski: That makes sense to me. From a QA perspective, testing adaptive MFA is significantly more complex - you basically need to simulate all these different environmental conditions. So keeping that separate is probably the right call. Hannah Liu: Agreed. And honestly from a product narrative standpoint, we can still tell a strong story with the rules-based engine. Being able to say you can set granular MFA policies per role, per app, that's already differentiated from what CyberNova offers right now. Ananya Sharma: Yeah I think that's right. CyberNova's IAM is pretty much all-or-nothing on MFA from what I've seen. Hannah Liu: Okay so let's try to nail down some rough timelines. If we're targeting the rules engine for Q2, what does that look like sprint by sprint? I know it's early but even a rough shape would help me with planning. Ananya Sharma: So, rough shape - I'd say February and into early March is design finalization and we start building out the policy schema, the data model. Mid-March through April is core implementation. And then ideally late April we're handing off to Nina's team for testing, which gives us... a May release window if everything goes smoothly. Nina Kowalski: May is tight but not impossible. The thing I'd flag is that late April hand-off only works if the spec is really locked before we start testing. Last time, and I don't want to relitigate this, but last time we got a build that was still in flux and we wasted like a week and a half. Ananya Sharma: No that's a totally fair callout, and I take ownership of that - the spec on the last feature wasn't clean enough when it went to QA. What I'd suggest is we set a hard cutoff, like spec is locked two weeks before the hand-off date, and if it's not locked, we don't hand off. Hannah Liu: I'm supportive of that. And from my side, I'll make sure the acceptance criteria are written into the spec from the beginning so Nina's team isn't guessing at what done looks like. Nina Kowalski: That would genuinely help a lot. If we have acceptance criteria upfront, we can start building test cases in parallel with development instead of waiting. Hannah Liu: Good, let's make that the standard going forward for Identity work. Okay, so - SSO connectors. Do we want to talk about prioritization? Like which connectors do we tackle first? Yeah, so I've been looking at this. Based on what sales has been logging in the CRM, Okta is by far the most requested. After that it's Azure AD, then Google Workspace. Everything else is pretty scattered - Ping Identity comes up occasionally, Duo, a few others. Ananya Sharma: Okay so Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace as the first three. That actually makes sense from an engineering standpoint too because those three have the most mature and well-documented APIs, so we're less likely to hit weird edge cases. Nina Kowalski: From a testing standpoint I'll need access to sandbox environments for all three. Okta I'm pretty sure we have a dev account already. Azure AD and Google Workspace I'd need to confirm. Ananya Sharma: We definitely have the Okta dev account. Azure AD - I think we have one through our internal Nextera agreement but I'd have to check with IT. Google Workspace I'm not sure about. Hannah Liu: Can you both just check and send me what you find? I'd rather know now if there's a gap so we can sort it out before it becomes a blocker in March. Ananya Sharma: Yeah I'll check on the Azure one this week. Nina Kowalski: Same, I'll figure out the Okta account situation and confirm it's still active. Hannah Liu: Great. Okay I think we're in decent shape on the high-level plan. Let me just recap what I've got - MFA policy rules engine is the Q2 priority, spec locked mid-April, hand-off to QA late April, targeting May GA. SSO connectors, starting with Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace. And I'm following up on the infra staging environment ticket. Does that sound right to everyone? Ananya Sharma: That covers it from my side. The one thing I'd add is we should probably schedule a mid-point check-in, like sometime in March, just to make sure we're on track before things get too far along. Hannah Liu: Agreed. I'll put something on the calendar for mid-March - same group, probably thirty minutes. Nina Kowalski: Works for me. Hannah Liu: Alright, I think that's everything. Thanks both, this was a useful sync. Ananya Sharma: Yeah, good to get on the same page. Talk soon. Nina Kowalski: Thanks everyone, bye.
topics: identity roadmap, mfa policy engine, sso connectors, qa process, sprint planning, infrastructure bottleneck
action_items: Hannah Liu: Follow up with the infra lead to prioritize the dedicated Identity staging tenant ticket | Ananya Sharma: Check on Azure AD sandbox account availability through the internal Nextera agreement | Nina Kowalski: Confirm the Okta dev account is still active and available for QA testing | Hannah Liu: Schedule a mid-March check-in for the same group to review progress against the Q2 plan

title: Aegis / Bridgeport Health - Renewal Finalization
summary: James Mitchell led a renewal call with Evelyn Park of Bridgeport, joined by Kevin O'Brien (Solutions Architecture) and Ravi Gupta (DevOps). Evelyn shared overall positive feedback on Aegis Protect and Identity modules, while raising concerns about a six-hour Detect outage in March. Ravi provided a technical explanation of the incident and remediation steps taken. The team aligned on renewal terms including flat pricing, Comply v2 access at no charge for year one, a 20% seat expansion rider, and several follow-up deliverables.
transcript_text: James Mitchell: Alright, I think we've got everyone on - Evelyn, can you hear us okay? Evelyn Park: Yes, loud and clear. Good morning James, good to see you again - well, virtually. James Mitchell: Ha, always virtually these days. Um, so we've also got Kevin O'Brien from our solutions architecture team and Ravi Gupta from DevOps on the line - I wanted to make sure you had the full crew here for this one. Kevin O'Brien: Hey Evelyn, great to finally put a name to a face - or I guess a name to a voice. Evelyn Park: Same here Kevin. And Ravi, I think we've actually interacted a bit over support tickets, right? Ravi Gupta: Yeah, that's right - a couple of times over the past few months. Good to formally connect. James Mitchell: Perfect. So, Evelyn, today's really about finalizing the renewal for Bridgeport and making sure you're set up well going into the next contract year. But honestly, I also just wanted to take a step back and hear how things have been feeling from your side before we get into the paperwork side of things. Evelyn Park: Yeah, no, I appreciate that approach. I'll be honest - we've had a big year. Healthcare has just been, uh, relentless in terms of the compliance and threat landscape, so I've been leaning on the platform pretty heavily. James Mitchell: Totally understandable. Can you tell us a bit about where you feel like Aegis has been delivering for you and - and equally where you feel like there's been friction? Evelyn Park: Sure. So, Protect has been rock solid honestly. Our backup posture is way better than it was eighteen months ago. We had an incident internally - nothing Aegis-related - but we did a test restore and it just worked, which was kind of a relief because in my previous org that was always the nightmare scenario. Kevin O'Brien: That's really good to hear. Those restore validation moments are kind of the ultimate test. Evelyn Park: Exactly. And Aegis Identity - the SSO and MFA rollout - that was painful to implement, I won't sugarcoat it, but your team was really helpful and now that it's running it's genuinely made a difference. We had a phishing attempt last quarter that didn't go anywhere because of MFA. So, you know, wins are wins. James Mitchell: That's - honestly that's the story we love to hear. That's exactly the kind of thing that, um, doesn't always make it back to us but it really matters. Evelyn Park: Right. Now - and I want to be fair here - Detect was a concern. The outage in March, the what, six hours of no visibility? That was not great. I was getting calls from my board. James Mitchell: Yeah, and I want to address that head on because I know we've had some back and forth over email but I'd love for Ravi to just kind of walk through what actually happened and what we've done since, if that's okay. Evelyn Park: Please, yeah. I'd appreciate hearing it directly. Ravi Gupta: Absolutely. So the March 10th incident - the root cause was essentially a single point of failure in our event ingestion pipeline. We had a cascading failure that propagated across the processing layer and that's what caused the monitoring gap. It lasted about six hours before we had full visibility restored. And I know that six hours in healthcare feels like an eternity. Evelyn Park: It does. It really does. Ravi Gupta: So what we've done - and this is deployed and live now - we've implemented redundant processing nodes so there's no single failure point in that ingestion path anymore, and we've layered in a circuit breaker pattern so that if one node degrades it isolates before it can cascade. We've also updated our internal alerting thresholds so we're catching these things faster internally. Kevin O'Brien: And we can get you the full post-incident report - I know you may have already seen a version of it but we have the final documented version with the architecture changes if you want that for your own internal audit trail. Evelyn Park: Yes, actually, that would be helpful. Our compliance team has been asking about it and honestly that brings me to the other thing I wanted to talk about which is Comply v2. James Mitchell: Oh good, yes - let's talk about that. It launched earlier this month, April 7th, and I'm really excited about it especially for a healthcare org like yours. Evelyn Park: Yeah, so we saw the announcement and I've had my compliance manager poking around in the new interface a bit. The on-demand reporting - that's huge for us. We do HIPAA audits and we're working toward our SOC 2 Type II and the idea that we can just pull those reports when we need them rather than doing a big manual data gathering exercise every time is... I mean that's going to save us real hours. Kevin O'Brien: Exactly, and it's not just HIPAA and SOC 2 - you've got PCI DSS and ISO 27001 in there too, all from the same interface. And the reporting engine pulls directly from your environment data so it's not a static template, it's actually reflecting your current posture. Evelyn Park: That's the part that impressed me when I saw the demo. Because we've had tools before where you get a report and then you look at it and you're like, well this is from three weeks ago so what does it actually tell me. So having it be real-time or near real-time is genuinely useful. Kevin O'Brien: Completely agree. And for a HIPAA audit specifically - the way the framework mapping works in v2 is a lot more granular. You can drill down to individual controls and see exactly which assets or configurations are tied to each requirement. It makes the auditor conversation so much smoother. Evelyn Park: I want to set up a deeper session on Comply v2 with my compliance manager and maybe one of your solutions folks - Kevin, would that be something you could support? Kevin O'Brien: Absolutely, yeah, a hundred percent. We can get that on the calendar, probably next week or the week after depending on your team's availability. Evelyn Park: Great. Okay so - James, where are we on the renewal terms? Because I've had finance breathing down my neck a little bit. James Mitchell: Ha, yeah, let's get into that. So the proposal I sent over last week - you're renewing all four modules, same seat count, and we've held pricing flat from your current contract. Given the March outage I actually went to bat internally to make sure we weren't asking you to absorb any kind of increase this cycle. Evelyn Park: I really appreciate that, James. That gesture did not go unnoticed, I'll say that. James Mitchell: Of course. And then the one thing I wanted to flag - we've added the Comply v2 access at no additional cost for the first year as part of the renewal. The upgraded reporting features are included. After year one we'd have a conversation about the tier you're on based on your usage, but we want you to actually get value from it before we talk about any kind of add-on pricing. Evelyn Park: That's - yeah, that's a good structure. I like that. Gives us time to actually stress test it with real audits rather than committing to something sight unseen. James Mitchell: Exactly. And honestly, I think once your compliance manager gets into it they're going to love it, and then the year two conversation will be easy. Evelyn Park: One thing I did want to ask about - we're growing. We're acquiring a smaller regional clinic probably mid-year and I want to make sure the contract has some flexibility to add seats or expand scope without having to renegotiate the whole thing from scratch. James Mitchell: Yes, great point. The renewal terms do include an expansion rider - basically you can add up to twenty percent additional seats at the current per-seat rate without a contract amendment. Anything beyond that we'd do a quick order form but the core terms stay in place. Evelyn Park: Twenty percent is probably enough for the near term. The clinic we're acquiring is small. That should cover us. Evelyn Park: Perfect. And Ravi, from an onboarding standpoint if they do expand mid-year, how does that typically look for a new site getting added into an existing Aegis environment? Ravi Gupta: Yeah, so for an existing customer it's pretty streamlined - we're essentially extending your current tenant configuration to the new environment. Agent deployment, policy inheritance, getting them into the Identity setup - depending on their current IT state it usually takes a few weeks end to end, not months. And we'd have someone assigned to walk your team through it. Evelyn Park: That's reassuring. The last acquisition we did the IT integration was honestly the hardest part and we had a different vendor at the time. It was not fun. Kevin O'Brien: Well, we'll make sure it goes a lot smoother on our end. We can even do a pre-acquisition readiness check if you want - just a quick look at their environment before the deal closes so we know what we're walking into. Evelyn Park: Oh that's actually a really smart idea. Yes, let's do that. Can you add that to whatever follow-up notes James is keeping? James Mitchell: Already in there. Okay so to summarize where we are - renewal of all four modules, flat pricing, Comply v2 included for year one, twenty percent seat expansion rider, post-incident report from Ravi's team, a Comply v2 deep-dive session with your compliance manager and Kevin, and a pre-acquisition readiness check when you get closer to that deal closing. Does that capture everything? Evelyn Park: That's a really complete summary actually. Yeah, I think that covers it. I'm - honestly I came into this call a little bit nervous just because of the March thing, but I feel good about where we are. The Aegis relationship has been positive overall and I think you've handled the hard moments well. James Mitchell: That means a lot, Evelyn. Genuinely. We take the trust that a healthcare organization puts in a platform like ours really seriously - there's real stakes here and we don't take that lightly. Evelyn Park: Agreed. Alright - send me the final docs and I'll get them to our legal and finance team. I don't anticipate any drama there. I think we can wrap this up by end of month. James Mitchell: Perfect. I'll get everything over to you today. And Evelyn - thank you for the time and for the honest conversation. This is exactly the kind of partnership we want to have. Evelyn Park: Same here. Looking forward to year two. Thanks everyone - Kevin, Ravi, good to meet you properly. Kevin O'Brien: You too, take care! Ravi Gupta: Thanks Evelyn, talk soon.

title: Detect Team - Sprint Planning
summary: The team held a sprint twelve planning meeting that began with a quick retrospective on sprint eleven, where seven of nine tickets were completed. Key carry-overs include alert deduplication and a pipeline latency investigation that revealed a significant single point of failure in the event ingestion layer. The team agreed on primary sprint twelve commitments: deduplication carry-over, pipeline architecture remediation, and a CI gate improvement, with detection rule versioning pushed to a stretch goal or sprint thirteen. Capacity constraints and QA bandwidth were key factors in scoping decisions.
transcript_text: Chris Lee: Alright, I think we've got everyone. Let me just pull up the board real quick. Ananya Sharma: Yeah I'm here, just give me one sec, I'm closing out some tabs. Chris Lee: Mike, you on? Mike Romano: Yep, I'm here. Good to go. Chris Lee: Nina, looks like you just joined too, cool. Okay so let's get started, we've got a lot to get through today for sprint twelve. Nina Kowalski: Yeah sorry, my previous call ran over a bit. Chris Lee: No worries, we just started. So, um, first thing - I want to do a quick retro on sprint eleven before we get into planning. Just high level, shouldn't take more than five minutes. Anyone want to kick that off? Mike Romano: I can. So sprint eleven, I think we got through about, what, seven of the nine tickets we committed to? The two that slipped were the alert deduplication work and the pipeline latency investigation. The dedup one slipped because the spec changed midway through, and the pipeline thing just... it's bigger than we scoped it. Ananya Sharma: Yeah the pipeline latency investigation has been sitting in my queue and honestly the more I dig into it the more I think we have a deeper architectural issue with the event ingestion layer. Like it's not just latency, there are some single point of failure concerns I want to flag. Chris Lee: Okay yeah, let's put a pin on that, that's actually on the agenda for today. We'll get to it. What about from a QA perspective, Nina, anything notable from eleven? Nina Kowalski: Uh, a couple things. The test coverage on the new correlation rules was thin, we flagged that but it didn't get addressed before the sprint ended. And there was a regression in the alert severity scoring that we caught late - like day nine of the sprint, which is not great. Mike Romano: Yeah that regression was on me, I merged a config change without running the full suite. That won't happen again. Nina Kowalski: I mean, it happens, but we should probably look at whether we can gate that in CI. Like that shouldn't be a manual discipline thing. Ananya Sharma: Agreed, let's add that as a chore ticket for this sprint. Okay, moving on - let's talk about sprint twelve priorities. Chris, what's coming down from product? Chris Lee: So the big ones from product this sprint are: finishing the alert deduplication feature, continuing the pipeline latency work, and there's a new ask around improving detection rule versioning so customers can roll back rule changes. That last one is, uh, medium priority but product wants it in the next two sprints. Mike Romano: The rule versioning thing, do we have a spec for that yet or are we starting from scratch? Chris Lee: There's a rough doc, I'll share it after this call. It's not fully baked but enough to start scoping. Ananya Sharma: Okay. So my concern is capacity. If we're carrying over two tickets from eleven and adding rule versioning on top of the pipeline work, that's... I don't think we can realistically commit to all of that in one sprint. Mike Romano: Yeah I was going to say the same thing. The pipeline work alone, if we're actually doing it right, is probably a twelve to fifteen point story. And that's if we don't find more stuff buried in there. Chris Lee: What's your current estimate on the deduplication carry-over? Mike Romano: I'd say five points. The spec is stable now, it's just implementation and tests. Chris Lee: Okay so if we're looking at roughly five for dedup, twelve to fifteen for pipeline, and then whatever rule versioning scopes out to - Nina, what does QA bandwidth look like this sprint? Nina Kowalski: So I have the full two weeks but I'm also trying to finalize the regression suite improvements, which I'd really like to not push again. So I can support testing on the dedup work and probably the pipeline work, but if rule versioning lands mid-sprint I'm going to need a heads up. Chris Lee: That's fair. I think the honest thing to do is scope rule versioning as a stretch goal this sprint and make it a primary commitment for sprint thirteen. Product might push back a little but I'd rather set realistic expectations. Mike Romano: I agree with that. And honestly the pipeline work is more important right now. Like if the ingestion layer has the issues Ananya's describing, that's not something we want to defer. Chris Lee: Can you walk us through what you're seeing there, Ananya? Like at least a summary so we can make sure we're scoping it right. Ananya Sharma: Yeah, so basically the event ingestion pipeline right now has... it's all running through a single processing node with no fallback. If that node goes down or gets overwhelmed, we lose event visibility entirely. There's no circuit breaker, no redundancy. I think we need to add redundant processing nodes and probably implement a circuit breaker pattern to prevent cascading failures. Chris Lee: Okay so that's significant. How long has this been the case? Ananya Sharma: Honestly? Probably since the original implementation. It just wasn't a problem when we had lower event volumes but we're growing and it's becoming a real risk. Chris Lee: Alright, yeah that needs to be a primary workstream this sprint. No question. Let's make sure we break that into sub-tasks so it doesn't become one giant blob of work. Ananya Sharma: I was going to suggest that - I can draft the sub-tasks today and share them in the team channel so everyone can review before we finalize the board. Chris Lee: That'd be great. Okay, so to recap: primary commitments are dedup carry-over, pipeline architecture work, and the CI gate improvement Nina flagged. Stretch goal is starting rule versioning. Does that feel right to everyone? Mike Romano: Works for me. Nina Kowalski: Yeah, that's a reasonable scope. Ananya Sharma: Fine by me. I'll get those sub-tasks written up. Chris Lee: Perfect. Okay, anything else before we wrap? We've got about five minutes left. Mike Romano: Just a quick heads up - I'm out Thursday afternoon for a dentist appointment, so if there's anything blocking me I'd want to know by Wednesday. Chris Lee: Noted. Anyone else? Okay, I think we're good then. I'll update the board and send a summary to the channel. Standup as usual tomorrow at ten. Nina Kowalski: Sounds good, thanks everyone. Ananya Sharma: Thanks. Mike Romano: Yep, talk tomorrow.

action_items: Chris Lee: Share the rough detection rule versioning spec doc with the team after the call | Ananya Sharma: Draft pipeline architecture sub-tasks today and share in the team channel for review before the board is finalized | Chris Lee: Update the sprint board and send a summary to the team channel | Nina Kowalski: Create a chore ticket for CI gating to prevent unvalidated config merges

title: Aegis / Redwood Clinical - Product Feedback Session
summary: Daniel Okafor and Lisa Park held a structured feedback session with Thomas Hargrove from the healthcare vertical to discuss pain points with Aegis Comply after eight months of use. Thomas outlined four prioritized feature gaps: granular control-family filtering in HIPAA reports, scheduled automated report delivery to stakeholders, an executive summary layer, and period-over-period delta tracking for compliance posture. Thomas noted that while Protect and Identity modules are performing well, Comply feels behind and could eventually prompt evaluation of competing tools like VaultEdge if gaps persist. The call concluded with agreed next steps including a written summary, follow-up on scheduled delivery roadmap status, and an introduction to the healthcare vertical product liaison.
transcript_text: Daniel Okafor: Alright, I think we're all on now - Thomas, can you hear us okay? Thomas Hargrove: Yeah, loud and clear. Good to go. Daniel Okafor: Great, great. So, Thomas, thanks for making time today - I know February is always kind of a weird month for healthcare IT, end of quarter planning and all that. Thomas Hargrove: Ha, yeah, you could say that. We've got our annual risk assessment coming up in March so the timing is actually... it's fine, this is relevant for us. Daniel Okafor: Oh good, I'm glad to hear that. And I'll just introduce Lisa here - she's been on your account for a few months now and she's really the one who flagged that we should get this session on the calendar. Lisa Park: Hi Thomas, yeah we've exchanged a few emails but I don't think we've actually spoken live before so it's nice to properly connect. Thomas Hargrove: Same, yeah. Good to put a voice to the name. Thomas Hargrove: Yeah, no, that makes sense. Our team has been using Comply for, I want to say, about eight months now? And we have some thoughts. Can you walk me through what that looks like in practice? Like what's the actual workflow that's breaking down? Thomas Hargrove: Sure. So, when our compliance officer - her name's Priya - when she needs to prep for an audit, she's going into Comply, pulling the HIPAA report, and it gives her this flat document basically. But if the auditor comes back and says hey, we want to look specifically at, um, access controls or encryption standards, she has to go back through the whole thing and find those sections manually. There's no way to filter or generate a focused view on a specific control family. Daniel Okafor: Got it, yeah. title: Aegis / Nimbus Platform - Comply v2 Preview
summary: Kevin O'Brien demoed Comply v2 to Keith Donovan of Nimbus ahead of its April 7th general availability launch. The demo highlighted on-demand multi-framework compliance reporting (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001), cross-module data integration with Protect and Detect, and auditor-ready PDF output. Keith expressed strong enthusiasm, particularly around PCI DSS reporting given Nimbus's new financial services partnership. They aligned on a timeline to get Nimbus live on v2 by April 21st, with Keith's security engineering lead Priya handling the technical onboarding.

Keith Donovan: Yeah, no kidding, it's been a crazy couple of weeks on our end, but I'm glad we made it work - this is a call I've actually been looking forward to. Kevin O'Brien: Same, same. So before we jump in, how are things going at Nimbus? I saw you guys announced that new data platform partnership last week - that looked like a big deal. Keith Donovan: Yeah that was - that was a long time coming, honestly. It opens up a whole new set of customers for us in the financial services space, which is exciting but also, you know, comes with its own compliance headaches, which is actually very relevant to why we're here today. Kevin O'Brien: Oh perfect, yeah that's a great segue actually. So, um, the whole reason I wanted to get this call on the books is that we've got Comply v2 going GA on April seventh - so like a week from today - and I really wanted to get you guys in front of it early, kind of a sneak peek before the broader announcement goes out. Keith Donovan: Yeah I appreciate that. And honestly, the timing is - it's almost too good, like we were literally in a board meeting two days ago where our CFO was asking about our compliance posture going into Q2 and I didn't have a great answer for him on the reporting side. Kevin O'Brien: Okay so let's fix that. Let me share my screen here and I'll walk you through what we've built - and Keith feel free to just interrupt me whenever, this is not meant to be a one-way demo. Keith Donovan: Absolutely, yeah I'm not a passive audience kind of guy so you'll hear from me. Kevin O'Brien: Perfect, that's exactly what I want. Okay so, uh, you can see the new dashboard here - and the biggest headline with v2 is the on-demand reporting engine. So previously, as you know, generating a SOC 2 report was kind of this... painful, manual export process. That's gone. Keith Donovan: Okay yeah because I remember when we went through our last SOC 2 audit and my team spent like three days just pulling data together. Three days. That's not a compliance process, that's just suffering. Kevin O'Brien: Ha - yeah, suffering is a good word for it. So what you're looking at now is - you click here, select your framework, and the report generates. Full audit-ready SOC 2 report, on demand. Keith Donovan: Wait, how long does that actually take? Like when you click generate, what's the - what's the actual wait time? Kevin O'Brien: So it depends on the size of your environment, but in our testing with accounts similar to Nimbus in terms of scale, we're seeing somewhere between, uh, ninety seconds and about four minutes for a full SOC 2 Type II report. Keith Donovan: Four minutes versus three days. That's - yeah, that's a meaningful difference, Kevin. Kevin O'Brien: Right? And it's not just SOC 2 - so v2 launches with multi-framework support out of the gate. You've got SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 all in the same interface. And given what you just said about financial services customers, PCI DSS is probably relevant now in a way it maybe wasn't six months ago. Keith Donovan: That is - yeah, that is extremely relevant. We've been kind of, um, putting off the PCI conversation internally because nobody wanted to deal with the overhead of standing up a whole new reporting workflow. If this just... works, that changes the conversation completely. Kevin O'Brien: And that's exactly the intent. Like the whole philosophy behind v2 was, compliance reporting shouldn't require a project. It should just be part of how you operate. So - let me show you the framework selector here. Keith Donovan: Yeah go ahead, I'm watching. Kevin O'Brien: So you click frameworks, you get this dropdown, and you can actually - this is something our customers have loved - you can run reports for multiple frameworks simultaneously. So if you need SOC 2 and ISO 27001 at the same time for a customer who's asking for both, you just check both boxes, hit generate, and it queues them up. Keith Donovan: Okay I need to send this recording to my head of security engineering because he has been building, like, a custom internal tool to do exactly this and I think I just saved him about three months of work. Kevin O'Brien: Ha, yeah - well, you know, we've heard that from a few accounts actually, people who had kind of started building something in-house and then saw v2 and were like, oh, okay, we don't need to do that anymore. Keith Donovan: That's a win. Okay, so - walk me through the output. Like what does the actual report look like? Is it something I can hand directly to an auditor or is there still cleanup work to do? Kevin O'Brien: Great question and honestly this is where v2 really shines. The output is a structured PDF - it's formatted specifically for auditor consumption, so it's got your control mapping, your evidence artifacts, timestamps, everything organized by control category. We worked with a few of our customers' auditors directly in the design process to make sure the format actually worked in the real world. Keith Donovan: You worked with actual auditors? That's - I mean that's the right way to do it, most vendors just guess at what auditors want and then you end up with this beautiful PDF that your auditor looks at and goes, I can't use any of this. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah exactly, we've been on the receiving end of those complaints too so we wanted to get it right from the jump. Let me actually show you a sample output - I've got one pulled up here from a test environment. Keith Donovan: Yeah please. Kevin O'Brien: So this is a SOC 2 Type II sample - you can see the trust service criteria on the left, the controls mapped to each one, and then for each control there's a linked evidence section that pulls directly from your Aegis environment. So like here, for availability, it's pulling in the uptime data, the incident logs, backup verification records from Protect - it all connects. Keith Donovan: The cross-module data pull is - that's actually huge. Because right now we're stitching that together manually across three different tools and it's - it's a mess. Having it come out of a single platform is a massive operational improvement. Kevin O'Brien: Yep, and that's really the power of having Protect and Comply sitting in the same ecosystem. Um, I want to ask you something actually - you mentioned you're also using Detect, right? Are you on the full suite or just Protect and Comply? Keith Donovan: We're on Protect, Comply, and Detect. We're not on Identity yet - that's actually something we've been evaluating but haven't pulled the trigger on. Kevin O'Brien: Got it, okay. I'll put a pin in Identity for now. But the reason I ask about Detect is - and this is something I wanted to mention - Detect also feeds into the compliance reports in v2. So your threat monitoring data, your detection events, your incident response logs - those surface in the relevant control sections automatically. Keith Donovan: Oh that's interesting. So when an auditor asks about our incident detection and response capability, the evidence is just... already in the report. Kevin O'Brien: Exactly. You don't have to go pull it separately, it's baked in. Now - and I want to be transparent here - there was a period in March where Detect had some availability issues, you may have noticed that, the outage around March tenth through the eighteenth. We've made significant infrastructure changes since then - redundant processing nodes, circuit breaker architecture - so the reliability story is much stronger now, but I wanted to flag that proactively. Keith Donovan: Yeah we did notice that, and honestly I appreciated the communication during it - your team was pretty on top of the status updates. It wasn't fun but I felt like we knew what was happening. And the fix sounds solid, the circuit breaker pattern is the right call for that kind of cascading failure scenario. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah our engineering team was - they moved fast on it and I think the architecture is genuinely better for it. Okay so - let me swing back to Comply v2, I want to make sure we cover the onboarding side of this since that's really the point of today's call. Keith Donovan: Yes, yeah - let's talk about what actually getting live on v2 looks like for us. What's the migration path from current Comply? Kevin O'Brien: So the good news is there's no big bang migration here. v2 is deployed as an upgrade to your existing Comply instance, your historical data comes with you, your custom configurations and any existing scheduled reports are preserved. The typical onboarding for an account your size is - we're looking at kind of a one to two week window to get fully configured and validated. Keith Donovan: One to two weeks is very manageable. And is there a dedicated resource from your side for that, or is it more of a self-serve setup with documentation? Kevin O'Brien: So you'd have me as your SA throughout, and we'll also loop in a dedicated onboarding specialist from our CS team - they'll run the technical setup sessions with your team. It's not self-serve, we're hands-on for the whole window. Keith Donovan: That's great to hear, honestly. The last time we onboarded something new it was basically a Confluence page and good luck to you, so this is a different experience. Kevin O'Brien: Ha, yeah, we try to make it a little more human than that. Okay, so - given that v2 goes GA on April seventh, what would your ideal timeline look like? Do you want to be in the first wave of production upgrades, or do you want to let it bake for a few weeks? Keith Donovan: Honestly, given the PCI angle and the board conversation I mentioned, I'd love to be in the first wave. Like if I can go back to my CFO in mid-April and say we have on-demand PCI DSS reporting live and ready, that's a very good story to tell. Kevin O'Brien: I love that. Okay, so let's talk about what we'd need to do to make that happen - I'd want to get the upgrade scheduled for the week of April seventh, kick off the onboarding sessions the week of the fourteenth, and target you being fully live and validated by April twenty-first. Does that rough timeline work for your team's bandwidth? Keith Donovan: April twenty-first is - yeah, that works. I'd want to loop in my security engineering lead, Priya, she'd be the one running point on the technical side. Can I have her connect with you directly after this call to get the details? Kevin O'Brien: Absolutely, yes - have her shoot me an email and I'll get the onboarding specialist intro'd right away. And Keith, honestly, I'm really excited about this one - I think v2 is going to genuinely change the way your team experiences compliance and I can't wait to see you use it with auditors for real. Keith Donovan: Same, yeah - this has been one of those calls where I feel like I'm getting off with more than I expected to, which is a good feeling. Thanks for the early look, Kevin, really appreciate it. Kevin O'Brien: Of course, that's what we're here for. I'll send over a recap and the onboarding guide this afternoon, and I'll hold a spot for you in the April seventh first-wave rollout. Looking forward to it. Keith Donovan: Perfect. Alright, I'll talk to you soon Kevin - appreciate the time. Kevin O'Brien: You too, Keith. Take care.

title: Aegis / Coastal Living Co - Protect Module Expansion
summary: Kevin O'Brien from Aegis spoke with Vanessa Cruz at Coastal Living about deploying Aegis Protect for their hybrid backup and recovery environment following a successful spring collection launch. Vanessa described a fragmented backup setup across CloudPrime and on-prem systems totaling 80-100TB across 40-50 workloads, with poor visibility being the primary pain point. Kevin outlined a phased three-part implementation plan, confirmed compatibility with their infrastructure, and discussed RPO/RTO requirements for their critical customer data platform. The call concluded with plans for a kickoff meeting the following Wednesday and next steps around onboarding documentation.
transcript_text: Kevin O'Brien: Hey Vanessa, good morning! Can you hear me okay? Vanessa Cruz: Yes! Hi Kevin, I can hear you perfectly. Good morning - thanks for making time for this. Kevin O'Brien: Of course, of course. I've been looking forward to this one actually. So, uh, how's everything going at Coastal Living? You guys just wrapped up your spring collection launch, right? Vanessa Cruz: We did, yeah! It went really well actually. Traffic was way up compared to last year, which is great but also... you know, it puts a lot of pressure on the backend systems. So that's kind of part of why we're talking today. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, absolutely, that makes total sense. More traffic, more data, more things that need to be protected. So let's dig into that. Before I jump into anything, can you just walk me through where you're at right now with your backup and recovery setup? Like what does that look like today? Vanessa Cruz: Sure. So right now we have, um, kind of a patchwork honestly. We've got our e-commerce platform on CloudPrime, we've got some on-prem systems still - legacy stuff from before my time - and we've been using a third-party backup tool that... it does the job but it's not really built for what we're doing at scale now. Kevin O'Brien: Got it. And when you say it's not built for scale, is that more of a performance issue, or is it more around visibility - like you can't see across all your environments from one place? Vanessa Cruz: Both, honestly. The visibility is probably the bigger pain point for me personally. My team is going into like three different dashboards to figure out whether a backup job actually completed successfully. And during peak season that's... that's just not sustainable. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, that's a really common thing we hear, especially from retail customers. The seasonality angle is huge. And that's actually one of the areas where Aegis Protect really shines - you get that single pane of glass across your hybrid environment. So whether it's your CloudPrime workloads or your on-prem stuff, it's all in one place. Vanessa Cruz: Yeah, that's what drew me in when I was looking at the documentation. That unified view is - I mean, that alone would save my team probably a few hours a week during busy periods. Kevin O'Brien: Exactly. And it adds up, right? A few hours a week times however many engineers you have touching this stuff... that's real time back. So, okay, tell me more about the environment. How many workloads are we roughly talking about that you'd want to bring under Protect? Vanessa Cruz: So we've got around... let me think... probably 40 to 50 workloads total. The core e-commerce platform, our inventory management system, we've got a customer data platform that's really critical, and then some internal tools - HR stuff, finance systems. Those are less urgent but we'd want them covered eventually. Kevin O'Brien: Okay, that's a solid scope. And do you have a sense of total data volume? Rough order of magnitude is fine. Vanessa Cruz: We're probably looking at, um, somewhere around 80 to 100 terabytes across everything. With the customer data platform that's the big one - that's where most of it lives. Kevin O'Brien: Perfect, yeah that's very much in our sweet spot. And the customer data platform - is that something where you have specific RTO and RPO requirements? Like from a recovery standpoint, if something went wrong, what does the business need? Vanessa Cruz: Great question. So for the CDP specifically we'd want an RPO of no more than an hour, and RTO... ideally under four hours. That's kind of the threshold where it starts impacting our customer experience in a meaningful way. Kevin O'Brien: That's very achievable with Protect. We can actually get you to sub-one-hour RPO on that with continuous backup enabled - it's essentially near-real-time snapshotting. And on the recovery side, with our orchestrated recovery workflows, four hours is very conservative, you'd likely be looking at faster than that in practice. Vanessa Cruz: Oh that's - yeah, that's really good to hear. Because honestly, one of my nightmares is a data loss event during like Black Friday or peak sale periods. We can't be down for hours. Kevin O'Brien: Totally understandable. Retail is one of those industries where a few hours of downtime has a direct, measurable revenue impact. It's not abstract. And that's actually something we can help you model out as part of the onboarding - we have a business impact analysis template that a lot of customers find really useful for internal stakeholder conversations. Vanessa Cruz: Oh interesting, I'd love that. My CFO always wants to see the numbers tied to risk, so that would be - yeah, that would actually be really helpful for getting full buy-in internally. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, I'll make sure to include that in the onboarding package. Okay so let's talk about the onboarding itself. Typically for a deployment of your scope - hybrid environment, 40 to 50 workloads - we're looking at a phased approach. We don't just try to flip everything on at once. Vanessa Cruz: Good, because I was going to ask about that. My team has bandwidth constraints right now. We just came off the spring launch so everyone's a little fried, and I don't want to dump a massive migration on them all at once. Kevin O'Brien: Totally, yeah, we take that into account. So typically what we'd do is - phase one is your tier-one critical workloads, so in your case that's probably the CDP and your e-commerce platform. We'd get those onboarded first, get your team comfortable with the Protect console, and then phase two we roll out the inventory systems and other business-critical stuff. Phase three is everything else. Vanessa Cruz: That structure makes a lot of sense. How long does each phase typically take? And, um, how much of my team's time are we realistically looking at per phase? Kevin O'Brien: So phase one usually runs about two to three weeks. Time commitment from your side is honestly pretty light - you'd have one or two engineers working with my implementation team, and it's more coordination and validation than heavy lifting. We do most of the configuration work. Vanessa Cruz: Oh that's less than I expected. I think I was bracing for like a months-long project with lots of engineering hours. Kevin O'Brien: Ha, yeah we get that reaction a lot. We've really tried to streamline the implementation process. We've got automation for a lot of the agent deployment, especially on the CloudPrime side - it connects right into your existing infrastructure without a lot of manual configuration. Vanessa Cruz: That's huge. Honestly that was one of my concerns - I didn't want my team spending weeks just getting agents installed everywhere. Kevin O'Brien: Right, and with the on-prem piece it's a little more manual but not dramatically so. We've got a connector that works with most legacy environments - what operating systems are your on-prem servers running? Vanessa Cruz: It's a mix. Mostly Windows Server 2019, and then a couple of older Linux boxes - I think they're running CentOS 7. I know, I know, that's a legacy concern but we're working on it. Kevin O'Brien: No, that's fine, we support all of that. CentOS 7 is fully supported so no issues there. I'll just make a note so our implementation team is aware going in. Vanessa Cruz: Great. And what about training? Is there like a formal training program for my team, or is it more self-serve documentation? Kevin O'Brien: Both, actually. We have a dedicated onboarding specialist who'll run live sessions with your team - usually two or three sessions covering the console, backup policy configuration, and recovery workflows. And then we have a full knowledge base and video library they can reference on their own time. Most teams feel pretty confident after those live sessions. Vanessa Cruz: Perfect. My team learns better in live sessions honestly - they like being able to ask questions in real time. So that's great. Kevin O'Brien: Absolutely. And your onboarding specialist will also be your point of contact for the first 90 days, so if questions come up after the sessions they have someone specific to go to rather than just a generic support queue. Vanessa Cruz: Oh I love that. Nothing worse than getting routed through a support ticket system when you're trying to just get a quick answer. Kevin O'Brien: Exactly, yeah. Okay so I want to also just flag - you guys are also going to have access to Aegis Comply, right, as part of your package? Vanessa Cruz: Oh yeah, we've been hearing about the v2 launch - that just went GA recently, right? We haven't dug into it yet but it's on my radar. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, just launched April 7th actually. And given that you're dealing with customer data at scale - payment info presumably - the PCI DSS reporting out of Comply v2 might be worth a separate conversation down the line. Just something to keep in mind. Vanessa Cruz: Definitely, yes. PCI compliance is always a headache for us. Let's put that on the list for a follow-up after we get Protect up and running. One thing at a time. Kevin O'Brien: Agreed, absolutely. Okay so I think the next step is I'll send over a formal onboarding plan document - it'll outline the three phases, timelines, resource requirements from your team, and I'll include that business impact analysis template I mentioned. Does early next week work for a kickoff call with the implementation team? Vanessa Cruz: Yeah, early next week is great. Tuesday or Wednesday would work best for me. I'll get my two senior engineers looped in - they're the ones who'll be hands-on with this. Kevin O'Brien: Perfect. I'll send a calendar invite for Wednesday with the implementation lead copied in. Vanessa, I'm really excited about this one - I think the Protect deployment is going to make a real difference for your team heading into the summer season. Vanessa Cruz: Me too, honestly. This has been one of the more energizing vendor conversations I've had in a while - you actually answered my questions without just throwing a slide deck at me, so... I appreciate that. Kevin O'Brien: Ha! I'll take that as a win. Alright, I'll get everything over to you by end of day tomorrow. Thanks so much for the time today, Vanessa. Vanessa Cruz: Thank you Kevin. Looking forward to it. Talk soon!
