title: Support Case #8179 - Clearwater Medical Overage Charges Dispute
summary: Clearwater Medical's Ajay Mehta (Compliance Manager) and Natalie Simmons (IT Director) contacted Aegis Cloud Security to dispute a $4,000+ April invoice. The primary dispute involves $3,200 in Comply module overages tied to report generation during the v2 launch on April 7th, where Ajay explored multi-framework reporting features with no knowledge of plan limits and no in-app alerts - which turned out to be a misconfiguration affecting migrated accounts. An additional $840 Detect module overage appears potentially linked to replay traffic generated by Aegis's own March outage, which is being investigated. Sarah Chen committed to escalating both disputes as high priority, with a written Comply dispute response within 48 hours and a Detect log analysis by end of day.

We're a healthcare organization, we need to demonstrate compliance across HIPAA, SOC 2, we're also starting a PCI DSS review. So yeah, I ran reports. I was exploring the feature set. But I had absolutely no warning that I was going to blow past some threshold and rack up thousands of dollars in charges. Natalie Simmons: Was there any in-app notification, any banner, anything that said hey you're approaching your limit? Because if there was and he missed it that's one thing, but if there wasn't- Sarah Chen: That's - yeah, I want to look into that. Marcus, do we have any record of in-app threshold alerts being triggered or sent for this account? Marcus Williams: I'm checking the notification logs now... I'm not seeing any threshold alert sent for this account. There's a flag here actually - it looks like the overage alert configuration for Comply on-demand reports may not have been enabled by default on existing accounts that were migrated to v2. Natalie Simmons: Wait - so you're saying existing customers were upgraded to v2 and the overage alerts weren't even turned on? So we had no way of knowing we were racking up charges? Sarah Chen: I hear you, Natalie, and that frustration is warranted. We value the relationship and I want to make sure we get this resolved correctly, not just quickly. I'll send you both a written summary of this call and the next steps before end of business today. Ajay Mehta: Alright. We'll look for that. Thank you both for at least being straight with us. Sarah Chen: Of course. We'll be in touch shortly - thanks Ajay, thanks Natalie.

title: Support Case #3536 - Stratos Cloud LogVault Integration Timeout
summary: Damien Rowe from Stratos Cloud contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding consistent timeout errors when Aegis Detect attempted to push event data to their LogVault HTTP Event Collector endpoint, an issue that had been ongoing since April 18th. David Kim and team lead Priya Patel diagnosed the root cause as a circuit breaker payload threshold introduced in the April 8th remediation build (v4.1.2) being triggered by Stratos's high event volume of 8,000-12,000 events per minute during peak hours. The fix involved switching the LogVault integration from batched to streaming mode to distribute load more evenly, followed by a retroactive backfill of four days of missed event data. Damien expressed serious frustration, noting this was the second major disruption this year and that his team was questioning whether to remain on the Aegis Detect platform.
transcript_text: David Kim: Hi, this is David Kim calling from Aegis Cloud Security support, I have case number 3536 here for Stratos Cloud - am I speaking with Damien? Damien Rowe: Yeah, yeah that's me. Damien Rowe. Thanks for calling back, I've been waiting on this for like - look, we submitted this ticket yesterday morning and this is kind of urgent for us. David Kim: I completely understand, Damien, and I apologize for the wait. I also have my team lead Priya Patel joining us on the call today, she's been looped in given the priority of the case. Priya Patel: Hi Damien, thanks for your patience. We definitely want to get to the bottom of this with you today. Damien Rowe: Okay, sure. I appreciate that. So - look, I'll just get into it. We've been running Aegis Detect integrated with our LogVault environment, right, and starting around - I want to say April 18th, maybe 19th - we started seeing consistent timeout errors when Detect tries to push event data to our LogVault HTTP Event Collector endpoint. It's not intermittent, it's basically every... every batch that goes through. David Kim: Okay, so consistent timeouts hitting the HEC endpoint. And when you say every batch - are these on a scheduled interval or is this continuous streaming from Detect? Damien Rowe: We have it set to push every five minutes. And it was working fine, totally fine, for months before this. Nothing changed on our end - we didn't update LogVault, we didn't change the HEC token, nothing. So whatever broke, it broke on your side. David Kim: I hear you, and I want to be careful not to make assumptions before we dig into the logs, but I do want to look at this thoroughly. Can I ask - are you seeing any error codes coming back, or is it just a straight connection timeout with no response from the HEC endpoint? Damien Rowe: It's a connection timeout. We're not even getting a response code. The connection just... hangs and then drops. Our LogVault team confirmed the HEC endpoint itself is healthy - they're receiving data from other sources without any issues. Priya Patel: Okay so LogVault HEC is healthy, other sources pushing fine, only Aegis Detect is timing out. David, I'm wondering if this could be related to the event processing changes that were pushed in the pipeline update earlier this month. David Kim: Yeah, I was thinking the same thing. Damien, I want to ask - do you happen to know your Aegis Detect tenant version? It should be visible in the platform under Settings and then About. Damien Rowe: Uh, hold on. Let me - yeah, give me a second, I'm pulling it up now. Okay it says... Detect pipeline version 4.1.2, event processor build April 8th. David Kim: April 8th build. Okay. Priya, that would be the post-remediation build from after the March incident, right? Priya Patel: Yes, that's correct. So Damien, I don't know if you were made aware - in mid-March we had a significant incident with the Aegis Detect event processing pipeline. There was a cascading failure that caused monitoring gaps, and we pushed a remediation update that included redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern in the ingestion layer. Damien Rowe: Oh, I am very aware of that outage. Yeah, we were one of the customers affected. Six hours of no visibility - that was a really bad week for us. We had to explain to our own leadership why we had blind spots in our threat monitoring. That was not a fun conversation. Priya Patel: Yeah, we - we really do understand that, and I'm sorry again for the disruption that caused. What I'm wondering now though is whether the circuit breaker implementation in that fix might be contributing to what you're seeing with LogVault. If the outbound connector to your HEC endpoint is getting tripped by the circuit breaker under certain load conditions, that could explain the timeout pattern. Damien Rowe: So you're telling me the fix for one problem might have caused a new problem? That's - I mean, come on. That's not great to hear. Priya Patel: I want to be clear that I'm not confirming that yet, we need to look at the logs before I say anything definitively. But it's a hypothesis worth investigating. David, can you pull the outbound connector logs for Stratos on the Detect side? David Kim: Already on it. Damien, while I'm doing that - can you tell me roughly what volume of events Detect is processing in your environment? Like ballpark events per minute during peak hours? Damien Rowe: Uh, we're a pretty active environment. I'd say during peak - probably somewhere between eight and twelve thousand events per minute. We're a technology company, we've got a lot of infrastructure generating signal. David Kim: Okay, yeah that's - that's actually useful context. So I'm looking at the connector logs now and... okay, yeah. I'm seeing the circuit breaker state flipping to open on the LogVault HEC connector. It looks like it's tripping because the payload size on the five-minute batch is exceeding the default threshold that was set in the 4.1.2 build. Damien Rowe: So what does that mean exactly? In plain terms. David Kim: So the circuit breaker that was added to protect the pipeline - it has a payload threshold, and at your event volume, the five-minute batch is generating a payload that's hitting that limit. When the circuit breaker trips, it stops the outbound push to LogVault and the connection just drops, which is why you're seeing the timeout with no response code. Damien Rowe: So it's stopping itself from sending data to our SIEM. That means we've had gaps in our LogVault data since the 18th? That's - that's four days of incomplete data. Do you understand what that means for us from a security monitoring standpoint? Priya Patel: I do, and I want to be transparent with you - yes, the events during the tripped periods would not have been forwarded to LogVault. They are retained within Aegis Detect itself, so the data isn't lost, but it hasn't been pushed to your HEC endpoint during those windows. Damien Rowe: Okay so the data exists on your side. Can we backfill it? Can you push the missed events retroactively to our LogVault instance? David Kim: That's actually something we can do, yes. We have a manual replay function for the outbound connector. What I'd want to do first though is fix the underlying threshold issue so we're not in the same situation after the backfill. Damien Rowe: Yes, absolutely do that first. What's the fix? David Kim: So we have two options. One - we can adjust the circuit breaker payload threshold for your tenant specifically to accommodate your event volume. Two - we can switch your LogVault integration to use a streaming mode instead of batched pushes, which would distribute the load more evenly and avoid hitting the threshold altogether. Honestly for your volume, streaming is probably the better long-term configuration. Damien Rowe: How long does switching to streaming take to configure? And is there any disruption during the switchover? David Kim: The configuration change itself is pretty quick on our end, maybe fifteen minutes to apply and validate. There'd be a brief pause in forwarding during the switch - we're talking under a minute typically. And then we'd do the backfill right after to make sure you have everything. Damien Rowe: Okay. Do the streaming mode. And I want a written summary of what happened here - the root cause, the timeline, what data was affected, and what was done to fix it. I need to take that to my leadership and frankly I'm going to need to share it with our security team so they can assess any gaps in coverage. Priya Patel: Absolutely, Damien. I'll personally make sure a detailed incident summary is drafted and sent to you - I'd say end of business tomorrow at the latest. And I want to flag that given this is the second significant disruption to your Detect environment this year, I'd like to schedule a call with you and our customer success team to review your overall configuration and make sure we're set up in a way that's more resilient for your environment going forward. Damien Rowe: Yeah, that conversation needs to happen. I'll be honest with you - my team has been asking questions about whether Aegis Detect is the right platform for us. We're a fast-growing company, we can't be absorbing incidents like this. So that conversation with customer success, fine, but it better be substantive. Priya Patel: Understood, and I appreciate you being direct with us about that. That feedback is important and I won't minimize it. Let's get the immediate fix applied today, get you the backfill, and then we'll make sure the follow-up conversation is meaningful. David, can you go ahead and initiate the streaming mode switch for Stratos now? David Kim: Yeah, doing it now. Damien, you might see a very brief pause in the LogVault feed - like I said, under a minute - and then it should resume and you'll see the stream mode active. I'll confirm with you on the call when it's validated. Damien Rowe: Fine. And the backfill - how long will that take to actually show up in LogVault? David Kim: Given the volume we're talking about, probably one to two hours for the full four-day backfill to complete. It runs as a background job. I'll send you a confirmation email when it kicks off and another when it completes. Damien Rowe: Alright. I'll take that. Look - I appreciate you both getting on the call and actually diagnosing this today. I'm still frustrated with the situation, I won't pretend I'm not. But at least we have a path forward. Priya Patel: That's completely fair, Damien. We'll get everything wrapped up and make sure you have the documentation you need. Keep an eye out for my email and I'll be in touch as soon as the backfill is confirmed running. Damien Rowe: Sounds good. Thanks.
topics: technical issue, logvault integration, data backfill, circuit breaker, churn risk, incident follow-up
action_items: David Kim: Switch Stratos Cloud's LogVault integration to streaming mode and initiate the four-day event data backfill, sending confirmation emails when the job starts and completes | Priya Patel: Draft and send a detailed incident summary including root cause, timeline, affected data, and remediation steps by end of business tomorrow | Priya Patel: Schedule a substantive follow-up call with Damien Rowe and the customer success team to review Stratos Cloud's overall Aegis Detect configuration and address platform reliability concerns

title: Aegis / Summit Trust - Platform Concerns Discussion
summary: Maria Santos (CSM) met with Alicia Monroe from Summit Trust to address concerns ahead of their upcoming renewal. Alicia raised critical issues with Aegis Identity, including inconsistent MFA enforcement in their loan origination system and internal reporting portal, as well as SSO session timeouts occurring well before the configured 60-minute policy. Alicia also disclosed that her CISO has initiated exploratory conversations with competitor VaultEdge due to concerns that the IAM solution does not feel enterprise-grade, and brought up a six-hour Detect outage earlier in the month that damaged internal trust. Maria acknowledged the support escalation pattern as unacceptable and committed to several concrete follow-up actions to retain the account.

Alicia Monroe: And I want to be fair - it's not all bad. The Comply module has been... actually things have been okay there, better than expected, and I heard there's a new version coming? title: Aegis / Crestline Wealth - Identity Module Deployment
summary: Rachel Torres (Senior Account Manager) and Sofia Petrov (Senior Engineer) at Aegis held a pre-deployment discovery call with Derek Owens at Crestline to discuss adding the Aegis Identity module to their existing Protect and Detect deployment. Derek's organization has ~340 users on Entra ID with a mixed MFA environment and needs to address privileged access management gaps flagged in a February audit. Sofia outlined a three-phase deployment approach covering directory sync, MFA policy migration, and PAM, with an end-of-July target that is feasible given Crestline's environment. Derek also expressed interest in Aegis Comply v2 as a future add-on, which Rachel noted would benefit from the audit data generated during the Identity deployment.
transcript_text: Rachel Torres: Alright, I think we've got everyone on - Derek, can you hear us okay? Derek Owens: Yeah, loud and clear. Good to go. Rachel Torres: Perfect. Okay so, welcome everyone - I'm Rachel Torres, Senior Account Manager here at Aegis, and I have Sofia Petrov with me today, she's one of our Senior Engineers on the Identity side of things. Sofia, you wanna say a quick hi? Sofia Petrov: Hey Derek, great to meet you. Really excited to be working with Crestline on this - Identity deployments in financial services are kind of my favorite thing to dig into, so, yeah, looking forward to the conversation. Derek Owens: Likewise, honestly. I've been looking forward to this one. We've had Protect and Detect running for a while now and the team's been happy, so adding Identity feels like a natural next step. Rachel Torres: That's great to hear, and yeah, that's - that's kind of the pattern we see with a lot of our financial services customers. They start with backup and threat monitoring and then once Identity is on the roadmap it sort of becomes a priority real fast, especially given the regulatory environment you're dealing with. Derek Owens: Exactly, yeah. We had our annual audit in February and the auditors flagged some gaps around privileged access management and MFA coverage across our admin accounts specifically. So that sort of lit a fire under us to get this moving. Rachel Torres: Okay, that's - that's actually super helpful context, Derek, thank you. So Sofia, that kind of shapes where we should probably start today, right? Sofia Petrov: Yeah, absolutely. So Derek, before I get into the actual deployment steps, can you give me a quick picture of your current identity landscape? Like, what are you using today for SSO or directory services, if anything? Derek Owens: Sure, so we're running Azure AD - or I guess it's Entra ID now, still getting used to that name - for our primary directory. We've got about 340 users total, around 40 of those are in elevated or admin roles. MFA right now is a mix of, uh, Nextera Authenticator and some legacy SMS-based auth that we've been meaning to deprecate for a while but just haven't gotten around to it. Sofia Petrov: Okay, great. And the SMS-based stuff - is that mostly for a specific group of users or is it kind of scattered across different departments? Derek Owens: Honestly it's a bit scattered. I think it's probably 20, maybe 25 users, a lot of them are in our wealth advisory group. Some of the senior advisors have been resistant to changing their auth flow, if I'm being honest. Sofia Petrov: Ha, yeah, that's - that's a very common story. We hear that a lot. The good news is Aegis Identity has some tooling around phased MFA policy rollout that makes that transition a lot smoother. You can essentially grandfather users into a migration window rather than doing a hard cutover, which tends to reduce the, uh, the pushback significantly. Derek Owens: Oh that's actually really good to know. My manager was asking about that specifically - like whether we'd have to do a big bang cutover. I was not looking forward to that conversation with the advisory team. Sofia Petrov: You can tell your manager that's a hard no on the big bang approach. We've got you. Rachel Torres: I love it. Okay so Sofia, do you want to walk Derek through sort of the high level deployment phases? I think that'll help frame the rest of the conversation. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, definitely. So, at a high level we're looking at three phases for a deployment like yours. Phase one is directory sync and SSO configuration - basically getting Aegis Identity talking to your Entra ID environment, setting up the SAML or OIDC connectors, depending on what your apps support. Phase two is MFA policy configuration and enrollment, which is where we'd handle that phased migration you mentioned. And then phase three is privileged access management, which sounds like it's actually going to be really important for you given what the auditors flagged. Derek Owens: Yeah, the PAM piece is huge for us. Can you tell me a bit more about what that looks like in practice? Like, are we talking just session recording, or is there more to it? Sofia Petrov: So it's quite a bit more than just session recording, which I think you'll find pretty compelling. Aegis Identity gives you just-in-time access provisioning for admin roles, so instead of users having standing admin privileges 24/7, they request elevated access for a specific window, it gets approved through a workflow, and then it auto-expires. You still get full session recording and audit logs, but the just-in-time piece is really what closes that standing privilege gap that auditors love to flag. Derek Owens: Okay, that's - yeah, that's exactly what we need. That's honestly the thing that's going to make my auditors happiest. We've had a few instances where terminated employees still had admin access longer than they should have because the offboarding process wasn't fully automated, and that's a conversation I don't want to have again. Sofia Petrov: The automated deprovisioning is actually one of the things our financial services customers consistently call out as like a - a real pain point solved. We can tie it directly into your HR system or your ticketing system so the moment an offboarding ticket is triggered, access is revoked automatically. No manual steps, full audit trail. Derek Owens: We're using ServiceNow for ITSM, would that work? Sofia Petrov: ServiceNow is one of our, uh, supported integrations out of the box, yeah. We've got a native connector. Derek Owens: Perfect. Okay I'm taking notes furiously over here. Rachel Torres: Ha, I love to hear it. So Derek, just while we're talking timelines - you mentioned the audit flagged some gaps. Do you have a target date in mind for when you want to have the Identity module fully deployed? Like, is there a next audit or a compliance checkpoint you're working toward? Derek Owens: Yeah, so our next internal compliance review is in August, and I'd really love to have everything buttoned up by end of July at the latest so we have time to generate some reports and actually show progress. Is that - is that a realistic window? Sofia Petrov: End of July is very doable. If we can get the kickoff scheduled within the next week or two, we're looking at roughly ten to twelve weeks of deployment work depending on how complex the app integrations get, and that puts us comfortably in the early July range for full deployment. Derek Owens: That's - yeah, that's better than I was expecting honestly. I had budgeted for like a four month process in my head. Rachel Torres: I mean, it can get longer if there are a lot of custom app integrations or if there's a lot of back and forth on MFA policy decisions, but for your environment as you've described it - 340 users, existing Entra ID foundation - we've got a really solid baseline to work from. Sofia's done probably a dozen of these in the financial services space at this point. Sofia Petrov: Closer to fifteen actually, but who's counting. Derek Owens: Ha, even better. Oh, one thing I did want to mention while I have you both - I saw the announcement about Aegis Comply v2 that went out earlier this month. We're not currently on the Comply module but the on-demand SOC 2 and the multi-framework reporting - that caught my eye. Is that something we could potentially layer in down the road? Rachel Torres: Oh, absolutely. And honestly the timing is great because the Identity deployment is going to generate a ton of the underlying audit data that Comply v2 pulls into those reports. Like, all of the access logs, the privileged session records, the MFA enrollment status - that all feeds directly into the compliance reporting engine. So by the time you're ready to look at Comply, you'll already have months of clean data to work with. Derek Owens: Oh that's a really good point, I hadn't thought about it that way. So it's not like starting from scratch with Comply, we'd already have a head start. Rachel Torres: Exactly. And just so you know, Comply v2 has SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 all supported now as of the April launch. I know financial services customers often need to juggle multiple frameworks, so having all of that in one place on demand - no more waiting for quarterly report runs - it's pretty compelling. Derek Owens: Yeah, I'm going to bring that up with our Chief Compliance Officer. She's been asking about the SOC 2 reporting specifically. But let's - let's get Identity locked in first and then circle back on Comply. One thing at a time. Rachel Torres: Totally, that's the right approach. Okay so in terms of next steps - I'm going to send over a deployment plan document after this call that Sofia will put together, it'll have the three phases laid out with rough timelines, the integration checklist for the Entra ID connector and ServiceNow, and what we'll need from your side to get started. Does that work? Derek Owens: Yeah, that's perfect. If you can also include the MFA migration framework stuff Sofia mentioned - the phased rollout approach - that would be great because I'm going to want to share that with my manager before the kickoff. Sofia Petrov: I'll include a section on that specifically, and I'll flag the just-in-time PAM stuff too since that sounds like it'll be an important talking point for your audit preparation. Derek Owens: Awesome. This has been - yeah, this has been really helpful. I feel a lot more confident about the timeline than I did going into this call. I'll loop my manager in on the doc once I get it and then let's get that kickoff on the calendar. Sofia Petrov: Sounds great. We'll aim to get the document to you by end of day Monday, and then we can do a quick kickoff call early next week if that works. Rachel, does that align with what you're thinking? Rachel Torres: Yep, that works perfectly on our end. Derek, I'll send a calendar invite with a few options for early next week. And as always, if anything comes up before then, don't hesitate to reach out - you've got my direct line. We're really excited to get this moving with the Crestline team. Derek Owens: Likewise, thanks so much Rachel, thanks Sofia. Talk soon. Sofia Petrov: Take care, Derek!
topics: identity deployment, privileged access management, mfa migration, compliance audit, entra id integration, compliance reporting

title: Detect Team - Sprint Planning
summary: The team held a sprint planning meeting to review carryover items and commit to work for the upcoming sprint. Nina flagged two edge cases in DETECT-219 related to wildcard regex matching that Tyler needs to fix before the ticket can be closed. Ananya raised an architectural concern about a single-node ingestion pipeline and proposed a design spike to address redundancy and failover, which Ravi agreed to scope collaboratively. The team settled on 13 story points for the sprint, including carryover, QA work, the design spike, and the alert deduplication ticket DETECT-231, intentionally leaving buffer after overcommitting last sprint.
transcript_text: Sofia Petrov: Alright, I think we've got everyone - let me just pull up the board real quick. Tyler Washington: Yeah, I'm here. Sorry I was a couple minutes late, my previous meeting ran over. Sofia Petrov: No worries, we were just getting started. Ravi, you on? Ravi Gupta: Yep, I'm here. Can everyone hear me okay? Sofia Petrov: Loud and clear. Okay so, uh, let's just do a quick run through of what we're carrying over from last sprint and then figure out what we're committing to for this one. Nina, do you have the QA status on the event filtering tickets? Nina Kowalski: Yeah so, DETECT-214 is done, that's fully verified. DETECT-219 is still in progress - Tyler's fix came through but I found two edge cases that need to be addressed before I can close it out. Tyler Washington: Oh, the - is that the one with the regex matching issue on the custom rule engine? Nina Kowalski: Yeah exactly. So when you pass in a rule with a wildcard at the start of the pattern, it's not matching correctly against certain log formats. I can send you the repro steps after this. Tyler Washington: Yeah please do, I thought I had that covered but... apparently not. I'll take a look today. Sofia Petrov: How long do you think that fix will take, Tyler? Because I want to factor that into what we're pulling into this sprint. Tyler Washington: Uh, honestly if it's just the wildcard handling, maybe a couple hours? But I don't want to commit to that without actually seeing Nina's repro first. Sofia Petrov: Fair enough. Let's call it a two-point carryover for now and adjust if needed. Ananya, what's the status on the ingestion pipeline work? I know you were heads-down on that last week. Ananya Sharma: So, uh, the core refactor is done - I finished that Thursday. But I want to flag something, and I think this is actually worth a conversation for sprint planning. The current architecture has a single ingestion node that everything funnels through, and I'm a little uncomfortable with that given the load we're projecting for Q2. Ravi Gupta: Yeah I've had the same thought honestly. What are you thinking, like introducing redundancy at that layer? Ananya Sharma: Right, or at minimum some kind of failover mechanism. If that node goes down, we basically have a blind spot in event processing. That's not great. Sofia Petrov: I mean, agreed in principle, but is that realistically something we can scope into this sprint? That feels like a pretty significant chunk of work. Ananya Sharma: Probably not a full implementation, no. But maybe we scope it as a design spike this sprint and carry the build work into next sprint? At least we'd have the architecture figured out. Sofia Petrov: That makes sense to me. Ravi, from an infra standpoint what would redundant nodes actually look like? Like are we talking a lot of new infrastructure or is it relatively contained? Ravi Gupta: So it depends on how we want to handle state. If the nodes need to share state, then it gets complicated fast - we'd need some kind of coordination layer. If they're stateless and we just route around failures, it's simpler. I'd want to sit down with Ananya and look at what the node is actually doing before I give a real estimate. Sofia Petrov: Okay, let's do this - Ananya and Ravi, can you two block some time this week, maybe Wednesday, to look at that together and come back with a rough scope? We don't need to solve it today. Ravi Gupta: Works for me. Ananya Sharma: Yeah, I'm free Wednesday afternoon. Sofia Petrov: Great. Okay so for this sprint - carryover on 219, the ingestion refactor from Ananya landing and going through QA, the design spike on redundancy, and then what else were we planning to pull in? I had a few new tickets flagged. Tyler Washington: DETECT-231 is the alert deduplication improvement. That one's been sitting in the backlog for a while and product has been asking about it. Sofia Petrov: Right, yeah. How are we estimating that? Tyler Washington: I put it at five points. It's not super complex but there's a fair amount of testing surface - like we need to make sure we're not accidentally suppressing legit alerts while we're deduplicating. Nina, you'd probably need to write a decent set of test cases for that. Nina Kowalski: Yeah, that one's going to need a solid test matrix. I'd want to cover at least twenty or so distinct scenarios. Five points sounds right to me - maybe push it to eight if we're being conservative. Sofia Petrov: Let's say five for now and flag it if we're running into issues mid-sprint. I don't want to over-inflate points just out of caution if the engineering side is relatively clean. Nina Kowalski: Fine by me. Ananya Sharma: What about DETECT-240, the latency metrics dashboard? I know Ravi had some thoughts on that. Ravi Gupta: Yeah so I actually think that one should wait. We're in the middle of some infra changes and I don't want to build a dashboard off metrics that might shift once we've stabilized the environment. I'd rather do it after we've landed those infra changes so we're actually measuring the right thing. Sofia Petrov: That's a reasonable point. Okay, we'll push 240 to next sprint. What's our total looking like then? Carryover 219 at two, ingestion refactor QA... Nina what are you estimating for that? Nina Kowalski: Probably three points for QA, assuming the code is clean. If Ananya's refactor introduces anything unexpected I might need more time but let's start at three. Sofia Petrov: Okay so two plus three plus the design spike - what are we calling that, three points? - and then 231 at five. That's thirteen, which is pretty comfortable. Sofia Petrov: Yeah I agree, let's not do that again. Thirteen is fine. If we're burning through it early, we can always pull something in. Ananya Sharma: Sounds good. Are we doing the usual check-in cadence - async updates in Slack, then syncing Thursday? Sofia Petrov: Yeah, same as always. Daily async, Thursday sync at two. Tyler Washington: Nope, good to go. Sofia Petrov: Alright, good. Okay everyone, talk Thursday. Thanks.

title: Support Case #7537 - Forge Industries Detect Recovery Confirmation
summary: Elena Vasquez from Aegis Cloud Security support called Dana Moretti of Forge Industries to discuss the recovery and closure of support case 7537 related to a Detect platform outage. The outage began March 10th with approximately six hours of complete threat monitoring visibility loss caused by a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer, followed by degraded performance through March 15th. Aegis implemented architectural fixes including redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern, with full restoration confirmed March 18th. Dana needs documentation for her CISO, including a data recovery summary for the blind-spot window and a formal post-incident report.
transcript_text: Elena Vasquez: Hi, this is Elena Vasquez from Aegis Cloud Security support, am I speaking with Dana Moretti? Dana Moretti: Yeah, that's me. Hi Elena, thanks for calling back on this. Elena Vasquez: Of course, so I'm calling regarding support case number 7537, the Detect recovery confirmation for Forge Industries - is this still a good time? Dana Moretti: Yeah, yeah, now works. I've got about thirty minutes so let's get into it. Elena Vasquez: Perfect. So, uh, just to level set, I wanted to walk through with you what happened over the past several days with the Detect platform, confirm the current status from your end, and then just make sure we've covered everything before we close out the case. Dana Moretti: That works for me. Yeah, I mean, it's been a rough week honestly. We lost visibility for, what, around six hours on - I think it was the twelfth? Elena Vasquez: So the outage actually started on March 10th and the full restoration was confirmed by our team on March 18th, which is today. The most acute period - the window where event processing was completely down - that was approximately six hours starting late on the tenth, you're right about the duration. Dana Moretti: Okay, right, right. The tenth. Yeah, that's when our alerts just stopped coming through entirely. My team flagged it maybe an hour in and then we opened the ticket. Elena Vasquez: Yeah, and we received that, we logged it. So let me just walk you through the root cause at a high level, because I want to make sure you have that documented on your end as well. Dana Moretti: Please, yeah, I need to put something together for my CISO this week so any detail you can give me is helpful. Elena Vasquez: Absolutely, so the root cause was a cascading failure in the event processing pipeline. Essentially what happened is there was a single point of failure in our event ingestion layer - so when that component went down, it took the entire processing pipeline with it, which is why you saw a complete loss of threat monitoring visibility rather than just degraded performance. Dana Moretti: Right, and that's - I mean, that's the part that concerns me from an architectural standpoint. Like, a single point of failure in something as critical as threat monitoring, that's... that's not a small thing. Elena Vasquez: No, you're right, and I'm not going to minimize that. It's a significant issue and our engineering team has been very direct internally about that as well. Dana Moretti: Okay. So what did you actually do to fix it? Like, is this a patch or a real architectural change? Elena Vasquez: It's a real architectural change, not just a patch. Two things were implemented. First, redundant processing nodes were added to the event ingestion layer - so there's no longer a single point of failure there, if one node goes down the others pick up the load. And second, a circuit breaker pattern was implemented, so if a component does start to fail, it isolates that failure before it can cascade through the rest of the pipeline. Dana Moretti: Okay, the circuit breaker pattern, yeah, that makes sense. And those are both live now, as of today? Elena Vasquez: Both are live and confirmed in your environment as of this morning, yes. Dana Moretti: Alright. And in terms of - okay, so during that six-hour window, we had no visibility. What does that mean for our alert history? Like, are there gaps in our logs, did we lose any event data, or was it captured somewhere and just not processed? Elena Vasquez: That's a good question and I want to give you an accurate answer here. Events that arrived during the outage window were queued but the processing queue itself was affected by the failure, so there is a gap in your processed alert history for that window. Raw ingestion data - some of it was preserved depending on where in the pipeline the failure hit, but I wouldn't rely on full fidelity there. I can get you a specific data recovery summary from our backend team if that's something you need for your documentation. Dana Moretti: Yeah, I'd actually really appreciate that. Because my CISO is going to ask whether we need to treat that six-hour window as a blind spot from a forensic standpoint, and I need to be able to answer that clearly. Elena Vasquez: Understood, yeah. I'll flag that as a follow-up action item on this case and have our backend team put together a summary of what was and wasn't captured during that window. I'll target getting that to you by end of week. Dana Moretti: End of week works. That's Thursday or Friday? Elena Vasquez: Let's say Friday to be safe, but I'll push for Thursday. Dana Moretti: Okay. And then - sorry, I'm jumping around a little bit - what about the monitoring during the recovery period? So after the six-hour outage, were we at full functionality or was there still some degraded state we should know about? Elena Vasquez: Yeah, so there was a phased recovery. After the initial outage was resolved, the platform came back up but event processing throughput was running below normal capacity for a period while the redundant nodes were being fully provisioned. That would have been roughly from the eleventh through about the fifteenth. During that window you may have seen some latency in alert delivery, so alerts were coming through but potentially with some delay. Dana Moretti: Okay, yeah, my team did notice that actually. We had some alerts coming in that were timestamped earlier than when we received them. I wasn't sure if that was a data backfill or just latency. Elena Vasquez: Most likely latency during the recovery period, yeah. Some of it may also be backfill as the queue drained, so a mix of both probably. That should have normalized by around the sixteenth. Dana Moretti: It did, actually. Things looked normal by - yeah, I'd say by the sixteenth or seventeenth we weren't seeing the timestamp discrepancies anymore. Elena Vasquez: Good, that tracks. And as of today you're fully confirmed back to normal alert volumes and processing? Dana Moretti: Yeah, from what I can see in the dashboard it looks normal. I mean, I'd love some kind of confirmation from your side that our tenant is specifically healthy rather than just going off the UI, if that's possible. Elena Vasquez: Absolutely, I can pull your tenant metrics right now actually. Give me just a second. Dana Moretti: Sure, take your time. Elena Vasquez: Okay so I'm looking at the Forge Industries tenant now - event ingestion rate is at normal baseline for your account, alert processing latency is under two seconds which is within SLA, and I'm not seeing any queue backlog. Everything looks healthy from the backend. Dana Moretti: Okay, good. That's helpful to have confirmed. Can you include that in the case notes so I have a record of it? Elena Vasquez: Already adding it as I speak, yeah. I'll also attach a timestamp to that health confirmation in the case record. Dana Moretti: Appreciate it. Um - and I guess the last thing I want to ask, and this is more of a process question, is there going to be any kind of formal post-incident report or RCA document that we'd receive? Because I've seen some vendors do that and it's useful for our own internal reviews. Elena Vasquez: Yeah, our team is producing a post-incident report, it's in draft right now. I can make sure that's shared with you once it's finalized. It'll cover the root cause, the timeline, the remediation steps - essentially everything we discussed today but in a formal written format. title: Support Case #8749 - Coastal Living Co SAML Certificate Rotation Bug
summary: Vanessa Cruz from a retail company contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding a critical SAML certificate rotation issue affecting 60-70% of her workforce on a Sunday. Support engineer Elena Vasquez identified the root cause as a known bug in Aegis Identity version 3.4.1, where the certificate rotation wizard fails to propagate new certificate metadata to all service provider connections. The team worked on a manual workaround requiring Vanessa's engineer Priya to re-import the new certificate metadata across all 14 SP connections. Vanessa expressed broader frustration with platform reliability, citing this bug alongside a recent Detect outage, and Marcus committed to escalating her concerns to customer success.

Vanessa Cruz: I mean, it shouldn't matter what day it is, this shouldn't be happening at all, right? Vanessa Cruz: How many SP connections are we talking about, like, do you know how many integrations we have configured? Marcus Williams: I'm pulling up your account right now - it looks like you have fourteen service provider connections active. Vanessa Cruz: Fourteen. title: Support Case #3546 - Meridian Capital SCIM Provisioning Request

Sarah Chen and Marcus Williams confirmed that native SCIM 2.0 is on the roadmap but not yet generally available, and recommended using Aegis's REST API with Okta Workflows as an interim solution. The team agreed this API approach could meet Meridian's 24-hour deprovisioning compliance requirement, with audit logs accessible through Aegis Comply. Next steps include sending API documentation, logging the SCIM feature request with Meridian's specific use case, and looping in the account manager for a roadmap discussion.

title: Aegis / Frostbyte AI - Product Feedback
summary: Rachel Torres and Sofia Petrov met with Victor Zheng of Frostbyte to discuss pain points after approximately eight months on Aegis Identity. Victor highlighted two key product gaps: the lack of hierarchical role inheritance in the flat role model, which causes manual permission duplication and complicates their ongoing SOC 2 audit, and the inability to configure session timeout policies per role or resource. Victor also praised Aegis Comply v2's on-demand SOC 2 reporting as a significant time-saver. He clarified he is not evaluating alternatives but wants assurance that Aegis Identity can scale with Frostbyte's rapid growth over the coming quarters.
transcript_text: Rachel Torres: Hey Victor, thanks for making time today - I know your calendar's been pretty packed lately. Victor Zheng: Yeah, no worries, it's been a busy quarter but this is - this is on my list, so happy to make it happen. Rachel Torres: Good, good. So I've also got Sofia Petrov on with me today, she's one of our senior engineers on the Identity side, and I figured having her here would be more useful than me trying to take notes and relay everything back. Sofia Petrov: Hey Victor, thanks for having us. Really looking forward to hearing what you've been running into. Victor Zheng: Hey Sofia, yeah, appreciate you jumping on. Okay so - where do I start. So we've been on Aegis Identity now for, I want to say, about seven months? Maybe closer to eight. Rachel Torres: Yeah, that tracks, I think you all went live around mid-September last year. Victor Zheng: Right, yeah. So overall - look, it's been fine. The SSO integration was pretty smooth once we got through the initial SAML configuration, and the MFA rollout went better than I expected honestly. Sofia Petrov: That's good to hear. That SAML piece can be... yeah, it can be a little finicky depending on the IdP. Victor Zheng: It was, yeah, we had a couple of back-and-forths with your support team on that, but it got resolved. So no complaints there. The reason I wanted to have this call is really around some gaps we're hitting on the IAM side - specifically around how Aegis Identity handles role management at scale. Sofia Petrov: Okay, yeah, tell me more. What does scale look like for Frostbyte right now in terms of, like, users and roles? Victor Zheng: So we're sitting at roughly - and this has grown a lot this year - we're at about 1,400 users across the organization. And the role taxonomy is... it's gotten complicated. We've got engineering, ML infrastructure, data, product, and then all the corporate functions on top of that. Sofia Petrov: Right. Victor Zheng: And the issue we keep running into is that there's no good way to do nested role inheritance within Aegis Identity. Like, I can define roles, I can assign permissions, but I can't say - this team lead role inherits everything from the senior engineer role, plus these additional permissions. It's all flat. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, that's - that's a known limitation in the current version, I'll be straight with you. The role model right now is flat, there's no hierarchical inheritance baked in. It's something that's been on the roadmap for a while. Victor Zheng: So it is on the roadmap? Do you have any sense of timeline? Sofia Petrov: I don't want to - I don't want to give you a number I can't stand behind, honestly. Rachel, do you have anything more concrete from the product side on that? Rachel Torres: Not a GA date, no. The last I heard from our product team, hierarchical roles is in active development, but I haven't seen a committed date for release. I can definitely follow up with our product management contact and get you something more specific, Victor. Victor Zheng: Yeah, that would be helpful. Because right now what we're doing is - we're basically duplicating permissions manually across roles, which is, uh, it's error-prone and it's a pain to audit. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, I get that. That's exactly the kind of thing hierarchical inheritance would fix. Can I ask - when you say it's hard to audit, are you running into issues specifically around access reviews, or is it more the day-to-day management overhead? Victor Zheng: Honestly both, but the access review piece is becoming more urgent. We're going through a SOC 2 audit right now - we're actually using Aegis Comply for some of that, which, by the way, the v2 stuff that came out earlier this month is pretty solid. Rachel Torres: Oh good, yeah the on-demand reporting in Comply v2 - I was hoping that would land well for your team. Victor Zheng: Yeah the on-demand SOC 2 report generation is saving us real time. But - the issue is that when the auditors start pulling on the thread of who has access to what and why, the role structure in Identity doesn't tell a clean story because everything is kind of manually duplicated. Sofia Petrov: That makes sense. So there's almost a compounding problem where the flat role structure creates noise in your compliance reporting even if the underlying access is technically correct. Victor Zheng: Exactly. Yeah, you said it better than I did. Rachel Torres: Okay, that's a really useful framing. Sofia, I want to make sure we capture that for the product feedback - the compliance audit angle specifically, because that might actually bump the priority on this. Sofia Petrov: Agreed, yeah. Victor, is there anything else on the Identity side beyond the role hierarchy piece, or is that the main one? Victor Zheng: There's - yeah there's one other thing. It's maybe a smaller ask, but it's been bugging us. The session timeout policies - right now it seems like you can only set one global timeout, right? There's no way to do it per role or per resource. Sofia Petrov: That's correct, yeah. One global session timeout config right now. Victor Zheng: So what we'd really want is to say - okay, for users accessing our ML training infrastructure, we want a shorter timeout, maybe 30 minutes, because those environments are sensitive. But for, like, someone just accessing our internal wiki through SSO, a four-hour timeout is totally fine. We shouldn't have to apply the most restrictive policy globally. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, that's a reasonable ask. Role-based or resource-based session policies. I don't believe that's on the short-term roadmap but - honestly, Victor, I'm going to be honest, I'd have to check. I don't want to guess. Victor Zheng: No, that's fine, I appreciate the honesty. I'd rather you check than tell me something's coming and it doesn't. Rachel Torres: Yeah, and I'll make sure both of these - the hierarchical roles and the session policy granularity - are written up formally and submitted to product. And I'll loop in your CSM so there's visibility on our end into how this gets prioritized. Victor Zheng: Great. And - look, I want to be clear, I'm not raising this because I'm about to go evaluate alternatives or anything like that. It's more that - we're growing fast, and I want to make sure Aegis Identity can grow with us. If these things get addressed in the next couple of quarters, we're in good shape. Rachel Torres: That's helpful context, Victor, and I appreciate you saying that. It helps us frame the urgency appropriately when we're talking to product. Victor Zheng: Yeah, for sure. One thing I'd also find useful - and maybe Sofia you'd know this - is there a way for us to track these feature requests? Like, is there a customer portal or anything where I can see if something moves from 'requested' to 'in progress'? Sofia Petrov: So right now that kind of visibility goes through your account manager - Rachel's your best touchpoint for that. We don't have a self-serve feature request tracker that's customer-facing, at least not yet. Victor Zheng: Okay, noted. Yeah, that's - that's another thing that would be nice to have someday, but I understand. Rachel Torres: It's fair feedback and I'll pass that along too. Okay, I think we've covered the main items - I'll send you a summary email after this with what we discussed, the two feature requests, and what our next steps are on our end. Does that work? Victor Zheng: Yeah, that works. Thanks both of you - this was a good call. Appreciate the time. Sofia Petrov: Thanks Victor, really helpful to get this context directly from you. Rachel Torres: Absolutely, we'll be in touch. Talk soon.

Mike Romano: Yeah, and to Ravi's point, the architecture review we did back in February specifically called out those failure modes and I think the team addressed them really thoroughly. I feel a lot better about the resilience story on this one. Ananya Sharma: Same. Okay, good. The feature flag means we can instantly revert to v1 behavior without redeploying anything - just flip the flag back. The infrastructure changes are additive, not replacing anything, so the v1 reporting service stays running in parallel until we're confident. We can decommission that after, uh, I was thinking two weeks post-GA. Ananya Sharma: Two weeks sounds right to me. I'll update the runbook today with the alert config action item and the warm-up ping note, and I'll send it around for a final review by EOD Thursday. Does anyone have anything else they want to flag before we wrap up? Mike Romano: Nothing from me. I'm honestly just pumped to ship this. It's been a long road. Ravi Gupta: Same, I'm really proud of what the team put together. This is going to be a good one. Ananya Sharma: Agreed. Okay, let's do it. Thanks everyone - I'll see you in Slack, and Ravi and Nina, I'll let you two coordinate on those alerts. Good call today! Nina Kowalski: Thanks Ananya, talk soon! Mike Romano: Bye everyone.

title: Support Case #6539 - Steelpoint Manufacturing LDAP Sync Failures
summary: Harold Jensen, IT Director at Steelpoint Manufacturing, called regarding a 3-day-old unresolved LDAP sync failure with Aegis Identity affecting 200+ employees on a 24/7 manufacturing floor. Marcus Williams diagnosed the root cause as an SSL handshake failure caused by an internal CA-issued certificate renewed during a maintenance window on March 18th that was not trusted by the Aegis connector. The issue was resolved live on the call by uploading the internal CA root certificate into the Aegis Identity TLS Configuration settings. Harold expressed significant frustration over the slow initial support response and broader confidence concerns about Aegis following a prior Detect outage, and Marcus committed to escalating the response time failure and arranging a follow-up call with the account manager.
transcript_text: Marcus Williams: Thanks for calling Aegis Cloud Security support, this is Marcus Williams, how can I help you today? Harold Jensen: Yeah, hi Marcus, this is Harold Jensen, IT Director over at Steelpoint Manufacturing. I've got a case open - it's case number 6539 - and honestly I'm pretty frustrated at this point because this has been going on for a few days now. Marcus Williams: I completely understand Harold, and I appreciate you calling in. Let me pull up case 6539 right here... okay I'm seeing it, LDAP sync failures with Aegis Identity. Can you walk me through what you're experiencing on your end? Harold Jensen: Sure, so - basically our Active Directory sync through Aegis Identity just stopped working. Users aren't getting provisioned, group memberships aren't syncing, and we've got about, uh, I'd say 200 plus employees who can't get into systems they need access to. This is a manufacturing floor environment, Marcus. People can't do their jobs. Marcus Williams: Yeah, that's - that's a serious impact and I hear you. When did you first notice the sync failures? Do you have an approximate timestamp? Harold Jensen: It started March 19th, around 7 AM our time, Central. And look, I submitted the case that same morning and it took almost 24 hours to get a response, which is not acceptable for something this critical. Marcus Williams: You're right and I - I want to apologize for that response delay, that shouldn't have happened on a case with this kind of operational impact. I'm going to personally own this from here on out. Now, the 19th... let me check something real quick on our end. Harold Jensen: Okay, and while you're doing that - I also want to mention that we had some issues earlier in the month with Aegis Detect, the outage you guys had, and now this. My leadership is starting to ask questions about whether we made the right call going with Aegis and that's a conversation I really don't want to be having. Marcus Williams: I understand, and that's a fair concern. The Detect outage was - yeah, that was a significant incident and I know it affected a lot of customers. We've made infrastructure changes since then. But let's focus on getting your LDAP sync resolved right now because that's what's actively hurting you. So I'm looking at our sync logs for your tenant... Harold Jensen: Right, yeah. Marcus Williams: Okay so I'm seeing a high volume of sync errors starting the 19th, you're correct. The error codes being thrown are mostly - it looks like connection timeout errors and then some authentication failures against your LDAP endpoint. Can you tell me, did anything change in your environment around that time? Any firewall rule updates, certificate rotations, anything like that? Harold Jensen: That's - hm, that's actually a good question. We did have a scheduled maintenance window on the 18th, overnight. Our network team pushed some firewall policy updates. I didn't think that would affect the LDAP connector but... Marcus Williams: Yeah that could absolutely be it. The Aegis Identity LDAP connector needs outbound access on port 389 for standard LDAP or 636 for LDAPS - are you running LDAPS by any chance? Harold Jensen: We are, yeah, we're using LDAPS. Port 636. Marcus Williams: Okay, so there's two things I want to check then. First, can you verify with your network team that port 636 is still open from our connector's IP range? I can send you the current list of Aegis egress IPs. And second - did anything happen with your SSL certificate on the LDAP server during or after that maintenance window? Harold Jensen: I - I'm not sure about the certificate. I'd have to check. But I'll tell you what, this is information that should have been asked three days ago when I first filed the case. I had to chase your team for a response and now we're just starting the basic troubleshooting. Do you understand how that feels from my side? Marcus Williams: Yes, and honestly Harold, you're completely right. There's no excuse for the delay and I'm not going to try to make one. What I can do right now is move fast. Can you get your network team on a quick message while we're talking to check that port 636 egress rule? Harold Jensen: Yeah, let me - hold on, I'm going to ping Dave on our network team right now via Teams. Give me just a second. Marcus Williams: Of course, take your time. And while you're doing that I'm going to look at the specific authentication error details more closely. The error is... okay so it's saying SSL handshake failure. Which actually - Harold, that points more to a certificate issue than a firewall issue. Harold Jensen: Okay, Dave's responding. He says the firewall rules look - yeah he says 636 should be open. So it's not the firewall. Marcus Williams: Right, which is consistent with what I'm seeing. The SSL handshake failure means our connector is trying to establish the encrypted connection and something's going wrong on the certificate side. Two possibilities - either your LDAP server's SSL cert was renewed or changed during maintenance and the new cert isn't trusted by our connector, or the cert expired. Can you have Dave check the certificate on your Active Directory server? Harold Jensen: Okay I'm asking him now... he's checking... oh for the love of - Marcus, he's saying the SSL certificate on the AD server was renewed as part of the maintenance on the 18th and, uh, it looks like it was issued by an internal CA. Would that cause a problem? Marcus Williams: That is exactly the problem. If your certificate was issued by an internal certificate authority, our connector doesn't inherently trust that CA. You need to upload your internal CA's root certificate into Aegis Identity so that we can validate the chain. This is why the handshake is failing. Harold Jensen: Okay so - three days of my people not being able to work because of a certificate. That's - I'm glad we found it but I'm also really annoyed that it took this long. Marcus Williams: I hear that completely. Let me walk you through uploading the CA cert right now so we can get this fixed in the next few minutes. In Aegis Identity, go to Settings, then Directory Connectors, find your LDAP connector and click into it. Harold Jensen: Alright, I'm in Identity, going to Settings... Directory Connectors... okay I see our LDAP connector listed here, it's showing a red status icon. Marcus Williams: Yeah that red status is the sync failure. Click into the connector and you should see a tab called Security or TLS Settings - it might vary slightly depending on your version. Harold Jensen: I see... there's a tab that says TLS Configuration. Is that it? Marcus Williams: Perfect, yes. In there you should see an option to upload a custom CA certificate. You'll need the root CA cert from your internal certificate authority - your team should be able to export that as a PEM or CER file. Harold Jensen: Okay I'm asking Dave to pull that cert. He should have it... yeah he's exporting it now, says he'll have it in a minute. And Marcus - look, while we're waiting - I need to understand why this wasn't documented anywhere. Like shouldn't there be some kind of alert or error message in the UI that says 'hey your certificate is untrusted' instead of just showing a generic sync failure? Marcus Williams: That is a completely valid piece of feedback and honestly you're not the first person to raise that. The current error messaging in the connector is not specific enough and I'm going to log this as product feedback with our Identity team. A more descriptive SSL error message would have made this much faster to diagnose. Harold Jensen: Yeah it would have saved us three days. Okay, Dave just dropped the cert in our shared drive, I'm downloading it now. It's a.cer file, is that going to work? Marcus Williams: CER should work, yep. Go ahead and upload it through that TLS Configuration tab - there should be an Upload Certificate button. Harold Jensen: Uploading... okay it's uploaded. Now do I just save and it'll try to reconnect automatically? Marcus Williams: Hit Save and then there should be a Test Connection button - click that to trigger a manual test before you do a full sync. Harold Jensen: Okay saving... and Test Connection... it's running... Marcus, it says Connection Successful. The status icon just turned green. Marcus Williams: That's what we want to see. Now trigger a manual sync from the sync options and let's make sure user provisioning starts flowing correctly. Harold Jensen: Running manual sync now... okay it's running and I'm already seeing sync events populating. Users are coming through. This looks like it's working. I'm glad it's fixed but I - yeah, I still want to talk about the support response time issue because this cannot happen again. Marcus Williams: Absolutely, and I want to make sure that's addressed. I'm going to escalate the response time failure internally and make sure your account is flagged for priority routing on future cases. I'd also like to set up a brief call with your account manager this week so we can have that broader conversation about your experience, including the Detect outage and now this. Harold Jensen: Yeah, I think that's a good idea. I need someone from Aegis leadership to understand the impact this has had on Steelpoint. We're a 24-7 manufacturing operation - downtime isn't abstract for us, it's real dollars and real people standing around. Marcus Williams: I completely understand that and I will make sure that message gets communicated. I'll document everything in the case notes today and reach out to your account manager to schedule that follow-up. Is there anything else I can help you with right now while I have you? Harold Jensen: No, I think we're - we're good for now. Sync looks like it's running clean. Just make sure those case notes are thorough and that someone actually follows up with me. I've had cases fall through the cracks before. Marcus Williams: You have my word on that Harold. I'll send you a case summary email within the hour and copy your account manager. Thank you for your patience today and again I'm sorry for the trouble this caused. Harold Jensen: Alright. Thanks Marcus. Bye.
