title: Aegis / Ironworks Corp - Vendor Comparison Discussion
summary: Maria Santos met with Catherine Page and Russell Tang to address serious concerns about Aegis following a six-hour monitoring outage in March that affected their manufacturing OT environment, poor communication during the incident, and gaps in compliance reporting functionality. Catherine disclosed that their organization is actively evaluating a competitor, Fortiguard Pro, partly driven by these issues. Maria acknowledged the failures directly, informed the team that Aegis Comply v2 had just launched with improved ISO 27001 reporting, and proposed concrete next steps to rebuild trust. The call ended constructively with the customer open to continuing the relationship provided key commitments are met.
transcript_text: Maria Santos: Hey Catherine, thanks for making time today - I know you mentioned last week things have been pretty hectic on your end. Catherine Page: Yeah, hectic is one word for it. We've got an audit coming up end of May and honestly our whole security stack is under a microscope right now. Maria Santos: Understood, totally get that. And Russell, good to have you on as well - I think this is actually the first time we've spoken directly, right? Russell Tang: Yeah, first time. I've been kind of the one in the weeds on the day-to-day with the platform so Catherine thought it made sense for me to jump on this one. Maria Santos: Absolutely, and honestly I'm glad you're here because I think a lot of what I want to talk through today is going to be pretty technical. So, where do you want to start - should I just sort of set an agenda or do you guys have things you want to get straight to? Catherine Page: I think we should just get into it, Maria. I'll be honest with you - and I don't want this to feel like an ambush - but we've been having some pretty serious conversations internally about whether Aegis is still the right fit for us. Maria Santos: Okay. I appreciate you saying that directly, Catherine. Can you help me understand what's driving that? Is this across the board or is it specific areas? Catherine Page: It's - well, it's a few things. Russell, do you want to start with the Detect stuff since that's kind of where it kicked off? Russell Tang: Sure. So, look - the outage in March. That was a really bad week for us. We're a manufacturing environment, we've got operational technology, we've got floor systems that we're trying to keep visibility on, and for roughly six hours we had nothing. Zero threat monitoring. And I found out about it because one of my guys noticed alerts had stopped coming in, not because Aegis told us. Maria Santos: Yeah, and that's - Russell, I hear you and I want to acknowledge that because that outage was, um, it was a significant failure on our part. The event processing pipeline had a cascading failure and it exposed a single point of failure in our ingestion layer that frankly should not have existed. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Russell Tang: I mean, at least you're saying that. But the communication piece is what really stung. We're paying for a platform that's supposed to be our eyes and ears and we essentially found out through the back door that it was blind. Maria Santos: That's a fair criticism and it's one I've already escalated internally. The post-incident review identified that our customer notification process was too slow and too passive. We've since put in redundant processing nodes and implemented a circuit breaker pattern so that kind of cascade can't happen again, but I also want to be clear - the communication gap was a separate failure and it's one we're actively fixing. Catherine Page: Okay but here's my thing, Maria - and I want you to really hear this - we're in manufacturing. We've got ISO 27001 we're working toward, we've got customers asking us about SOC 2 now, and we cannot have a situation where our security monitoring just goes dark and we don't know about it for hours. That's not a 'we're fixing the process' situation, that's a trust issue. Maria Santos: I completely understand, and I don't want to minimize that. Can I ask - since the remediation went in, have you seen any further gaps or performance issues with Detect specifically? Russell Tang: No, it's been stable since then. But stable for three weeks after a six-hour blackout isn't exactly confidence inspiring, you know? Maria Santos: That's fair. And I'm not asking you to just take my word for it. I can get you a formal RCA document and the engineering team can actually walk you through the architecture changes if that would help rebuild some confidence. Catherine Page: That might actually be useful, yeah. But - and I don't want to just pile on here - there's also the compliance piece. Russell and I were looking at the reporting functionality last quarter and it just felt really... limited? Like we couldn't get the kind of on-demand reporting we needed. Maria Santos: So this is actually something I do want to flag because it's timely - Aegis Comply v2 just went GA last week, on April 7th. And one of the headline features is exactly that - on-demand compliance reporting across SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001. Like, you mentioned ISO 27001 a minute ago, that's now a supported framework. Russell Tang: Wait, when did that launch? Maria Santos: April 7th. So literally last week. I know the timing is - I wish I'd been able to get you a preview of it earlier, that's on me, but the functionality that you were frustrated about should be significantly different now. Catherine Page: Okay well that's... I mean, that would have been helpful to know about sooner. We've been going through this whole evaluation partly because of the compliance reporting gaps. Maria Santos: And I take responsibility for that communication gap on my end. You should have been looped in on the Comply v2 roadmap well before GA. Can I ask - what does the evaluation look like right now? Are you in active conversations with other vendors? Catherine Page: Yeah, we've been talking to Fortiguard Pro. They reached out to us actually, about six weeks ago, and their pitch was pretty compelling especially on the compliance and reporting side. Maria Santos: Okay, good to know. And how far along are those conversations? Catherine Page: We've had two demos and they're putting together a proposal. Russell, what's your read on them technically? Russell Tang: Honestly their UI is cleaner. Alert triage feels a bit more intuitive. But I've got questions about how they handle OT environments specifically because a lot of their case studies seem very IT-centric and we've got Siemens PLCs on the floor that I need visibility on. Maria Santos: That's a really important point and it's actually one of the areas where I think Aegis Detect has genuine depth - the OT and ICS coverage specifically. But I don't want to just tell you that, I'd rather show you. Have you actually stress-tested Fortiguard Pro against your OT environment or is that still pending? Russell Tang: Still pending. Their proposal is supposed to address it but we haven't seen it yet. Maria Santos: Okay. So here's what I'd like to propose - and tell me if this feels like too much - but I'd like to set up a technical session with our OT security specialist and your team specifically around the manufacturing use case, Siemens environment included. And separately, I want to get you into a Comply v2 demo because I genuinely think what you see is going to be different from what you've experienced before. Russell Tang: I mean, I'm open to it. Catherine? Catherine Page: I'm open to it too but I want to be honest - we're not going to be swayed just by demos at this point. The March outage shook our confidence and we need more than a good product presentation to feel like Aegis is the right long-term partner. Does that make sense? Maria Santos: It makes complete sense. And I respect you for saying it that way. What would it take - like, genuinely, what would rebuilding that trust look like for you? I want to understand what success looks like from your side. Catherine Page: Honestly? A few things. We want the RCA documentation Russell mentioned. We'd want some kind of SLA commitment or credit structure for monitoring downtime specifically - not just generic uptime guarantees. And we want to actually see the Comply v2 reporting in action for ISO 27001 because that audit in May is real and we need to be able to produce documentation. Maria Santos: All of that is reasonable and I can work toward all three. The RCA I can get you this week. The SLA conversation I'll need to pull in our account executive and potentially our VP of Customer Success, but I don't think what you're asking for is out of reach. And the Comply v2 demo - I can have that scheduled within the week. Would next Tuesday or Wednesday work? Catherine Page: Wednesday works better for me. Russell? Russell Tang: Wednesday's fine. Maria Santos: Great. I'll get that on the calendar today. And look - I know this call was hard and I appreciate that you came to me directly instead of just going quiet. I'd rather have the honest conversation than find out after the fact that we'd lost you. We've got work to do to earn back your confidence and I'm not taking that lightly. Catherine Page: We appreciate that. Like I said, we're not looking to leave just for the sake of leaving - switching vendors mid-audit cycle would be a nightmare. But we need to feel like Aegis has its house in order. Maria Santos: Understood. I'll follow up with a summary email this afternoon - RCA timeline, the Wednesday Comply v2 demo, and next steps on the SLA discussion. Anything else before we wrap? Russell Tang: No, I think that covers it. Thanks Maria. Catherine Page: Thanks, Maria. Talk soon.
topics: outage, compliance reporting, competitive threat, ot security, trust recovery, sla negotiation
action_items: Maria Santos: Send RCA documentation for the March outage to Catherine and Russell this week | Maria Santos: Schedule Comply v2 demo with ISO 27001 focus for Wednesday and send calendar invite today | Maria Santos: Engage account executive and VP of Customer Success to develop a monitoring-specific SLA and credit structure proposal | Maria Santos: Set up a technical session with the Aegis OT security specialist tailored to the customer's manufacturing and Siemens PLC environment

title: Detect Reliability - 30-Day Review
summary: This 30-day post-incident review covered the March 10-18 Detect module outage, which caused six hours of complete threat monitoring blindness for 47 affected accounts due to a single point of failure in the event ingestion pipeline. The engineering team confirmed fixes including redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern, both deployed by March 29th, with a clean 30-day window since. Customer Success raised concerns about two key accounts - Meridian Financial (August renewal at risk due to compliance audit impact) and Treswick Healthcare (HIPAA documentation concerns) - and the team discussed potential remediation strategies including early access to the Detect telemetry dashboard and a Comply v2 upsell conversation. The team aligned on several follow-up actions including drafting a customer-facing incident summary and improving internal communications protocols.
transcript_text: Tyler Washington: Alright, I think we've got everyone. Diana, Chris, can you both hear me okay? Diana Reeves: Yeah, I'm good. Just pulled up the incident doc so I can follow along. Chris Lee: Same here. Let me get my screen share ready in case we need to walk through the architecture diagram. Tyler Washington: Perfect. So, uh, today's agenda - this is officially the 30-day post-incident review for the Detect outage that happened March 10th through the 18th. We want to cover what happened, where we landed with the fixes, and then Diana, I know you have some customer impact stuff you want to walk through. Diana Reeves: Yeah, exactly. And I want to make sure we have time at the end to talk about messaging, because I'm still getting questions from a few accounts and I need to know what I can and can't say. Chris Lee: Totally fair, we'll get there. Tyler, do you want to just do a quick recap of the root cause first for the record? Tyler Washington: Sure, yeah. So the short version - the event processing pipeline had a single point of failure in the event ingestion layer. What happened was we had a cascading failure that started around 11 PM on the 10th and by about 5 AM on the 11th we had essentially zero threat monitoring visibility for customers on the Detect module. Six hours of complete blindness. Diana Reeves: And just to be clear for this review, this wasn't a security breach, right? Like the data itself was fine, it was just the monitoring layer that went down. Tyler Washington: Correct, yes. No data loss, no unauthorized access. The pipeline that processes incoming threat events just stopped processing. So events were queuing but nothing was being analyzed or alerted on. Diana Reeves: Right, and that distinction actually matters a lot for how some of our customers interpreted it initially. A few of them - I'll get into this later - a few of them thought their environments had been compromised because they stopped seeing alerts. Chris Lee: Yeah, that was... that was a comms problem as much as a technical problem, honestly. Tyler Washington: We can talk about that. Let me just finish the technical recap and then Diana you can take us through the customer side. So, um, root cause confirmed as the single ingestion node - no redundancy, no failover. When that node got overloaded due to a spike in event volume from one of our larger tenants, it effectively took down the whole pipeline. Diana Reeves: And that's fixed now? Like what did we actually ship? Tyler Washington: So we shipped two things. First was redundant processing nodes - we now have three ingestion nodes running in parallel with automatic failover. If one goes down, the other two absorb the load. Second thing was implementing the circuit breaker pattern, which basically means if we detect that a downstream component is failing, the system stops trying to push work to it and routes around it instead of just hammering it until everything collapses. Chris Lee: When did those go live? Tyler Washington: The redundant nodes were deployed March 24th. Circuit breaker pattern was fully validated and in production as of, uh, March 29th I believe. Chris Lee: And we've had no recurrence since then, right? Like the 30-day window has been clean? Tyler Washington: Yeah, clean. We had one minor hiccup on March 31st where latency spiked briefly but the circuit breaker caught it and we never lost visibility. Customers didn't see anything. Diana Reeves: Okay. Good. That's actually - I didn't know about the March 31st thing. Was that documented somewhere? Chris Lee: It's in the internal runbook notes. Probably should have looped you in on that one just as an FYI even though it was a non-event from a customer perspective. Diana Reeves: Yeah, I'd appreciate that going forward. Even if it's just a Slack message saying hey, we had a blip, circuit breaker fired, all good. Just so I'm not getting caught flat-footed if a customer asks. Chris Lee: Noted, that's a fair ask. We'll add that to the on-call runbook - any circuit breaker activation gets a heads up to Customer Success. Diana Reeves: Thank you. Okay so - customer impact. Let me pull up my notes here. So we had... forty-seven accounts on Detect that were affected. Of those, eleven filed formal support tickets during the outage window. Three accounts requested executive briefings afterward. Tyler Washington: Executive briefings - were those with our execs or their execs or both? Diana Reeves: Both, in two cases. One of them was just their CISO wanting to talk to me directly, which was fine. That conversation went okay - they were frustrated but they understood once I explained what actually happened and what the fix looked like. Chris Lee: What about the other two? Diana Reeves: One was Meridian Financial - they're a large account, been with us about two years. Their VP of IT Security was pretty unhappy. They had an internal compliance audit scheduled for March 15th and the fact that they couldn't show continuous monitoring coverage for those six hours was a problem for them. Like a real problem, not just a perception problem. Tyler Washington: That's... yeah, that's rough. Is that audit risk still open for them? Diana Reeves: We provided them with a formal incident report and a letter from our CTO explaining the nature of the outage and the remediation steps. Their auditors apparently accepted it as a documented exception. So it's closed but it left a bad taste. Chris Lee: And what's their renewal situation? Do we know? Diana Reeves: They're up in August. I'm watching it closely. They haven't said anything explicitly threatening but I'm not comfortable with where the relationship is right now. We need a good next few months. Tyler Washington: Is there anything engineering can do to help with that? Like, would it help if we could offer them some kind of enhanced monitoring visibility or a preview of upcoming Detect improvements? Diana Reeves: Actually, yeah, that might be worth exploring. We're planning to roll out the expanded event telemetry dashboard in Q2 anyway - could we get Meridian into a beta or an early access program? Tyler Washington: I'd have to check with product on timeline but I don't see why not. Chris, thoughts? Chris Lee: I think it's doable. The dashboard work is about 60% done. We could have something meaningful to show by mid-May. I'd rather not promise anything before I talk to Priya about the scope but conceptually I'm supportive. Diana Reeves: Okay, let's flag that as a follow-up action. Who owns that conversation with Priya? Chris Lee: I'll take it. I'll ping her today and loop you in on the thread, Diana. Diana Reeves: Great. So the third executive account - that was actually a smaller one, Treswick Healthcare. They were more worried about the regulatory angle, specifically HIPAA. They use Detect as part of their security monitoring for covered systems. Same situation - the gap in monitoring coverage was a documentation headache for them. Tyler Washington: Did we pull the Comply team into that conversation at all? Because, um, actually - today's kind of a relevant day for this. Comply v2 just went GA this morning, right? Chris Lee: Ha, yeah it did. And actually that's kind of relevant because Comply v2 has the on-demand HIPAA reporting. If Treswick was running Comply they could pull an audit trail report that would show, you know, here's exactly what happened and here's the documented gap. That's actually more defensible than us writing a manual letter. Diana Reeves: Are they on Comply currently? Tyler Washington: I don't know off the top of my head. I'd have to check. But if they're not, this might be a moment to have that conversation with them. Diana Reeves: Yeah, I'll look into their contract. That's actually a good angle - turning a service recovery situation into a broader platform conversation. I like that. Chris Lee: Okay, so to wrap up on the action items - Tyler owns the technical documentation for the 30-day review, Chris is going to talk to Priya about the Meridian early access thing, and Diana you're going to check on Treswick's Comply status. Anything else we're missing? Diana Reeves: I want to make sure we have a finalized customer-facing summary of the incident and the resolution. Something I can point people to if they ask. Right now I'm working from my own notes and the internal doc, but I'd like something I can actually share. Chris Lee: Tyler, can you take a pass at drafting that? You've got the technical detail. Keep it non-technical enough for a customer to read but specific enough that it's credible. Tyler Washington: Yeah, I can do that. I'll have a draft to you both by end of week. Diana, do you want to review before it goes anywhere? Diana Reeves: Definitely. Send it to me first, I'll give you feedback on the tone and then we can finalize. I don't need it to go through legal unless Chris thinks it needs to. title: Support Case #7572 - Brightpath Commerce Invoice Discrepancy
summary: Kendra Wallace, CTO of Brightpath Commerce, contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding a $1,400 discrepancy on her February invoice. Marcus Williams identified an overage charge of 2.31 terabytes under the Aegis Protect module, which was traced to a backup policy change made on January 3rd that added five new workloads including database instances. The team clarified that billing is calculated on pre-compression raw data, meaning the policy expansion unintentionally pushed usage over the 10 TB contracted tier. Marcus agreed to document the findings in a case summary and connect Kendra with account manager Devon Park to discuss a potential billing adjustment.

Marcus Williams: Hey there, Marcus Williams, good to be on. Kendra Wallace: Hi Sarah, hi Marcus, this is Kendra Wallace, I'm the CTO over at Brightpath Commerce - thanks for getting this scheduled quickly, I know it's end of month so I appreciate it. Sarah Chen: Of course, yeah, end of month is always a busy time so we wanted to get eyes on this sooner rather than later for you. Marcus Williams: So, just to frame this up - the case notes say you're seeing a discrepancy on your February invoice, is that right? Kendra Wallace: Yes, exactly. So we received the invoice on, I think it was February 20th, and the total came in about fourteen hundred dollars higher than what we were expecting based on our contract. Marcus Williams: Okay, and the contract - is that the renewal you signed back in, uh, Q4 of last year? Kendra Wallace: Yeah, November. We renewed in November and locked in pricing for Aegis Protect and Aegis Detect, those are the two modules we're currently on. Sarah Chen: Got it. And do you have the invoice number handy? I want to pull it up on my end while we're talking. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, one sec - it's INV-2026-0847. Marcus Williams: INV-2026-0847, okay pulling that up now. Sarah Chen: While Marcus is pulling that up, Kendra, can you tell me a little more about what specifically looked off - was it a line item that seemed wrong, or was it more like an unexpected charge category entirely? Kendra Wallace: So there's a line item that says, um, overage charges - data retention overage - and it's for something like 2.3 terabytes. And we just, we weren't expecting that at all. We've been pretty consistent in our data footprint, we're a retail operation, not a huge amount of log volume. Marcus Williams: Okay yeah I see it, I've got the invoice open. The overage charge is listed under Aegis Protect, it's flagging 2.31 terabytes above your contracted tier. Kendra Wallace: Right, and that's what surprised us because we're on the, I believe it's the 10 terabyte tier, and we've never come close to that. Sarah Chen: Yeah, so your contracted limit is 10 TB for Protect - Marcus, can you check what the usage reporting shows for January? That's the billing period this invoice covers. Marcus Williams: Already on it, yeah. So... okay this is interesting. The usage report is showing 12.31 terabytes for the January period, but let me cross-check that against the actual backup logs. Kendra Wallace: And is that, um - is that 12 terabytes compressed or uncompressed? Because I know that can sometimes be the thing. We did actually - our infrastructure team made some changes to our backup policy configuration in, I want to say early January. We added a few additional workloads to the backup scope. Sarah Chen: That would do it, yeah. If you added workloads mid-cycle or even at the start of January, those would count toward the raw ingestion metric for the whole month. Marcus Williams: Let me see if I can pull the backup policy change log for Brightpath's org. Give me just a moment. Kendra Wallace: Sure, no problem. Sarah Chen: And Kendra, while he's doing that - does your team have visibility into the usage dashboard in the portal? Sometimes customers aren't aware that we have a real-time usage tracker under the Protect module settings. Kendra Wallace: Honestly I'm not sure if my team checks that regularly. I'm more on the strategy side, our infrastructure lead would be the one managing that day to day. Sarah Chen: That's fair. It might be worth looping them in after this call - there's also an option to set usage threshold alerts so you get notified before you hit your limit, rather than finding out on the invoice. Kendra Wallace: Yeah that would actually be useful, we'd want that enabled going forward. Marcus Williams: Okay, I've got the change log - so there's a policy update on January 3rd, looks like five new workloads were added to the Brightpath backup scope, and that includes what appears to be a couple of database instances that weren't in the previous config. Is there anything that can be done about the charge given that it was essentially, you know, a configuration thing and not like intentional overuse? Marcus Williams: That's a fair point to raise. I don't have authority to adjust billing charges directly, that would need to go through your account team - but what I can do is document this in the case notes with the full context, the policy change date, the workloads added, so that when your account manager reviews it they have everything they need to make a determination. title: Aegis / Brightpath Commerce - Detect Module Deployment
summary: James Mitchell (AE) and Kendra Wallace (Brightpath) held an onboarding planning call for the Aegis Detect deployment across Brightpath's CloudPrime and Azure environments. They discussed deployment sequencing, timeline (roughly one month end-to-end), and the importance of completing the rollout before Brightpath's spring peak season in late March. Key integrations with PagerDuty and LogVault were confirmed as natively supported, and the system's seven-day observation/baseline mode was highlighted as a solution to Kendra's alert fatigue concerns. A December reliability incident was raised by Kendra and addressed transparently by James, who agreed to share the post-incident report.
transcript_text: James Mitchell: Hey Kendra, thanks for making time today - I know your schedule's been packed. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, it has been, but this is an important one so I made sure to block it off. Good to connect, James. James Mitchell: Absolutely. So the plan for today - I wanted to walk through the Aegis Detect deployment for Brightpath, kind of go over the onboarding steps, talk through your environment specifics, and make sure we're set up for a smooth rollout. Does that work for you? Kendra Wallace: Yeah that works. I've got our infrastructure lead, Marcus, looped in on some of the technical details so I may reference some notes he sent over. He couldn't make the call today unfortunately. James Mitchell: No problem at all, happy to follow up directly with Marcus as well after this. So, just to level-set - Brightpath is running primarily on CloudPrime, correct? With some Azure footprint for certain workloads? Kendra Wallace: That's right. We're about seventy percent CloudPrime, the rest is Azure. We use Azure mainly for some of our analytics pipelines and a couple of internal tools. Core commerce infrastructure - storefront, order management, payments - that's all CloudPrime. James Mitchell: Got it, that's helpful context. Aegis Detect handles both environments natively so that's not a concern, but it does affect how we sequence the deployment. Typically we recommend starting with the primary cloud environment first, getting the agents and event collectors stabilized there, and then extending to the secondary. Kendra Wallace: That makes sense. So CloudPrime first, then we layer in Azure. What's the typical timeline for something like that, for an environment our size? James Mitchell: For a mid-market retail footprint like Brightpath's - and I'm ballparking here based on what you shared in the scoping doc - you're probably looking at two to three weeks for the initial CloudPrime deployment to get to a stable monitored state. Azure would be an additional week, week and a half maybe. Kendra Wallace: Okay so roughly a month end to end. That's... that's workable. We were hoping to have something operational before our spring peak season, which starts ramping up in late March. James Mitchell: Yeah, and that's actually why I wanted to get this call in this week. If we kick off deployment by end of next week, mid-February, we should be comfortably ahead of that window. You'd have at minimum the CloudPrime side fully operational with time to spare. Kendra Wallace: Good. That's good. Okay, so what does the actual kickoff involve? What do we need to prepare on our end? James Mitchell: So the first thing is IAM permissions - we'll need read access to your CloudPrime CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and if you have GuardDuty enabled we'll want to pull from that as well. Our onboarding team will send over a specific permissions template, it's pretty straightforward, a predefined IAM role with least-privilege scoping. Kendra Wallace: We do have GuardDuty running, yes. And CloudTrail is enabled across all regions. VPC Flow Logs - I'd have to check with Marcus on that one, I believe we have them enabled for production VPCs but maybe not all of them. James Mitchell: That's fine, we can work with partial coverage initially and expand. It's not a blocker. The other thing we'll need is a point of contact on your infrastructure team for the technical onboarding sessions - that'd probably be Marcus? Kendra Wallace: Yeah, Marcus Okonkwo, he's our head of cloud infrastructure. I'll make sure he's looped in. He's very hands-on so honestly once you get him the technical docs he'll probably have it half done before the onboarding call even happens. James Mitchell: Ha, I love that type. That makes the process a lot smoother honestly. Okay so - on the Detect side specifically, I want to make sure we talk about alerting configuration because that's usually where onboarding takes the most time. You can get the data flowing pretty quickly, but tuning the alerts so you're not buried in noise - that's the art of it. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, alert fatigue is a real concern for us. Our security team is small - it's two dedicated security engineers plus myself staying involved. We can't have them chasing false positives all day. James Mitchell: Totally understandable, and that's a really common scenario especially in retail where you've got... a lot of legitimate high-volume traffic patterns that can look suspicious if you don't tune for them. Aegis Detect has baseline learning built in - it runs in observation mode for the first seven days and builds a behavioral baseline before it starts generating production alerts. Kendra Wallace: Oh, that's actually - I didn't know that. That's a good feature. So it won't just start firing off alerts the moment it's connected? James Mitchell: Right, exactly. You can override that and go straight to active alerting if you want, but for most customers we recommend the observation period. Gives the system time to understand your normal traffic patterns - your order processing spikes, your batch jobs, whatever recurring patterns you have - and it significantly reduces that initial false positive noise. Kendra Wallace: That's going to make my security team much happier. Okay. What about integrations - we use PagerDuty for incident response, and our logging goes into LogVault. Does Detect play well with those? James Mitchell: Both are supported out of the box. PagerDuty integration is pretty much plug and play - you configure your API key in the Detect settings, map your severity levels to PagerDuty escalation policies, and alerts route through automatically. LogVault is also a native integration, we can push event data and alert context into your existing LogVault indexes. Kendra Wallace: Perfect. That's - yeah that's what we needed to hear. We weren't sure if we'd have to do custom work there. James Mitchell: Nope, no custom development required for either of those. There's a configuration guide in the onboarding portal that walks through it step by step. Marcus should be able to knock that out without too much trouble. Kendra Wallace: Good. Um - okay, I do want to ask about something. I was reading some community forums, I think it was a security subreddit, and someone mentioned there had been some reliability issues with Detect recently? I don't know if that was... accurate or if it was FUD from a competitor or what. James Mitchell: Yeah, I appreciate you bringing that up directly. There was an incident - it was in December, I believe - an event processing issue that caused some monitoring gaps for a period of time. I'd rather be straightforward about it than have you find out through the grapevine. Kendra Wallace: What happened exactly? James Mitchell: The short version is there was a failure in the event ingestion pipeline - a cascading failure that resulted in a single point of failure being exposed. Monitoring visibility was interrupted. Our engineering team identified the root cause and the fix that went in was adding redundant processing nodes and implementing a circuit breaker pattern so that kind of cascading failure can't propagate the same way again. Kendra Wallace: How long was the outage? James Mitchell: It was a few hours. I don't want to give you an imprecise number - I can send you the post-incident report if you want the specifics. We published it internally and shared it with customers. Kendra Wallace: Yeah, please do send that. I'd want to review it and share it with Marcus and our security team. We need to understand the risk profile before we're fully dependent on this for monitoring. James Mitchell: Absolutely, I'll include it in the follow-up email today. And I think it'll give you confidence when you see the remediation steps - the architecture changes are substantial. It wasn't a patch, it was a real structural fix. Kendra Wallace: Okay. I appreciate the transparency on that. It would have been more concerning if you'd tried to brush it off. James Mitchell: Yeah, no - that's not how I operate and it's not how Aegis operates. Issues happen, what matters is how you respond to them. Alright, let me also touch on the onboarding support model so you know what to expect. You'll be assigned a dedicated onboarding engineer - they'll run the technical sessions with Marcus, be available for questions during the deployment, and they stay with you through the first thirty days post go-live. Kendra Wallace: Is that the same person throughout or does it rotate? James Mitchell: Same person throughout the onboarding period, yes. After the thirty days you transition to our standard support team but you'd still have me as your AE point of contact for anything account-level. Kendra Wallace: That's good. Continuity matters. Okay - I think I have what I need for today. What are the concrete next steps coming out of this call? James Mitchell: From my side - I'll send the post-incident report, the IAM permissions template, and the onboarding portal credentials this afternoon. I'll also loop in our onboarding team to schedule the kickoff session with Marcus, aiming for early next week. From your side, if you can confirm Marcus as the technical contact and maybe do a quick check on those VPC Flow Log configurations, that'd set us up well. Kendra Wallace: I can do that. I'll send you Marcus's contact info after this call and I'll let him know to expect outreach. He'll probably want to get on a call with your onboarding engineer before the formal kickoff just to go through architecture questions. James Mitchell: Perfect, we can absolutely set that up. I'll make sure the onboarding engineer knows to expect a technically detailed conversation - in a good way. Kendra Wallace: Ha. Yeah, Marcus doesn't do surface-level. Alright James, I think this was a good call. Let's get moving on this. James Mitchell: Agreed. You'll have everything from me by end of day. Thanks Kendra, talk soon. Kendra Wallace: Thanks, bye.
topics: onboarding, deployment planning, alert fatigue, reliability incident, cloud infrastructure, integrations
action_items: James Mitchell: Send post-incident report, IAM permissions template, and onboarding portal credentials to Kendra by end of day | James Mitchell: Loop in onboarding team to schedule kickoff session with Marcus Okonkwo, targeting early next week | Kendra Wallace: Send Marcus Okonkwo's contact information to James and notify Marcus to expect outreach from the onboarding team | Kendra Wallace: Check with Marcus on VPC Flow Log configuration coverage across all production environments

title: All Hands - April Update
summary: The team held an April all-hands covering three main topics: a retrospective on the March Detect outage, the Comply v2 launch status, and Q2 roadmap planning. The Detect outage post-mortem revealed a single point of failure in the ingestion layer that caused a six-hour customer-facing blackout, with redundant nodes and a circuit breaker pattern now deployed but a chaos engineering validation still needed. Comply v2 launched on April 7th with multi-framework compliance reporting and is showing early positive adoption, though two open bugs remain around PDF formatting and concurrent report timeouts. For Q2, the team agreed to prioritize reliability and observability work on Detect over new features, deferring pure feature additions to Q3.
transcript_text: Ravi Gupta: Alright, I think we've got most people on now - Hannah, you there? Hannah Liu: Yeah, I'm here, sorry - just had another call run long. Ravi Gupta: No worries, Ananya and Alex are on, Nina just joined - okay good, let's just get started. Nina Kowalski: Morning everyone. Alex Reyes: Hey Nina. Hannah Liu: Okay so, uh, this is the April all-hands update - I sent the agenda doc around yesterday, hopefully everyone had a chance to at least skim it. Ananya Sharma: I looked at it this morning, yeah. Ravi Gupta: Same, I skimmed most of it. Hannah Liu: Okay great. So I want to cover a few things - we'll do a quick retrospective on the March Detect outage, then talk about the Comply v2 launch, and then get into Q2 planning for the roadmap. Should take us under an hour. Nina Kowalski: Works for me. Hannah Liu: So starting with Detect - Ravi, do you want to walk us through where we landed on the post-mortem? Ravi Gupta: Sure, yeah. So, uh, for those who maybe weren't as close to it - the outage ran roughly six hours in mid-March, March 10th through the 18th was the window where we were seeing instability, but the main event was that six-hour gap on the 10th where the event ingestion pipeline just... collapsed. Ananya Sharma: Right and that was a cascading failure, not a single point thing - or, well, it started as a single point of failure and then cascaded, right? Ravi Gupta: Exactly, yeah. The root cause was we had a single point of failure in the ingestion layer - one node goes down, nothing has a fallback, and then the backpressure just propagates upstream and the whole thing falls over. Alex Reyes: And customers had zero visibility into their threat monitoring for that whole window? Ravi Gupta: Yeah, effectively. Alerts weren't firing, the dashboard was showing stale data - it was not great. Hannah Liu: I know customer success had a rough week after that. I got looped into like three customer escalations. Nina Kowalski: So what's the fix look like at this point? I know we deployed something but I'm not clear on the details. Ananya Sharma: So we went with redundant processing nodes and we implemented the circuit breaker pattern on the ingestion side. Basically if one node degrades past a threshold, traffic gets rerouted before it can cascade. It's been stable since we pushed that. Nina Kowalski: Has QA validated that path? Like have we actually tested a node failure scenario end to end? Ananya Sharma: We did a tabletop sim, yeah. The ISO 27001 one in particular, that was a gap for us before, and we're seeing uptake there. Hannah Liu: What about new logo deals? Has it moved any pipeline? Alex Reyes: Sales is pointing to a couple of deals where it was a factor - I don't want to overstate it, it's early. But the positioning against, say, VaultEdge on compliance reporting is cleaner now. That was always a weak spot. Ravi Gupta: Yeah VaultEdge was beating us on that pretty consistently in competitive deals from what I heard. Hannah Liu: Okay, any known issues post-launch? Nina, anything from QA's perspective that's still open? Nina Kowalski: There are two open items - one is a formatting inconsistency on the PCI DSS export, it's a PDF rendering thing, not a data accuracy issue, but it looks sloppy. And then there's a minor edge case on the multi-framework run where if you queue more than three reports simultaneously it occasionally times out. Ananya Sharma: Is the timeout one reproducible consistently or is it intermittent? Nina Kowalski: Intermittent, maybe... two out of five tries? It's not consistent but it's frequent enough that we should fix it before we start pushing the concurrent reporting use case in marketing. Hannah Liu: Okay that's fair. Ananya, can you take the timeout bug? And I'll get the PDF formatting thing assigned to someone on the front-end side. Ananya Sharma: Yeah I'll pick it up, I want to look at the queue handling anyway - there might be a broader issue there. Hannah Liu: Alright. Let's jump into Q2 planning. Ravi Gupta: On Detect - I want to flag that we should be careful about piling too much onto that module right now. The team just went through a really stressful period and we're still stabilizing. Ravi Gupta: I know, but pushing features at the expense of reliability work seems like the wrong call after what just happened. Hannah Liu: Can we try to split the difference? I'll send out a summary with the action items - Ravi on the chaos engineering scope, Ananya on the timeout bug, and the Q2 prioritization framework. Thanks everyone. Ravi Gupta: Thanks Hannah. Ananya Sharma: Thanks, talk soon.

title: Support Case #3266 - Trailhead Marketplace Detect Alerts Not Firing
summary: Isaac Brennan, infrastructure lead at Trailhead Marketplace, called Aegis Cloud Security support in frustration over a complete 15+ hour outage of Aegis Detect's event processing pipeline, leaving his retail platform blind to threats. Elena Vasquez and David Kim confirmed the issue is platform-wide, stemming from a cascading failure in the event ingestion layer, with no confirmed ETA for resolution. Isaac expressed serious concern about PCI compliance and fraud exposure during the outage, and was particularly upset that no proactive communication had been sent despite his status page subscription. Elena escalated the case to P1, committed to a two-hour update, and logged a formal request for a full written incident report by end of week. Isaac warned that the future of the contract depends on how the situation is handled in the next 24 hours.
transcript_text: Elena Vasquez: Hi, thanks for calling Aegis Cloud Security support, this is Elena Vasquez, I have my colleague David Kim on the line with me as well - how can we help you today? title: Competitive Landscape Review
summary: Jordan Whitfield and Tom Bradley conducted a competitive landscape review in preparation for an upcoming product review meeting. They discussed four key competitors: SentinelShield (threatening Detect with a strong SIEM integration story), VaultEdge (a growing threat to Protect and potentially Comply), CyberNova (aggressive pricing in Identity for mid-market), and Fortiguard Pro (a legacy incumbent). The most pressing concern identified was a gap in the LogVault connector experience compared to SentinelShield, which Jordan plans to surface as a risk item for leadership at next week's review. Jordan agreed to update and share the competitive deck before EOD the following day.
transcript_text: Jordan Whitfield: Hey Tom, you there? I think you might be on mute. Tom Bradley: Oh, yeah sorry, I was - yeah, I had myself muted. Can you hear me now? Jordan Whitfield: Yeah, loud and clear. Okay cool, so I figured we should probably carve out some time to actually go through the competitive landscape before the product review next week, because I feel like we've been kind of operating on vibes a little bit. Tom Bradley: Yeah no, agreed. I got the deck you sent over this morning. Hadn't had a chance to fully go through it but I did skim the section on SentinelShield. That one stood out to me. Jordan Whitfield: Right, yeah. So that's kind of where I wanted to start actually, because they've been showing up more in deal cycles lately. I've been hearing that from the sales team - like Marcus's team specifically flagged them twice in the last month. Tom Bradley: Mm. What's the - what's the pitch they're running? Like what's SentinelShield leading with? Jordan Whitfield: So from what I've been able to piece together - and some of this is from public stuff, some of it is from what reps are hearing in calls - they're leading pretty hard on the SIEM integration story. Like native integrations with LogVault, with Nextera Sentinel, and they're positioning that as kind of a no-rip-and-replace approach. Tom Bradley: Okay. And how does that actually compare to what we have in Detect right now? Jordan Whitfield: Honestly? We're not as strong there. We have the LogVault connector but it's - it's kind of janky, right? I know the team has been working on it but I don't think it's at parity with what SentinelShield is showing in demos. Tom Bradley: Yeah I'd push back on calling it janky, but... it's not polished. The connector works, the issue is more around the configuration experience. There's like a lot of manual steps that honestly shouldn't be manual. Jordan Whitfield: Okay, that's a fair distinction. But from a buyer's perspective, right, if they're seeing a slick demo from SentinelShield where it's like, here's our three-click setup, and then they're talking to us and there's like a six-page config guide... that's a perception gap regardless of whether the underlying tech is actually better. Tom Bradley: Sure, yeah. That's fair. I don't disagree with that. We've got it on the roadmap but it's been deprioritized a couple times because of other things that were more urgent. Jordan Whitfield: Right, okay. So let's - let's park SentinelShield for a second and talk about VaultEdge, because I think they're a different kind of threat. They're not really going after Detect, they're going after Protect. Tom Bradley: Yeah, backup and recovery. What are you seeing from them? Jordan Whitfield: So VaultEdge is making a lot of noise about their RTO and RPO numbers. They're claiming like sub-fifteen-minute recovery times for enterprise workloads, which, I mean, that's a pretty aggressive claim. Tom Bradley: Mm-hmm. Do we know if that's, like, validated anywhere or is that just marketing? Jordan Whitfield: I mean, it's mostly marketing as far as I can tell. There's one Gartner Peer Insights review that kind of backs it up but it's a single data point. What I think is more interesting is that they're starting to bundle in some compliance reporting features, which starts to get adjacent to what we're doing with Comply. Tom Bradley: Oh that's - yeah, that's worth watching. Like, are they doing real compliance reporting or is it more like checkbox stuff? Jordan Whitfield: From what I can see it's pretty surface level right now. Like they're doing some basic audit log exports, maybe some pre-built report templates. But it's not - it doesn't seem like a serious compliance play yet. But the concern is they're moving in that direction. Tom Bradley: Right. Well, the good news there is we've got a lot coming with Comply in the next couple months. I don't want to get too deep into roadmap stuff but the on-demand reporting capabilities are going to be a significant step up from what we have today. Jordan Whitfield: Yeah, I know. And I think that's going to be a strong differentiator. I just want to make sure we're timing the competitive messaging right, because if VaultEdge is building toward this space, we want to be out front before they get there. Tom Bradley: Agreed. Okay, what about CyberNova? I feel like I don't have a great read on them. Jordan Whitfield: Yeah so CyberNova is kind of the interesting one. They're not - they don't have the brand recognition of SentinelShield, they're smaller. But they've been very aggressive on pricing, like significantly undercutting on Identity specifically. And they've got a decent SSO story. Tom Bradley: How are they on MFA? Because that's where we tend to have more depth. Jordan Whitfield: MFA is where they fall down a bit, from what I can tell. They support the standard stuff - TOTP, push notifications - but they don't have the hardware key support or the adaptive authentication policies that we have in Identity. So like, for mid-market it might be a closer call, but for enterprise buyers who care about that stuff, we're still in a good position. Tom Bradley: Okay. And then Fortiguard Pro - I mean, they're a different category of competitor really, aren't they? Like they're so broad. Jordan Whitfield: Yeah, Fortiguard Pro is more of a legacy incumbent situation. They show up in deals but usually in larger enterprises that already have a relationship with them. The main thing I hear is that customers who are using Fortiguard are often frustrated with the complexity and the cost of professional services to do anything. So our consolidation play works well against them. Tom Bradley: Right, the platform story. Yeah. Okay so if I'm summarizing - SentinelShield is the most immediate threat in Detect, VaultEdge is one to watch in Protect and potentially Comply, CyberNova is a pricing threat in Identity for mid-market, and Fortiguard is the big incumbent we're differentiating against on simplicity. Jordan Whitfield: Yeah, that's roughly the picture. And I think the thing I want to flag for next week's review is that the LogVault connector thing - like, the SentinelShield gap - is probably the most actionable near-term thing we should be thinking about prioritizing. Tom Bradley: I hear you on that. I'm going to push back a little though, because engineering bandwidth right now is pretty constrained, and I don't want to make commitments that we can't actually back up with capacity. Jordan Whitfield: No, that's fair. I'm not asking you to commit to anything today. I just think we need to at least surface it as a risk in the review so that leadership has visibility into the tradeoff. Tom Bradley: Yeah, okay. I can get behind that framing. Surface the gap, let the conversation happen at the right level, and then we see what prioritization shakes out. Jordan Whitfield: Exactly. Okay, I think that's probably enough to work with for now. I'll clean up the deck, add a summary slide with that competitive matrix you basically just articulated, and share it before EOD tomorrow. Tom Bradley: Sounds good. Yeah, send it over and I'll take a proper look before the review. Appreciate you pulling this together. Jordan Whitfield: Yeah of course. Alright, talk soon. Tom Bradley: Yep, take care.
topics: competitive analysis, product gaps, siem integration, compliance features, pricing pressure, roadmap prioritization
action_items: Jordan Whitfield: Clean up the competitive deck, add a summary slide with the competitive matrix, and share before EOD tomorrow | Tom Bradley: Review the updated deck thoroughly before the product review meeting next week | Jordan Whitfield: Frame the LogVault connector gap as a risk item for leadership visibility in the product review | Tom Bradley: Assess engineering bandwidth feasibility around improving the LogVault connector configuration experience

title: Aegis / Nova Retail Group - Renewal Discussion
summary: Aisha Johnson (CSM) met with Stephanie Blair from Nova Retail ahead of their end-of-next-month renewal to assess account health. Stephanie expressed significant frustration stemming from a six-hour Aegis Detect outage on March 10th, ongoing compliance reporting pain in Aegis Comply, dashboard signal-to-noise issues, and a slow support ticket resolution. She disclosed that Nova is actively evaluating competitor SentinelShield, having completed two demos. Aisha acknowledged accountability, outlined technical remediation steps taken post-outage, previewed the upcoming Aegis Comply v2 launch with on-demand compliance reporting, and committed to a set of concrete follow-up actions to help Stephanie rebuild confidence for the renewal.
transcript_text: Aisha Johnson: Hi Stephanie, thanks for making time today - I know you've got a lot going on. Stephanie Blair: Yeah, it's been a week, honestly. But yeah, I wanted to have this conversation so, here we are. Aisha Johnson: I appreciate it. So, um, I wanted to reach out specifically because your renewal is coming up at the end of next month and I just - I want to make sure we're in a good place and that you're getting value out of the platform. Stephanie Blair: Aisha, I'll be straight with you. We're not in a great place right now. And I think you probably know why. Aisha Johnson: The outage. Stephanie Blair: Yes. The outage. We had six hours - six hours - where we had zero visibility into our threat environment. Do you understand what that means for a retail operation our size? We're processing transactions, we've got customer data, we've got POS systems across 200-plus locations. Six hours is not a blip, Aisha. That's a liability. Aisha Johnson: I completely understand, and I want to be very clear - I'm not here to minimize what happened. The Aegis Detect outage on March 10th was serious, and I know it hit a lot of our customers hard, but frankly, a customer like Nova with your threat surface, I - yeah, I know it was especially painful. Stephanie Blair: Painful is one word for it. Our CISO was asking me why we were paying for threat monitoring that wasn't monitoring anything. And honestly I didn't have a good answer. Aisha Johnson: That's a really hard position to be in and I'm sorry you were put there. Can I - can I share what we've actually done in response? Because I don't want this to feel like a PR answer but I do think the remediation work is meaningful. Stephanie Blair: Go ahead. Aisha Johnson: So the root cause was a single point of failure in our event ingestion pipeline. Essentially when one node got overwhelmed it cascaded. What we've done since is deploy redundant processing nodes across the pipeline and implement a circuit breaker pattern so that if one component starts failing it doesn't bring down the whole system. We've also increased our alerting thresholds so our on-call team gets flagged much earlier. Stephanie Blair: Okay, but - and I say this with all due respect - why wasn't that architecture in place to begin with? That's not a novel engineering concept. Circuit breakers, redundancy, these are table stakes for a platform that's supposed to be enterprise-grade. Aisha Johnson: You're right. And I don't have a satisfying answer for that. It's a gap that shouldn't have existed and it did and we're - we're accountable for that. Stephanie Blair: I appreciate the honesty at least. Look, we've been with Aegis for - what is it, almost three years now? This isn't coming from a place of just wanting to switch for the sake of switching. But I do have to make decisions that I can defend to my board and to our security team. Aisha Johnson: Of course. And that's exactly the kind of conversation I want to have. What - what are the specific things that would need to be true for you to feel confident going into a renewal? Stephanie Blair: Well, a few things. One is obviously the reliability concern we just talked about. Two is - and this has been a slow-burn frustration for us - our compliance reporting situation. We are under PCI DSS obligations, we've got some HIPAA-adjacent data from our pharmacy locations, and right now generating those reports out of Aegis Comply is... it's manual, it's painful, it takes my team days to pull together what should be a few clicks. Aisha Johnson: Okay, that's - that's actually really important feedback and I want to come back to that specifically because there's something relevant there. What's the third thing? Stephanie Blair: The third thing is that we've been talking to SentinelShield. And I want to be transparent about that because I think you deserve to know. Aisha Johnson: I appreciate you telling me that. How far along are those conversations? Stephanie Blair: We've had two demos. We haven't asked for a formal proposal yet, but we're close. Their threat detection coverage looks solid and they made a pretty compelling case for their uptime SLAs, which given everything is - yeah, it's on our radar. Aisha Johnson: Understood. And I'm not going to sit here and trash SentinelShield, that's not my style. But I do want to make sure you have the full picture on where we are and where we're going, because I think some of what you've described - especially on the compliance side - is actually about to change significantly. Stephanie Blair: What do you mean? Aisha Johnson: So Aegis Comply v2 is launching on April 7th - which I know is after your renewal window opens, so I want to be upfront about that - but it includes on-demand reporting for PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Multi-framework, no manual aggregation, you can pull a report in real time. The workflow your team is dealing with today basically goes away. Stephanie Blair: On-demand meaning... what exactly? Because I've heard 'on-demand' from vendors before and it means 'we queued your report and it'll be ready in four hours.' Aisha Johnson: Ha - fair. No, I mean genuinely on-demand. The data's already being ingested and mapped against the control frameworks continuously, so when you click generate, you're getting a live report. We're talking minutes, not hours. I can get you into a preview environment if that would help you evaluate it before the decision. Stephanie Blair: That would actually be useful. My compliance lead has been pulling her hair out over this so - yeah, let's do that. Aisha Johnson: Great, I'll set that up. Now I also - going back to the SentinelShield piece - I want to ask you something directly. Is the Detect outage the primary driver here or is it more of a cumulative frustration thing? Because those are kind of different problems. Stephanie Blair: Honestly? It's both. The outage was the thing that made this feel urgent. But if I'm being real with you, we've had some grumbles about support response times, about the Detect dashboard being a bit clunky for our team, and the compliance stuff has been a background annoyance for a while. So it all kind of... crystallized. Aisha Johnson: That makes a lot of sense. And I don't want to dismiss any of those. The dashboard feedback - can you tell me more about what specifically feels clunky? Is it the alert triage flow, the filtering, or something else? Stephanie Blair: Um, it's mostly the alert volume and the signal-to-noise ratio. We're getting flagged on things that are clearly not threats for our environment and then when something real comes through it can get buried. My SOC analyst - she actually flagged this to your support team back in January and I don't think she got a satisfying resolution. Aisha Johnson: I'm going to pull that ticket after this call and personally follow up. That should not have been left unresolved for two months. I'm sorry about that. Stephanie Blair: I'd appreciate that. Look, Aisha, I want to be clear - I'm not trying to be difficult here. I actually like working with you and I think the Aegis platform has genuinely helped us. But I have to be able to justify this to leadership and right now the story has some holes in it. Aisha Johnson: I hear you. And I think that's completely fair. So let me propose this - I'll set up the Comply v2 preview with you and your compliance lead, I'll personally chase down that support ticket and get you a resolution, and I'd also like to put together a written summary of the Detect remediation steps with our updated SLA commitments so you have something concrete to bring to your CISO. Does that seem like a reasonable set of next steps? Stephanie Blair: Yeah, that seems reasonable. I'd also want to have a conversation about whether there's any flexibility on the commercial side given... everything. I'm not saying that's a dealbreaker but it's something I'd need to at least explore. Aisha Johnson: Absolutely, and I'll loop in my account executive on that piece. I want to make sure if we're talking numbers we're having the right conversation. I don't want to throw something out without being able to back it up properly. Stephanie Blair: That works. Okay. I think - I came into this call pretty frustrated, so I'll give you credit, this was a more useful conversation than I expected. Aisha Johnson: I'm glad. And Stephanie, genuinely - I want to earn the renewal, not just retain the contract. There's a difference and I take that seriously. Stephanie Blair: I appreciate that. Alright, send me the calendar invite for the Comply preview and I'll get Sarah from our compliance team on it. Aisha Johnson: Will do. I'll have something out to you by end of day Monday. Thanks again for being so direct with me today, it actually helps me help you. Stephanie Blair: Yep. Talk soon.
topics: renewal, service outage, compliance reporting, churn risk, competitive evaluation, product feedback
action_items: Aisha Johnson: Set up Aegis Comply v2 preview environment for Stephanie and her compliance lead Sarah before the renewal decision | Aisha Johnson: Pull and personally resolve the unresolved January support ticket regarding Detect alert signal-to-noise from Stephanie's SOC analyst | Aisha Johnson: Prepare a written summary of Detect remediation steps and updated SLA commitments for Stephanie's CISO | Aisha Johnson: Loop in account executive to explore commercial flexibility and set up a pricing conversation with Stephanie

title: Aegis / Bridgeport Health - Compliance Review
summary: Maria Santos and Solutions Architect Kevin O'Brien met with Evelyn Park to discuss her organization's compliance challenges ahead of a HIPAA audit in late May/early June. Evelyn's team has been using Aegis Comply for eight months primarily for SOC 2, but identified gaps in HIPAA support and frustration with treating multiple frameworks as separate workstreams. Kevin outlined near-term technical recommendations including evidence library restructuring and PHI access logging, while previewing the upcoming Comply v2 multi-framework feature that would allow single evidence items to map across HIPAA, SOC 2, and other frameworks simultaneously. The call concluded with plans to schedule a Comply v2 preview session and for Kevin to deliver a SOC 2 to HIPAA control mapping document.
transcript_text: Maria Santos: Evelyn, hi! Thanks so much for making time today, I know your calendar's been absolutely packed. Evelyn Park: Maria, are you kidding? I've been looking forward to this one. We've got a lot to catch up on. Maria Santos: That's great to hear. And I also have Kevin O'Brien on the line with me today - he's one of our Solutions Architects, and he's been deep in the weeds on everything Comply-related, so I wanted to bring him in for this one. Kevin O'Brien: Hey Evelyn, really glad to be here. I've been doing a lot of work with healthcare customers lately so hopefully I can add some useful context. Evelyn Park: Perfect, love that. Kevin, welcome. And yeah, compliance has just been - it's been front and center for us this quarter, so the timing of this call is actually really good. Maria Santos: So maybe let's just start there - what's been driving the urgency on the compliance side? Is it an upcoming audit, internal pressure, or...? Evelyn Park: It's honestly a little bit of everything. Maria Santos: That's a lot of moving pieces all at once. Evelyn Park: Yeah, it really is. And the honest truth is, our current compliance reporting process is - it's painful. We're still pulling together spreadsheets, chasing down evidence from like six different teams, and by the time we have a report ready it's already out of date. Kevin O'Brien: Okay yeah, that's a really common pain point we hear, especially in healthcare orgs at your scale. Can I ask - are you currently using Aegis Comply at all, or is this more exploratory? Evelyn Park: We are using it, we've been on it for about eight months now. We're using it primarily for SOC 2 right now, and it's been - honestly it's been a night and day difference from what we were doing before. But HIPAA specifically, that's where we feel like there are gaps. Kevin O'Brien: That makes a lot of sense. So the SOC 2 workflow is working well for you - that's great to hear. And the HIPAA gap, is that more about the framework mapping itself, or is it the evidence collection, or...? Evelyn Park: It's kind of both, if I'm being honest. Like, I can see where controls overlap between SOC 2 and HIPAA in theory, but the platform right now makes me basically treat them as two completely separate workstreams. And that's just - that's not sustainable for my team. Maria Santos: Right, right. And that's actually - Kevin, do you want to jump in here? Because I think what Evelyn's describing is exactly what we've been building toward. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, absolutely. So Evelyn, this is something we've heard from a lot of customers in healthcare and financial services, and it's something the product team has been heads-down on. Without getting too far ahead of ourselves, what's coming in the Comply v2 roadmap is really designed to address exactly this - multi-framework support where a single piece of evidence can map across HIPAA, SOC 2, and other frameworks simultaneously. Evelyn Park: Oh that's - okay, tell me more about that. Because if I can collect evidence once and have it satisfy controls across multiple frameworks, that would be... I mean that would be huge for us. Kevin O'Brien: That's exactly the idea. So instead of your team going to three different places for three different audits, you'd have one unified evidence library and the platform handles the cross-framework mapping for you. Maria Santos: And I know you mentioned the board asking more questions too - one thing that's really exciting about where Comply is going is the reporting side. Like, being able to generate an on-demand report for a board meeting rather than spending a week pulling it together manually. Evelyn Park: Oh gosh, yes. Our last board presentation, I kid you not, my team spent four days on the compliance section alone. Four days. That's time we're not spending on actual security work. Maria Santos: Yeah that's - that's a real cost, right? And it's hard to quantify sometimes but when you think about your team's time and attention, it adds up fast. Evelyn Park: Totally. And honestly, one of the things I really appreciate about Aegis Comply versus what we looked at with some other vendors - I think VaultEdge was one - is that your framework actually integrates with our cloud environment natively. We're not just uploading PDFs and checking boxes. Kevin O'Brien: That's a really important distinction and I'm glad it's landing that way. The native integration piece is something we've invested in heavily, especially for healthcare customers where you've got such a complex environment - different EHR systems, cloud workloads, on-prem infrastructure... Evelyn Park: Exactly, yeah. We've got Epic, we've got Azure, we've got a couple of legacy on-prem systems that we're slowly migrating, so getting all of that into one compliance view has been... a journey. Maria Santos: A journey, I love that. Very diplomatic. So, in terms of the HIPAA audit prep - when is the actual audit, do you know yet? Evelyn Park: We're looking at late May, early June. Evelyn Park: The Detect integration - yeah, that's been working really well actually. Maria, is that something we could arrange? Maria Santos: Absolutely, yeah. Evelyn, I think we could set up a preview session - we've been doing that with a handful of strategic customers and the feedback has been really positive. Would that be useful for you? Evelyn Park: Yes, please. That would be - yeah, that's exactly what I want. Even just to be able to show my team what's coming so they can see there's a light at the end of the tunnel. Maria Santos: I love that framing. Okay, so let me think about next steps - I'll follow up with you on scheduling that Comply v2 preview, and Kevin, can you send over a framework mapping document that shows the SOC 2 to HIPAA control overlap? Something Evelyn's team can actually use as a working guide. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, for sure. I'll put together a healthcare-specific version of that, pull in some of the PHI-related controls specifically. I'll have it to Maria by end of next week. Evelyn Park: That would be incredibly helpful. My compliance lead, she's going to be very happy when I forward that to her. Maria Santos: And one more thing - Evelyn, you mentioned PCI earlier, or actually I think it was... wait, no, you didn't mention PCI. Sorry, I was thinking of another customer. Are PCI requirements on your radar at all or is it really just HIPAA and SOC 2? Evelyn Park: No, PCI isn't really relevant for us on the clinical side. We do have some billing systems but those go through a third-party processor so we're mostly scoped out. HIPAA and SOC 2 are the big two. Maria Santos: Got it, good to know. Okay, I think we've covered a lot of ground today. Evelyn, any other questions or concerns you want to make sure we address before we wrap up? Evelyn Park: Honestly, no - I feel really good about where this is heading. I was a little nervous going into this call because Q2 feels like it's sneaking up on me, but talking through it, I think we've got a solid plan. I really appreciate you both making time. Maria Santos: Of course! That's what we're here for. And Evelyn, seriously, your team has done great work getting to where you are with the platform in eight months. A lot of organizations take much longer to get to this point. Evelyn Park: Thank you, that means a lot. Alright, I'll keep an eye out for Kevin's framework doc and the preview session invite. Looking forward to it. Maria Santos: Perfect. We'll be in touch soon. Thanks everyone, take care!

title: ESCALATION: Northstar Pharma - Detect Outage Impact on Compliance
summary: Aegis Cloud Security support rep Elena Vasquez spoke with Grace Yoon and Frank Delaney (VP of IT) of Northstar, a pharmaceutical company, regarding a platform-wide outage of the Aegis Detect event processing pipeline that had been ongoing for approximately nine to ten hours. The customer was never proactively notified of the outage, which Elena acknowledged as a serious communication failure. The outage is particularly critical because Northstar handles HIPAA-regulated patient data and is currently in a SOC 2 audit cycle, creating potential compliance findings. transcript_text: Elena Vasquez: Thank you for holding, this is Elena Vasquez from Aegis Cloud Security senior support, I have your case pulled up here - am I speaking with Grace?
