title: Aegis / Helix Data - Post-Incident Review
summary: Maria Santos and Kevin O'Brien from Aegis held an urgent call with Charles Ng from Helix to address a six-hour outage in their threat monitoring pipeline caused by a single point of failure in the event ingestion system. Charles expressed significant frustration that his team was not alerted for nearly two hours and had to manually audit logs afterward, costing 12-15 person-hours. He disclosed that Helix is actively reviewing their security vendor stack and has been in conversations with competitor VaultEdge, citing both the outage and ongoing concerns about false positive alert noise and cumbersome custom rule configuration. The Aegis team committed to delivering a technical remediation brief for Charles's CTO, scheduling a detection tuning session, and presenting a broader make-right proposal before a follow-up call mid-next week with Helix's security lead Priya.
transcript_text: Maria Santos: Alright, I think we're all on now - Charles, can you hear us okay? Charles Ng: Yeah, I'm here. Audio's fine on my end. Maria Santos: Great. And Kevin just joined too, so we're all set. Charles, thanks for making time - I know this week has probably been, uh, a lot for your team. Charles Ng: Yeah, 'a lot' is one way to put it, Maria. It's been a rough few days, honestly. Maria Santos: Completely understood. And that's exactly why we wanted to get on a call sooner rather than later - not just to send an email but actually, you know, sit down and walk through what happened and where we go from here. Kevin, you want to kick us off with the technical summary? Kevin O'Brien: Sure, yeah. So, Charles, first - I just want to say I'm sorry. Your team should not have experienced what happened, and I want to be straightforward with you about the root cause. What we had was essentially a single point of failure in our event ingestion pipeline. One component went down and, uh, it cascaded. It took the whole processing layer with it. Charles Ng: Right, so for - what was it, six hours? - we had zero threat monitoring visibility. None. Our security team was flying blind. Kevin O'Brien: That's correct. Six hours, approximately. And I - yeah, there's no softening that. That's a significant window. Maria Santos: Kevin, can you tell him what the fix looks like? Because I think that's important context. Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, absolutely. So we've already implemented redundant processing nodes - so there's no longer a single point of failure in that ingestion layer. And we've also put a circuit breaker pattern in place, which means if one node starts degrading, it gets isolated before it can take down the rest of the pipeline. This is already in production as of this morning. Charles Ng: Okay. And I appreciate you explaining that, Kevin, I do. But - and I want to be honest with you both here - that doesn't fully address my concern. The concern isn't just what caused it. It's that it happened at all, and that we didn't know it was happening until almost two hours in. Maria Santos: That's a fair point, Charles. Charles Ng: Two hours before we got any notification. My team was the one who flagged it to your support desk. We noticed our dashboards had gone stale before Aegis even sent us an alert. That's - I mean, that's backwards. A threat monitoring product should be monitoring itself. Kevin O'Brien: You're absolutely right, and that's - honestly, that's the part that stings the most from our side too. The alerting on the internal failure was not working the way it should have. That's a gap we've identified and it's being addressed alongside the pipeline fix. Maria Santos: Charles, can I ask - and I want to understand the full picture here - what was the actual impact on Helix during that window? Did anything slip through, or was it more of an exposure risk that you had to manage? Charles Ng: Fortunately - and I say fortunately with a lot of emphasis there - nothing slipped through that we've found. But we spent, I don't know, twelve, fifteen person-hours doing a manual review of logs after the fact just to confirm that. My team basically had to do Aegis Detect's job manually for six hours and then audit it afterward. That's not a small thing for us. Maria Santos: Yeah, that's - yeah. That's a real cost and I don't want to minimize it. Charles Ng: And look, I like you guys. I've always liked working with your team. But I have to be transparent - this isn't happening in a vacuum. We've been having internal conversations about our security stack, and, um, we've been talking to VaultEdge as part of a broader vendor review. I'm not saying that to be threatening, I just - you should know where we're at. Maria Santos: I appreciate you telling us that, Charles. I really do. Can you tell us a bit more about what's driving that review - is it primarily this incident, or were there concerns before? Charles Ng: Honestly? It's both. This incident accelerated the conversation, but we've had some lower-level grumbles for a while. The alert noise from Detect has been higher than we'd like - a lot of false positives that my team has to triage. And the custom rule configuration, it's... it's more cumbersome than it should be for a platform at this price point. Kevin O'Brien: The false positive rate - is that something you've flagged with support previously, or has it mostly been absorbed internally? Charles Ng: Mostly absorbed internally, which I'll admit is partly on us for not escalating sooner. But there's also an expectation that a product this mature should have better out-of-the-box tuning, you know? Maria Santos: Yeah, that's fair feedback and I want to make sure we capture that properly. On the rule configuration side - Kevin, is that something we can get eyes on specifically for Helix's environment? Kevin O'Brien: Absolutely. Charles, I'd actually like to set up a separate working session just on the detection tuning - look at what rules you have configured, where the noise is coming from, and get you to a better baseline. That's something we can do in the next week or two. Charles Ng: I mean, I'm open to that. I just want to make sure it's not a band-aid. Like, if the underlying product has structural issues, tuning sessions aren't going to change my view on the platform. Maria Santos: That's completely reasonable and I hear you. I don't want to oversell a tuning session either. What I'd want to understand better is - when you're talking to VaultEdge, what is it that they're showing you that's resonating? Because I want to understand if there are genuine capability gaps on our side. Charles Ng: Uh, well - their detection pipeline architecture, from what they've shown us, is distributed by design. Which, in light of what just happened, is obviously appealing. They've also been talking about their alert correlation engine, which is supposedly a lot better at suppressing redundant alerts. We haven't done a full POC yet so I can't say for sure how it actually performs. Kevin O'Brien: Okay, that's helpful. And just so you know - the redundant node architecture we've now deployed is functionally similar to what a distributed-by-design approach would give you. I want to make sure you're evaluating the current state, not where we were a week ago. Maria Santos: Kevin, can you - would it make sense to put together something in writing that documents the architecture changes? Like a proper technical brief that Charles can share with his leadership? Kevin O'Brien: Yeah, I can do that. I can have a technical summary of the remediation and the new architecture ready by end of this week. Charles Ng: That would actually be useful. My CTO is asking questions and right now I'm the one translating the situation upward, so having something formal would help. Kevin O'Brien: Totally, and I'll make it CTO-readable - high level but technically substantive, not just marketing language. Maria Santos: Charles, I also want to put something on the table - and I want to be thoughtful about how I say this because I don't want it to feel transactional. But given the impact this caused, I want to talk about what we can do to make this right beyond just the technical fix. I'd like to bring a proposal to you by end of week. Charles Ng: I appreciate that, Maria. I'll be honest, though - it's going to take more than a service credit to rebuild my confidence here. I need to see that this kind of failure mode is genuinely off the table going forward. Maria Santos: Understood. And I think the combination of the architecture brief from Kevin, the tuning session, and whatever we put together commercially - I want all of that to come together as a package, not just a check in a box. Can we plan to reconnect next week to go through it together? Charles Ng: Yeah, next week works. I'd say mid-week - Tuesday or Wednesday. And I'd want my security lead, Priya, on that call as well. Maria Santos: Perfect, we'll get that scheduled. And Charles - again, I'm sorry. This shouldn't have happened and I want to make sure that when we talk next week, you feel like we've actually addressed the things you've raised today, not just acknowledged them. Charles Ng: I hear you. I'll see how next week looks. Thanks for getting on the call today, both of you. Kevin O'Brien: Thanks Charles, talk soon.

title: Aegis / Pinnacle Insurance - Detect Roadmap Review
summary: Rachel Torres (CSM) met with Sandra Keating (customer in insurance/financial services) to discuss Detect product roadmap and feature requests. Sandra raised two primary feature gaps: granular alerting thresholds by entity type with custom behavioral baselines, and in-product pipeline health visibility following a six-hour outage in March. Rachel shared upcoming roadmap items including native LogVault integration and a threat intelligence correlation layer, and the call closed with a discussion of Comply v2's new SOC 2 on-demand reporting feature, with a demo planned for Sandra and her compliance lead Marcus.
transcript_text: Rachel Torres: Hi Sandra, thanks for making time this afternoon - I know Tuesdays tend to get a little chaotic. Sandra Keating: Yeah, no kidding, I had three back-to-backs before this so I appreciate you being flexible on the time. Rachel Torres: Of course, absolutely - okay so, I've got the agenda pulled up, we wanted to walk through some of the Detect roadmap items, and I know you had some specific feature requests you wanted to put on the table today. Sandra Keating: Right, yeah, that's the main thing I want to get into. Rachel Torres: Before we jump in - how are things going on your end generally, like from a security posture standpoint, anything major come up since we last spoke? Sandra Keating: I mean it's been a pretty busy quarter, we had an internal audit wrap up last week, and honestly the compliance side of things has been eating a lot of our bandwidth, but we can get to that in a sec. Rachel Torres: Sure, sure, yeah we can definitely touch on that - I know the Comply v2 launch just happened last week actually, so there might be some relevant stuff there. Sandra Keating: Yeah I saw that announcement, I want to circle back to that, but let's do Detect first because that's kind of the more pressing thing for my team right now. Rachel Torres: Totally, let's do it - so do you want to just kick us off with what you're seeing as the gaps, or would it be helpful if I first walked through what's on the roadmap for the next two quarters? Sandra Keating: Let me start with the gaps because I think it'll be useful context for whatever you're about to tell me. Rachel Torres: Perfect, go ahead. Sandra Keating: So the primary thing - and I've been saying this for a couple of quarters now - is that we really need more granular alerting thresholds by entity type. Rachel Torres: Right, can you walk me through specifically what you mean by entity type in your context? Sandra Keating: Sure, so - in the insurance world we're dealing with a lot of different categories of users and systems, right, so you've got your claims processing systems, your underwriting platforms, your customer-facing portals, and the risk profile for each of those is very different. Rachel Torres: Mm-hmm. Sandra Keating: But right now in Detect, when we're setting alert thresholds, it's basically a one-size-fits-all situation, and that creates a ton of noise on the low-risk endpoints and then potentially under-alerts on the high-value systems. Rachel Torres: Yeah that's - that's a fair point and actually that lines up with feedback we've been getting from a few other financial services customers as well, so it's definitely something that's been getting traction internally. Sandra Keating: Good, because it should be, honestly - the alert fatigue is real, my SOC team is dealing with a lot of false positives and it affects their ability to respond to the things that actually matter. Rachel Torres: Understood, and I don't want to get too far ahead without checking - are we talking about thresholds on the behavioral side, like anomaly detection thresholds, or also on the signature-based rules? Sandra Keating: Both, but honestly the behavioral side is where it's most painful because the baselines are being calculated across everything and they just don't reflect the actual behavior patterns of, say, a claims adjuster versus a network admin. Rachel Torres: Got it, okay - so what you'd really want is the ability to define entity groups and then have separate baseline models trained per group, essentially. Sandra Keating: Exactly, yes, that's exactly it - and ideally you'd be able to map those groups to your own org hierarchy, not just some generic taxonomy. Rachel Torres: Okay, I'm noting all of this down - and I do want to be upfront with you, Sandra, that the entity grouping with custom baselines is something our product team has been scoping, it's not GA yet, it was targeted for Q3 in the roadmap I have, but I want to get you connected with our product team directly so they have this context. Sandra Keating: Q3, so like July-September timeframe? Rachel Torres: That's the current target, yeah - but I want to be careful not to commit to that because roadmaps shift, as you know. Sandra Keating: Yeah, I appreciate the honesty, I'd rather know the real situation than get a date that slips. Rachel Torres: Right, exactly - okay so that's the first item, what else is on your list? Sandra Keating: The second thing, um, this is a little more sensitive to bring up but I think it needs to be on the table - the outage in March. Rachel Torres: Yeah, I was going to bring that up too - I know we sent the incident report and the RCA but I wanted to make sure you had a chance to ask questions directly. Sandra Keating: So we were dark for, what, six hours - and look, I understand things happen, infrastructure fails, I've been in this industry long enough to know that, but for us specifically, that's six hours where we had no visibility into threats across our environment, and given our regulatory obligations that's not a small thing. Rachel Torres: No, absolutely not, and I want to acknowledge that directly - that outage was a significant failure on our part, it was a cascading failure in the event ingestion pipeline, single point of failure that we should have architected around, and we did not. Sandra Keating: Right, that's what the RCA said. Rachel Torres: And the fix - we've implemented redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern so that if one node in the pipeline degrades, it doesn't take everything down with it, and that's been live since mid-March. Sandra Keating: Okay, so my follow-up question on that is - and this goes to the feature request angle - is there any way for customers to have visibility into the health of the Detect pipeline itself, like a status indicator within the product? Rachel Torres: That's actually a really good one and it's something I've heard from a couple of other accounts too - right now the status page is external and it's sort of - it's not surfaced inside the product itself. Sandra Keating: Yeah because we only found out about the outage because someone on my team noticed the alert volume had dropped to zero and then went and checked the status page - that's not a great discovery mechanism. Rachel Torres: No, I completely agree, and that's - I'll be honest, that's a gap in the product experience, and I'm going to log that as a formal feature request, in-product pipeline health status with proactive alerting if ingestion drops below a threshold. Rachel Torres: Understood, and I think that's a very reasonable ask - I'm going to make sure that goes to the right product team with your name on it so they have the customer context. Sandra Keating: Appreciate that. Rachel Torres: Okay so let me also share a few things that are on the Detect roadmap that I think are relevant to what you're describing - there are two items I want to highlight specifically. Sandra Keating: Sure, go ahead. Rachel Torres: First one is expanded SIEM integration - we're adding native connectors for a couple of the major SIEM platforms in Q2, which I know you're running LogVault, so that should reduce the time from event to alert in your existing workflow. Sandra Keating: That would actually be helpful, yeah - right now the LogVault integration is a little manual, we're doing some custom scripting to get the data in there. Rachel Torres: Yeah so that should get a lot cleaner - I'll send you the details on that after this call, it's a Q2 item so should be coming up relatively soon. Sandra Keating: Okay, and the second thing? Rachel Torres: Second one is - we're building out a threat intelligence correlation layer, so essentially Detect will be able to cross-reference events against external threat intel feeds in near real-time, which should improve the signal-to-noise ratio on the alerts that are actually meaningful. Sandra Keating: That's interesting - what feeds are you pulling from? Rachel Torres: The initial launch is going to include a few of the major ones - I don't want to get into specifics that I haven't confirmed with the product team, so let me get you the accurate list rather than guess. Sandra Keating: Fair enough, yeah, please do send that over - the feeds matter a lot, some of them are better for financial services specific threat actors than others. Rachel Torres: Absolutely, I'll include that in the follow-up - and actually, is there a specific feed you're already using or want to see prioritized? Sandra Keating: We're subscribed to FS-ISAC feeds and I'd want to see that included, that's probably the most relevant for our threat landscape. Rachel Torres: FS-ISAC, got it, I'm writing that down - that's a very reasonable ask for a financial services customer and I'll flag that specifically to the product team. Sandra Keating: Yeah I mean that one feels like a no-brainer for any insurance or banking customer you're working with. Rachel Torres: Agreed - okay, you mentioned the compliance audit earlier, do you want to spend a few minutes on Comply before we wrap up? Sandra Keating: Yeah just quickly - we're coming up on a SOC 2 Type II renewal and honestly the reporting process last time was pretty painful, lots of manual exports and spreadsheet work. Rachel Torres: So this is actually really timely because Comply v2 launched last week - April 7 - and one of the headline features is on-demand SOC 2 reporting, so you can generate the report without the manual export process, it pulls directly from the data in the platform. Sandra Keating: Okay, that's - yeah that could actually save us a lot of pain, when can we see that in action? Rachel Torres: I can set up a demo for your team, I'm thinking we loop in your compliance lead too - would that be the right person to have in the room? Rachel Torres: Perfect, I'll reach out to coordinate schedules - okay let me just do a quick recap of the action items before we lose track of everything. Sandra Keating: Yeah please. Rachel Torres: So from my side - I'm logging two formal feature requests: entity grouping with custom behavioral baselines, and in-product pipeline health status with proactive degradation alerts. Sandra Keating: Correct, yes. Rachel Torres: I'm also going to send you the confirmed list of threat intel feeds for the correlation layer, including whether FS-ISAC is on the roadmap, and the details on the LogVault native connector timeline. Sandra Keating: That all sounds right. Rachel Torres: And then I'll set up the Comply v2 demo with you and Marcus - I'm thinking we can probably do that within the next two weeks? Sandra Keating: Two weeks works, yeah - try to avoid the last week of April if you can, I think we've got some internal stuff happening. Sandra Keating: That's all I ask - okay I've got a hard stop in about two minutes so let's call it there. Rachel Torres: Sounds good - thanks Sandra, I'll have everything in your inbox by end of week. Sandra Keating: Great, talk soon.

title: Support Case #6573 - Ridgeline Logistics Detect Data Gaps
summary: Mark Ellison, Infrastructure Lead at Ridgeline Logistics, contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding a complete outage of his Detect dashboard that began around 11 PM on March 11th. Elena Vasquez and Sarah Chen confirmed this is a platform-side issue caused by a failure in the event ingestion pipeline affecting multiple accounts. Mark expressed serious concern given that his company's OT networks, SCADA systems, and production floor infrastructure have had zero threat monitoring visibility for nearly 24 hours. The call concluded with commitments to escalate the case to Sev 1, provide a status update within two hours, investigate data backfill options, and loop in the account manager regarding potential SLA credits.
transcript_text: Elena Vasquez: Hi, thanks for joining - this is Elena Vasquez from Aegis Cloud Security support, and I also have my colleague Sarah Chen on the line with me today. Sarah Chen: Hi there, yeah, Sarah Chen here as well - I specialize in the Detect module so Elena looped me in given what we're seeing in your ticket. Mark Ellison: Yeah, hi, Mark Ellison here - Infrastructure Lead at Ridgeline Logistics. Thanks for, uh, getting on a call quickly I guess, though honestly I'm pretty frustrated that we're even here right now. Elena Vasquez: Totally understandable Mark, and we appreciate you taking the time. Can you walk us through what you're seeing - just in your own words, even if it overlaps with what's in the ticket? Mark Ellison: Sure, yeah. So we started noticing - I want to say it was sometime yesterday morning, March 12th - that our Detect dashboard was just... not updating. Like the last event we could see was from around 11 PM the night before, March 11th, and then there's just nothing after that. Sarah Chen: And this is across all your monitored environments or is it specific to certain agents or regions? Mark Ellison: That's - okay so that's actually a good question. It looks like it's everything. We have agents deployed across our three main data centers - two in the midwest, one on the east coast - and none of them are showing any event data. Zero. Like the dashboard is just... frozen. Sarah Chen: Right, okay. And are the agents themselves still running? Like if you check the agent status locally, are they active? Mark Ellison: Yeah that's what makes this so confusing and frankly alarming. The agents are running fine. We can see them locally, they're processing, but none of that data is actually making it to the dashboard. It's like there's a black hole somewhere between our infrastructure and your platform. Elena Vasquez: Okay, Mark, I want to be transparent with you - we are aware of an issue on our end right now with the event processing pipeline in Detect. We started seeing signals on our side around... Sarah, correct me if I'm wrong, but it was late March 11th? Sarah Chen: Yeah, that's right, late evening March 11th is when our internal monitoring started flagging it. We have engineers actively working on it right now. Mark Ellison: Wait - so this is a platform-level issue? Like this isn't something on my end at all? Elena Vasquez: Based on what we're seeing, yes - this appears to be on our side. We're not asking you to do any configuration changes or anything like that. Mark Ellison: Okay well that's - I mean that's good to know I guess, but it doesn't make it any less of a serious problem. We're a manufacturing company. We have operational technology networks, we have SCADA systems, we have production floor infrastructure that your platform is supposed to be monitoring for threats. And right now we have literally zero visibility. Do you understand how unacceptable that is? Sarah Chen: We absolutely do, Mark, and I want to say we don't take that lightly at all. Especially given your environment - OT networks are exactly the kind of infrastructure where a monitoring gap is really critical. Elena Vasquez: And we genuinely apologize for the impact here. Can I ask - do you have any secondary monitoring tools in place, even basic ones, that your team has been able to lean on in the meantime? Mark Ellison: We have some basic network monitoring but nothing close to what Detect provides for threat detection specifically. I mean, that's why we pay for your platform. My team has been manually reviewing logs all morning which is... not sustainable. Elena Vasquez: That's a terrible position to be in and I hear you. Sarah, can you share any more detail on what we know about the root cause at this point? Sarah Chen: Yeah, so what I can share right now - and some of this is still being confirmed by the engineering team - is that it looks like there's a failure in the event ingestion layer. Essentially the pipeline that takes in events from the agents and processes them for the dashboard hit some kind of cascading issue. We're still diagnosing exactly where the breakdown is. Mark Ellison: A cascading issue. Okay. So how long has this been going on - and more importantly when is it going to be fixed? Because we're now going on almost 24 hours of no threat monitoring visibility. Sarah Chen: I don't want to give you a hard ETA right now that I'm not confident in, because I'd rather be honest with you than give you a time that slips. What I can tell you is this is the highest priority incident on our side right now. Mark Ellison: That's... I mean, that's not really an answer though, is it? I have to go back to my CISO and tell him something. I can't just say 'they're working on it.' Elena Vasquez: I completely understand that pressure, Mark. Let me see what I can do - I can escalate internally to get you a more concrete status update within the next two hours. I'll personally make sure that happens. Is email okay for that or would you prefer a direct call? Mark Ellison: Both. I want something in writing and I want someone to call me. And honestly I'd like this to be flagged as a Sev 1 on your end if it isn't already. Elena Vasquez: Completely fair. We will make sure this support case is marked as Sev 1 - I'll do that right now actually while we're on the call. Sarah Chen: And Mark, just to make sure we have everything we need from your side - can you confirm the account ID and which specific Detect workspace you're working out of? I want to make sure engineering has eyes on your telemetry specifically. Mark Ellison: Yeah it's - hold on, let me pull it up. Okay, account ID is RLL-4482, and the workspace is ridgeline-prod-detect. There's also a secondary workspace, ridgeline-staging-detect, but I'm less concerned about that one. Sarah Chen: Got it, I'm noting both of those. And just to double check - you mentioned the last events visible were around 11 PM on March 11th. Is that the timestamp shown in the dashboard or are you also confirming that against your local agent logs? Mark Ellison: Both actually. Dashboard shows 11:04 PM as the last event, and when I looked at the agent logs on one of our nodes it was actively generating events well after that. So the agents are definitely sending, something is just not receiving it or processing it on your end. Sarah Chen: That's really helpful and consistent with what we're seeing across affected accounts. The agents are healthy, the issue is downstream in the ingestion pipeline. Mark Ellison: Great. And when this is fixed - are we going to get backfilled data? Because if I have a gap of 24 hours or more in my threat monitoring history, that's a compliance issue for us. We need that audit trail to be complete. Sarah Chen: That's a really important question and I want to be careful how I answer it. The agents are generating and queuing event data locally - so the raw data does exist. Whether backfill is feasible depends on how the engineering team resolves the pipeline issue. I'm going to make sure that question is explicitly raised in our internal escalation. Mark Ellison: It needs to be more than raised - it needs to be answered. I don't want a resolution that just fixes the live feed going forward and leaves me with a hole in my historical data. Elena Vasquez: Noted, and I will make sure that's explicitly called out as a requirement in the escalation. You have my word on that. Mark Ellison: Okay. I also - look, I want to ask this because I have to - is there any indication of what caused this? Like was this a configuration error, was it something that could have been prevented? Because if this is a systemic reliability issue with your platform I need to know that. Sarah Chen: I understand why you're asking and I think it's the right question. I don't have a definitive root cause analysis to share right now - engineering is still actively diagnosing - but we will provide you with a full incident report once this is resolved. That will include root cause, remediation steps, and what we're doing to prevent recurrence. Mark Ellison: I'll hold you to that. I need that in writing. And frankly depending on how long this goes on and what that report says, we're going to have a conversation about SLA credits. This is a significant breach of what we're paying for. Elena Vasquez: That's a completely reasonable thing to raise and your account team will be the right people to have that conversation with. I'm going to flag this case to your account manager as well so they're in the loop and can proactively reach out. Mark Ellison: Fine. Yeah. Okay. Is there anything else you need from me right now or... I mean I need to get back to my team. Elena Vasquez: No, I think we have everything we need. Just to recap - we're escalating this to Sev 1, I'll have an update to you within two hours via email and a direct callback, and we're specifically flagging the data backfill requirement to engineering. Does that cover everything? Mark Ellison: Yeah, that covers it for now. I really hope the next call is with better news because this is - this is not a good situation. My team is stressed, my CISO is asking questions, and we're flying blind on threat monitoring. Just... please fix it. Elena Vasquez: We hear you Mark, and we're going to do everything we can to get this resolved as quickly as possible. Thank you for your patience and we'll be in touch very soon.

title: Support Case #3677 - Coastal Living Co MFA Token Failures
summary: Vanessa Cruz, VP of Engineering at Coastal Living Co, contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding a critical MFA token failure affecting approximately 40-45 users since 7 AM. The issue involves TOTP validation failures (error 4031) for users authenticating through an Okta SSO integration with Aegis Identity. Support agent Elena Vasquez determined the issue is likely on Aegis's end after ruling out client-side clock drift, and escalated it as a P1 business-critical incident. A temporary workaround using email OTP was implemented to unblock the engineering and ops teams while the root cause is investigated.
transcript_text: Elena Vasquez: Hi, this is Elena Vasquez from Aegis Cloud Security support, am I speaking with Vanessa? Vanessa Cruz: Yes, hi Elena, Vanessa Cruz here, VP of Engineering at Coastal Living Co - thanks for picking this up, I've been waiting on a callback for a bit. Elena Vasquez: Yeah, I apologize for the delay on that, Vanessa, we've had a higher than normal queue today - but I've got your case pulled up here, case number 3677, MFA token failures, is that right? Vanessa Cruz: That's correct, yes, and honestly it's been - it's been a pretty rough morning because of this, so I'm really hoping we can get to the bottom of it today. Elena Vasquez: Absolutely, let's dig in - can you walk me through what you're seeing, like when did this start and which users are affected? Vanessa Cruz: So it started, um, I'd say around 7 AM this morning, and it's not all users - it seems to be specifically the users who are enrolled in TOTP-based MFA through Aegis Identity, they're getting token validation failures even though the tokens are generating correctly on their authenticator apps. Elena Vasquez: Okay, TOTP failures, and are these users on a specific SSO integration or are they authenticating directly through the Aegis Identity portal? Vanessa Cruz: They're going through our Okta SSO integration that we have set up with Aegis Identity, so the flow is Okta, then it hands off to Aegis Identity for the MFA step. Elena Vasquez: Got it, and roughly how many users are hitting this - is it like a handful or is it widespread across your org? Vanessa Cruz: It's - I mean it's significant, we're talking probably 40, maybe 45 users who can't get in right now, and these are people on our engineering and ops teams who need access to production systems, so this is not a minor inconvenience, Elena. Elena Vasquez: No, I completely understand, that's a critical situation and I'm treating it as such - let me check a few things on the backend here while we talk. Vanessa Cruz: Yeah please do, and I also want to flag that we had users try regenerating their TOTP secrets through the self-service portal and re-enrolling their authenticator apps and it didn't fix anything, same error. Elena Vasquez: Hmm, okay, that's actually a really useful data point - if re-enrollment isn't resolving it that does suggest this might not be a user-side clock drift issue, which was my first instinct. Vanessa Cruz: Right, and I mean we checked device times, everything looks synced, I had two of my engineers verify that specifically because I knew that would be the first question. Elena Vasquez: Smart, okay - I'm pulling up your tenant now and I'm looking at the authentication logs... give me just one second here... Vanessa Cruz: Sure, and while you're doing that I just want to say - we evaluated Aegis Identity specifically because of the reliability promises, we're a retail company, we have tight operational windows, we can't have engineering staff locked out of systems, especially heading into our spring inventory cycle. Elena Vasquez: That's completely fair and I hear you on that, the timing is terrible - okay, I'm seeing something in your logs, there are a high volume of TOTP validation attempts all returning a 4031 error code, which is... okay, that's interesting. Vanessa Cruz: What does 4031 mean, is that something on your end? Elena Vasquez: So a 4031 is a token validation window mismatch, but - and this is the part that's odd - it's usually caused by a time sync issue on either the client or our validation server, but given that you've already ruled out client-side, I want to check if there's something going on with our validation service configuration for your tenant specifically. Vanessa Cruz: So you're saying this could be a bug on Aegis's side? Elena Vasquez: I - I don't want to confirm that definitively yet without escalating to our Identity engineering team, but based on what I'm seeing in these logs and the fact that re-enrollment didn't help, it does look like the issue may be on our end, yes. Vanessa Cruz: Elena, that's - okay, I appreciate you being honest about that but that is really frustrating to hear, because this is a production impacting issue and my team has been blocked for hours. Elena Vasquez: I know, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it, this is a problem and we need to fix it - what I can do right now is flag this as a P1 escalation to our Identity engineering team, and I also want to offer a temporary workaround while we investigate. Vanessa Cruz: What kind of workaround are we talking about? Elena Vasquez: So within Aegis Identity, admins have the ability to temporarily switch affected users to email-based OTP as a fallback method - it's not ideal, I know, but it would unblock your team immediately while the TOTP validation issue is being investigated. Vanessa Cruz: Email OTP... I mean that's less secure and my security team is going to push back on that, but I understand you're trying to help - how long would this workaround need to be in place? Elena Vasquez: I honestly can't give you a hard timeline without the engineering team weighing in, but P1 escalations for Identity are supposed to have an initial response within two hours and a resolution path within four - I will personally stay on this case and keep you updated. Vanessa Cruz: Two to four hours - Elena, my team has already been down for several hours, that's potentially most of the workday for some of these folks. Elena Vasquez: I know, and I'm sorry - I'm escalating this right now as we speak, I'm marking it as business critical with active user lockout, that should push it to the front of the engineering queue. Vanessa Cruz: Okay, fine - and can you also tell me, is this affecting other customers or is it just us? Elena Vasquez: I'm going to be transparent with you - I don't have visibility into other tenant logs, but I'm not seeing any broader incident reported for Aegis Identity on our internal status board, so right now it looks like it may be specific to your tenant configuration, possibly related to the Okta integration setup. Vanessa Cruz: So something in our configuration, but we haven't changed anything on our end - nothing was touched, no updates, no config changes since last week. Elena Vasquez: I hear you, and I believe you - there may have been a backend update or configuration push on our side that affected certain tenant setups, that's something the engineering team will need to confirm. Vanessa Cruz: Alright, okay - so what do I need to do right now, walk me through the email OTP workaround steps so I can at least get my team unblocked. Elena Vasquez: Sure, so if you go into the Aegis Identity admin console, navigate to Authentication Policies, and then under the MFA methods for your primary user group, you should see an option to enable email OTP as an allowed fallback - I can stay on the line while you do that. Vanessa Cruz: Okay, I'm in the admin console now... Authentication Policies... yeah I see it, I see the MFA methods section. Elena Vasquez: Great, and you should see a toggle or checkbox for email OTP - enabling it there should allow affected users to choose it as an alternative at the next login attempt. Vanessa Cruz: Okay... I'm enabling it now, and I'll have someone ping the affected users to try logging in again - but Elena, I need a follow-up from you today, not tomorrow, today, with an actual update on what caused this. Elena Vasquez: Absolutely, you have my word - I'll follow up via email with an update by end of business today, and if engineering identifies the root cause before then you'll hear from me immediately. Vanessa Cruz: Alright, I'm going to hold you to that - and honestly we're going to need to have a broader conversation about reliability with our account team because this is not the first time we've had hiccups, but that's a separate discussion. Elena Vasquez: Understood, and that's a fair conversation to have - I'll make a note for your account team to follow up on that as well, for now let's get your team back in and I'll be in touch shortly, okay? Vanessa Cruz: Okay, thanks Elena - I hope to hear from you soon.
topics: mfa failure, totp, okta sso integration, p1 escalation, user lockout, reliability concern
action_items: Elena Vasquez: Escalate case 3677 as P1 business-critical to Identity engineering team with active user lockout flag | Elena Vasquez: Send follow-up email to Vanessa with root cause update by end of business today | Elena Vasquez: Notify Vanessa's account team to schedule a broader reliability discussion | Vanessa Cruz: Enable email OTP fallback in Aegis Identity admin console and notify affected users to retry login

title: Support Case #3615 - Nimbus Platform Custom Report Request

title: Competitive Response Strategy
summary: James Mitchell convened a competitive strategy call with Rachel Torres, Tom Bradley, Jordan Whitfield, and Kevin O'Brien to address SentinelShield's aggressive positioning against Aegis in three recent late-stage deals. Tom Bradley explained the root cause and remediation of the March platform outage, confirming that redundant processing nodes and a circuit breaker pattern have been in production since March 28th. Jordan Whitfield highlighted Comply v2, launched April 7th, as a strong differentiator with native cross-module compliance reporting for SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001. The team aligned on next steps for the at-risk Hartfield Manufacturing deal and identified materials needed to support the competitive response.

Kevin O'Brien: Here, sorry, just pulling up my notes. James Mitchell: No worries. Okay, so, the reason I called this is - we've had three deals in the last two weeks where SentinelShield came up pretty aggressively in late-stage conversations, and I want to make sure we're all aligned on how we're positioning against them going forward. Rachel Torres: Is this primarily on the Detect side or is it across the board? James Mitchell: Mostly Detect, honestly. Which is - and I'll be candid here - not a surprise given what happened in March. Tom Bradley: Right, yeah. The outage. James Mitchell: Exactly. That's, um, that's not entirely surprising but it's still frustrating to hear. James Mitchell: Tom, can you give us a quick rundown of where we stand on the March incident from a technical remediation standpoint? So - the root cause was a single point of failure in the event ingestion pipeline. When the primary node went down, the failover didn't trigger the way it was supposed to, and that created a cascading failure across the processing layer. Total visibility loss was roughly six hours. Kevin O'Brien: Six hours is a long time in threat monitoring. Tom Bradley: It is. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. But - and this is important - what we've done since then is we've implemented redundant processing nodes across all three availability zones, and we've added a circuit breaker pattern that will isolate a failing component before it can cascade. Lisa Park: Alright, I'll get a follow-up invite on the calendar for next week, I'll send over the implementation plan draft and the dashboard demo agenda before then so you and your team can review ahead of time. Raymond Burke: Sounds great, I'm really looking forward to it - thanks Lisa, thanks Aisha, this was a really productive session. Aisha Johnson: Thank you Raymond, we're really excited to be working with Vanta Health on this, talk soon! Lisa Park: Take care Raymond, we'll be in touch!

title: Support Case #9856 - Silverline Brands Backup Window Exceeded
summary: Dominic Flores, IT Director at Silverline Brands, called Aegis Cloud Security support regarding a two-week-old open case about backup jobs significantly overrunning their scheduled 1 AM-5 AM window, with SQL Server backups now taking up to 8-9 hours and causing production performance degradation. Support engineer David Kim identified a dramatic throughput drop from ~800 MB/s to ~180-220 MB/s, potentially linked to backend network routing changes made during a March remediation effort for a separate module (Aegis Detect). David initiated immediate workarounds including a manual agent update to version 4.2.0 and SQL job priority adjustments, and escalated the issue as P1 to the infrastructure team. A follow-up call was scheduled for the next morning at 10 AM Central with a Protect platform engineer to review root cause findings.
transcript_text: David Kim: Thank you for calling Aegis Cloud Security support, this is David Kim, how can I help you today? Dominic Flores: Hey David, yeah, this is Dominic Flores, IT Director over at Silverline Brands, I've got case number 9856 open, the one about our backup windows? David Kim: Yes, absolutely, I pulled up the case right before you called actually - so you're seeing backup jobs running well past their scheduled windows, is that right? Dominic Flores: That's the short version, yeah. I mean, look, this has been going on for about two weeks now and it's - it's becoming a real problem for us, especially with our retail operations. We're a 24/7 environment basically, and when backups are running into business hours it's causing performance degradation on our production systems. David Kim: I completely understand, and I appreciate you flagging this - two weeks is way too long to be dealing with something like this, so let's dig into it today and figure out what's going on. Dominic Flores: Yeah I mean, I submitted the case on - I think it was the 4th? And honestly I expected a faster response, I'll be honest with you. We're paying for premium support. David Kim: You're right, and I - I want to own that, the initial response time on this case wasn't where it should've been and I'm sorry about that. I want to make sure we make good use of this time right now though. Can you walk me through what you're actually seeing? Like, what was the original backup window you had configured? Dominic Flores: So we had it set to run from 1 AM to 5 AM, that's our four-hour window, which historically has been plenty. But now these jobs are running until - I've seen it go to 9, 9:30 in the morning. That's four to five hours of overage and that's right in the middle of when our warehouse and e-commerce teams are ramping up. David Kim: And this started roughly two weeks ago you said, so that would be around March 29th or so? Dominic Flores: Yeah, give or take. March 28th, 29th is when we first noticed it. My team thought maybe it was a one-off thing, like a large data change set or something, but it's been happening every night since. David Kim: Okay, and are all of your backup jobs affected or is it specific workloads - like, is it just certain VMs, certain datasets, or is this across the board? Dominic Flores: That's a good question. It seems like it's - it's pretty broad, but the worst offenders are our SQL Server instances. We've got three pretty beefy SQL servers running our e-commerce database and our inventory management system, and those are the ones really blowing past the window. Some of the smaller file server backups are also slow but not as dramatic. David Kim: Got it, so SQL workloads are the primary pain point. And are these incremental backups that are running nightly or are you doing full backups every night? Dominic Flores: Incrementals nightly, fulls on Sunday. And the Sunday fulls are - I mean those are also taking longer but that's kind of expected, the incrementals are what's really alarming me because they should be fast. David Kim: Right, yeah, incrementals ballooning like that is definitely a red flag. A few things I want to check - have you seen any significant growth in your data change rate? Like, is there any reason your daily change set might have gotten larger around that time, end of month processing, new application rollouts, anything like that? Dominic Flores: I mean, we did have our spring inventory sync run around that time, but we do that quarterly and it's never caused this before. And even if the change set was bigger it shouldn't be adding four hours, that seems excessive. David Kim: Yeah, no, you're right, a quarterly process shouldn't account for that magnitude of slowdown. I want to pull up your backup job logs from the Aegis Protect console, do you mind if I take a minute to look at those? Dominic Flores: Go ahead, yeah. David Kim: Okay, so I'm looking at your environment here... and yeah, I can see the job durations, oof - yeah that's significant. Your SQL backup for, looks like it's the instance labeled SQLPROD01, that one's averaging about eight hours over the last ten days. That's uh, that's not good. Dominic Flores: Right, exactly! And I keep getting told by my team to just expand the window but that's not a real fix, I shouldn't have to carve out more production hours for backups that used to run in under two hours. David Kim: No, absolutely not, that's a band-aid, not a solution. Let me look at the throughput metrics here... okay so I'm seeing the backup throughput dropped pretty substantially - it looks like you were averaging around 800 megabytes per second before March 27th and now you're sitting around 180 to 220. That's a massive drop in throughput. Dominic Flores: So something changed on your end? Because we didn't change anything on our infrastructure around that time, I specifically asked my team about that. David Kim: I hear you, and I want to be transparent - so looking at our platform logs, around March 10th through the 18th we had a significant incident with Aegis Detect, our threat monitoring pipeline, and as part of the remediation work we pushed some backend infrastructure updates. Now, Protect and Detect run on separate systems, but some of the underlying network routing configurations were touched as part of that work, and I'm wondering if - and I need to confirm this with our infrastructure team - if some of those changes affected the data transfer paths for backup jobs in your region. Dominic Flores: Wait, so a problem with a completely different module potentially broke our backups and nobody flagged this to customers? That's - I mean, I'm sorry David but that's pretty alarming to me. David Kim: I understand your frustration, Dominic, and I'm not going to spin this - if that's what happened, it shouldn't have happened that way and customers should have been proactively notified. I'm still confirming the root cause but I want to be upfront with you about what I'm seeing rather than tell you nothing. Dominic Flores: Okay. I - I appreciate that, at least. So what are the next steps here? Because I need this fixed before tonight, we cannot have another morning where our warehouse team is fighting with a sluggish inventory system because backups are still running. David Kim: Okay so here's what I can do right now - I can escalate this internally to our Protect infrastructure team with the throughput data I'm looking at, and I also want to check your backup agent version because I'm seeing you're running 4.1.2, and we released 4.2.0 about three weeks ago which had some improvements to the data transfer compression algorithms. That could help even before we nail down the root cause. Dominic Flores: Why wasn't that update pushed automatically? We're on managed updates. David Kim: That's a fair question - 4.2.0 was staged as an opt-in update rather than automatic because of some compatibility flags for SQL Server environments, which is ironic given your situation. But let me get that queued up for your environment, I'll push it out as a manual deployment through the console and you should see it applied within the hour if you can confirm your agents are reachable. Dominic Flores: They should be, yeah. And that update - is that going to fix the throughput issue or is that just going to help a little bit? David Kim: Honest answer? It should help, probably meaningfully, but I don't want to promise you it's the full fix until I understand whether there's a network routing issue on our backend. I'm going to get the infra team on this today - I'm flagging it as a P1 on my end - and I want to schedule a follow-up call with you tomorrow morning, before your backup window starts, so we can walk through whatever findings we have. Dominic Flores: Tomorrow morning works. And I want someone from your engineering team on that call, not just - no offense - not just a support engineer. I need someone who can actually make changes on the backend if needed. David Kim: None taken, I'll make that happen. I'll have a Protect platform engineer on the call. Can we say 10 AM your time? And what timezone are you in? Dominic Flores: We're Central, so 10 AM Central works. David Kim: Perfect, I'll send a calendar invite to the email on your account within the next 30 minutes. And Dominic, one more thing - is there anything I can set up as a temporary workaround for tonight? For example, I can look at adjusting the backup job priority settings and throttling some of the lower-priority file server jobs so the SQL workloads get more of the available bandwidth during the window. Dominic Flores: Yeah, yeah, let's do that. The SQL servers are the priority, the file servers we can live with being a little slower if it means the SQL jobs finish closer to on time. David Kim: Okay, I'm going to make those priority adjustments now in your policy configuration, and combined with the agent update that should - hopefully - get tonight's run into a better place. I'll also set up an alert so if the SQL job duration exceeds six hours I get paged directly, and I'll check in on it tomorrow morning before our call. Dominic Flores: Alright. I mean, look, I'm still frustrated that we're two weeks into this and I'm just now getting real traction, but - I do appreciate you being straight with me about what you're seeing and not just giving me the runaround. Let's see what tomorrow brings. David Kim: That's fair, Dominic, and I get it. We'll make this right. I'll have that invite and a case update email to you within the half hour, and I'll see you tomorrow at 10 Central with the engineering team. Dominic Flores: Sounds good. Talk to you then. David Kim: Thank you Dominic, talk soon.

title: Protect Team - Quarterly Planning

title: Support Case #6635 - Nova Retail Group SSO Login Failures
summary: Nova Retail Group VP Stephanie Blair and senior security engineer Andre Coleman contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding an SSO outage affecting approximately 38-42% of their 1,200 users since February 10th. Aegis support identified a likely regression introduced by a patch deployed on February 9th affecting SAML NameID format handling in the Identity module. A temporary workaround was provided via bulk per-user local auth override in the admin console, while a permanent fix is estimated within 48 hours. Stephanie expressed significant frustration over the four-day outage coinciding with Valentine's Day, one of Nova Retail's busiest sales days, and the lack of proactive communication from Aegis.
transcript_text: Sarah Chen: Hi, thanks for joining - this is Sarah Chen from Aegis Cloud Security support, and I also have my colleague Elena Vasquez on the line with me today. Elena specializes in our Identity module so I wanted to bring her in given what you described in the case notes. Stephanie Blair: Great, yeah. This is Stephanie Blair, VP of Technology at Nova Retail Group, and I have Andre Coleman on with me - he's one of our senior security engineers and he's been in the thick of this since it started. Andre Coleman: Hi everyone, Andre here. Yeah, happy to be on - well, not happy about the situation, but you know what I mean. Elena Vasquez: Totally understand, and hi Andre, hi Stephanie. We've reviewed the case notes you submitted but I'd love to just hear directly from you - can you walk us through what you're experiencing? When did this start? Stephanie Blair: So it started - Andre, was it Tuesday morning? Around like 9 AM? Andre Coleman: Yeah, Tuesday February 10th, roughly 8:50, 8:55 AM central time. We started getting a flood of tickets from users saying they couldn't log in through SSO. They'd hit the login page, get redirected to our IdP, authenticate fine, and then come back and just get... a generic error. Something like 'authentication failed, please contact your administrator.' Sarah Chen: And this is affecting - I want to make sure I understand the scope - is this all of your users or a subset? Stephanie Blair: That's what's so frustrating about this, honestly. It's not all users. It's roughly - Andre, what are we at, like 40 percent? Andre Coleman: Yeah, we've been tracking it. About 38 to 42 percent of our user base is hitting the failure. We have around 1,200 users in Aegis Identity and somewhere between 450 and 500 of them are completely locked out. And there's no obvious pattern - it's not department-based, it's not role-based, it doesn't seem to correlate with when they were provisioned or anything like that. Elena Vasquez: Okay, that's really helpful context. And just to confirm - you're using Okta as your identity provider, correct? That's what's in the case. Andre Coleman: That's right, Okta. SAML 2.0. We've been running this configuration for, what, eight, nine months without any issues, and then Tuesday just - boom. Elena Vasquez: And nothing changed on your Okta side? No config updates, no certificate renewals, anything like that? Andre Coleman: Nothing. I went through everything. Our Okta config is untouched. The SAML app settings are exactly what they've been. I even pulled the metadata and compared it to what we had exported three weeks ago - identical. Sarah Chen: Okay so, and I want to be transparent here - we do have some reports from a couple of other customers about SSO intermittency, and our engineering team is actively investigating. I don't want to say definitively this is a platform bug yet, but it's something we're taking seriously. Elena, do you want to talk about what we've been looking at on our end? Elena Vasquez: Yeah, absolutely. So um, what we've identified so far is there may be an issue with how Aegis Identity is processing certain SAML assertion attributes - specifically around the NameID format. There was a minor update pushed to the Identity module on February 9th, which was the day before you started seeing issues, and we think it may have introduced a regression in how we're handling persistent versus transient NameID formats. Stephanie Blair: Wait - there was an update pushed the day before this started and you're just telling us this now? We've had 500 users locked out for four days. Sarah Chen: You're absolutely right to be frustrated by that, Stephanie, and I'm sorry. The update was a minor patch - it wasn't expected to affect SSO behavior and it didn't trigger our standard pre-release SSO regression tests the way it should have. That's a gap in our process and I don't want to gloss over that. Stephanie Blair: I mean, look - I get it, things happen. But four days is a long time. We've got retail operations staff who literally cannot access the security platform. We're a retail company, Valentine's Day is today, this is one of our biggest sales days of the year, and we have team leads who can't get into the system. Elena Vasquez: Understood, and that context is really important - thank you for sharing that. Let me ask you this - in the interim, as a workaround, have your affected users tried using local username and password login instead of SSO? I know that's not ideal but it would at least get them access while we work on the fix. Stephanie Blair: We did try that for a handful of users. The problem is we enforced SSO-only as a security requirement, so local auth is disabled for most of our user accounts. Andre, is that still the case across the board? Andre Coleman: Yeah, we have local auth disabled for about 90 percent of users. It's a security policy thing - we went SSO-only specifically because it was the recommended configuration in Aegis's own documentation. So the workaround kind of doesn't apply to us. Sarah Chen: Right, okay. So Elena, can we talk about the admin override option? Because I think that might be relevant here. Elena Vasquez: Yes - so Stephanie, Andre, there is an option in the Aegis Identity admin console where a super admin can temporarily re-enable local authentication on a per-user basis without changing your global policy. It's under Identity Settings, User Management, and then you'd select the affected user, go to Authentication Override, and toggle on 'Allow local auth - temporary.' It sets a 72-hour window by default. That would let your affected users in today at least. Stephanie Blair: Okay, that's... actually useful. Andre, can you look at that while we're on the call? Andre Coleman: Yeah, pulling it up now. Identity Settings... User Management... okay I see it. Authentication Override, yeah. So I'd have to do this for each of the 450 affected users individually? Elena Vasquez: There is a bulk selection option - if you filter your user list and select multiple users, the bulk actions dropdown should have the Authentication Override option. It's a little buried, I'll be honest. Andre Coleman: Okay, yeah, I see the bulk action. That's... manageable. Not great, but manageable. I'll take it. Elena Vasquez: Good. And I want to be clear that this is a stopgap - we are working on a proper fix. Our engineering team has identified the regression in the NameID handling and a patch is being tested right now. I can't give you a hard commit time, but the current estimate from engineering is that we're targeting a fix deployment within 48 hours. Stephanie Blair: 48 hours. So that's... Sunday at the earliest. We will have had users locked out for almost a week by then. That's really not acceptable, Elena. Sarah Chen: I hear you. I'm going to escalate the priority on this case when we get off this call and push engineering to see if there's any path to accelerating that timeline. I can't promise a different date but I will personally follow up with you by end of day today with an updated ETA. Stephanie Blair: I'd also like to understand - are there any other customers affected by this? Because if this is a widespread issue I'd expect a status page update or some kind of proactive communication, and I haven't seen anything. Sarah Chen: That's a fair point. We have seen reports from a small number of other customers - I don't have exact numbers in front of me - and you're right that a status page update should have gone out sooner. I'm going to flag that internally as well. You shouldn't have to check in with support to find out if there's a known issue affecting your platform. Stephanie Blair: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. Look, I want to be clear - we're not going anywhere, we're committed to Aegis, but this has been a rough week and I need to see some responsiveness here. Our CISO is asking me questions I don't have great answers to right now. Elena Vasquez: Completely understood. I want to make sure you have everything you need to communicate internally. Would it help if we drafted a brief incident summary email that you could share with your CISO? Something that lays out the root cause, what we know, and the remediation plan? Stephanie Blair: Actually, yeah. That would be helpful. Something I can forward that doesn't come from me trying to paraphrase a support call. Sarah Chen: We'll put that together and send it over within the hour. And Andre - as you go through the bulk override process, if you run into any issues or it doesn't behave the way I described, please ping us directly in the case thread and we'll jump back on immediately. Andre Coleman: Will do. And just to confirm the next steps I'm hearing - you'll escalate the patch timeline, you'll send an incident summary we can share internally, and you'll follow up by end of day today with an updated fix ETA. Is that right? Sarah Chen: That's exactly right. And we'll keep the case thread updated in real time as we get information from engineering. You won't have to chase us. Stephanie Blair: Okay. I appreciate that. I'm still frustrated, I'm not going to pretend otherwise, but at least we have a path forward. Let's see how the next 24 hours go. Elena Vasquez: That's completely fair, Stephanie. We'll earn back your confidence here. Thank you both for your time today and I'm sorry again for the disruption, especially on a day like today. Andre Coleman: Thanks. Talk soon.
topics: sso outage, identity module regression, saml configuration, incident communication, workaround, patch deployment

title: All Hands - February Wrap

Comply v2 is tracking toward an April GA with backend milestones met, though QA coverage is slightly behind at 62% versus a 70% target, contingent on two QA resources rotating over from the Detect team in March. A customer loss to competitor VaultEdge and two upsell opportunities totaling ~$240K ARR were discussed on the customer success front. A potential bottleneck in the Detect event ingestion pipeline was elevated as an item needing immediate attention, and March priorities were set including code freeze for Comply v2 and early access briefings for strategic accounts.

title: Aegis / Maplewood Goods - SOC 2 Prep Review

title: Comply v2 - Design Review
summary: Hannah, Ananya, and Mike held a design review call for Comply v2 ahead of the April GA launch. They aligned on an async report generation model with P90 latency of 45 seconds to 2 minutes, and confirmed a unified evidence store architecture to handle overlapping compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, PCI DSS). PDF export was confirmed in scope using headless rendering, while report annotations were deferred to v2.1. The team expressed strong confidence in the April date, with a load test planned for mid-March to validate queue performance under concurrent usage.
transcript_text: Hannah Liu: Okay, I think we've got everyone, let me just - yeah, okay, great. Hi guys, thanks for jumping on. Ananya Sharma: Hey Hannah, hey Mike. Mike Romano: Hey, good morning. Or good afternoon for you, Ananya, right? You're EST today? Ananya Sharma: Ha, yeah, I'm in New York this week visiting family so, uh, slightly less jet-lagged than usual. Hannah Liu: Nice, nice. Okay so - should we just dive in? I know everyone's got a packed afternoon. Mike Romano: Yeah let's do it. Hannah Liu: Alright, so the purpose of today's call is really to do a proper design review for Comply v2 before we lock the spec. We've got the April GA date on the calendar and I want to make sure engineering is fully unblocked after this call. Um, I also want to talk through the on-demand reporting architecture because there are a few open questions I flagged in the doc. Ananya Sharma: Yeah I saw those, I've been thinking about them actually. The one around report generation latency is - I think we have a pretty solid answer for that now. Hannah Liu: Oh great, yeah, that was the one I was most curious about. Walk us through it? Ananya Sharma: Sure, so the concern was basically - if a customer kicks off, say, a SOC 2 report on demand, how long does that take and is the UX acceptable? And what we landed on is an async generation model where the report job gets queued, the user gets an immediate acknowledgment with a job ID, and then they either poll or we push a notification when it's done. Mike Romano: And what's the expected generation time in the P90 case? Like, worst case realistic scenario. Ananya Sharma: So we benchmarked it against our internal compliance data and for a full SOC 2 Type II report across a twelve-month window, we're looking at roughly... forty-five seconds to two minutes depending on data volume. Which honestly is way better than I expected. Hannah Liu: Yeah that's - that's actually really good. I was worried we'd be talking like five, ten minutes and that would've been a harder sell to customers. Ananya Sharma: Right, and even at two minutes, you know, with the async pattern the user isn't just sitting there staring at a spinner. They can go do something else and come back. So the perceived wait time is much lower. Hannah Liu: Okay yeah I love that. Mike, you had some thoughts on the multi-framework support side, right? I remember you sent something in Slack last week. Mike Romano: Yeah, yeah. So my main concern - and it's less a concern now, more just a design question - is how we're handling the control mapping layer when you've got overlapping frameworks. Like SOC 2 and ISO 27001 share a ton of controls conceptually, and I want to make sure we're not duplicating evidence collection or doing redundant data pulls. Hannah Liu: That's such a good point actually, and this is one of the things customers are going to care about a lot. Like, nobody wants to re-audit the same thing four times. Ananya Sharma: Exactly. So, um, the way we've architected it - and Mike, you can poke holes in this - is that we have a unified evidence store underneath, and the framework-specific report generation is basically a different lens or projection on top of that same evidence set. So the control mapping lives in a config layer and the evidence collection is framework-agnostic. Mike Romano: Okay, that's - yeah, that's the right pattern. I was a little worried you were going to say each framework had its own collector but this is much cleaner. Ananya Sharma: No no, we definitely considered that early on and it was just a nightmare from a maintenance standpoint. Like, the moment a framework updates its control list you'd have to touch four different collectors. Hannah Liu: Yeah, agreed. And from a PM perspective, that also makes it way easier to add new frameworks down the road, which is kind of a roadmap priority for H2. So that's a win. Mike Romano: Totally. HIPAA and PCI DSS are the four GA frameworks, right? Those are locked? Hannah Liu: Yeah, SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 - those are the four for v2 launch. We might soft-launch GDPR as a beta flag but I don't want to commit to that in the April release notes yet. Ananya Sharma: That's probably wise. GDPR mapping is... complicated. I'd rather do it right than rush it. Hannah Liu: Completely agree. Okay, um, let's talk about the reporting UI side for a second because I got feedback from the design team this morning and there are a couple of things I want to flag. One is the export formats - customers really want PDF natively, not just CSV or JSON. Where are we on that? Mike Romano: PDF is in scope, yeah. We're using a headless rendering approach, basically generate the report as structured HTML and then render to PDF server-side. The output looks really clean actually, I'm pretty happy with how it came together. Hannah Liu: Oh that's great to hear. Can you share a sample? I'd love to show something to the field team before launch. Mike Romano: Yeah for sure, I'll drop a sample in the shared drive today. It's still using placeholder data but the structure is there and it looks pretty polished. Hannah Liu: Amazing, thank you. Okay, the other UI thing is around - so customers want to be able to annotate the report before they share it externally. Like, add a note to explain a gap or an exception. Is that in scope for v2 or are we punting that? Ananya Sharma: Hmm. I mean, I think annotations are really valuable but... honest answer, building it properly is not trivial. You'd need to track annotation history, tie it to specific control sections, probably have some kind of approval workflow eventually. What's the customer expectation - is this like a nice-to-have or is this table-stakes for someone to buy? Hannah Liu: Honestly? Based on the customer interviews I've done it's more of a nice-to-have for most folks. The main ask is just - let me export a clean PDF and share it with my auditor. The annotation stuff came up in like two out of eight interviews. Mike Romano: Yeah, I'd say let's punt that to v2.1 then. Keep April clean and get the core on-demand generation solid. Annotations on top of a shaky foundation would be worse than no annotations at all. Hannah Liu: Yeah, agreed, I'll move that to the backlog. Good call. Alright, I think we're in really good shape overall honestly. I'm feeling a lot more confident about the April date after this conversation. Ananya Sharma: Same, yeah. The big unknowns feel pretty resolved at this point. Mike Romano: I do want to flag one thing before we wrap - just making sure we have a proper performance testing plan in place before GA. On-demand report generation at scale, like if fifty customers all kick off reports simultaneously, I want to know the queue doesn't fall over. Ananya Sharma: Yes, a hundred percent, that's on the testing checklist. We've got a load test planned for mid-March. We'll simulate concurrent report jobs and make sure the queue depth and worker scaling behaves well. Hannah Liu: Perfect. Okay I think that's everything on my list. Anything else from either of you before we let everyone go? Mike Romano: Nope, I think we're good. Really solid session. Ananya Sharma: Same, I feel good about where we're landing. Thanks everyone. Hannah Liu: Great, thanks guys. I'll update the spec doc today with what we agreed and send it around for a final review. Have a good rest of your day!
topics: design review, compliance reporting, multi-framework support, pdf export, performance testing, roadmap planning
