title: Support Case #1750 - Vanta Health Systems SIEM Connector Issue
summary: Vanta Health Systems contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding a critical issue with their LogVault SIEM connector dropping event data since February 8th, including complete 45-minute to 1-hour blackout windows. Sarah Chen and Priya Patel identified the root cause as a known bug in connector version 3.4.1 where connection timeouts from F5 load balancer throttling cause the buffer to flush instead of retry. Immediate workarounds were provided (adjusting F5 connection limits and enabling the undocumented retry_on_timeout parameter), with a permanent fix available via upgrade to version 3.5.0. Dr. Cheng expressed significant frustration with the 10-day support response delay, undocumented parameters, and lack of proactive notification about the known bug in a healthcare/HIPAA environment.
transcript_text: Sarah Chen: Hi, good afternoon, this is Sarah Chen from Aegis Cloud Security support, I have Dr. Cheng and Mr. Burke on the line from Vanta Health Systems, and my colleague Priya Patel is joining as well - Priya, you there? Priya Patel: Yeah, I'm here, hi everyone. Dr. Linda Cheng: Hello, yes, Dr. Linda Cheng here, and Raymond is with me as well. Raymond Burke: Raymond Burke, yeah, hi, thanks for getting us on quickly. Sarah Chen: Of course, so I've had a chance to look at your case notes, Support Case 1750, and I understand you're seeing issues with your SIEM connector in Aegis Detect - can you walk us through what you're experiencing from your end? Dr. Linda Cheng: Sure, Raymond, do you want to take this one since you've been dealing with it directly? Raymond Burke: Yeah, absolutely - so, um, we integrated Aegis Detect with our LogVault SIEM environment about six weeks ago, and for the first couple of weeks it was working fine, events were flowing through, we were getting alerts, everything looked good - but starting around, I want to say February 8th or 9th, we started noticing significant gaps in event data reaching LogVault. Sarah Chen: And when you say gaps, are we talking about partial data loss or like, complete windows of missing events? Raymond Burke: Both, honestly - there are periods where we're getting maybe 20 or 30 percent of the expected event volume, and then there are windows, sometimes 45 minutes to an hour, where we get absolutely nothing into LogVault. Dr. Linda Cheng: I want to underscore something here - we are a healthcare organization, we're dealing with PHI, we have HIPAA obligations, and having blind spots in our threat monitoring is not, it's not acceptable from a compliance and security posture standpoint, this is genuinely concerning to us. Sarah Chen: Dr. Cheng, I completely understand, and I want to be transparent with you - that concern is absolutely valid and we're taking this seriously, which is why Priya joined me on this call. Priya Patel: Yeah, and I want to add - we've escalated this internally on our side as well, so you have our full attention on this, I promise. Dr. Linda Cheng: I appreciate that, but I have to be honest with you, we've been sitting on this issue for almost ten days now, we submitted the case on the 9th, we've had two email exchanges, and this is the first time we're actually talking to someone - that response time is not what we were sold on when we signed up for the enterprise tier. Priya Patel: That's - yeah, that's a fair point and I'm not going to make excuses for that, the delay in getting to a live call was not acceptable and I'm sorry for that, let's use this time to actually dig in and get you some answers. Sarah Chen: Thank you - okay, so Raymond, can you tell me which version of the Aegis Detect SIEM connector you're running, and what your connector configuration looks like in terms of the forwarding mode? Raymond Burke: Yeah, give me one second, I have the config pulled up - okay, so we're on connector version 3.4.1, and we're using the push-based forwarding mode, not pull, and the endpoint is pointing to our LogVault HEC endpoint on port 8088. Sarah Chen: Okay, and are you using TLS on that HEC connection? Raymond Burke: Yes, TLS 1.2, with a self-signed cert - and look, I already know what you're going to say about the self-signed cert, but we verified the cert pinning configuration in the connector, that's not the issue. Sarah Chen: Okay, fair enough, I wasn't going to go straight there actually - um, what I'm more interested in is, are you seeing any errors or backpressure indicators in the connector logs on the Aegis side, like, do you have access to the connector diagnostic logs and if so what are they showing around those gap windows? Raymond Burke: We do have the logs, yeah, and I actually exported them before this call - what we're seeing is a lot of, um, connection timeout errors to the HEC endpoint, and then the connector seems to just... drop the buffer instead of retrying, which is - that seems like a bug to me, honestly. Priya Patel: Connection timeouts dropping the buffer instead of queuing for retry - okay, Sarah, I think I know what this might be. Sarah Chen: Yeah, I think I'm landing in the same place - Raymond, can you confirm, is your LogVault HEC endpoint behind a load balancer, and do you have any rate limiting or connection throttling configured on that endpoint? Raymond Burke: Yes to the load balancer - we have an F5 in front of it, and I think, yeah, there is a connection rate limit set, I'd have to check the exact number but I believe it's something like 50 concurrent connections. Sarah Chen: Okay so here's what I think is happening - in connector version 3.4.1, there's a known issue where if the HEC endpoint returns a connection timeout, specifically due to upstream throttling from something like an F5, the connector's retry logic doesn't kick in correctly, it treats the timeout as a terminal error rather than a transient one, and it flushes the buffer. Raymond Burke: So we're losing events - not just delayed, actually losing them. Sarah Chen: In those specific timeout scenarios, yes, the events in that buffer window would be dropped - I want to be straightforward with you about that. Dr. Linda Cheng: That is - okay, that's a significant problem, and I have to say, if this is a known issue in 3.4.1, why were we not notified proactively, why did we have to discover this ourselves after ten days of degraded monitoring? Priya Patel: That's a completely legitimate question and honestly I don't have a good answer for why you weren't notified, and I'm going to flag that internally as a process failure on our part - customers on affected versions should have been alerted. Dr. Linda Cheng: I mean, look, I'm not trying to be difficult here, we chose Aegis Detect specifically because of the reliability promises around healthcare environments, and right now I'm sitting here wondering if we made the right call. Sarah Chen: I hear you, and I understand why you're feeling that way - what I can tell you is that connector version 3.5.0 has a fix for exactly this retry behavior, it was released on February 3rd, and upgrading to that version should resolve the buffer drop issue. Raymond Burke: And the upgrade process - how disruptive is that, because we can't just, you know, take down our SIEM connector in the middle of the day, we need to plan for that. Sarah Chen: The connector upgrade itself is typically a rolling restart, it usually takes about 3 to 5 minutes and the interruption to event flow is minimal - we're talking a very brief gap, not anything close to what you're experiencing now - but I'd strongly recommend doing it during a lower-traffic window just to be safe. Raymond Burke: Okay, and is there anything we can do right now, like today, to reduce the event loss while we plan the upgrade, because we're still in a degraded state. Sarah Chen: Yes - there are two things you can do immediately: first, if you can increase the connection rate limit on your F5 to something like 100 or 150 concurrent connections, that'll reduce the frequency of the timeouts triggering the bug, and second, you can actually adjust a parameter in the connector config called retry_on_timeout and set it to true, that's not the full fix but it'll enable some retry behavior even on the older version. Raymond Burke: Wait, there's a retry_on_timeout parameter that we can set manually - is that documented anywhere, because I did not see that in the connector documentation. Sarah Chen: Uh... honestly, it's a configuration parameter that was added in a patch but the docs weren't updated at the same time - which is, yeah, I know, that's not great, and I'll flag that for our documentation team as well. Dr. Linda Cheng: Undocumented parameters, delayed support response, proactive notification failures - I'm keeping a list here, and I do want to have a broader conversation with our account team about the support experience, but let's finish resolving the immediate issue first. Priya Patel: Understood, and I think that conversation is absolutely warranted - I'll personally make sure your account executive knows to reach out to you this week. Sarah Chen: Okay - Raymond, I'm going to send you an email right after this call with the exact config syntax for the retry_on_timeout parameter, the steps for upgrading to 3.5.0, and the recommended F5 connection limit settings - does that work? Raymond Burke: Yes, that works, and can you also include whatever documentation exists on that parameter, even if it's just internal notes, because I want to understand the full behavior before I push any config changes to production. Sarah Chen: Absolutely, I'll include everything I have - and I'd also recommend we schedule a follow-up call for after you've done the upgrade to 3.5.0, just to verify the event flow is healthy and you're not seeing any more gaps. Dr. Linda Cheng: Yeah, let's do that - and Sarah, Priya, I want to say I appreciate that you actually dug in and found something today, that's more progress than we've made in ten days of emails, I just - the overall experience getting here has been frustrating. Priya Patel: I completely understand, and your frustration is warranted - we'll do better, and we're going to make sure this gets fully resolved for you. Raymond Burke: Alright - thank you both, we'll apply the interim config change today and plan the upgrade for this weekend, and we'll expect that follow-up email shortly. Sarah Chen: You'll have it within the hour - thank you Dr. Cheng, Raymond, we'll talk soon.

title: Support Case #6147 - Summit Trust Detect Alert Delays
summary: Alicia Monroe (Risk Manager) and Gregory Fisk (IT Director) from Summit Trust contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding threat alert delays of 20-45 minutes in their Detect platform, which is critical given their financial services regulatory obligations. David Kim identified the root cause as Summit Trust's tenant being placed on an overloaded processing node cluster during post-outage infrastructure remediation in March. Additionally, it was revealed that Summit Trust had never been notified of a significant platform outage in March (March 10-18) involving six hours of reduced visibility, which raised serious compliance concerns. David submitted an emergency rebalance request during the call and committed to delivering a formal incident summary document by end of business the following day.
transcript_text: David Kim: Hi, this is David Kim from Aegis Cloud Security support, I have support case number 6147 open here - am I speaking with Alicia Monroe? Alicia Monroe: Yes, hi David, this is Alicia, and I also have Gregory Fisk our IT Director on the line with me today. David Kim: Gregory, Alicia, great - thanks for jumping on. I've reviewed the case notes you submitted, but I'd love to hear it in your own words. What exactly are you seeing with the alert delays? Alicia Monroe: Yeah, so - okay, I'll let Gregory kind of walk through the technical side, but from my perspective as risk manager, the core issue is that we're in financial services, we have regulatory obligations, and our threat alerts are coming in anywhere from 20 to 45 minutes late. That is not acceptable for us. Gregory Fisk: Right, and to add to what Alicia said - we started noticing this around, I want to say, April 9th or 10th, so just last week. Our SOC team flagged it because they were correlating timestamps on alerts versus when the actual events were logged in our SIEM, and there's a consistent lag. It's not occasional, it's every single alert. David Kim: Every single alert, okay - and Gregory, when you say you're comparing against your SIEM, what are you using on that side, just so I have the full picture? Gregory Fisk: We're running LogVault for our primary SIEM integration, and we have Aegis Detect configured to push alerts via webhook. The events are hitting LogVault with the correct original timestamps, but the Aegis alert notification - the one our security team acts on - that's the thing that's delayed. David Kim: Okay, that's helpful. And - I do want to be upfront with you both - you may be aware that we had a significant outage with Detect back in mid-March, the event processing pipeline issue. We addressed that with some architectural changes. I want to make sure what you're seeing now isn't a residual effect of those changes. Alicia Monroe: Wait, hold on - what outage? We weren't notified of any outage. Gregory Fisk: Yeah, I was going to ask the same thing. We had no communication from Aegis about a platform outage affecting Detect. When did this happen? David Kim: So the outage was March 10th through the 18th - it was a cascading failure in our event ingestion pipeline, approximately six hours of reduced visibility. There were status page updates posted, and there should have been email notifications to primary account contacts. I - I'm genuinely sorry if that communication didn't reach you, that's something I'm going to flag internally. Alicia Monroe: David, six hours of no threat monitoring visibility and we're hearing about it right now, on April 15th? That is - I mean, Gregory, are you as frustrated as I am right now? Gregory Fisk: Very much so. Look David, I don't want to pile on you personally here, you're support, I get it - but this is a serious gap. We have examiners who ask us whether our security tooling was operational. If we didn't know there was an outage, we can't accurately answer that question. David Kim: That is completely fair, and I hear you both. I'm documenting this specifically - the communication failure - as a separate escalation item on top of the technical issue. Your account team needs to follow up on that. But let me stay focused on what's happening right now because the delays you're seeing, the 20 to 45 minutes - that's a current, active problem and I want to fix it today if I can. Gregory Fisk: Okay, yeah - let's figure out what's going on. I pulled our Detect configuration settings this morning, I can share my screen if that helps. David Kim: That would be great, but actually let me start by pulling up your tenant on our backend first - um - okay, Summit Trust, I'm looking at your Detect configuration now. Gregory, can you tell me what alert priority thresholds you have set? Are you filtering on severity levels at all? Gregory Fisk: We're set to receive all severity levels, so critical, high, medium, and low. We didn't want to filter anything out. David Kim: Okay, so you're ingesting the full volume. And your webhook endpoint - is that pointing to an internal receiver or a third-party relay? Gregory Fisk: It's going to an internal middleware layer we built, it normalizes the payload before it hits LogVault. But again - the timestamps tell us the delay is happening before the webhook fires, not in our middleware. The event timestamp and the alert-sent timestamp in the Aegis payload itself have a 20-plus minute gap. David Kim: Right, okay - yeah that's actually really telling. If the delay is baked into the payload itself, that means it's happening on our processing side, not yours. Let me look at... okay, so I'm looking at your event processing queue metrics and - hm. Yeah, I'm seeing something here. Alicia Monroe: What are you seeing? Because honestly at this point I'm just hoping there's a clear answer. David Kim: So - and I want to be careful not to over-promise here - but what I'm seeing is that your tenant is sitting on a processing node cluster that's running significantly higher queue depth than it should be. This is likely connected to the redistribution work we did after the March outage, when we moved to redundant processing nodes. It looks like Summit Trust got placed on a cluster that's, uh, handling a disproportionate share of event volume right now. Alicia Monroe: So you fixed your outage problem and accidentally caused our latency problem. Is that what you're telling me? David Kim: I - yeah, that's essentially what the data is suggesting. I want to be honest with you rather than dance around it. The remediation work introduced an imbalance in tenant distribution across our processing infrastructure, and Summit Trust appears to be on the short end of that. Gregory Fisk: Okay. So what do we do about it? What's the fix and what's the timeline? David Kim: The fix is migrating your tenant to a less-loaded node cluster. I can initiate that request right now as an emergency rebalance - that goes to our infrastructure team with a priority flag. Typically that kind of migration completes within two to four hours with zero downtime on your end. Gregory Fisk: Two to four hours - okay. And we'd see the latency drop after that? David Kim: That's what I'd expect, yes. I want to set the expectation that there may be a brief period - maybe 10, 15 minutes - during the migration where queue processing pauses momentarily, but you shouldn't see an alert gap, alerts will catch up immediately after. I'll monitor it on my end and I'll send you a direct update when the migration is complete. Alicia Monroe: Alright. Gregory, does that make sense technically to you? Gregory Fisk: It does, yeah. David, I'd also ask - can we get some kind of written summary of what happened? The March outage, the root cause of the latency we're experiencing, and what was done to fix it? Because I need to be able to document this for our risk register and potentially for our next regulatory review. David Kim: Absolutely, yes. I'll put together a formal incident summary - it'll cover the March pipeline event, the remediation steps taken, the unintended impact on tenant node distribution, and the resolution we're implementing today. I can have a draft to you by end of business tomorrow. Alicia Monroe: That would be really helpful. And I'd like that to go to our account manager as well, not just this support ticket, because we have a QBR coming up and this needs to be part of that conversation. David Kim: Noted, I'll loop in your account manager explicitly. And Alicia, I just want to - I want to acknowledge again that the communication piece of this, not being notified about the March outage - that's a real failure on our side and it shouldn't have happened. That's going to be a separate escalation I document today. Alicia Monroe: I appreciate you saying that. I'm not - look, we're not looking to be difficult customers, we're trying to run a secure operation and we rely on Detect to do that. When it's not working right and we don't even know it's not working right, that's when it becomes a real problem for us. David Kim: No, I completely understand. You're right to be frustrated. Okay - let me go ahead and submit that emergency rebalance request right now while we're on the call. I'm submitting it as I speak... okay, that's in, ticket reference for the infrastructure team is internal IR-8842, I'll include that in your summary doc. Gregory Fisk: Perfect. And David, just one last thing - is there any way to set up some kind of monitoring alert on our end, or on yours, so that if alert latency creeps above a threshold we know about it proactively? Rather than our SOC team manually catching it? David Kim: That's a great question and honestly it's something we should have had in place. Right now in Detect there isn't a native self-monitoring latency alert for customers, but - and I'll flag this as product feedback - that's a gap. In the short term, I can work with you on setting up a synthetic monitoring check using your existing LogVault infrastructure that compares event timestamps against alert-received timestamps on a schedule. It's a workaround but it'd give you early warning. Gregory Fisk: Yeah, let's do that. Can you send us documentation on how to set that up? David Kim: I will include that in the follow-up email along with the incident summary. Alright - I think we have a clear path forward here. Rebalance request is submitted, I'll monitor progress, you'll have a written summary by EOB tomorrow, and I'll reach out directly once the migration is confirmed complete. Any other questions before I let you go? Alicia Monroe: I think that covers it for now. We'll be watching our alert latency closely and we expect to hear from you. David Kim: You will. Thank you both for your time, I'm sorry this happened, and we'll get it sorted. Take care.

title: Aegis / Ironclad Financial - Account Recovery Check-in
summary: Maria Santos and Solutions Architect Kevin O'Brien met with Robert Langston and Tanya Desai (Security Engineering) to address a six-hour Detect platform outage and discuss contract renewal ahead of end-of-Q2. Kevin explained the root cause as a cascading single point of failure in the event ingestion pipeline and outlined remediation steps including redundant nodes and a circuit breaker pattern. Robert and Tanya outlined clear conditions for renewal justification: a formal written post-mortem, updated SLA language with uptime teeth for Detect, and a configuration review. The call also surfaced an upcoming Comply v2 launch with on-demand compliance reporting relevant to the customer's June PCI audit.
transcript_text: Maria Santos: Alright, I think we've got everyone now - Robert, Tanya, good to see you both. Thanks for making time today. Robert Langston: Yeah, of course. Kevin O'Brien: You're right, and I'm not going to sit here and defend the original architecture. Tanya Desai: Can you send us documentation on those changes? Like, actual architecture diagrams, not just a summary email. Kevin O'Brien: Yes, absolutely. I'd want to do a config review with you. Robert Langston: Let's put that on the action items list. I'll have Maria set that up separately. Maria Santos: Done. I'll reach out next week to schedule that with Tanya's team. Robert Langston: Okay. So let's talk about the renewal because that's technically why we're here. title: Support Case #7615 - Crestline Wealth Group Policy Sync Delay
summary: Derek Owens from a wealth management firm contacted Aegis Cloud Security support regarding persistent policy sync delays and provisioning issues in Aegis Identity, some taking 4-5 hours to propagate. Support engineer Sarah Chen investigated the tenant logs and identified a sync worker queue backup issue on a shared cluster tier, potentially related to remediation work done after a mid-March Detect incident. Sarah offered two immediate actions: escalating the case to P1 for engineering review and migrating Derek's tenant to a dedicated sync worker to alleviate the delays. Derek expressed frustration over the 5-day response gap and raised concerns about renewal given the support experience.
transcript_text: Sarah Chen: Hi Derek, thanks for holding - this is Sarah Chen from Aegis Cloud Security support, I've got your case pulled up here, case number 7615. Derek Owens: Yeah, hi Sarah. Thanks for getting back to me. Honestly I've been waiting on this for, uh, a couple days now and it's starting to become a real problem for us. Sarah Chen: I completely understand and I apologize for the delay in getting you on a live call. I do want to dig into this with you today and get it resolved. So the notes in the case mention a policy sync delay in Aegis Identity - can you walk me through what you're seeing? Derek Owens: Sure. So basically, we push policy updates through Identity - role assignments, access group changes - and they're just... not propagating. Or they are, but it's taking, like, four, five hours sometimes. And in a financial services environment that is not acceptable. We had a situation last Thursday where we provisioned a new analyst and she couldn't access core systems until the next morning. Sarah Chen: Okay, so we're talking about provisioning sync delays, not just policy rule updates - is that right? Or is it both? Derek Owens: It's both, honestly. But the provisioning one is the one that's really biting us. Role-based policy updates seem to eventually get there, but it's slow. The provisioning - that's where it's the worst. Sarah Chen: Got it. And when did you first start noticing this? Do you have a rough date? Derek Owens: I mean, we started noticing it, I want to say, around mid-March? Maybe a little before? But we thought it was just, you know, a temporary thing. It wasn't until it kept happening that we actually opened a ticket. Sarah Chen: Mid-March, okay. I do want to flag something - and I want to be transparent with you about this - we did have a significant incident with Aegis Detect in that timeframe, March 10th through the 18th, that was a pipeline-level issue. Now that was Detect, not Identity, but I want to check whether there were any downstream effects on shared services. Can you tell me - are you running Detect alongside Identity? Derek Owens: Yeah, we have Detect and Identity, we don't have Protect or Comply. Well - actually we're supposed to be getting Comply soon but that's a whole other conversation. Sarah Chen: Okay, noted. So the reason I'm asking is - there were some shared event ingestion components between Detect and Identity in certain tenant configurations, and I want to see if your environment is one of those. Can you give me your tenant ID? I should have it in the case but I want to double-check. Derek Owens: Yeah it's, uh, CWG-04471. That's our primary tenant. Sarah Chen: CWG-04471, perfect. Okay, give me just a second here while I pull up the sync logs for your tenant... okay I'm in. Derek Owens: While you're looking at that - I just want to say, like, this is impacting us more than I think the ticket description conveys. We're a wealth management firm. We have compliance requirements. We have auditors. If someone has access they shouldn't have, or doesn't have access they should have, that's not just an inconvenience, that's a potential audit finding. Sarah Chen: No, you're absolutely right and I take that seriously. Financial services environments have zero tolerance for this kind of lag and I'm not going to minimize it. Derek Owens: I appreciate that. It just - it feels like we report these things and then it kind of goes into a black hole, you know? I submitted the ticket on the 22nd and I got one automated response and then nothing until you called today. Sarah Chen: That's fair feedback and I'll make sure that's flagged internally. You should not have had a five-day gap with no human response on a Priority 2 case. That's on us. Okay, so I'm looking at your sync logs now and... yeah, I'm seeing what you're describing. There are queue depth spikes - significant ones - on your Identity sync worker. They're clustering around, it looks like, every few hours. Derek Owens: So is that a known bug or what? Like what's causing it? Sarah Chen: So, I'm looking at your configuration and I think I can see what's happening. Your sync worker is configured with a pretty aggressive polling interval - looks like it's set to sixty seconds - but your directory size, you've got a pretty large AD environment, right? How many users roughly? Derek Owens: We're around 800 users, give or take. Sarah Chen: Okay so 800 users, and you're on a shared sync cluster tier - I can see that here - and what's happening is the polling cycle is completing but the write queue is backing up because the worker isn't getting enough processing headroom between cycles. It's essentially falling behind itself. Now whether that's purely a configuration issue or whether there's an underlying bug causing the worker to be slower than it should be, I want to be honest, I'm not a hundred percent sure yet. Derek Owens: Well, I mean - we haven't changed our configuration. This was working fine before mid-March. So something changed on your end. Sarah Chen: That's a fair point and I don't want to dispute that. Something may have shifted in how the shared cluster is handling workloads, possibly related to the remediation work we did after the Detect incident. I want to get our backend engineering team to look at this because if the circuit breaker changes we made affected cluster resource allocation, that could be contributing to what you're seeing. Derek Owens: So basically you fixed one thing and possibly broke something else. Great. Sarah Chen: I understand why that's frustrating. I'm not going to make excuses. What I can do right now - there are a couple of things. First, I can escalate this to a P1 and get engineering eyes on it today, not tomorrow, today. Second, I can make a configuration change on your sync worker right now - I can move you off the shared cluster tier to a dedicated worker, which should immediately reduce the queue backup. It won't fix the root cause but it should get you back to normal sync times while we investigate. Derek Owens: Okay. Yeah, let's do that. How long does the dedicated worker change take? Sarah Chen: It's usually - it's a backend change, so I need to submit a provisioning request, it typically takes about 30 to 45 minutes to propagate. You might see a brief sync pause of like two or three minutes during the cutover but it shouldn't be disruptive. Derek Owens: Okay. And is there anything I need to do on my end or does it just happen? Sarah Chen: Nothing on your end. I'll initiate it right after this call and I'll send you an email confirmation when it's done. I'd ask you to monitor sync times over the next couple of hours and let me know if you're still seeing delays above, let's say, ten minutes - because on a dedicated worker at your directory size, you should be well under that. Derek Owens: And the root cause investigation - what's the timeline on that? Because if this is a bug I want to know it's actually being fixed, not just worked around. Sarah Chen: That's the right question. I'm going to escalate this case with my notes and the log data I'm pulling right now. Engineering's SLA for a P1 investigation is 48 hours to root cause determination. I can't promise a fix in 48 hours but I can promise you'll have a definitive answer on what caused it and a remediation plan. And I will personally follow up with you - not an automated email - on Wednesday. Derek Owens: Wednesday. Okay. That's, uh - I'm going to hold you to that, Sarah. Sarah Chen: Please do. And Derek - I know you mentioned Comply is coming up for you. Once this is stabilized I'd actually recommend making sure your Identity configuration is reviewed before that goes live, just to make sure the integrations are set up cleanly. But that's a conversation for after we get this sorted. Derek Owens: Yeah, yeah that makes sense. One thing at a time. I just - look, I like the platform overall, I really do, but when stuff like this happens and it takes days to even get someone on the phone, it makes me nervous about renewal conversations. Sarah Chen: I hear you, and that's feedback I'm going to make sure gets to the right people. Your account team should be aware of this experience regardless of the technical outcome. I'll flag it. Derek Owens: Okay. Alright. Yeah, let's go ahead and do the dedicated worker thing and I'll watch the sync times this afternoon. Sarah Chen: Perfect. I'll get that initiated right now. You'll get an email from me within the hour with confirmation and I'll include a direct line for this case so you don't have to go through the queue again. And Wednesday at the latest you'll hear from me with an engineering update. Derek Owens: Alright. Thanks Sarah. I appreciate you actually digging into it. Sarah Chen: Of course. I'll be in touch shortly. Take care.
topics: provisioning sync delay, identity policy propagation, shared cluster performance, support response time, renewal risk, compliance requirements

title: Aegis / Frostbyte AI - Identity Module Setup
summary: This was an onboarding kickoff call for Aegis Identity with Victor Zheng and Olivia Strand as the new customers, joined by James Mitchell (account manager) and Ananya Sharma (senior engineer, technical point of contact). Ananya outlined a two-to-three week timeline for baseline SSO configuration and MFA rollout, faster than the customer anticipated. Next steps were clearly established, including Victor completing Okta API token setup and a user attribute mapping template before scheduling a live working session.

Really excited to finally get this kicked off. Olivia Strand: Same here, yeah. Thanks for making time on a Thursday afternoon, I know you all are heads down on a lot right now. Ananya Sharma: Hi everyone! Really happy to be working with you. I've actually looked through the notes from your sales calls and the infrastructure questionnaire you filled out, so I have a decent picture of where you're starting from. Ananya Sharma: Eight tools, yeah that's - okay, that's definitely something we can help consolidate. What's your current identity provider situation? Are you on Okta, Azure AD, something homegrown? Victor Zheng: We're on Okta right now but we've been pretty underwhelmed with it honestly. It does the basics but the MFA policy management is clunky and we've had some issues with our contractors not getting provisioned correctly. Ananya Sharma: That contractor provisioning issue is something I hear a lot actually. And Aegis Identity handles that really well - you can set up conditional access policies that treat contractors differently from full-time staff, different MFA requirements, session timeouts, all of that. Victor Zheng: Oh that's - yeah, that's exactly the kind of granularity we've been missing. Olivia, that's the thing you mentioned in the board meeting right? Olivia Strand: Yeah exactly. We had a security review last quarter and one of the findings was that our contractor access controls weren't differentiated enough. So this is directly addressing that. James Mitchell: Perfect, and that's actually a really common driver for this kind of implementation in tech companies especially. You're scaling fast, you're bringing in contractors for specific projects, and the identity perimeter gets blurry really quickly. Victor Zheng: Exactly, yeah. I want to say around four hundred users, maybe a few dozen contractors on top of that. Ananya Sharma: For that size, the initial sync is usually done in under an hour. It's really the validation step that takes time - you want to do spot checks, make sure groups are mapping correctly, that kind of thing. I'd budget maybe half a day for that. Victor Zheng: That's much faster than I expected honestly. Ananya Sharma: Yeah we've really streamlined it over the last few releases. And then from there we'd move into SSO configuration for your applications. Can you share what those eight tools are? That'll help me flag any that might need custom SAML work versus the ones we have prebuilt connectors for. Victor Zheng: Yeah let me just - I have a list somewhere. Okay so we've got Slack, GitHub, Jira, Confluence, Figma, MetricFlow, Snowflake, and then our internal admin portal which is custom built. Ananya Sharma: Okay great, so the first seven - all of those have prebuilt connectors in Aegis Identity, so those are basically click-to-configure. The internal admin portal is where we'd need to do a bit more work, but as long as it supports SAML 2.0 or OIDC, we're in good shape. Olivia Strand: It does SAML, yeah. Victor built it so he can speak to that better than I can. Victor Zheng: Yeah it's SAML 2.0, we actually built it with federation in mind so it should be pretty straightforward to hook up. We were thinking it would be closer to six weeks. Ananya Sharma: Ha, well I don't want to overpromise - some things do take longer than expected, especially if we hit any surprises in the user attribute mapping. Like what's the first action item on our side? Ananya Sharma: A couple things - I'll send you an Okta API token request guide, it's basically step by step, shouldn't take more than twenty minutes. You can tie MFA method requirements to user groups and also to the specific application being accessed. So you could say - access to Snowflake requires hardware key, full stop, regardless of whether you're on-prem or remote. Olivia Strand: Oh that's - yeah that's powerful. We couldn't do anything close to that with Okta. Victor Zheng: Alright, I think we've covered a ton of ground today. Really feels like this is going to come together well. James, anything you wanted to add before we wrap up? James Mitchell: Just that - yeah, I'm really glad we're at this point. title: Aegis / Ridgeline Logistics - Identity Roadmap Discussion
summary: Daniel Okafor (CSM) met with Paula Schneider from Ridgeline to review their experience with Aegis Identity after eight months on the platform. Paula raised several operational pain points including clunky shared workstation session management, lack of granular session timeout policies by device group, and inflexible MFA policy exceptions for service accounts. Daniel confirmed these items would be escalated internally, including a January support ticket that had gone unanswered, and noted an upcoming RBAC enhancement that may address some of her concerns. The call also touched on a potential SSO integration with a new fleet management platform and a Q3 renewal on the horizon.
transcript_text: Daniel Okafor: Paula, hey, thanks for making time today. I know Thursdays are usually pretty packed for you. Paula Schneider: Yeah, no, it's fine. We had a planning session move to next week so actually the morning opened up a bit. Good timing. Daniel Okafor: Perfect. Well I appreciate it. So the agenda I had in mind - I wanted to walk through where we are on the Identity roadmap, get your input on some of the features we're scoping, and then just make sure we're aligned on what Ridgeline actually needs over the next couple of quarters. Does that work? Paula Schneider: Yeah that works. I've got a few things on my end I wanted to raise too, so we can weave those in. Daniel Okafor: Absolutely, let's do it. So, starting with Aegis Identity - you've been on the platform, I think it's been about eight months now since you fully deployed the IAM module. How's day-to-day been with it? Paula Schneider: It's been okay. I mean, the core IAM stuff works fine, provisioning and deprovisioning is faster than what we had before. MFA rollout went smoother than expected honestly, given that we're dealing with, you know, warehouse floor workers who aren't exactly used to that kind of workflow. Daniel Okafor: Yeah that's actually a use case we hear a lot from manufacturing customers specifically. The non-desk worker angle is tricky. Paula Schneider: Right, and we made it work, but it required some customization on our end. Which brings me to one of the things I wanted to flag - we need better support for shared workstation scenarios. So like, on the floor we have terminals that multiple workers log into across shifts, and right now the session management is kind of clunky. There's no clean handoff. Daniel Okafor: Okay, yeah. Can you describe what clunky looks like? Is it a timeout issue, is it a re-auth issue, or...? Paula Schneider: It's kind of both. So the session timeout is set globally right now, and we can't scope it by device group or location. So a desk employee in corporate gets the same timeout window as a warehouse terminal, which doesn't make sense. And then when worker A logs out and worker B logs in, sometimes the previous session data is still cached and that creates... it creates issues. We've had a couple of incidents where someone had residual access they shouldn't have had. Daniel Okafor: Got it. So you're really asking for two things - granular session timeout policies by device or group, and then cleaner session termination on the shared workstation side. Paula Schneider: Exactly. And I've submitted a support ticket on this, I think it was back in January, but I haven't seen any movement. I don't know if it got escalated or just, uh, sat somewhere. Daniel Okafor: I'll track that down after this call. I want to make sure it's actually in the right queue. And I'll be honest with you, the session policy granularity piece - that is something our product team has been scoping. It's not in the current release but it's been flagged as a near-term priority. I can't give you a hard date yet but it's actively being looked at. Paula Schneider: Okay. I mean, near-term is a bit vague but I understand you probably can't commit to a date. Is there any way to get visibility into where it sits on the roadmap? Even just a rough quarter? Daniel Okafor: I can set up a call with our product manager for Identity, his name is Marcus. He can give you a more specific picture. I'd rather him speak to it directly than me guess and then you hold me to the wrong timeline. Paula Schneider: Yeah, that would be useful. I'd rather get it from the source anyway. Daniel Okafor: Good, I'll set that up. Okay, the other thing I wanted to cover - on the SSO side. You're using our SSO integration with, I think it's primarily your ERP and your warehouse management system. Are there other apps you're looking to bring in? Paula Schneider: Yeah, we're evaluating a new fleet management platform right now. It's called Translog, I don't know if you've heard of it. And the question is whether Aegis Identity can support the SSO integration natively or if we'd have to go custom. Daniel Okafor: Translog - I'm not immediately familiar with that one. Do you know if they support SAML 2.0 or OIDC? Paula Schneider: I believe they support SAML. I'd have to double-check with their team. We're still mid-evaluation so nothing's been decided but I want to make sure we're not creating an integration problem for ourselves down the road. Daniel Okafor: That's the right time to ask the question, honestly. If they're SAML 2.0 compatible, we should be able to handle it natively. I can have our integration team do a quick compatibility check once you have the vendor's technical docs. Just send those over to me. Paula Schneider: Okay, I can do that once we get further along. Probably another few weeks before we have the full technical spec from them. Daniel Okafor: Perfect, no rush. Just keep me looped in. Paula Schneider: Will do. The other thing - and this is maybe more of a, uh, feature request in the traditional sense - we need more flexibility around MFA policy exceptions. Right now it's pretty binary, either MFA is required or it's not. But we have certain service accounts and automated processes where MFA enforcement breaks the workflow, and managing those exceptions is a pain. Daniel Okafor: So you're looking for like a conditional exclusion model? Where you can carve out specific account types or identity classes without just turning MFA off globally? Paula Schneider: Yes. And with some kind of audit trail so I can demonstrate to our auditors that those exclusions are intentional and documented. Not just, you know, someone flipped a switch. Daniel Okafor: That's actually a really good point and I think that ties into what we're building for the compliance side too. Um, have you looked at Aegis Comply at all? I know you're primarily on Identity and Protect right now. Paula Schneider: We've seen the overview but we haven't done anything with it. We handle compliance reporting separately through a third-party tool right now. Daniel Okafor: Noted. I'll just say we have some things coming on that front that might be relevant to you, but that's probably a separate conversation. I don't want to sidetrack from Identity today. Paula Schneider: Sure, we can table that. Okay so back to the MFA exceptions - is that something that's on the roadmap or is this new information for you? Daniel Okafor: Honestly it's something I've heard from a few customers but I want to make sure it's formally captured from Ridgeline specifically. The more customers who articulate the same need, the stronger the case for prioritization. So I'll make sure this is logged as a feature request with your name on it. Paula Schneider: Yeah, please do. I mean, it's not a blocker right now but it's adding operational overhead and that compounds over time. Daniel Okafor: Understood. I want to make sure our product team understands the operational impact, not just the technical ask. So I'll frame it that way when I log it. Paula Schneider: Good. I think that covers the main things I had. Is there anything on your side - you mentioned you had things to cover from the roadmap perspective? Daniel Okafor: Yeah, a couple of things. One is around role-based access control enhancements - we're planning to ship more granular RBAC controls in the next release, and I wanted to flag that because I think it touches on some of what you've described. Especially around those shared workstation scenarios, being able to scope roles more tightly at the device level. Paula Schneider: Okay, that's good to know. Is there documentation on that I can review? Daniel Okafor: Not public yet but I can share a preview doc under NDA. I'll send it over after the call. Paula Schneider: That works. We already have an NDA in place so no issue there. Daniel Okafor: Great. And then the other thing I just wanted to touch on quickly - your renewal is coming up in, I think, Q3. I just want to make sure we're not getting to that conversation cold. If there are things we should be addressing between now and then, I'd rather know early. Paula Schneider: Honestly the things I've raised today are the main things. If those are moving in the right direction, I don't anticipate any issues at renewal. But I'll say - the shared workstation thing is probably the most pressing for us operationally. If that's still unresolved by summer, it's going to be a talking point. Daniel Okafor: I hear you. I'll make sure that one has the right visibility internally. Okay - so to recap next steps: I'll track down that support ticket from January, I'll set up the call with Marcus on the product side, I'll log the MFA exception request formally, and I'll send over the RBAC preview doc. Does that cover it? Paula Schneider: Yeah, that covers it. And I'll send you the Translog technical specs once we have them. Daniel Okafor: Perfect. Thanks Paula, this was really useful. I'll get those follow-ups out to you by end of week. Paula Schneider: Sounds good. Talk soon.

title: Protect Performance - Scalability Concerns
summary: The team convened to discuss alarming performance issues in the Protect module, triggered by load testing results showing backup job queue times spiking to 47 minutes at 2x P95 customer scale. Two compounding root causes were identified: a job scheduler not built for concurrent dispatch at current scale, and a synchronous I/O bottleneck in the snapshot deduplication layer. The full scheduler fix is estimated at six to eight weeks, raising concern about an upcoming growth quarter where sales is actively bundling Protect with Comply v2. As interim measures, the team agreed to throttle per-tenant job concurrency, fast-track an async fix for the dedup issue, and have a proactive conversation with sales about slowing Protect onboarding pace.
transcript_text: Chris Lee: Alright, I think we're all on - can everyone hear me okay? Nina Kowalski: Yeah, I can hear you. Tyler Washington: Yep, good here. Sofia Petrov: Same, I'm on. Chris Lee: Okay good, so - let's just dive in because I don't want this to run long. The reason I called this is, uh, we've been getting some pretty alarming signals from the Protect module over the last couple of weeks and I think we need to talk through what's actually happening before this becomes a customer-facing issue. Nina Kowalski: Yeah, I'm glad we're finally having this conversation honestly. I've been flagging some of these benchmark numbers for like three weeks now and it feels like nothing's moved. Chris Lee: Okay, let's not - I hear you Nina, and I want to get to that, but let's just start with the actual data so we're all on the same page. Tyler, you ran the load tests last week, can you walk us through what you saw? Tyler Washington: Sure, yeah. So we ran a simulated backup workload at roughly 2x our current P95 customer scale, and the results were... not great. Throughput started degrading at around the 60% load mark, and by the time we hit full simulated load we were seeing backup job queue times spike to like - I think the worst number was 47 minutes for a job that should complete in under five. Sofia Petrov: 47 minutes? I - sorry, did you say 47? Tyler Washington: Yeah. 47. And that's not even worst-case, that's just what we observed in the test window. It could be worse under sustained load. Sofia Petrov: That's... I mean that's genuinely bad. Like that's not a tuning problem, that's a fundamental architecture concern. Tyler Washington: Right, which is sort of what I've been trying to say. The scheduler - and look, I don't want to throw anyone under the bus here - but the job scheduler isn't built to handle concurrent dispatch at this scale. It was designed for, I don't know, a much smaller customer footprint than where we're heading. Nina Kowalski: Okay and this is exactly what I documented in QA-1847 back in, uh, late February. The concurrency ceiling on the scheduler queue was a known risk item. I flagged it as high severity. Chris Lee: Nina, I know you flagged it. It was on the backlog. We were dealing with - look, we had the Detect outage in March, that pulled a lot of engineering bandwidth, and some things got deprioritized. That's just the reality. Nina Kowalski: I understand that, Chris, and I'm not trying to relitigate prioritization decisions. But I think we have to acknowledge that we knew about this and we're now sitting here looking at 47-minute queue times. That's... that's uncomfortable. Chris Lee: It is uncomfortable. I'm not disagreeing. Let's focus on what we do about it. Sofia Petrov: So I've been doing some digging since Tyler shared the numbers yesterday, and I think there are actually two separate issues tangled together here. One is the scheduler concurrency problem which Nina flagged, and the other is - and this one I actually didn't expect - the snapshot deduplication layer is doing a lot of synchronous I/O that it really shouldn't be. Like it's blocking on disk reads mid-job. Tyler Washington: Oh, yeah - I actually saw that too in the traces. There's this dedup check that happens inline and it's just... it's not async. It never was. Sofia Petrov: So that's compounding the queue problem. Because jobs are blocking longer than they should, which backs up the queue, which makes the scheduler worse. Nina Kowalski: It's like, it's a pressure cooker situation. Each problem makes the other one worse. Great. Chris Lee: Okay, so realistically - what are we looking at in terms of effort to fix the scheduler concurrency issue? Sofia, you know that codebase better than anyone. Sofia Petrov: Honestly? It's not a quick fix. The scheduler wasn't designed to be horizontally scalable. To do this properly we'd probably need to refactor the dispatch layer, introduce some kind of distributed queue - I keep thinking something like a partitioned queue model would actually solve this - but we're talking weeks of work. Plural. Not two weeks, more like... six to eight minimum if we want to do it right and not create new problems. Chris Lee: Six to eight weeks. Okay. And we're heading into what's supposed to be a growth quarter for Protect. Sales has been pushing it pretty hard post the Comply v2 launch - they want to bundle them together. Tyler Washington: Which is great for the business but if we scale the customer base and the infrastructure can't handle it, we're going to have outages. Real ones. Customer-impacting ones. Nina Kowalski: And that's the last thing we need right now. After March, after the Detect thing - honestly our credibility with some of these enterprise customers is already fragile. Another major incident would be... it would not be good. Chris Lee: Yeah, I think about that a lot. The Detect outage - the six hours of no visibility - that shook some people. I know we fixed it, the redundant nodes, the circuit breaker stuff, all of that. But trust takes a while to rebuild and piling a Protect failure on top of that is not something I want to explain to leadership. Tyler Washington: So what do we do in the meantime? Like is there a stopgap? Because six to eight weeks for a full refactor doesn't help us if we're onboarding new customers next month. Sofia Petrov: There might be some things we can do at the config level. Like we could tighten the job concurrency limits per tenant - basically throttle how many concurrent backup jobs any single customer can run - which buys us some headroom on the queue. It's not a fix, it's a band-aid, but it could prevent the worst-case blowups. Nina Kowalski: Yeah but then we're artificially limiting the product for customers who are paying for, you know, enterprise-grade backup. That feels wrong. Sofia Petrov: It does feel wrong. But the alternative might be an outage, which is worse. Chris Lee: I agree with Sofia. A graceful degradation we control is better than an uncontrolled failure. We implement the throttle as a temporary measure, we communicate it internally, and we stay off the critical path while we do the real fix. Tyler Washington: And the async dedup issue - is that more tractable? Like can we decouple that faster than the scheduler work? Sofia Petrov: Yeah, actually I think the dedup thing is more isolated. If we move the deduplication check to an async worker and just do a quick hash lookup first with a fallback... I mean I'd need to prototype it but I think that's a one to two week effort. Maybe less. Chris Lee: Okay, that's at least something. That's one concrete thing we can actually move on quickly. Nina Kowalski: Can I ask something that might be uncomfortable? Do we need to be having a conversation about whether sales should be slowing down Protect commitments right now? Like, should we be having a conversation with them about customer onboarding pace? Chris Lee: Ugh. I mean - yes, probably. That's going to be a fun conversation. Sales is riding high on the Comply v2 momentum and they're not going to love being told to pump the brakes on Protect. Nina Kowalski: I know, but better to have that conversation now than to have it after a customer's backups fail during a ransomware event or something. Like, that's the scenario we're trying to avoid. Chris Lee: You're right. Okay. I'll set up time with the sales lead this week. I'll frame it as a scaling preparation conversation rather than a stop-selling conversation. But the message will basically be: let's be thoughtful about onboarding pace for the next six to eight weeks. Sofia Petrov: That's probably the right framing. And in parallel, Tyler and I can start sketching out the scheduler architecture? Like even just getting the design doc started so we know what we're actually committing to? Tyler Washington: Yeah, let's do that. I can pull together the load test traces and annotate them so you've got the full picture of where things are falling apart. Chris Lee: Good. Nina, can you put together a summary of the QA findings - the existing ticket plus anything new from the test results - so I have something to bring to leadership? I need to brief them this week and I want the data to speak for itself. Nina Kowalski: Yeah, I can have that to you by tomorrow morning. And I'll include the timeline of when things were flagged because I think that's... I think that context matters. Chris Lee: Understood. Okay - I think we have a rough path forward. It's not a great situation, I won't pretend it is, but at least we're not walking into it blind anymore. Let's regroup end of week and see where we are on the dedup fix and the design doc. Sound good? Tyler Washington: Works for me. Nina Kowalski: Same, I'll have the summary ready. Sofia Petrov: Yeah, sounds good. I'll ping Tyler offline to coordinate. Chris Lee: Alright. Thanks everyone. Not a fun call but an important one. Talk later.
topics: performance degradation, architecture scalability, technical debt, incident risk, sales alignment, backup infrastructure

title: Aegis / Atlas Precision - Annual Review & Renewal
summary: Daniel Okafor and engineer Mike Romano held an annual review call with Wayne Keller of Atlas Precision ahead of a May renewal. Wayne expressed overall satisfaction with the platform, highlighting the Comply module as the biggest win by significantly reducing his team's audit burden. The March Detect outage was discussed openly, with Wayne acknowledging the strong incident communication and the architectural fixes implemented. The call concluded with alignment on flat renewal pricing, a planned Identity module discovery call with Wayne's IT director, and a follow-up on OT anomaly detection roadmap details.
transcript_text: Daniel Okafor: Wayne! Good to have you on, man. How are things going out there in - is it still cold in Cleveland or have you guys finally gotten some spring weather? Wayne Keller: Ha, we actually had a really nice weekend, finally. Like sixties, sunny - my wife dragged me into the garden for the whole two days but I'm not complaining. Daniel Okafor: That's great, that's great. Hey I also have Mike Romano on with me - Mike's one of our staff engineers, he's been kind of the technical backbone on your account for the last few months. Mike, you want to say hey? I've been behind the scenes on a few of your support tickets and some of the Comply v2 migration stuff so, uh, looking forward to actually talking through things today. Wayne Keller: Yeah, likewise. I've seen your name in a lot of the ticket updates - appreciate the thorough notes by the way, that actually makes a big difference for my team. Mike Romano: Oh good, good to hear. We try to keep things documented especially on the technical side. Daniel Okafor: So Wayne, the whole purpose of today is really just - it's your annual review, renewal's coming up at the end of May, and I want to make sure we're doing right by you before we get into any of that paperwork stuff. So let's just start at a high level - how has the last year felt from where you're sitting? Wayne Keller: Yeah, honestly? It's been pretty solid. And I'll say that as someone who was, uh, fairly skeptical when we first signed on. Our previous vendor was - well, let's just say the bar wasn't super high coming in. Daniel Okafor: Ha, fair enough. What's kind of moved the needle the most for you? Wayne Keller: Honestly the Comply module has been the biggest win. We do a lot of work with defense contractors - secondary suppliers, not primes, but still - and the audit burden is real. Like, our compliance team was spending, I don't know, probably close to two weeks every quarter just pulling together documentation for various audits. And now that's... it's not zero but it's dramatically less. Daniel Okafor: That's huge. And that was - that's actually a great segue because the v2 launch just happened earlier this month, April 7th. Has your team had a chance to get into the new on-demand reporting features at all? Wayne Keller: Yeah, we've been, um, kind of slowly rolling through it. Mike actually helped us get set up on the ISO 27001 template which we hadn't been using before - that was a new one for us. Mike Romano: Right, yeah. So the ISO template in v2 is much more granular than what was available before - like you can actually map controls down to individual policies in your environment rather than just doing a top-level attestation. Did your team find that useful or was it a bit overwhelming at first? Wayne Keller: Little of both, honestly. The first time one of my engineers looked at it she was like, okay this is a lot. But once she got through the mapping exercise she said it basically gave her a complete picture she'd never had before. So yeah, initial friction, long-term value. Mike Romano: That's the typical arc, yeah. And once those mappings are saved you don't have to redo them - that's sort of the whole philosophy of the on-demand piece, the first report's the heavy lift and then it's like push-button after that. Wayne Keller: Yeah she figured that out and was very relieved. Daniel Okafor: Good, good. Hey Wayne, I do want to address the elephant in the room a little bit - the Detect outage back in March. I know we communicated through that in real time but I want to hear from you directly how that landed with your team. Wayne Keller: Yeah, so - look, I'll be honest, there were about thirty minutes in the middle of that where I was getting texts from our CISO and I was not having a great afternoon. Six hours of no monitoring visibility is not nothing for us. Daniel Okafor: Totally, and that's completely fair. I don't want to minimize that at all. Wayne Keller: But - and I want to give credit where it's due - the communication from your team during the incident was actually really good. Like, the status updates were frequent, they were honest about what you didn't know yet, and the RCA you sent afterward was detailed. My CISO actually read the whole thing and said it was one of the better incident write-ups she'd seen. So, points for that. Daniel Okafor: I really appreciate you saying that Wayne. And just for context, Mike was actually closely involved in the remediation work - Mike, do you want to touch on what we've done architecturally since then? Mike Romano: Sure, yeah. So the root cause was a single point of failure in the event ingestion pipeline - basically one component went down and it cascaded. What we've done since is deploy redundant processing nodes so there's no single point of failure anymore, and we also implemented a circuit breaker pattern so that if one node starts degrading it isolates before it can take down the whole pipeline. We've stress tested it pretty heavily since and we're confident in the fix. Wayne Keller: Yeah, I actually passed that along to our infrastructure team and they said the circuit breaker approach was the right call. So - yeah, look, it happened, it wasn't great, but you handled it well and you fixed it. I'm not going to hold it against you. Daniel Okafor: That means a lot, genuinely. Is that something that's on your radar at all or is IAM kind of handled elsewhere? Wayne Keller: It's... it's on the radar. We have kind of a patchwork situation right now - we're using one tool for SSO, something else for MFA, and honestly it's a mess. Our IT director has been complaining about it for like eight months. Daniel Okafor: Yeah that's a really common story in manufacturing actually - like the OT and IT environments both accumulate their own identity solutions and then nobody talks to each other. Aegis Identity was kind of built with that consolidation problem in mind. Would it be worth a separate conversation just to see if it actually fits your environment? Wayne Keller: Yeah, I think so. Loop in my IT director - her name is Priya Sanjay - she'd be the right person to have that conversation with. I can introduce you over email. Daniel Okafor: Perfect, yeah, please do. I'll make sure Mike's on that call too since it'll get technical pretty quickly. Mike Romano: Happy to be on it, yeah. Yeah, send it over and I'll take a look. I don't anticipate any major issues - honestly at this point you'd have to really mess something up for me to go shopping around. And I've heard mixed things about SentinelShield from a few peers, so... Daniel Okafor: Ha - yeah, we hear things. I won't comment on that but uh, we're glad you're staying in the family. Wayne Keller: Is there anything on the product roadmap side that you can share? Like, what's coming for Detect or Protect in the next couple quarters? Mike Romano: Yeah, I can touch on some of it - some of it's still under NDA so I'll be a little careful. But on Detect specifically, we're working on enhanced anomaly detection for OT environments, which is actually very relevant to you given your manufacturing setup. And Protect is getting some improved RTO tooling in Q3. I'll share the roadmap deck once it's cleared for external sharing - should be in the next few weeks. Wayne Keller: OT anomaly detection is interesting - yeah, definitely want to see that when it's available. We've had some weird stuff on the plant floor network that nobody's been able to fully explain. Daniel Okafor: Okay yeah, we should actually get that documented as a use case before that roadmap call - like if you can share some details with Mike that would help him frame whether the new capabilities actually address what you're seeing. Wayne Keller: Sure, I can pull together some notes on that. It's probably a conversation in itself. Daniel Okafor: Perfect. Alright, I think we're in really good shape here. To summarize - proposal comes to you this week, flat pricing on current modules, separate call with Priya on Identity, and Mike will loop you in on the OT roadmap details when they're cleared. Does that cover everything from your side? Wayne Keller: Yeah, I think that's it. This was a good call - I feel good about where things are heading. Appreciate you guys taking the time. Daniel Okafor: Always, Wayne. We appreciate Atlas Precision - seriously. Have a good rest of your week and enjoy the garden weather while it lasts. Wayne Keller: Ha, yeah. Thanks guys, talk soon.

title: Support Case #3286 - Vanta Health Systems API Integration Error

title: Detect Outage - Root Cause Analysis
summary: The team conducted a post-incident review of a cascading failure in their event ingestion pipeline that caused six hours of zero threat monitoring visibility for customers. Mike Romano explained that an out-of-memory error on a primary ingestion node triggered a cascade due to the absence of a circuit breaker and inadequate health checks that couldn't distinguish between liveness and readiness. The group identified three root technical causes: a single point of failure in ingestion, no circuit breaker pattern, and insufficient health checking. The team also acknowledged that the underlying single-point-of-failure risk had been flagged in Q3 of the prior year but was deprioritized in favor of feature work, and agreed the post-mortem should reflect that honestly.
transcript_text: Sofia Petrov: Okay, I think everyone's on now - Tyler, can you hear us okay? Tyler Washington: Yeah, yeah I'm here, sorry I was - had to grab the right headset, my other one died. Sofia Petrov: Alright, let's just get into it because honestly we've been in firefighting mode for the past four days and I want to actually understand what happened here. Ananya Sharma: Yeah, agreed. So, Mike, do you want to walk us through what you found? You were the one digging into the pipeline logs last night. Mike Romano: Sure, yeah. So, um, the short version is - we had a cascading failure in the event ingestion layer. There's essentially a single point of failure in how we're routing events through the processing pipeline, and once that node went down on Monday morning, everything backed up. Nina Kowalski: Wait, a single point of failure? Like, we've known about that risk for how long? I feel like that was flagged in Q3 last year. Mike Romano: It was flagged, yeah. It was in the backlog. It just... never got prioritized above the feature work. Sofia Petrov: That is honestly really frustrating to hear, Mike, because we had six hours - six hours - where customers had zero threat monitoring visibility. Like, Detect is supposed to be the thing that tells you when something bad is happening. Mike Romano: I know. I know, and I'm not trying to make excuses. The prioritization call was made above our level and at the time there were reasons, but obviously in hindsight- Ananya Sharma: In hindsight it was the wrong call, yeah. Tyler Washington: Can we talk about the actual failure sequence though? Like I want to understand technically what cascaded. Was it a memory issue, was it network, what actually triggered the initial node failure? Mike Romano: So from what I can tell in the logs, the primary ingestion node started throwing out-of-memory errors around 6:47 AM. And instead of failing gracefully, it just - it locked up. And then the queue started building, and because there was no circuit breaker, the downstream processors kept trying to pull from a source that wasn't responding. Ananya Sharma: Right, and that's what caused the cascading part. The downstream processors themselves started degrading. Mike Romano: Exactly. And by the time our alerting caught it - which was, ugh, almost 40 minutes later - the whole pipeline was basically dead. Nina Kowalski: Forty minutes before alerting kicked in? Why did it take that long? We have health checks on those services. Tyler Washington: The health checks were pinging the node endpoint, which was still technically responding - it just wasn't processing anything. So the check was returning healthy even though the service was completely stuck. Nina Kowalski: Oh, that's - okay, so the health check was essentially useless in this scenario. Tyler Washington: Pretty much, yeah. It was a liveness check, not a readiness check. Which is a gap we clearly need to fix. Sofia Petrov: Okay so we've got at least three things here - the single point of failure in ingestion, no circuit breaker pattern, and inadequate health checking. Is that a fair summary so far? Mike Romano: Yeah, that's how I'd characterize it. And I think the fix for the ingestion layer specifically is redundant processing nodes - at minimum two, probably three, with active load balancing. Ananya Sharma: And the circuit breaker - like, how complicated is that to implement? I don't want us to say 'we'll implement a circuit breaker' and then that also ends up sitting in the backlog for a year. Mike Romano: It's not trivial but it's also not like a three-month project. I think we could have a working implementation in two, maybe two and a half weeks if we actually focus on it. Nina Kowalski: I want that estimate in writing honestly, because I've heard 'two weeks' before and then it becomes six. Mike Romano: That's fair, Nina, that's fair. I'll put together a proper scope doc today. Tyler Washington: What about the communication side of this? Like, customers were in the dark for hours. Do we know how that was handled? Sofia Petrov: That's - yeah, that's a whole other conversation, but I will say the status page update was way too slow. That's something that needs to be escalated separately. Nina Kowalski: Agreed. And from a QA perspective, I'm also really bothered by the fact that we didn't have a test scenario for this kind of failure. Like, do we even have chaos engineering coverage on the ingestion pipeline? Ananya Sharma: We don't. Not really. We have some basic load testing but nothing that simulates a node going unresponsive. Tyler Washington: Yeah, that needs to change. Like, we should be deliberately killing nodes in staging on a regular basis to validate that the system handles it. Sofia Petrov: One hundred percent. I'm going to push for that as part of the remediation plan. It won't just be 'fix the code' - it needs to be 'build the testing practice too.' Ananya Sharma: Good. And honestly, uh, I think we need to be really transparent in the post-mortem doc about the fact that this risk was known and deprioritized. I don't think we should soften that. Sofia Petrov: I agree with that. If we're going to learn from this, we have to be honest about the decision-making chain that got us here, not just the technical failure. Mike Romano: Yeah. It's uncomfortable but it's the right call. Sofia Petrov: Okay, so action items - Mike is doing the scope doc for the circuit breaker and redundant nodes, Ananya and Tyler are looking at the health check improvements, and Nina, can you start scoping out what a chaos testing framework would look like for the pipeline? Nina Kowalski: Yeah, I can do that. I'll probably want to pull in Tyler for part of it. Tyler Washington: Works for me. Sofia Petrov: Alright. This has been a really rough week and I don't think anyone feels great about where we're at, but - let's make sure this doesn't happen again. I'll circulate the post-mortem draft by end of day tomorrow. Ananya Sharma: Thanks everyone.

title: Support Case #3103 - Silverline Brands Detect False Positives After Patch
summary: Sarah Chen from Aegis Cloud Security support spoke with Dominic Flores and Michelle Tan (Security Manager) regarding a surge of false positive alerts following the application of agent patch 4.2.1 on Friday night. The patch reset the behavioral detection baseline, causing over 300 false positive alerts on Saturday morning compared to their normal volume of 15-20, resulting in hours of wasted on-call time. Sarah identified the issue as a known problem with the 4.2.1 patch and initiated a baseline restore to the pre-patch profile from March 13th, while also recommending suppression rules for Saturday batch jobs during the relearning period. The customer expressed frustration over two incidents in two weeks and disclosed they are evaluating other vendors at renewal time.
transcript_text: Sarah Chen: Hi, this is Sarah Chen calling from Aegis Cloud Security support - am I speaking with Dominic Flores? Dominic Flores: Yeah, that's me. Hi Sarah. I've got Michelle Tan on the line too, she's our Security Manager - she's been dealing with this more directly than I have. Michelle Tan: Hi Sarah, yeah, I've been the one actually in the platform trying to figure out what's going on. Sarah Chen: Great, hi Michelle, thanks for jumping on. So I pulled up Support Case 3103 before this call - you're seeing a spike in false positives from Aegis Detect after a patch was applied, is that right? Dominic Flores: That's correct. And look, I want to be upfront - we're already pretty frustrated. This is the second issue we've had with Detect in, like, the past couple weeks. Sarah Chen: I completely understand, Dominic, and I appreciate you flagging that. Can you walk me through what you're seeing specifically? Like when did it start and what kind of alerts are triggering? Michelle Tan: So, um, we applied the agent patch - I think it was version 4.2.1 - on Friday night. Saturday morning I come in and my dashboard is just... lit up. Hundreds of critical alerts. Sarah Chen: Hundreds? Like, what's your normal alert volume on a Saturday? Michelle Tan: Maybe fifteen, twenty alerts on a slow day. We're a retail company, we have a lot of endpoints, but our baseline is pretty well established at this point. So going from twenty to, I don't know, I counted over three hundred by 9 AM - that's not normal. Dominic Flores: And our on-call person spent the entire morning triaging and every single one of them was a false positive. Every. Single. One. That's hours of wasted time right there. Sarah Chen: Yeah, that's - okay, I hear you, that's a significant operational impact. Michelle, do you know what categories of alerts were triggering? Like was it lateral movement, unusual login patterns, data exfiltration flags, or...? Michelle Tan: It was mostly the behavioral anomaly ones. Uh, specifically around process execution - we were getting flagged for what looked like, I think the alert type was something like 'suspicious child process spawning' or something along those lines. Sarah Chen: Okay. And those endpoints - are those your POS systems, back-office servers, or a mix? Michelle Tan: Mix, but predominantly back-office. Our inventory management system runs a lot of scheduled jobs on Saturday mornings - restocking workflows, that kind of thing. We've never had issues with those being flagged before. Sarah Chen: Right, right. So the patch may have reset or recalibrated the behavioral baseline thresholds. That's... yeah, that's a known issue we've been tracking with 4.2.1 actually. The patch included updates to the behavioral detection engine and in some environments it's basically starting the learning period over from scratch. Dominic Flores: I'm sorry - it's a known issue? Why weren't we notified before we applied it? Sarah Chen: That's a fair point, Dominic, and I'm not going to make excuses for that. The advisory did go out but I think it was posted to the release notes portal and honestly that's not sufficient for an issue of this scope. I'll be flagging that internally. Dominic Flores: We shouldn't have to check a portal every time we apply a patch to find out if it's going to break our alerting. We have an account manager, we have a support contract - this should be proactive communication. Sarah Chen: You're absolutely right. And I will make sure that feedback gets escalated after this call. Right now though I want to focus on getting you fixed up - can we do that? Michelle Tan: Yeah, okay. Yes. What do we do? Sarah Chen: So there are two things we can do. First, I can push a configuration update to manually restore your previous baseline snapshot - we keep a 30-day history of your tuning profiles, so we can roll back to where you were before the patch. That should stop the flood of false positives within a couple hours of applying it. Michelle Tan: Okay, that sounds good. And what's the second thing? Sarah Chen: The second thing is we need to get you on a supervised re-learning period so the engine actually learns your environment properly after the patch - rather than just resetting blind. I'd want to work with you to set some suppression rules for those Saturday batch jobs specifically, so they don't trigger during the relearning window. Dominic Flores: How long does the relearning period take? Because we can't have our team babysitting alerts for weeks. Sarah Chen: Typically seven to fourteen days for a retail environment with your endpoint count. But with the suppression rules in place and the baseline restore, you should be back to normal alert volumes pretty much immediately - the relearning just happens in the background.
